en: Now begins the first chapter, the first section: 1.
General Definitions.
1. The Sūtra of the Declaration:
Now, the ritual acts such as the *ācāra* (daily observances) and others are taken up. (ĀpGs 1.1)
Homage to Rudra! This unconfused commentary on the *Gṛhya-sūtra* composed by Āpastamba is now being produced by Haradatta.
Actions are of two kinds: those characterized by direct revelation (śruti) and those characterized by custom (ācāra).
Among these, those characterized by revelation have been explained.
Now, however, those actions beginning with marriage which are grasped—that is, known—from custom and practice, [are to be discussed].
Not because it is directly stated [in the scripture];
we shall explain those [details]. What is the purpose of the sūtra?
The eligibility for the *smārta* rites [is established];

by that, there is the restriction regarding the northern solstice (*udagayana*) and so forth. Furthermore, rules such as "in every case, when the fire has been kindled by itself" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 8.5) apply only to the domestic (*gārhya*) rites.
It is not [the case that it is] based on the Śruti.
Here, by the word "atha" (now), he indicates its dependence on that [Śruti], stating: "Immediately after the instruction of the Śruti, I shall provide the instruction of the Smṛti."
In that regard, there are these technical definitions (paribhāṣās): “He [performs] the three protections” (ĀpŚS Pariśiṣṭa 1.2);
“One should join the beginning of the ritual acts with the ends of the mantras” (ĀpŚS Pariśiṣṭa 2.1); and “The Raudra and Rākṣasa [rites]” (ĀpŚS Pariśiṣṭa 2.9).
“‘This indeed is the expiation for all [transgressions]’—these and other such [rules] apply here as well (these are the duties to be performed).”
I bow to that non-dual Hari, who is worshipped by the castes through their own eternal duties as impelled by scripture, and who bestows liberation upon them. //1//
I bow to the sage Āpastamba with the desire to benefit those of dull intellect, he who established the sequence for those distressed by the meaning of the steps to be performed. (2)
May that Kapardin, the knower of the true essence of the Vedas and their meanings, live long—he by whom the learned have come to revere this commentary as if it were the Veda itself. //3//
Even one of dull intellect, impelled solely by faith in the Veda, undertakes this determination of the purport of the Gṛhya-sūtras. (4)
The word "atha" (now/then) signifies immediate succession.
To explain its meaning, the preceding context is stated:
for here, sacrifices are of twenty-one varieties.
And therein are the seven forms of the *pākayajña*: the *aupāsana-homa*,
the *vaiśvadeva*, and so forth.
The Pārvaṇa, the Aṣṭakā, and the Māsi-śrāddha.
The *sarpabali* and the *rīśānabali*;
and the seven forms of the *haviryajña*: the *agnihotra*,...
The New and Full Moon sacrifices,
the Āgrayaṇa sacrifice, and the Cāturmāsya sacrifices.
The Nirūḍhapaśubandha, the Sautrāmaṇī,
the Piṇḍapitṛyajña, and others are called Darvīhomas.
(5) And there are exactly seven Soma-sacrifices: the Agniṣṭoma, the Atyagniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, [the Ṣoḍaśin, the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma].
The Ṣoḍaśī, the Vājapeya, the Atirātra, and the Aptoryāma.
And these [debts] are eternal, meaning they are caused by life which occurs at fixed times and directions.
Why are these eternal?

"Indeed, a Brāhmaṇa, being born, is born with three debts: to the Ṛṣis through studentship (brahmacarya), to the gods through sacrifice (yajña), and to the ancestors through progeny" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.10).

In this context, the singular form "yajñena" (by sacrifice) is intended to signify the class [of sacrifices], as the venerable Vasiṣṭha considers it to be so— just as in the case of "we shall explain sacrifice" (Āpastamba Paribhāṣā 1.1)— since his statement, "For these three debts are praised as obligatory" (Vasiṣṭha Saṃhitā 11.47), makes it clear that these must necessarily be performed.
Likewise: "In the evening and in the morning, and thereafter" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 7.19);
"One performs the Agnihotra as long as one lives";
and "One should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma in the spring" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 10.2.5).
By such statements as these, [it is said]:
"They are offered day after day" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.1.3), and "It is offered every half-month" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.2.8).
"His drinking of Soma becomes to be drunk again," (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.2.3).
From such passages as these,
and by the principle of the commencement of ritual acts (*karmārambhanyāya*), the repetition of performance is understood.

Likewise, because it is understood that a transgression arises from the non-performance of the Soma sacrifice and others, as evidenced by the prescription of expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) such as the Aindrāgna-Śunāsīrīya-iṣṭi;

and likewise, because it is understood from the passage, "He saw these four Hotṛ-offerings as means for ransoming himself" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.3.7), that the rites beginning with the Agnihotra and ending with the Soma sacrifice serve the purpose of ransoming the self.
But they are not merely optional (kāmya) like the Saurya sacrifice and others, because all the stated reasons for that are inapplicable;
and precisely because these are obligatory (nitya), it is said: "Not maintaining the sacred fires, theft... (Manu 11.65).

Thus, the state of not having established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgnitā*) is listed among the group of minor offenses (*upapātaka*). For this very reason, the establishment of the fires (*ādhāna*) is prompted by the injunctions concerning the obligatory (*nitya*) duties.

As for the accomplishment of desired results (*kāmyasiddhi*), let it be incidental (*prāsaṅgikī*), occurring through the performance of the obligatory rites themselves by way of an injunction regarding the fruit of a subordinate quality (*guṇaphala-adhikāra-vidhi*).
According to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas, although the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is enjoined by an injunction pertaining to optional rites (*kāmya-adhikāra-vidhi*),

and the fulfillment of the obligatory [rites] occurs as a byproduct (*prasaṅga*) through the performance of those optional ones; nevertheless, according to the methodology of the authors of the Kalpasūtras, it possesses its own independent qualification (*sādhikāratvena*).

Since it is possible for [the study] to be prompted by another [source] through the capacity for application and suitability, even the prompting by an obligatory injunction (*nityādhikāravidhi*) is established when there is no prompting from elsewhere;
as in the view of the *Vivaraṇa*, that "study is prompted by its own injunction.
Therefore, [this applies] to those of dull, middling, and superior intellects.

These [rites] must necessarily be performed by all members of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*). Yet, because they require various means of accomplishment, involve subsidiary elements found in various Vedic branches (*śākhā*), and contain verbal formulations whose precise meaning can only be determined through thousands of principles of Mīmāṃsā logic, they are difficult for those of dull intellect in the present day to perceive. Furthermore, being unable to perform them due to such ignorance, they might somehow incur sin. Therefore, with a mind filled with compassion, the author of the Sūtras [declared]: "We shall explain the sacrifice" (Āpastamba Paribhāṣā-sūtra 1.1).

Thus, having explained the twenty-one sacrifices in general and in brief within this introductory section (*paribhāṣā*), since that alone is insufficient for their performance, [the author] begins with "Now, therefore, the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*atha ato darśapūrṇamāsau*,
Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 1.1) and proceeds to describe the *Śrauta* oblation sacrifices (*haviryajña*) and the *Soma* rituals (*somasaṃsthā*).
The *kṣāmavatī* and other such occasional rites (*naimittika*), as well as those performed for specific desires (*kāmya*), have been explained in detail here as a matter of context.
Now, immediately following this:
from the word *ācāra*, the prefix *ā-* signifies uninterruptedness and pervasiveness as its intended meaning;
*cāra* means moving or engaging in activities.
This is because it is observed in such passages as "They perform the Piṇḍapitṛyajña" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 1.7.2).

Therefore, in all regions and at all times, by all the learned elders (*śiṣṭas*) versed in the three Vedas, [this practice] has been maintained without interruption even in the absence of any worldly purpose.
That which is respected through song—

and for that very reason, because no other source is possible, serves as the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for inferring the Veda which is its own root— is *ācāra* (customary practice). From that *ācāra*, by means of the Vedas inferred [therefrom], there are those rites such as the *aupāsana-homa* and others denoted by the term *pākayajña*, as well as the taking of the hand in marriage (*pāṇigrahaṇa*) and so forth.

The remaining rites intended for the purification of the body of one who is about to be authorized in the [sacrificial] acts are understood as those that must be performed; these we shall explain—this is the ellipsis.

Precisely because the domestic (gārhya) rites are to be understood from the Veda as inferred through established custom (ācāra), it was for this reason that the explanation of the Śrauta rites was performed first, even though they are to be practiced later than those [domestic rites].

Because, among those things enjoined by direct revelation, the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) occurs first, while the exposition occurs last, and because the exposition has the purpose of [fulfilling] that desire to know.

And here, by characterizing the domestic rites (*gārhya-karmāṇi*) as "according to custom" (*ācārāt*), he makes this known: even those items not explicitly recorded in this [text]—such as "the five-fold cutting for the Jamadagnis" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.18.2)—for which custom (*ācāra*) is pervasive across the entire region and so forth, these too must have the Veda as their source.

Furthermore, this pervasiveness across the entire region and so forth is to be determined through the observation of the Śrauta rites where there is an abundance of repetition, through other Gṛhya texts, through the Dharmaśāstras, by the force of logic (*nyāya-balena*), or by the words of traditionalists and commentators.
And this is the introductory sūtra;

it is stated in order to indicate that those [rites] which will be described hereafter— beginning with "ityādīni"— are for the purpose of domestic (gārhya) rituals, and to make known that even those Vedic (śrauta) rites, though universal, do not by themselves have this [domestic] purpose.
And this is because there is an absence of both common instruction and extension.

Some maintain that the term "rites" (*karmāṇi*) refers only to those intended for our own school which will be described in the *Gṛhya-sūtra*, and not to all matters as in the case of the Dharma-śāstras governed by the word "dharma.

Likewise, the section on domestic rites (*gārhya-adhikāra*) follows immediately after the section on Śrauta rites in order to ensure the application here of those universal dharmas mentioned in the Śrauta texts.

2. The rules for the seasons, beginning with the northern course of the sun: rites should be performed during the northern course of the sun, during the bright fortnight, on the day of the moon, and on auspicious days. (ĀpGs 1.2)

The prescription of the northern solstice (*udagayana*) and so forth is for the purpose of prohibiting the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) and so forth. There is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the northern solstice and the other [favorable times], not an option (*vikalpa*).

"Auspicious days" (*puṇyāha*) and "lunar mansions of the gods" (*devanakṣatra*) are well-known in the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*), as are the "mansions of Yama" (*yamanakṣatra*), which are prescribed therein.
The *udagayana* (northern course of the sun) and so forth are well known.

As for the "auspicious days" (*puṇyāha*), these are the five portions of the day divided into nine parts— namely, morning (*prātaḥ*), forenoon (*saṅgava*), midday (*madhyāhna*), afternoon (*sāyaṃ*), and evening (*parāhṇa*)— which are synonymous with "auspicious lunar mansions" (*puṇyanakṣatra*).
"There are five auspicious lunar mansions for the same day" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.5.6); "The time of union with Mitra— that is an auspicious,
radiant day" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.5.6).
This is because of such scriptural passages; moreover, even-numbered [days] are inauspicious, according to the Śruti: "There are four inauspicious [days]" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.5.6).
Some say that the divine lunar mansions beginning with Kṛttikā and ending with Viśākhā are auspicious days; "whatever one might do, one should do it during those very divine lunar mansions."
"Indeed, he performs [the rite] on an auspicious day," according to the Śruti (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.5.2).
This compound beginning with "udagayana" is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound.
In these [fires], the domestic rites (*gārhyāṇi*) are to be performed; this is the understood remainder.
There is a combination (*samuccaya*) of these, not an option (*vikalpa*).

And this general rule is set aside and restricted by specific rules in various instances. Thus, although there is a prescription for the northern solstice (*udagayana*) and so forth, in some cases an absence of restriction appears. "All seasons are [suitable] for marriage" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 2.12).

According to this statement, when a marriage takes place even during the southern transit of the sun (*dakṣiṇāyana*), the return home (*samāvartana*) should occur at a time very close to that [marriage].

Otherwise, if one who has returned during the northern transit (*udagayana*) were to marry in autumn, there would be a long interval; and in such a case, the rule "A twice-born man should not remain without an āśrama even for a single day" would be violated.
This is because there would otherwise arise the contingency of transgressing the prohibition [stated in] *Dakṣasmṛti* 1.1.

Furthermore, in the *Āśvalāyanagṛhya-sūtra*—in the passage "The tonsure ceremony (*caula*), initiation (*upanayana*), the godāna, and marriage should take place during the northern course of the sun (*udagayana*), in the waxing fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion" (Āśva.Gṛ. 1.5)—it is understood that since the godāna is a modification (*vikāra*) of the caula, the northern course of the sun is already applicable to it; therefore, its explicit prescription therein is intended to ensure that this restriction regarding the northern course does not cease to apply to other such modifications, namely, the return home (*samāvartana*).

Likewise, since the *samāvartana* rite is a modification of the *caula* according to the *Baudhāyanīya*, the fact that the rule for it is stated again despite the [general] attainment of the waxing fortnight (*āpūryamāṇapakṣa*) indicates that there is a restriction to the northern solstice (*udagayana*). Similarly, regarding the construction and entry into a house, because the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) is also prescribed in the *Jyotiḥśāstra* and because of the unopposed practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*), there is no restriction to the northern solstice.
Likewise, during the latter fortnight as well, until the fifth day, they perform the construction and entry into the house even at night;
similarly, when auspicious days are afflicted by the defects mentioned in the *Jyotiṣa*, they proceed even on inauspicious ones.

In the same way, when auspicious days are afflicted by the defects mentioned in the *Jyotiṣa*, people perform their rites without disagreement even on inauspicious days that possess the qualities mentioned therein;
such is the nature of the *Jyotiṣa* science as well.

Because it is an auxiliary of the Vedas, because no reason for its rejection is perceived, and because it is accepted by the learned, it is indeed to be respected, just like the Kalpasūtras and similar texts;
for in matters of determination, the learned are the authority in all cases.
3. The rule regarding the sacred thread, circumambulation, and so forth: [one should act] wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*). (ĀpGS 1.3)
The word "duties" (kāryāṇi) is understood to carry over [from the previous context].
The connection is with the word "rites" (*kāryāṇi*).

[Objection: But is not the wearing of the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) already established for *pākayajña* sacrifices by such rules as "towards the east" (*prāgapavargāṇi*, Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 2.15)?

In the case of sacrifices such as marriage and similar rites, as well as in recitations and the like, this rule is rendered redundant by such injunctions as "in the sacrifice and in the act of recitation" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.15.1).
Therefore, this specific rule here would be useless;
however, in rites such as the *pratyavarohaṇa* performed during the winter season, this rule indeed possesses its intended significance.
He should circumambulate [it] from left to right. (ĀpGs 1.4)
And those [fires] are to be circumambulated; "pradakṣiṇa" means having the right hand turned toward them. An example is the ritual strewing (*paristaraṇa*) and so forth.
Now, one might object: both of these are not things that can be enjoined.
Since these two have already been prescribed among the *śrauta* rites by the rule "the [offerings] for the gods" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.3.5),
it is stated there;
however, here, their application is also intended for the human rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and others.
This undertaking is for that purpose;
the connection is simply "the ritual acts.

However, this circumambulation by the right (prādakṣiṇya), although established as a technical rule (paribhāṣā-siddha) for the *pākayajñas* and for those rites belonging to their category, such as marriage and the like, [is here specifically enjoined].
If it is argued that a domestic chariot distinct from that is prescribed, it is exactly so.
The commencement is either from the east or from the north. ĀpGs 1.5.
This statement is for the purpose of establishing a rule where there was no fixed rule;
it is intended to prevent the commencement [of the action] from the right or the rear.
The spreading of grass and so forth serves as the illustrative example.
The word "kārya" (should be performed) is the ellipsis.
However, this [rite] is enjoined because it has not been prescribed in any of the domestic sacrifices (gārhya-yajña) that take the form of the Yajñāyajñīya.
Likewise, [the ritual for] final liberation. ĀpGs 1.6.
Their conclusion (*apavarga*) should also be understood in the same way; that is to say, it is either toward the east or toward the north. *Apavarga* means completion.

And here, a restrictive rule of equal application is not being made regarding the commencement and the conclusion—that what is commenced in the east must be concluded in that very place, and what is commenced in the north must be concluded in that very place.

Rather, the procedure follows according to what is possible; for example, in the case of the *paristaraṇa* (spreading of grass), since its conclusion in the east is impossible once it has been commenced there, its conclusion is toward the north.
In that case, the injunction for the conclusion [in the east] would be purposeless.
Because this has already been prescribed in the Śrauta rules as "ending toward the east or ending toward the north" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 2.15),
it is replied:
even if the rule regarding the direction of completion (*apavarga*) were not restated here, [it would still apply].

Regarding the statement, "Having built two huts to the west of the fire" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 19.14), it follows that they should end toward the south, because of the rule that the commencement [of the action] must be directed toward the north.
Therefore, this undertaking is intended so that, in the event of a conflict, the rule of completion (apavarga) shall prevail.
Otherwise, by the general maxim of "pradakṣiṇa," the general rule would be sublated; for it has been specified therein that "some rites are divine.
Here, however, regarding human actions and the like, the rule of completion is established for the purpose of attainment.
The meaning is that the completion of the ritual action should take place either to the east or to the north.

Now, one might object: since the rule "the commencement is to the east or to the north" already establishes the completion by implication in cases such as the circumambulatory sprinkling (*samantapariṣeka*), the rule "ending there" need not have been commenced.

We reply: No; for if this sūtra were not commenced, [the direction for] the drawing of lines toward the east, the purification of the grass-blades, and so forth, would not be established as being toward the north.
Furthermore, the completion of the rite of making the hut (*kuṭīkaraṇa*) and so forth would be toward the west and the south;
therefore, this [section] must indeed be commenced in order to override that.
Some [hold that] there is a northern commencement for the lines of those facing east.
And for those facing north, the conclusion is toward the east, because, as in the case of the strewing around the fire, it is impossible for both [directions] to be prescribed simultaneously. (2)
4. The rule for the ancestral rites beginning with the dark fortnight:
the ancestral rites are performed during the dark fortnight. (ĀpGs 1.7)
With the sacred thread worn over the right shoulder.
From left to right. // ĀpGs 1.9 //
The conclusion [of the rite] is toward the south.
Rites dedicated to the ancestors are to be performed during the latter fortnight;
as it is said, "The eighth day [festival] is that which follows the full moon of Māgha," therein the latter fortnight is prescribed.

This restriction, however, is intended to ensure that those rites such as the *gayā-śrāddha* and others—which have been taught by us as being performed for specific desires based on particular places or specific recipients—and which we have accepted [as valid], do not apply to the *pārvaṇa* [rite]; it is for the purpose of securing the attainment of the "latter fortnight" (*aparapakṣa*).
Therefore, for one who has died during the "former fortnight" (*pūrvapakṣa*), the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite must be performed during the latter fortnight, and not on the eleventh day.
And as for the performance on the eleventh day:
we shall explain the purpose of the monthly śrāddha according to the rules for the dark fortnight in that very place.

And this rule for the dark fortnight (aparapakṣa) is an exception to the entire [rule] beginning with the northern course of the sun (udagayana) and so forth, rather than being restricted to the previous [period] or the northward direction as appropriate.
An example is the ritual strewing (paristaraṇa) and other such acts.
Thus, this triad beginning with "wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (prācīnāvītī) is not something to be enjoined [as a primary rule].
[Objection: Because these have been defined only in the context of Śrauta rites;

[Response: It is said: These technical rules (paribhāṣās)—namely, "with the sacred thread over the left shoulder" (yajñopavītinā) and "moving to the right" (pradakṣiṇam), as well as "likewise at the conclusion" (tathāpavarge)—are recited here in this section without distinction. Since they are general technical rules, they would apply even to rites for the ancestors (pitrya); therefore, this [present rule] is stated in order to set aside that [general application].

And here, this rule for the *prācīnāvīta* applies only to those ancestral rites (*pitrya*) that proceed independently within their own lineage, but not to those performed as subordinate parts (*aṅga*) elsewhere.
Therefore, in rites for the gods (*daiva*) and for humans (*mānuṣa*), such as the formula "the fathers, the grandfathers," the *yajñopavīta* alone is used.
Another [teacher] says: "Therefore, the *Abhyātāna* formulas belong to the *vaiśvadeva* [rite]" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.4.6).
From this observation, it follows that because the formula “the fathers, the grandfathers” also pertains to the ancestors (*pitrya*), the *prācīnāvīta* arrangement would not apply [to it].

Likewise, under the heading “rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*) are performed in the dark fortnight,” it is stated that the *prācīnāvīta* applies without distinction to all ancestral rites (*pitrya-karman*) along with their constituent parts (*sāṅga*).

Therefore, in the rite for the ancestors, from the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings up to the *jaya* and subsequent rites, the sacred thread must indeed be worn over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*).
The injunction is simply "the rites are to be performed," and this injunction concerns the principal ancestral rite (*pitrya*) independently;
for there is no need to look toward an injunction regarding time for the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*), since they are to be performed together with the principal and thus share its timing.
And this is not merely a refutation of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
What then? It is another injunction for the purpose of refuting everything.
Ah! How is this known?
This is because of the indicative statement: "And one should not perform a *śrāddha* at night" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.17.23).
For if this were merely an exception to the rule regarding the first half of the month (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the rule would have been formulated differently].
Since there would be no possibility of [performing the rite] at night due to the absence of any exception to the three [periods] beginning with the northern solstice, there would be no prohibition;
yet, since there is indeed a prohibition, it is known that this must be a distinct injunction.

The purpose, however, is that optional *śrāddhas* should be performed without distinction even during the southern course of the sun (*dakṣiṇāyana*), during the waning fortnight (*aparapakṣa*), and on the day itself;
as for the monthly *śrāddha*, it is because of the rule: "It should be performed month after month" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.16.4).
By means of this distributive repetition (*vīpsā*), it is already established that [the rite] applies even during the southern course of the sun (*dakṣiṇāyana*).
But if this is so, what is the purpose of the injunction: "The monthly *śrāddha* [should be performed] in the dark fortnight" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 21.1)?
It is for the purpose of restriction; for it is thus: the *māsi-śrāddha* is to be performed only on the [lunar] dark fortnight, and not at other times due to either divine or human circumstances.

Just as when the latter fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) has passed due to an obstacle, one says, "The entire latter fortnight belongs to the full moon," and so forth, [the rite] must likewise be performed during the former fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*).
However, if there is a failure in the obligatory *smārta* rites already commenced, there is only an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
And that consists of a single oblation (*homa*) with the mantra "Bhūr bhuvaḥ suvaḥ svāhā," known as the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*).
"If it is unknown, one should recite all [the vyāhṛtis] beginning with bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ and offer them into the āhavanīya fire itself" (AiB 24.34).
According to this Śruti of the Bahvṛcas,
this [offering] is to be performed here in the aupāsana fire.

Because, according to the principles of logic, the word *āhavanīya* found in the Veda— which is devoted to a single specific rule— is intended to indicate any fire whatsoever used for ritual purposes that possesses the relevant characteristics; furthermore,
fasting must be observed upon the transgression of the obligatory rites prescribed by the Veda.
And for the violation of the vows of a *snātaka*, the expiation is fasting.
Thus, according to the statement of Manu;
and for one who possesses wealth, there is also the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) "in the case of transgressing another rule" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.12.18).
Because of this statement, there is indeed a combination (*samuccaya*) of these [penances] and not an option (*vikalpa*); for it is said:
"The penances heard in regard to a single fault should be combined" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 9.1.2).
Since this has been demonstrated,
the expiation is stated even when other [rites] are omitted as a consequence;
likewise, there is expiation for other *pākayajña* sacrifices that have been commenced in the event of their failure.
Even when the primary time has passed,
those [rites] are to be performed during the secondary time after first performing the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*).

However, if there is a lapse of many times for the *aupāsana* oblation, then prior to each of the eight [missed] oblation times, it must be performed individually after first performing the universal expiation.
The oblations (homāḥ) must be performed at dawn.
In this regard, the practice of fasting and breath-control (prāṇāyāma) is not observed.
However, even when the fire is being maintained thereafter, [the rule] "if it has gone out, it must be churned" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 5.17) applies.
These and other such [rules] apply to the expiation for the loss of the sacred fires, based on the scriptural statement: "If the fire is not offered for four nights, it becomes a worldly fire.

However, if one should remain for a long time with the fires extinguished due to laziness or other causes, then, according to another Smṛti, an appropriate penance such as the Kṛcchra, as well as the gift of materials for the oblation, must be understood [to be required].
However, for those *pākayajñas* whose time has not yet commenced, one should perform the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblation and then proceed with their commencement.

(4) Some [teachers] maintain that when the *pākayajñas* are not commenced at their proper times, or when those already commenced are not performed, or when the secondary time (*gauṇakāla*) has passed, one should offer oblations with clarified butter taken in four ladlings (*caturgṛhīta*), accompanied by the *graha* formula and the *saptahotṛ* formula.

For it is said: "One should cause him who has failed in the sacrifice to perform the sacrifice with the *saptahotṛ* formula and with clarified butter taken in four ladlings" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 14.14.11).
Thus, the *darvīhoma* prescribed by the Śruti is intended for the failure of a sacrifice;

nevertheless, having begun with the statement, "These *caturhotṛ* formulas are indeed the sacrifice for one who has not established the sacred fires" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 14.13.2), it concludes, "One who has established the fires should perform them [the *caturhotṛ*s]; the others [the *darvīhomās*] for both" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 14.15.5).
Because of this conclusion,
and because an explicit rule for expiation is required for a failure in domestic rites (*gārhya*), it is indeed appropriate that the same applies to a failure in those [śrauta] rites as well;
this was stated by Kapardisvāmin.
However, if the proper time for the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) and other such ceremonies has passed, they must be performed preceded by the performance of the universal expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*).
If there is an omission of the ancillary parts of a rite, however, there is the universal expiation and a breath-control exercise (*prāṇāyāma*).
The performance of the auxiliary rites that provide remote assistance (ārādupakāraka) continues until the completion of the ritual;
however, for those auxiliaries involving the preparation of materials (dravya-saṃskāra), this applies only as long as they are possible prior to the actual use of the material.
Furthermore, in the injunction regarding the initiation ceremony (upanayana), in the event of the failure of an auxiliary, one should offer [the oblation] with the mantra "amuṣmai svāhā."
The oblation is offered into the fire that is an auxiliary of the ritual (*karmāṅgāgni*).

There is also an oblation or a recitation (*japa*) with the three verses beginning with "anājñātam. Alternatively, there is an option between the word *bhuvaḥ* and the purpose of the injunction regarding what is unknown (*anājñātavidhyartha*).

This is because [the rule] "The rite is dependent on the Brāhmaṇa" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 2.10) and "The purificatory rite is based on the Śruti" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.1.9) serve the purpose of obtaining the expiatory rites prescribed by the Śruti.
[Objection: "Is it not the case that one offers in the Dakṣiṇāgni with the mantra 'nanv-abhavaḥ' and in the Āhavanīya with 'an-ājñātam'?

[Response: True; however, since those two fires are absent here, and because even occasional rites (naimittika), as being constituent parts (aṅga), ought to be offered in the primary fire (pradhānāgni) just like other constituent parts, [the offering must be made there]."

(4) Some say that regarding any omission in all *gṛhya* rites and their constituent parts, one should adopt what is not mentioned [in one's own text] from elsewhere, according to the maxim "what is not stated here should be taken from another source," and thus they cite the expiations (*prāyaścitta*) prescribed in other *gṛhya* texts; this, however, is to be considered.
Enough with this digression; let the subject at hand be discussed. As for the statement:
"The afternoon of the dark fortnight is more auspicious" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.16.50).
Thus, this is a restatement for the purpose of prescribing [the ritual] for the afternoon session;

just as in the case of the *pātnīvata* offering, where, although the absence of the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* is already established by the rule "In all cases there is no *anuvaṣaṭkāra*, except for those offerings to two deities, the seasonal cups, the Āditya cup, the Sāvitra cup, and the *pātnīvata*" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 12.24.2), it is further stated: "Or rather, one should perform the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* in a low voice" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 13.24.9, 10).
This is for the purpose of specifying the particular days;
that is, the monthly *śrāddha* is intended to be performed only on the days of the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*), and not even optionally on the days of the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Otherwise, if after the period of impurity has passed and during the latter fortnight, by chance an impurity should arise regarding a Śrāddha for the ancestors,
then once that impurity has indeed ceased, the Śrāddha is offered to them.

According to another Smṛti text, this [rite] may optionally take place even on the days of the first fortnight (pūrvapakṣa). However, as for the obligatory Śrāddha (nityaśrāddha), because of the force of the accusative case in the expression "thus for a year" (*evaṃ saṃvatsaram*, Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.18.13)—which denotes continuous connection—it must be performed during the first fortnight as well. //7//
The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "the rites for the ancestors (pitryāṇi) are to be performed.
However, this rule regarding the specific manner of arranging the garment applies to all ancestral rites, whether independent or dependent,
because the statement "the ancestral rites are to be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī)" is understood to apply without distinction.

Because, once the subject matter has been restricted solely to the ancestral rites (*pitrya*), if one were to intend to express independence regarding an unmentioned [subject], it would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*); furthermore,

even if the *prācīnāvīta* mode were to be prescribed for the subsidiary rites (*aṅga*), there would be no lack of requirement, as in the case of the statement, "The ancestral rites are performed in the dark fortnight."

Therefore, all those rites that are independent, such as the principal oblations (pradhānāhuti), as well as those that are dependent, such as the wiping of the two paths (dvitāyanimārjana) and so forth, must be performed by one wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī).
In this very same way, the rule "by one wearing the sacrificial thread" (yajñopavītinā) applies as well.
Therefore, even the subsidiary rites for the ancestors (pitrya), such as the āghāra libations and others, must be performed by one wearing the sacrificial thread.
However, for other subsidiaries, such as the preparation of the vessels and so forth, the rule follows exactly that of their respective primary rites.

Some maintain that it is logical for the subsidiary elements to possess the same ritual status as the principal rite; thus, they claim that the subsidiary elements belonging to the ancestors (pitrya) should be performed with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītin), while those belonging to the gods (daiva) should be performed with the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītin).
This, however, is to be considered.
The remainder is exactly the same. //9//
The word "in rites for the ancestors" (pitryeṣu kārye) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].

Here, because these three [rules] are already established by the general rule beginning with "wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (prācīnāvītī, Āpastamba-pariśiṣṭa 2.16), [the present rule serves to restrict them].
The rule [concerning the] fireless sacrifice, the obligatory rites, the sixteen śrāddhas, and so forth, is for the purpose [of these]. //10//
The rites performed on account of specific signs are those contingent upon such signs. ĀpGs 1.11.

The connection with the preceding sūtra is as follows: "with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), moving from left to right (prasavya), and concluding toward the south (dakṣiṇato 'pavargaḥ).

Regarding the causal occasions (nimittāni) and the rites occasioned by them (naimittikāni karmāṇi), these must be performed immediately upon observing the occasion; there is no requirement for the northern solstice (udagayana) or other such conditions in that regard.
These are the examples.
In that regard, because of the statement "at night on the new moon day," there is an extension [of the rite] to that extent.
Some maintain that the entering of the house is an occasional (naimittika) rite.
"No," say others. //8//
The occasional rites (*naimittika*), such as the *Āgrayaṇa*, the guest-offering (*atithya*), and the *Sīmanta*, depend upon specific occasions (*nimitta*).
The meaning is that the occasions themselves—such as the ripening of rice—are what are awaited for their performance, and not [general times] such as the northern solstice (*udagayana*).
In this case as well, there is no exception to the prior position (*pūrvapakṣa*) as far as it is possible. //11//

Having thus explained the connection with the preparatory rites (*prayoga-anubandha*) and the [details of] time and so forth, he now states the collection of preliminary and subsequent limbs—which constitute the common ritual procedure (*sādhāraṇatantra*) for all principal domestic oblations (*gṛhya-pradhāna-homa*)—according to their specific applications, beginning with "Having kindled the fire" (*agnim idhvā*) and ending with "The mantra is the name" (*mantraḥ sannāmaḥ*).
2. Definition of the Fire as the Mouth (*agnimukha-nirūpaṇa*):
1. Spreading the Grass, etc.:
Having kindled the fire, he spreads grass around the fire with its tips pointing eastward. (ĀpGS 1.12)
Or with the tips pointing toward the east or the north.
The general rules for the *pākayajñas* have been stated; now their common ritual framework (*sādhāraṇatantra*) will be explained: "Having kindled the fire.
This is called the "kindling of the fire," and it is an integral part of the ritual action.
What, then, is the fire in this case?

In connection with the wife, it is the *aupāsana* fire; others say it is the common worldly fire (*laukika*). Some, however, maintain that the acquisition of the fire begins from the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) onwards.
Others, however, say it begins from the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*); others say, "One should take hold of him at the point where he would place the final fuel-stick.
But where no fire has been established, one should fetch it from the house of a *śrotriya* or produce it by friction.

The phrase "wherever there is fire," however, constitutes a consecration of the location, which applies everywhere provided that the location has been prepared. Since "kindle the fire" was already mentioned in the context, the repetition of the word "fire" is so that the strewing around may also take place in those cases where the *tantra* (the ritual framework) does not otherwise apply—thus it says, "he strews around the fire in all cases. As for the placing of fuel, however, it is established there by the requirements of the situation.
Or with blades pointing eastward and northward.
Alternatively, the strewing is not performed with blades pointing only eastward on all sides; rather, it is done with blades pointing both eastward and northward.
Among these, those pointing northward are placed at the rear and at the front. //9//
And here, for the purpose of understanding the specific nature of the object "fire," fire as it appears in the Smṛtis is defined.
Regarding this, there is a statement by Yājñavalkya:
"A householder should perform the Smārta rites daily in the marriage fire."

Thus [it is said in Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.97]. The meaning of this is: a householder, that is, a married man together with his wife, should perform the *smārta* rites in the marriage fire, namely the *aupāsana* fire.

That action in the performance of which the wife’s partnership occurs through constituent elements such as the intention (*saṃkalpa*), the striking (*avaghāta*), the undertaking (*anvārambha*), the relinquishment of the substance (*dravyatyāga*), or the consent (*anumati*), that action one should perform in one's own *aupāsana* fire.

Alternatively, whatever action to be accomplished by means of fire has a fruit that accrues either directly or through the mediation of another action to the wife and husband—whether to both or to either of them—that action the householder should perform in his own *aupāsana* fire;
this is because of the hearing of the middle-voice ending (*ātmanepada*) in the word "kurvīta" (he should perform).
And thus, the Smārta *pākayajña* rites, such as the *sīmantonnayana* and others, are to be performed in the *aupāsana* fire.

Even the rite of entering the house (*gṛhapraveśa*) is to be performed in the *aupāsana* fire alone, because it serves the purpose of pacifying the site (*vāstuśānti*) resulting from that act and for the sake of the longevity of the wife, children, and so forth.
Likewise, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for one's father and others, as well as for one's maternal grandfather and others, is also to be performed in the *aupāsana* fire.

This is because the fruit of the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*—which consists in the cessation of the state of being a *preta* and the attainment of the status of a *pitṛ*—serves as the purpose for the recipient (*sampradāna*) in rites such as the *māsika-śrāddha* and others performed for prosperity; furthermore, the fruit of that rite accrues to both the wife and the husband.
For this very reason, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* should not be performed by all sons [simultaneously].
Since the status of being a recipient (*sampradānatva*) is established even by a single son acting as a father,
therefore, in a case where the wife’s partnership or the fruit of the ritual action accrues to both husband and wife, that rite is to be performed specifically in the *aupāsana* fire.

If, however, the son—being without sacred fire (*anagni*) and uninitiated (*anupanīta*)—performs the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* when the year is complete because it is mandatory, then he does so in a fire brought from the house of a *śrotriya*; for Bodhāyana states: "Or else, that *aupāsana* [fire] is taken precisely from the house of a *śrotriya*" (Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 6.2).
Because of this praise of the *aupāsana* fire and because of established custom,
even an uninitiated son is indeed entitled to perform the *śrāddha*;
for he is worthy [of performing it] even without the sacred fire and even without [the teacher's] presence.
Because of the statement [of Manu]:
"One should not utter the Veda or the word *brahman* except when offering the *svadhā* libation" (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 2.5).
Furthermore, because the word *svadhā* found in the statement of Gautama is intended to indicate all rites for the deceased (*ūrdhvadaihika*),
[it follows that]: "A brother, or a brother’s son, a *sapiṇḍa*, or even a disciple,
having performed the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*, should thereafter perform the *abhyudaya* (prosperity rite)."

Because of this statement, when a brother’s son or similar relative performs [the rite], then—since the aforementioned co-partnership and the sharing of the fruit are absent—it must be performed using fire brought from the sacrifice of one learned in the Vedas (śrotriya).

Others, however, maintain that even the attainment of the status of a father by a brother or others results in a reward going to the husband—just as the rewards such as purification resulting from a son accrue to the father—and that this applies to the *aupāsana* fire; but that should be considered carefully.

Likewise, the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), the tonsure (*caula*), the initiation (*upākaraṇa*), the completion (*samāpana*), the godāna, and the return home (*samāvartana*) are also [performed] in this manner.
So too is the leading near (*upanayana*).

Even according to the view that the leading near (*upanayana*) is for the purpose of accomplishing the status of a teacher (*ācāryakaraṇa*), it does not take place in the presence of the teacher’s sacred fire (*aupāsana*).
Because that [fire] must be maintained perpetually, it would contradict the Sūtra which states, "They maintain this fire for three days" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 11.19).
Furthermore, the marriage ceremony also takes place in this [fire].
Or [it may be performed] with the fire produced by friction,
because the *aupāsana* fire generated at marriage is impossible [in that case];
even if it were possible, [it would refer to] the first *aupāsana*.

There is no second or subsequent marriage with respect to that [fire], because of the understanding of a distinction between the *aupāsana* fires for each wife, as seen in the passage: "Whichever wife one might desire, 'May her offspring be sovereign,' for her [the fire] is in the *aupāsana*."
According to the Baudhāyana school, because of the injunction regarding the conjunction of two fires,
[this applies] to the consecrated site of the *aupāsana* fire intended for ritual acts,
or to another fire that has not yet been formally established (*anupasamāhita*).

The installation of the sacred fire (agnipratiṣṭhāpana) must be performed according to the procedure prescribed in the Dharmaśāstra by the rule: "Wherever [one may be], one should kindle the fire" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.1.13).
Some maintain that this nakedness is merely a part of the ritual action and must be performed with each specific rite, and that the maintaining of the fire is to be done in a cooking pot.

Now the Sūtra is explained: "having kindled the fire, one should kindle it" means that although the fueling of the fire is already implied by the sense of the matter, nevertheless, because of this specific statement, one should kindle it again even though it has already been kindled.

In this context, since the optative suffix (*liṅ*) and so forth could be understood as expressing an injunction, the mention of the suffix *ktvā* is for the purpose of restricting the priority of the act of strewing (*paristaraṇa*) to that of the fuel (*indhana*).
Consequently, the strewing must be performed immediately after the fuel;
however, it does not follow that other necessary tasks such as the voiding of urine or the preparation of ritual materials must necessarily be performed in the interval between those two.
[Objection: But surely, if both fuel and the spreading [of grass] were enjoined in a single sūtra, there would be a split in the sentence (vākyabheda). [Reply: True;
however, a split in the sentence is not a defect in a sūtra, because of the etymological derivation that "it is called a sūtra because it indicates (sūcana)."

This same explanation and purpose apply everywhere in the case of taking up grass-blades. He strews around the fire with darbha blades whose tips point eastward; he strews around the fire in all directions with kuśa grass whose tips point eastward. //12//
Alternatively, he strews grass around the fire with *darbha* blades;
on the south and north sides with blades pointing eastward, and on the west and east sides with blades pointing northward.
Because of the observation in the Śrauta [sūtra]: "The tips pointing upwards, both behind and in front" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.14.15),
he arranges these kuśa grasses so that they are directed from south to north.
And the northern [side] is below the southern,
because it is so stated in the Gṛhyasūtras of Baudhāyana and Bharadvāja:
"The right wing is on top, and the left is below."

In this context, although the fire has already been mentioned in the phrase "having kindled the fire," the repetition of the word "the fire" is for the purpose of restriction: he strews around the fire alone, and not any other subsidiary part [of the sacrificial ground].
Consequently, the water placed either to the north or to the east remains strictly outside.
Some [hold] that even in the case of rites not based on the Tantras, the fire must necessarily be strewn around; thus, [the rule] serves as a restrictive injunction (niyama). //13//
In rites for the ancestors, the blades of grass should have their tips pointing southward.
Or with the tips pointing south-east. ĀpGs 1.15.
There, the [blades] are pointed southward in the west and east. //10//
In rites for the ancestors, such as the monthly *śrāddha* and others, he strews grass with its tips pointing southward in all directions.
The sacrificer [should cover the ground] with darbha grass having their tips pointing southward in the west and in front;
and with tips pointing northward in the north and on the right side.
One should place the supports to the north, the highest, and to the south; likewise, having begun from the east, one strews [the grass] moving clockwise. //15//
2. The Arrangement of the Vessels (Pātraprayoga).
Having strewn darbha grass to the north of the fire, he arranges the vessels in pairs, turned face down, those associated with the gods.
Immediately after the surrounding strewing, he spreads darbha grass with tips pointing eastward to the north of the fire for the purpose of arranging the vessels.
The well-known spreading; he applies it, that is, he places it down.
"Nyāñci" means those which have become downward-turned.

And all materials that have a purpose are included by the term "taking up the vessels" (*pātragrahaṇa*). Therefore, even items such as the *mokhala* (threshing mortar) and so forth are set down at the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and other rites.
Among those, whatever are associated with the gods, he arranges them in pairs (*dvandva*).
The meaning is "two by two.
The rites for the gods include the *pārvaṇa* and others.
The mention of "fire" (*agni*) is redundant because [the rite] is not modified; thus, one says "having kindled the fire" (*agnim indhveti*).
This is for the purpose of indication; it indicates that this [procedure], which is prescribed for the strewing of grass around the fire, does not apply to the employment of the vessels.
When, then, does it apply? At the time of the absence of the *tantra* and when there is the introduction of the specific tip of the *darbha* grass.

Therefore, even in rites for the ancestors (pitrya), the spreading [of grass] must be with the tips pointing eastward, and [the placement] to the north of the fire; and because there is no use of vessels in the absence of a *tantra*, [the rule] applies only to the disposal (*pratipatti*) of the fire due to the governing context (*adhikāra*). Thus, both of those [points] would have to be understood as applying here.
The deity [is determined] from the context alone. //11//
Not far to the north of the fire, he spreads darbha grass; and these [blades] have their tips pointing eastward,
according to the Baudhāyana Gṛhya-sūtra.
The word *staraṇa* is [formed] with the prefix *pra*;
from the prefix *sam*, [the word *saṃstara* is formed]; and *udaka* is [formed] with the prefix *stara* and the suffix *apavarga*.

Even in rites for the ancestors (pitrya), the [grass] should be placed to the north of the fire with its tips pointing eastward; for although it is established by the rule, "The ritual movement (vihāra) is performed from the north" (Āpastamba Paribhāṣā-sūtra 2.10), the explicit statement here that "[it is] to the north" is also intended to apply here as well.

In the case of the fire under discussion as well, it is appropriate that the additional word "fire" (agni) refers to an additional purpose, since no specific distinction is stated— as is the case with the ritual strewing (paristaraṇa)—
and because the conclusion (apavarga) occurs only to the south.
The divine implements mentioned are those connected with divine rites;
the vessels refer to the ladles and so forth;
"in pairs" means two of each.
He turns the bowls downward,
prepares them, and sets them down.

But is it not the case that later on, since the distinction is already established by the qualifiers "connected with humans" and "connected with ancestors," the term "connected with gods" is redundant?

No; for divine rites are of two kinds: those consisting of human effort and those which are purificatory rites for men. In both cases, however, the purpose is to ensure the pairing of the vessels for the gods, such as the *darvī* ladle and so forth. //16//
In that regard, concerning certain vessels used for human purposes such as those for a potter, he states an exception:
"Those associated with humans [are purified] by a single [cleansing]. (ĀpGS 1.17)
Those vessels associated with human activities he employs only singly,
not in pairs;
"human activities" refers to marriage and the like.
The particle *eva* is for the purpose of prohibiting repetition (*abhyāvṛtti*) of the action.
Even if one is unable to place [the items] with both arms due to the multiplicity of vessels, they are to be placed all at once by means of some expedient.
Some, however, maintain that only those things associated with humans, such as the girdle (*mekhalā*) and so forth, are to be used only once.
Not for those intended for oblations;
we, however, have stated that they are connected with humans and connected with human activities. //12//

Items associated with humans—such as stones, garments, girdles, and so forth—which are connected through human agents, he employs only once, avoiding repetition of the action; even when there is a plurality of vessels, this is done by means of a specific method.
Some maintain that in rites for the purification of humans, implements such as the wooden ladle (*darvī*) and others are also employed only once. //17//
Each one individually is associated with the ancestors.
Those rites which have been prescribed for the ancestral ceremonies (pitr-karma), he performs them one by one; that is to say, one at a time. //13//
He prepares all at once the ladles and other implements required for the ancestral rites, as well as the vessels for the *svadhā* offering and so forth. //18//
3. The purification of the *pavitra* grasses:

the preparation of the two *pavitra* blades, their length and measurement, the preparation of the *prokṣaṇī* water, and the sprinkling of the vessels are performed silently, as in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice. (ĀpGS 1.19)
The consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the two *pavitra* strainers consists of [the preparation of] grass, wood, and so forth.
Regarding their length—their measurement in terms of extension—it is stated that they should be "a span long" (*prādeśamātra*).
The consecration by sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is described as: "Upon the *agnihotra-havaṇī* ladle covered with the *pavitra* strainers," and so on.
In this context, since the *agnihotrahavaṇī* ladle is not present here, one brings another vessel.
The sprinkling of the vessels begins with the words "the vessels face upwards" and so forth;
this indicates these four ritual items.
In this case as well, the procedure should be performed just as it is for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
The term "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*) is a prohibition of mantras.
Just as the action prescribed for the sprinkling of the vessels is established here, so too the loosening of the fuel-stick (*idhma*) is accomplished by its inclusion within that very process.
This statement, however, is for the purpose of restriction (niyamārtha), so that the measurement of length may apply only to the two strainers (pavitra),

and not to the fuel-sticks (idhma) or the tips of the darbha grass when they are being thrown into the clarified butter (ājya). But how could there be any possibility [of such an application] in that case?
This very point makes it known: here too, as in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is a silent consecration (*tūṣṇīṃ saṃskāra*).
The mention of "length" (*āyāma*) serves as a restrictive rule for the measurement of length of the two *pavitra* strainers; however, the number and measurement follow that of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.
Therefore, since the after-offerings (*anūyāja*) are not present here, the sacrificial fuel (*idhma*) does not consist of twenty-one pieces of wood.
The secondary offerings (upahoma), however, serve the purpose of the after-offerings (anuyāja). //14//
The consecration of the two *pavitra* blades should be performed similarly to that of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, with the exception of the mantras.
He prepares two *pavitra* blades from *darbha* grass whose tips are unbroken and which are a span (*prādeśa*) in length;
he cuts them after interposing either a blade of grass or a piece of wood, but not with his fingernail.
Then one should perform the ritual sipping (upaspṛśet),
according to the scriptural injunction; thereafter, the cleansing with water is performed starting from the roots of those two [the hands] up to their tips.
And the measurement of their length is exactly like that of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* [sacrifices].

Although the measurement of their length is already established as being like that [of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*] by the statement, "The consecration of the two strainers (*pavitra*) is like that of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*," nevertheless, when it is specified that "the measurement of their length is one span (*prādeśamātra*)," that alone is what is meant by "like that."
However, since there is no equality here even in terms of breadth, the phrase "the measurement by length" is stated again for that purpose.

Some [hold] that the measurement of length for the two *pavitra*s alone is as in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, but not for the *idhma* or for the tips of the *darbha* grass being cast into the clarified butter; thus, this repetition is for the purpose of restriction.

By the very fact of stating this, the author of the Sūtra has implicitly permitted the performance of the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the *idhma* and the tips of the *darbha* grass silently, just as in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice.
The procedure is likewise.
Therefore, the fuel-stick (idhma), made of *khadira* or *pālāśa* wood and bound with a cord, should be untied and sprinkled three times.
At the *Pārvaṇa* sacrifice, it should be bound on the preceding day.

And at the tip of the *darbha* grass, according to the injunction beginning with "grass or wood" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 1.11.7), one should prepare [the fuel] and place it into the clarified butter (*ājya*).
Although this matter is already established by either the term "lengthwise" (*āyāmataḥ*) or "measurement" (*parimāṇa*), it is stated in this way for the sake of another restrictive rule (*niyama*).
Whatever the measurement is in terms of length alone, that same [measurement] applies to the two sacrificial grass-bundles (*pavitra*), as in the case of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice;
the measurement is not determined by number.
Therefore, the numerical measurement of the fuel-wood (*idhma*) remains that of the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, namely: "the fuel-wood consists of twenty-one pieces of wood" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 1.5.6).

Thus, because the two strainers (*pavitra*) have been specifically restricted to the *āyāma* [offering], even though there is no need for twenty-one [strainers] due to the absence of the *anūyāja* offerings, nevertheless, by the force of this very [textual authority], the *jaya* and other [mantras] are to be postulated in their place. This has been stated extensively; for even when a rule is otherwise established through a previous explanation, they still postulate [such requirements] based on the Sūtra.
The consecration of the *prokṣaṇī* water is also performed silently, as in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice.

Having poured water into a vessel made of *vikaṅkata* wood that is covered by two northward-pointed *pavitra* strainers, one should sprinkle it three times with those two strainers and then perform the sprinkling of the vessels in the same manner, silently.
Having turned the vessels face upwards and loosened the fuel, he should sprinkle them three times with his hand, together with the sacrificial grass (*pavitra*), using those [waters]. //19//
4. The carrying forward of the *praṇītā* water:

Having poured water into a vessel placed behind the fire with strainers laid between, having purified it three times by means of two strainers with tips pointing northward, having drawn it up level with his breaths, and having set it down on *darbha* grass to the north of the fire, he covers it with *darbha* grass.

Immediately after the sprinkling of the vessels, having placed the strainer intended for the *praṇītā* water behind the fire, and having placed two strainers with tips pointing northward within it, he pours water into it and purifies it three times by means of the two strainers with tips pointing northward.
Ending toward the east;
the mention of "fire" is because of the governing context of the vessels.
A specific detail seen in another ritual manual (kalpa) is that [the fire should be grasped] with both hands turned upward, using the thumbs and the ring fingers.
Having purified them, he takes them away with his breath—
meaning, by means of his mouth.
Having taken them, he places them to the north of the fire on strewn darbha grass.
The taking up of the fire is performed with vessels so that there may be no obstruction;
having set it down, he covers it with *darbha* grass.
He performs all of this while holding the *pavitra* strainers in his hand. //15//
Not far behind the fire, having poured water into some vessel placed over the *pavitra* strainers, he purifies it three times with the two *pavitra* strainers whose tips point northward.

Here, because the two *pavitras* already under discussion are mentioned again, it is indicated that the tips of the hands [of the strainers] should point eastward as established by traditional practice (*ācāra*), and also that which was stated by Āśvalāyana: "with the thumbs and ring fingers of the two upturned hands" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.3.3).

Then, having taken those waters from the water-vessel with the thumbs and index fingers of both hands, and having drawn them up evenly through the nostrils, he places them to the north of the fire upon darbha grass that has been strewn again,
because of the statement "upon darbhas.
Others [place them] upon the previously strewn [grass].
Then one should cover it with *darbha* grass.
Here, the mention of "to the west of the fire" (*apareṇāgnim*) is intended so that [the covering] does not apply to the west of the vessels;
however, the phrase "to the north of the fire" (*uttareṇāgnim*) is for the purpose of precluding the removal of the vessels. //20//
5. The Invitation of the Brahman: Having seated a Brāhmaṇa on Darbha grass to the south. (ĀpGs 1.21)
Because the fire is the subject under discussion, [the direction] is to the south.
In that regard, some desire that one should pass behind the fire to the south, silently cast out a blade of grass, and then sit down;
others desire that one should circumambulate the fire from the front.
"Regarding the duties of the *hautra* and the *brahmatva*, having performed his own [duties] and sat upon the seat of the Brahman priest,
he should place his parasol, upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*), or water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) there and perform the other [rites]"— this is another ritual manual (*kalpa*).
In the case of clarified butter oblations (*ājya-homa*), the *paristaraṇa* (strewing of grass) has already been performed;
likewise, the *brahman* priest recites the two *ājyabhāga* verses, according to Āśvalāyana. //13//
Because of the context of the phrase "Agnim indhve" (You kindle the fire), one should seat some Brahmin on Darbha grass to the south of the fire;
however, this is not the case for a *brahmán* priest as in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, because the injunctions regarding the ritual procedure are identical.

Because there is no acquisition of those duties of the Brahman priest in this case in the absence of the indicative marks of the *codanā* (injunction), and because the entire procedure is prescribed by the rule, "Having seated the Brahman priest on the south among the *darbha* grasses," therefore, the duties of the Brahman priest— such as the covering [of the altar] and the removal of grass— are not to be performed here.
Even in the case where the officiating priests are regarded as the ancestors, there is no restrictive rule that the one who was the *brahmán* priest for the father must be the one seated here.
Others, however, [cite]: "In the Śrauta rite, the Brahman priest is seen seated on Darbha grass to the south of the fire;
likewise, in the Gṛhya texts of the Bahvṛcas and Chandogas, he is enjoined simply as 'the Brahman.
Therefore, here too, it says 'a Brāhmaṇa to the south.'"
Thus, by means of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), Brahman alone is being enjoined;
therefore, the attributes of Brahman that are possible [in that context] are also applicable here.

That is not so, because it is improper to resort to secondary indication for a word belonging to one's own school (*svagṛhya*)—namely the word *brāhmaṇa*—by abandoning its primary etymological meaning (*śrutyartha*) in favor of a word from another school (*paragṛhya*).
Furthermore, the author of the Sūtra does not intend for one who sits to the south of the Brahman priest to possess the status of a Brahman priest;
for if that were the case, [the text] would have stated: "If a learned Brāhmaṇa who knows the Vidyā should not attain glory" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 14.13.7).

In this case, one should say "He gives a boon to Brahman" with only a few syllables, and not, as would involve three more syllables, "He gives a boon to him who sits to the south" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 14.13.9).
When there is the possibility of obtaining [a shorter] ritual rule, the application of the corresponding mantras is likewise unavoidable.

Regarding the statement, "Having seated the Brāhmaṇa to the south," for those who claim that this constitutes an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*) of unmentioned mantras and so forth, their assertion is groundless; for when it is possible for the passage to be intended for its own context (*svārtha*), resorting to an exclusive specification fraught with the three defects is without justification. //21//

6. The consecration of the clarified butter (*ājya*). Having melted the clarified butter, and having poured it into a butter-pot over which a strainer has been placed to the west of the fire, one draws out embers toward the north, places [the pot] upon them, heats it over the flame, throws two tips of *darbha* grass into it, carries fire around it three times, and then removes it from the embers toward the north.
Having removed [the impurities] with two northward-pointed strainers, having purified [the water] three times by bringing it back again, and having thrown the two strainers into the fire. ĀpGs 1.22.
Now, regarding the preparation of the clarified butter (*ājya*): the melting of the *ājya* takes place in whichever fire is available, because the term *ājya* is used later on.
"Pouring out" (*nirvāpa*) means bringing it forward.
The repetition of the word *ājya* is so that the preparation of the *ājya* may take place even in a rite where no *āghāra*-libation is performed.
"One offers the clarified butter (ājya) everywhere after having set it aside" (nirupya).
"Setting aside" (nirūhaṇa) means separating [the portion].
The mention of the northward direction is so that it may apply even in the case of rites for daughters.

The removal [of the fire] has been explained. Illumination is the kindling by means of a burning blade of grass. Therein, having consecrated two tips of *darbha* grass like a purifier (*pavitra*), he throws them into the clarified butter (*ājya*).
The phrase "two or one" is for the purpose of prohibiting that option seen in the Agnihotra ritual;
therefore, even in the Agnihotra procedure (*tantra*), there are exactly two tips of *darbha* grass.

Then, he performs the *paryagni-karman* three times clockwise around that clarified butter (*ājya*)—he causes fire to revolve three times around the *ājya* on all sides—using either a blade of grass or a firebrand (*ulmuka*).
In that regard, they also desire the circumambulation by fire (paryagnikaraṇa) to be performed clockwise even for the ancestral rites;
"removal" (udvāsana) means carrying [the fire] out;
"shifting back" (pratyūhana) means bringing it back toward the fire without letting it touch it.
Having repeatedly brought the food back again and again,
these three winnowings are performed with their openings facing west;
the throwing-in [of the grains] follows from the context of the fires.
"Having loosened [the knot], one should touch it with water," according to another ritual manual.
Thus ends the first section in the Anākula commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra composed by Śrī Haradatta.

Although the melting [of the ghee] is established by the technical rule (paribhāṣā), "One should perceive the ghee as *ājya*," nevertheless, even if the *ājya* has already melted, one should melt it again for the purpose of the ritual action in the fire for the sake of the oblation (*homa*).

Then, one should pour that clarified butter (*ājya*) into the butter-pot (*ājyasthālī*) which has been placed behind the fire and covered with a purifier (*pavitra*). Although the context already states "having melted the *ājya*," the repetition of the word "*ājya*" is for the purpose of ensuring that the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) and other rites apply to the *ājya* alone, and not to the curd (*dadhi*), even though curd is a substance produced from an animal that may serve as a sacrificial offering— as in the case of the injunction, "He offers curd with his joined palms" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 22.10)— according to the principle that whatever is specified applies specifically to that.

Some [hold] that even in a rite not based on a specific tantra, the clarified butter (ājya) must be consecrated by means of pouring [into the fire] and other such purificatory acts; this is for that purpose.
"Behind the rock" refers specifically to the fire, not to the Brāhmaṇa;
some say this is for the purpose of [indicating] that the lamentation occurs behind another fire, while the pouring out of the oblation occurs only behind the fire intended for the *homa*.

Then, having drawn out the embers toward the north and prepared them, he places the clarified butter upon those embers, and having flickered it with a burning blade of grass— that is, having illuminated it with a downward-pointing flame—

Having placed two tips of *darbha* grass—which are of indefinite length—between blades of grass and the like, and having cut them, he should touch them with water and simultaneously cast them into the clarified butter (*ājya*). This is because of the word "two" (*dve*) being used as an additional term, and also because of established custom (*ācāra*).

Then, taking a firebrand (*ulmuka*), he should perform the rite of carrying fire around (*paryagni-karaṇa*) the clarified butter three times clockwise; having moved the fire all around it, he should remove it toward the north.

In this context, the completion toward the north for both the removal (*nirūhaṇa*) and the setting aside (*udvāsana*) is prescribed by the rule: "In that same manner [is] the completion" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 1.6).

Thus, this re-statement of what has already been established serves as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*): for these two [rites], the conclusion (*apavarga*) must always be toward the north; it is not the case that in rites for the gods (*daiva*) the conclusion may optionally be toward the east, nor that in rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*) it may be toward the south.

Likewise, in ancestral rites, the circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*), which stands between these two, must also be clockwise (*pradakṣiṇa*), just like in rites for the gods, according to the logic of the "tongs" (*sandaṃśanyāya*).
Such indeed is the conduct of the learned.
Then, having pushed back the embers previously established there and having again joined them with the fire located at its proper place—

because of the injunction for pushing back the embers used for the consecration of the clarified butter (ājya) before the rite has commenced (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa 4.21)— [the procedure continues].
Thus, they do not possess the status of being worldly (*laukika*).

However, in the case of the *avadeya* (the portion to be cut), the *udyotana* (illumination), and the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire), when these are taken from the [sacrificial] hearth (*āyatana*), then because those two fires have ceased their ritual function (*apavṛttakarman*), they are considered worldly, and thus there is a relinquishment [of the fire].
But when they are taken from the *nirūḍha* [hearth], then at that time, the casting [of the oblation] occurs into that very [fire].
Then, as before, having purified [the water] three times by drawing it up again and again with two strainers whose tips point northward—drawing it up repeatedly and purifying it three times;
in this case, beginning from the front, leading it to the back, and completing it at the front. Some say that due to the force of the prefix *ā*, the opposite is the case.

Then, having cast those two strainers into the fire, and having cast them in a manner favorable to the movement of the oblation—if there be a knot, then having untied it and touched them with water, one should cast them into the fire with their tips pointing eastward; such is the meaning. //22//
Thus ends the first section in the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya;
thus ends the first section in the *Āpastamba Gṛhyapraśna*.

Second Section: 7. The Purification of the Ladle (Darvī-saṃskāra). That with which one offers oblations is heated over the fire, wiped clean with *darbha* grass, heated again, sprinkled with water, and set down; then, having touched the *darbha* blades with water, one throws them into the fire. (ĀpGS 2.1)
Sweeping is easy;
heating refers to the heating of that which has been placed upon the fire.
The mention of "fire" is redundant.
Because heating is impossible elsewhere,

that [heating] is performed here for the purpose of obtaining those properties belonging to the sweeping in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; since the heating enjoined for either the *āhavanīya* or the *gārhapatya* fire occurs in this fire,
only the specific fire is different.
The rest is the same, beginning with "With the tips well-heated" (Āpa.
Śr. Sū. 2.4.4). The repetition of the word "in the fire" (*agnau*) indicates that the ritual rules pertaining to the wiping of the *sruk* ladle apply here as well.
Furthermore, in the *pākayajñas*, the oblation is offered with a *darvī* spoon.
Because it is seen in another ritual context and because it is explicitly shown:

in the sentence "Having taken the *darvī* at the *samāvartana*, he should offer [oblations] with clarified butter," which is intended for another purpose, it indicates that the *darvī* is already established [as the vessel]. Furthermore, when it says, "Having offered once by striking," it shows that the striking is performed from the *sthālīpāka*; that too is not possible with the *darvī*.
In that regard, there is one ladle for oblations of clarified butter;
for cooked messes of rice, there are two—one for the purpose of offering and one for the purpose of cutting portions;
for both types of offerings, there is the act of cleansing.
Since the *avadāna* (cutting of the portion) is for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*), just as the *sruva* spoon is used in the *agnihotra*,
it should be stated there that "one heats the *darvī* ladle over the fire. Why, then, is it said "with which one offers"?
[The rule] "with a middle or a small leaf of the *palāśa* tree" is stated so that it may apply here as well,
and so that it may apply within both the *agnihotra* and the *āgnihotrika* ritual procedures (*tantra*).
If this were the case, then by extension, the same would apply to the hollowed palms (*añjali*) as well.
This is established by an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*) in the case of marriages, snake-sacrifices, and so forth.

The fact that [the author] makes an effort here by stating "like the *Pārvaṇa* in the *Aupakārya*" indicates that the *añjali-homas* (hand-offering oblations) do not adopt [all] the ritual properties (*dharma*), but rather possess only those properties as explicitly stated.
Therefore, the triad beginning with the placing of the vessels (*sādana*) does not apply to the *añjali*. //1//

The passage beginning with "That vessel with which one offers— whether it be a ladle (*darvī*), a small spoon (*sruva*), or the hollowed palms (*añjali*)— one should heat it over the fire" has a clear meaning. Furthermore, the ladle's status as a sacrificial vessel is established by its appearance as an established fact in another sentence, namely, "Having placed [the oblation] in the ladle, he should pour clarified butter over it" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 12.9), as well as by traditional practice.

According to Baudhāyana, however, the disparagement of the *darvī* ladle in the passage "the *darvī* is seized by Nirṛti" is intended for the purpose of prescribing the *sruva* spoon, and not for the purpose of prohibiting the *darvī*.
Therefore, there is an option between the *darvī* and the *sruva*.
In that regard, for homas consisting solely of clarified butter (*ājya*), there is only one implement— the *darvī* or the *sruva*—
because of the absence of the under-layering (*upastaraṇa*) and other such rites.

In the case of oblations of caru and the like, however, there are two ladles (darvī) or two small offering spoons (sruva), for the purpose of under-spreading (upastaraṇa) and so forth, as well as for the purpose of the actual oblation.
Even that which serves the purpose of under-spreading and so forth undergoes consecration,
