because everything from the under-spreading up to the final offering constitutes the ritual act of oblation (homapadārtha).
Because the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *sruva* ladle is observed in the case of Śrauta rites, and because of established practice;
whereas for the three [utensils] beginning with the *darvī*, the refinement occurs only in the case of *tantra*-type oblations,
since the properties belonging to the *tantra* are not applicable in non-*tantra* rites.

Therefore, in such cases as "one should also offer with the *uttarā* [verse], even when following [the procedure]" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 5.20) and "mustard seeds mixed with husks" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 15.6), there is no requirement for the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the ladle (*darvī*) and other implements.

In this context, the mention of "fire" in the phrase "having heated it over this fire, he strikes it into the fire" is intended to indicate that this is not merely a name for the fire, but rather a complete injunction. Consequently, there is no possibility of applying here the ritual details (*dharma*) of the wiping of the *sruk* and *sruva* spoons belonging to the *iṣṭi* sacrifices— such as those beginning with "first [he wipes] the *sruva*" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.3.1)— since they would otherwise be inapplicable.

Some [hold] that because the text says "he heats it in the fire" and "he throws it into the fire," the ritual properties (*dharma*) pertaining to the *sruk*-ladle cleansing— which are devoid of any other purpose in that context— apply here as well;
however, the heating is in this very same fire,
and here the throwing of the *darbha* blades used for cleansing is also into the fire.
It is not, however, optional.
Likewise, regarding the general statement "with which one offers," it is specified as "with either the middle or the last leaf of the *palāśa* tree" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 22.4).
This is for the purpose of ensuring that even in non-tantric rites and in the Agnihotra ritual, there may be a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the vessel intended for the oblation. Furthermore,
by the rule "like the *parvan* [rites]" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 22.1), which serves to establish the portioning (*avadāna*) for the offering of cakes (*apūpa*) with cupped hands (*añjali*),
it follows that offerings made with cupped hands are original (*apūrva*) and possess only those specific characteristics as they are stated.
Because it is for the purpose of making known, it is not a *saṃskāra*. //1//

Śamyās are used in place of enclosing sticks (paridhi) during marriage, initiation, the return home from study, the parting of the hair, the tonsure, the clipping of the beard, and expiatory rites. (ĀpGS 2.2)
Then he lays down the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*).
Everything is done silently, as in the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice; after that, he places the two supporting fuel-sticks (*ādhārasamit*).

Why is this so? Because the permission [to proceed] is given as if it were already established, and because the statement "the *śamyā* is for the purpose of the enclosing-sticks" means that it serves the function of the enclosing-sticks.
*Śamyās* are well-known wooden pegs in the form of stakes placed in the holes at the ends of the *yūpa*; their binding together with fuel-wood constitutes the expiation (*prāyaścitta*),
which refers here to the expiation for extraordinary portents (*adbhutotpāta*).
In the case of marriage, for the purpose of the union of hearts, *śamyās* are used everywhere;

elsewhere than in marriage and similar rites, in all cases such as the *pārvaṇa* and others, only *paridhis* are used. The mention of the *caula* ceremony is redundant, as it is already established by the extension of the rule from the *sīmanta* ceremony.

The purpose of this [statement] as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) is to indicate that in this context, women are eligible only for those rites specifically mentioned, such as marriage and so forth, and not for those extended to them by analogy (*atideśa*).
Therefore, when the *puṃsavana* rite is extended from the *sīmanta*, it applies only to the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).

Likewise, in the case of cooked oblations (*pakvahoma*) such as the *pārvaṇa* and others, there is an extension [of the procedure] from the wedding *sthālīpāka* by virtue of the observation: "In this same manner, from now on. (2)
In rites such as marriage and others, in the place of the enclosing sticks— that is, in the function of laying the enclosing sticks—
the pins of the yoke (śamyā) are used; these are fashioned from any one of the [specified] woods such as Palāśa, with dimensions equal to the thickness and length of the enclosing sticks.
Because it occupies that very position;
and this is logical,
since regarding such subjects, the venerable author of the Vārttika has stated:
"Since the threshing-floor post (khalevālī) can be made of khadira wood, why is it specifically prescribed?
Thus [he asked].
Here, by the word "marriage" (vivāha), the marriage ceremony with all its constituent parts—excluding the *sthālīpāka*—is intended.
We shall explain the reason for excluding that [the *sthālīpāka*] later, under the section on the *pārvaṇa*.

Although the *śamyā* is already established by its inclusion in the *sīmantonnayana*, and thus its application would follow by extension to its derivatives—the *caula* and the *godāna* (which is a derivative of the *caula*)—the explicit mention of those two is for the purpose of precluding them from the *puṃsavana*, which is itself a derivative of the *sīmantonnayana*.
And the expiation is prescribed by [the rule] beginning with "In the case of the growth of a pillar in a house" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 23.9);
and here [it is further specified] as "made of Palāśa wood or Kārṣmarya" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 1.5.8).

The intention of the author of the Sūtra is that one should silently lay down the three enclosing sticks (paridhis), which are endowed with the qualities mentioned in such sūtras as "touching [the fire]," because of the injunction beginning with, "He lays down the enclosing sticks" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.3.7).

Because the *śamyā* is prescribed in its place after the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) have been accepted as established by the statement "for the purpose of the *śamyā*-enclosing sticks," and because of traditional practice. //2//
8. The first sprinkling around the fire:

he sprinkles water around the fire from the south, moving eastward, with the words, "O Aditi, give your consent"; from the west, moving northward, with the words, "O Anumati, give your consent"; from the north, moving eastward, with the words, "O Sarasvatī, give your consent"; and all around, with the words, "O God Savitṛ, impel [this sacrifice]. (ĀpGs 2.3)

Sprinkling with water is the act of pouring water around [the fire]. The mention of "the fire" is for the purpose of ensuring that [the sprinkling] does not take place outside the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), since the context concerns the enclosing sticks. It is said to be "toward the east and toward the north," meaning either to the northeast (*prāgudak*) or [specifically] toward the north.
The rite of sprinkling around is performed as prescribed for Aditi;
likewise, the conclusion [of the rite] is established by the technical definition itself.
The mantra is simply "O God Savitṛ, impel," because this much is seen in many other ritual manuals (kalpas).

And this is clearly stated in the *Baudhāyanīya*: "He causes [the officiants] to conclude the mantras with the words 'anvamaṃsthāḥ' (you have assented) and 'prāsāvīḥ' (you have impelled)" (*BaudhGṛSū* 1.4.7).
However, for the *Chandogas* alone, this is the beginning of the mantra.
The word *samantam* means "equally" (*sama*).
Therein, beginning from the east and proceeding clockwise, water is offered everywhere with each respective mantra. //3//
One sprinkles water around the fire alone, and not even around the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
He states the procedure for that with the words "O Āditi, give your consent," and so forth.
*Prācīnam* means extending toward the east.
Toward the north, extending northward;
on all sides, everywhere.
Here, the mantra is only this much: "O God Savitṛ, impel [us]."

The place for the *narca* offering is not [the same as] the initial location; likewise, in the subsequent sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), there is no modification (*ūha*) of the word "prasuva" such that one would say "aprāsāvīḥ.

This is because, in the *Vaiśvadeva-kāṇḍa*, within the section on the single fire (*ekāgni-vidhi*), these eight *yajus* mantras beginning with "O Aditi, protect us" are recited; and by virtue of their position in the scripture (*śruti-sthāna*), they are connected respectively to the eight operations consisting of the preceding and subsequent sprinklings.
Because the *ṛc* found in the section on the Vājapeya sacrifice is inherently unfit for application here as well;

because it would entail a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a collective whole at the initial location; and because an *ṛc* is not perceived within this group of eight mantras which predominantly consist of *yajus*.
Because, in the case of modification (*ūha*), there would be the consequence of subverting the Vedic reading of the seers (*ārṣapāṭha*);
because it would entail the adoption of that which is contradicted by the Ṛgvedic scripture stating, "Therefore, one should not modify a *ṛc*"; and because of our own traditional practice.
This is very clear among the followers of Baudhāyana, according to whom [it is stated]:
"He causes the mantras to conclude with 'anvamaṃsthāḥ' and 'prāsāvīḥ'" (BaudhGṛS 1.4.37).

And thus, at the subsequent sprinkling (uttara-pariṣecana), there is the recitation of only the specific portions following the previous mantras—namely 'anvamaṃsthāḥ' and 'prāsāvīḥ'—and not the entire texts again.
As in the case of fire: "With this very *triṣṭubh* metre, I place this brick.
Furthermore, the word "name" (*nāman*) here is used figuratively.
For this very reason, these mantras are to be studied after beginning the *Vaiśvadeva* section and prior to its conclusion.
And [the same applies] to the Brāhma-yajña and the Pārāyaṇa. //3//
Regarding the paternal rites, one should remain silent throughout. ĀpGs 2.4.
If the particle *eva* were not employed, this [statement] would serve the purpose of prohibiting the mantra during the sprinkling all around (*samantapariṣecana*).
However, because of the particle *eva*, there is the exclusion of the triad beginning with "to the south" and "eastward. //4//
In the rites for the ancestors (*paitṛka*), he sprinkles water all around;
not from the south toward the east, and so forth.
And that [sprinkling] is done silently (*tūṣṇīm*). //4//
9. The placing of the fuel and the pouring of the libations:
having placed the fuel, he pours the two libations silently, as in the New and Full Moon sacrifices. (ĀpGS 2.5)
Because the term *idhma* (fuel) refers to the collection as a whole, one places the fuel consisting of fifteen pieces of wood all at once.

Regarding the instruction "having sprinkled [the butter]," there is an alternative ritual procedure (*kalpāntara*) similar to that of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; however, according to the injunction beginning with "having brought it along the northern joint of the enclosing sticks" and "having brought it along the southern joint of the enclosing sticks," the word "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*) serves as a prohibition against the utterance of mantras.
Therefore, even this [injunction], "meditating on Prajāpati with the mind," does not apply here;

for, considering that the mental recitation of the mantra is what is prescribed there, the optional *āghāra* rituals do not operate in this context, as they pertain to the archetypal model (*prakṛti*).
Some, however, desire the first *āghāra* to be performed with the *sruva* ladle.
Others, however, maintain that since both the *darvī* and the *upabhṛt* ladles are absent, the *upayamana* grass-bundle is also not used;
moreover, one offers the subsequent *āghāra* libation while remaining seated and does not breathe over it.
We shall state the proof for this later on. //4//
He places fuel on the fire;
and that [fuel] is made of *khadira* or *palāśa* wood, fifteen in number, and characterized by a thickness and length according to the purpose, because of the name "fuel" (*idhma*).
And because it is observed in the Śruti; furthermore,
the laying of the fires occurs simultaneously, since the singular number in the word "fuel" (*idhma*) indicates that the collection as a whole is intended.
And that [offering] is performed silently, because no mantra is prescribed for it.

Others, however, treating the passage beginning with "tūṣṇīm" as a single sūtra, explain that the mantra of the Hiraṇyakeśins, namely "ayaṃ ta idhmaḥ," should not be incorporated according to the principle that "what is not stated here may be taken from elsewhere.
According to their view, the sprinkling around (samantapariṣecana) in rites for the ancestors would have to be performed with the mantra.
Some [hold this] from another Gṛhya text:
"The fuel-stick (idhma) is to be sprinkled with clarified butter and then placed on the fire."
The two oblations named *āghāra* are two types of *homa*.
One performs the *āghāra* by offering with a long, continuous stream,
as in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice.

"Having brought [the ladle] along the northern joint of the enclosing sticks... while pouring the *āghāra* libation straight and continuously toward the south-east with the *jyotiṣmatī* formula, he causes all the fuel-sticks to touch [the flame]" (ĀpŚS 2.12.7);

"having brought [it] along the southern joint of the enclosing sticks" (ĀpŚS 2.13.11), etc.; "The two [libations] are to be poured straight and eastward, or crosswise, either interlaced or not interlaced" (ĀpŚS 2.12.8).

Thus, these three optional alternatives regarding the *āghāra* libations must be performed in the same manner as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices; however, the alternative of not performing the *āghāra* at all— namely, "one should offer in the eastern half, the middle, or the western half" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 2.14.8)— is not permitted.

And he silently offers both of these two oblations with the ladle (*darvī*), because, as these *durvī*-oblations are not previously established, there is no application of the ritual properties of the *iṣṭi*-type *āghāra* offerings nor of their mantras.
Regarding the term "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*), it refers to the rule: "Having offered five oblations of clarified butter silently" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 22.4).
This is for the purpose of excluding the utterance of *svāhā* as well. Therefore, Prajāpati is the deity for both libations; that which is performed silently belongs to Prajāpati.
[This is] because of the Śruti text: (Tai.Brā. 2.1.4).
But how are these two [rites] oblations of the *darvīhoma* type, given that there is no injunction (*codanā*) stating "he offers" (*juhoti*)?

It is replied: although there is no such injunction as "he offers," nevertheless, because the injunction "he pours the libation" (*āghārayati*) has the sense of a "long-poured" (*dīrghadhāra*) offering, it functions as an injunction for the *juhoti* rite.
Furthermore, according to the consensus of ritualists, these are indeed *darvihomas*.
Moreover, in the passage "Then he offers the two *ājyabhāgas*" (*Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra* 2.6), the two *ājyabhāgas* are explicitly *darvihomas*.
By association with that [soma], the two *āghāra* libations are likewise [understood as subsidiaries].

Just as the *aṃśu* cup, though studied outside of any specific context (*anārabhyādhīta*), is connected to the ritual application of *soma* due to its association with the *adābhya* cup despite not being a subsidiary (*aṅga*) [of soma], so too is this the explanation: "He performs the two *āghāra* libations."

Following this principle of superiority and in accordance with the Gṛhya-paribhāṣā rule, "likewise [the sprinkling] ends toward the west" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.6), he offers with two long streams of oblation that end either toward the east or toward the north, but not with those ending toward the intermediate directions.
Nor do the *iṣṭi*-related rules and mantras apply,
precisely because [the rite] is unprecedented (*apūrva*);
however, for the first [offering], Prajāpati is the deity, just as in the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
The meaning is that Indra is the deity for the second [libation].
"Silently" (tūṣṇīm) is as before.

Others, however, hold that "the two Āghāras" is a technical name intended to extend the ritual characteristics of the Āghāra offerings of the iṣṭi sacrifices, just as in the case of the statement, "He performs the Agnihotra for a month."

In this context, since all the characteristics of the *āghāra* offerings and their respective mantras would otherwise apply— based on such rules as "having taken clarified butter from the *dhruvā* with the *sruva*, while seated, he pours another *āghāra*" (ĀpaŚrSū 2.12.7) and "saying 'O Juhū, come,' he takes the *juhū*" (ĀpaŚrSū 2.13.2)— the statement "he pours the two *āghāras*" is intended as a restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*).
The statement "he pours out" (āghārayati) indicates that one should perform only those two oblations characterized by a long stream,
and not those with other characteristics.
The word "silently" (tūṣṇīm) is for the purpose of excluding the mantras, which are sub-divisions of those [ritual] characteristics.

They say that [the rule] "like the Darśapūrṇamāsa" is indeed purposeless; but that is not so, because for the two *darvīhomas*, which are previously unestablished (*apūrva*) and specifically subordinate (*aṅga*) elements,
there is no dependence on the extension of ritual properties (*dharmātideśa*).
Furthermore, because it is illogical for the name itself to possess the characteristics of a ritual act (*dharma*);

because, when another interpretation is possible, an exclusive specification (*parisaṅkhyā*) is improper; and because an exclusive specification of ritual acts other than the *āghāra* would render the extended application (*atideśa*) futile.

Furthermore, since it has been stated by [the author] himself that the word "like the Darśapūrṇamāsa" would be redundant because—even if the restriction were applied to the mantras—the word "silently" (tūṣṇīm) would result in being purposeless;
and because if the two words "he pours the two Āghāras" were intended for the purpose of extension (atideśa) and restriction (parisaṅkhyā), there would be no word enjoining the oblation (homa);

and because if one were to abandon the restriction in order to establish that [oblation], it would lead to the performance of all the ritual properties (dharma) of the Āghāra, which would contradict established practice (śiṣṭācāra).

If one were to accept such an extension (*atideśa*) for the *ājyabhāga* offerings and others as well, it would follow that all the ritual details (*dharma*) belonging to the *iṣṭi*-type *ājyabhāga* and so forth must also be performed there.
Therefore, the previous explanation alone is correct;
for the two *āghāra* libations are indeed unprecedented (*apūrva*).
And because there is the general rule: "And there is an absence of the *samidh* [offering], with the exception of the *agnihotra*" (Āpastamba Paribhāṣā-sūtra 3.8, 9).
For this very reason, there is the cessation of the *āghāra* libations and the *samidh* fuel-sticks.
Others perform them;
according to that view, they are performed immediately after the placement of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Because it is so observed in the Śrauta ritual;

the *anūyāja* fuel-stick (*samit*) is omitted precisely because of the absence of the *anuyāja* offerings. Therefore, the binding of the sacrificial wood (*idhma-sannahana*), together with the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), is divided into eighteen parts.
Or rather, it is twentyfold, and not twenty-onefold. //5//
10. The two *ājyabhāga* oblations.

Now he offers the two *ājyabhāga* oblations: with "To Agni, svāhā! in the eastern part of the northern half; and with "To Soma, svāhā! in the eastern part of the southern half, level with the former. (ĀpGS 2.6)

The northern part of the front is the "northern half" (uttarārdha), and the eastern part is the "eastern half" (pūrvārdha); the space between those two is the "northeastern quarter" (uttarārdhapūrvārdha). "Equally" means in terms of spatial extent.
The meaning is that those two should be offered equally, not unequally.
Since the immediate succession following the *āghāra* offerings is established by the instruction itself, the word "atha" (now) is for the purpose of formal introduction.
What is thereby established?
The commonality between the two *āghāra* libations and the two *ājyabhāga* offerings is thus established.
Therefore, the oblation into the fire is performed with the *jyotiṣmatī* verse;
this is the well-known rule for the two *āghāra* libations.
The application of that [procedure] extends even to the two *ājyabhāga* offerings.
Likewise, the well-known characteristics of the two *ājyabhāgas*— namely, performing the oblation while seated and the absence of exhaling—
also apply to the two *āghāra* libations.
Therefore, what was stated—that in the subsequent offering (uttarāghāra) as well, there is neither a fixed place nor an intention—is established as valid.
"Ājyabhāgau" is the designation for the two oblations.
The purpose [of this designation] is for such injunctions as "from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the Ājyabhāgas," and so forth. //6//
Immediately after the *āghāra* libations, and even without performing the ritual duties (*arthakṛtya*), he performs two extraordinary *homa* offerings named *ājyabhāga*.
Therein, first, with the mantra "To Agni, svāhā!", [he offers] in the northeastern quarter of the fire, that is, in the direction between the north and the east.
The second [offering] is made with "To Soma, svāhā! in the eastern part of the southern half—that is, in the south-eastern quarter.

Taking the junction of the two *āghāra* libations as the limit equal to the previous one, he offers the northern [libation] at exactly the same interval from the junction as the first was offered, using a diagonal cord.
But it is neither proximate nor remote. //6//
11. The prescription for the *jaya* and subsequent oblations following the principal oblations (*pradhāna-homa*).
Having offered the principal oblations according to the instruction, he offers the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, *rāṣṭrabhṛt*, *prājāpatya*, the *vyāhṛti*s separately, and the *sauviṣṭakṛtī* oblation, saying:
"Whatever in this rite I have done in excess, or whatever I have done here deficiently..."
May Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make all this well-sacrificed and well-offered; Svāhā! ĀpGs 2.7.

"According to the instruction" means: in whichever ritual action whatever principal oblations are taught— for instance, "the subsequent oblations [are offered] while she maintains contact" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 14.2).
The term *ṛta* refers to those [verses] that have been recited;
the *jayās* are those beginning with "Thought and thinking" (*cittaṃ ca cittiśca*), as found in Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.4.4.
The *abhyātāna* [verses] begin with "Agni of beings" (*Tai. Saṃ. 3.4.5*).
The *rāṣṭrabhṛt* [verses] begin with "The upholder of truth, the establisher of truth" (*Tai. Saṃ. 3.4.7*).
The verse "O Prajāpati, these [beings] are not yours" is dedicated to Prajāpati.
The *vyāhṛtis* are well known.
The expression "unveiled" (*vidṛta*) is for the purpose of excluding everything else;
these [other mantras] are not taught here because they are already established [as being included].
The *sauviṣṭakṛtī* [offering] is recited because it is not well-known [otherwise].

But is this not also recited in the Sūtra during all expiations (*sarvaprāyaścitta*)? “Whatever I have overdone in this rite, or whatever I have done here deficiently—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make all that well-sacrificed and well-offered, Svāhā! (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 3.12.9).
In that case, this indicates that this procedure for the *pākayajña* is common to some others as well.

Indeed, it is observed that the Kālagireyas engage in this [procedure] during rites such as marriage; therefore, this [text] is intended to provide them with the instruction on the proper time for those oblations (*homa*) which are enjoined in those [rites].
It does not mean that the principal offerings (*pradhānāhuti*) are to be made before the *jaya* and other [offerings], and after the two *ājyabhāga* portions.
For this reason, because both [procedures] have been taught in that very context:

"Having offered the subsequent oblations after the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the *ājyabhāga* offerings," there is an application [of those rules] there due to the extended application (*atideśa*) of the rule "he offers from the *sthālīpāka*.
However, in the case of the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha], it is so; we shall explain this in the section on the procedure for the *āgneya-sthālīpāka*.

Now, in cases such as the *paṇya-phalīkaraṇa-homa* where there is no statement that "it ends with the *ājyabhāgas*" or "one proceeds with the *jayas*, etc.," this [rule] is stated for the purpose of obtaining those [elements]. In rites such as marriage (*vivāha*), the injunction [to perform the *jayas*, etc. would otherwise be redundant because of the statement: "One proceeds with the *jayas*, etc., at the end of the *ājyabhāgas*. Therefore, the *paṇya-homas* and others are *apūrva* (unique/original) acts, possessing only those ritual properties (*dharma*) as far as they are explicitly mentioned.

In that case, this [tantra] should apply even to those oblations (prayodana) mentioned by other authorities— whether they be obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), or optional (kāmya)— if they are performed by people such as ourselves, so that the application of this tantra may occur therein as well.

But is this not already established by the observation of the extension (atideśa) of the pārvaṇa rite, according to the principle that "those things which are not specifically prohibited are governed by established practice" (ācāra)?
It is true that [the rule] is established for cooked oblations, but not for oblations of clarified butter, such as those involving the *Kūśmāṇḍa* mantras with ghee,
because that [rule] pertains to uncooked substances.

In rites such as marriage and the like, for the purpose of establishing the rules for the tantric procedure— in those cases where the domestic fire is enjoined— the statement that "from the kindling of the fire up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, the *jaya* and subsequent rites are performed" indicates that the tantric procedure (*tantra*) applies precisely there.
By this, it is established that the *paṇya-homa* and similar offerings possess only those characteristics (dharma) as explicitly stated.

The mention of the "principal oblations" (*pradhānāhuti*) is for the purpose of establishing that [the sequence] includes everything from the *jaya* offerings up to the *ājyabhāga* portions. In the expression "he offers additionally" (*upajuhoti*), the prefix *upa-* signifies immediate succession;
therefore, the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) follow immediately after the principal oblations.
Therefore, at the sacrifice of Īśāna, the offering of the *bali* occurs after the final sprinkling (*pariṣecana*).

Or, in the case of a *śrāddha*, it is not prescribed; and in the *sthālīpāka*, the throwing of the remainder outside is called the *sauviṣṭakṛtī* [offering], for the purpose of making known that Sviṣṭakṛt is the deity.
By this, the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) occurs in cooked offerings (*pakvahoma*). //7//

Having offered those oblations according to the prescribed rules— by means of the same sacrificial materials such as clarified butter (*havis*) and so forth with which the principal oblations were taught for marriages and other rites— one offers the thirteen *jaya* oblations with the formula: "The *jayas*, the *cittas*, and *svāhā*" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.4.42).
There are twenty-two *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings.
Among them, having recited "ṛtāṣāṭ," he offers the first oblation with the words ending in "tasmai svāhā.
He offers the latter [oblation] with only the words "tābhyaḥ svāhā."
Thus there are five formulas.
In this context, the phrase "This Brahmā is indeed he" is to be supplied [to each],
as is the phrase "Svāhā to them."
The thirteenth [verse] is: "O Lord of the world... with blessings, svāhā!
There follow four cycles beginning with "Parameṣṭhī," as before.
The twenty-second [verse] is: "Grant us, O Lord of the world... bestow, svāhā!"
The verse "O Prajāpati, these [beings] are not yours" belongs to Prajāpati;
for the Śruti states: "With the verse belonging to Prajāpati, one should pour it into the mound of an anthill" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 3.7.2).

The author of the Sūtra likewise says: "Having poured it into the mound of an anthill with the verse belonging to Prajāpati, 'O Prajāpati, these [beings] are not yours'" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 9.2.4).
Because it has been explained thus;
the *vyāhṛtis* are recited as "Bhūḥ svāhā,
Bhuvaḥ svāhā, Suvaḥ svāhā."

The verse for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is "yad asya... (RV 10.2.31), beginning with the words "of this ritual. Here, its designation as having *Sviṣṭakṛt* as its deity is easily understood from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) itself.

The knowledge of the deity is also a constituent part of ritual action, as established by such scriptural passages as: "Whosoever, indeed, performs a sacrifice or teaches with a mantra whose seer (*ṛṣi*), meter (*chandas*), deity (*devatā*), and explanatory portion (*brāhmaṇa*) are unknown, he strikes against a wooden stump. And: "He who teaches or even recites [a mantra] without knowing its seer, meter, deity, and application, becomes a sinner."
This is established by the traditional teaching (smṛti).
Therefore, it is understood that in cases where there is no such rule regarding the knowledge of the ṛṣis and so forth, those [details] are optional (pākṣika).
In this way, these [rites] beginning with Jaya and the rest [are to be understood].
He offers fifty-eight oblations immediately after the principal oblations (*pradhānahoma*).
Even in cases such as the *sarpabali*, where the *sviṣṭakṛt* is extended from the *pārvaṇa* rite, these [oblations] likewise occur immediately after the principal oblations;
thereafter follows the *sviṣṭakṛt*.
[The suffix] *ktvā* [is applied], and [the augment *m* is added] after the prefix *upa*.

Some maintain that the *jaya* and subsequent offerings follow immediately after the *sviṣṭakṛt*, because the statement "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second" (*Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra* 7.7) indicates that the *sviṣṭakṛt* shares the same ritual properties as the principal offerings.

Now, one might ask: if the *jaya* and other offerings have already been taught as common to all principal oblations immediately following them, for what purpose is there the specific injunction in various places stating, "one performs the *jaya* and so forth"?
It is said: this statement is intended to mean that where these words do not exist—as in the case of the *pārvaṇa* and other rites—there the *jayā* and other offerings are not performed.
If that is so, then the general injunction here would be purposeless.
No; for it serves not only the purpose of enjoining the *jayā* and other offerings.
Otherwise, even the *anvārambha* (the ritual grasping of the hand) would have to take place at the wedding and other such occasions.

Furthermore, if this [general rule] were absent, the long passage beginning with "The *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, etc. and ending with "the teacher" would have to be recited again and again in each respective instance.
Therefore, this general injunction is intended both to exclude the *anvārambha* and other such rites from these occasions and to ensure brevity of the text.

Some say: wherever the *purastāt-tantra* (the preliminary ritual procedure) ends with the *ājyabhāga* offerings, there the *uttara-tantra* (the subsequent ritual procedure), beginning with the *jaya* offerings, applies everywhere.

This is because the principal oblations (*pradhāna-homa*) are prescribed by the remainder of the rule, "In the interval between these two, the principal oblations according to the instruction," and so forth.
Furthermore, the *jaya* offerings and others are indeed present even in the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice dedicated to Agni.

Thus, because the subsequent tantra beginning with "jayādi" is taught by the sūtra consisting of these two words, and because there is an extension of the rule by the statement "by means of the pārvaṇa [rite]" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 7.23) regarding the monthly śrāddha and other such occasions.

In the case of *ājya* oblations, after the *jaya* and other rites, one should silently cast the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) into the fire as in the *śrauta* ritual and then offer them with the residue from the ladle (*darvī-saṃsrāva*); for it has been stated that the enclosing sticks and their consecrations are permitted according to the *śrauta* rule, because those whose purpose has been fulfilled require a final disposal (*pratipatti*), and because this is also the established custom.
If they are *śamyā* [wooden pins], they are to be removed at this time,
because of the statement of Bodhāyana, "Now, having pushed the *śamyās* under [the fire]" (BaudhGṛS 1.4.37), and because of established practice. //7//
12. The final sprinkling of water is to the north of the fire.
As before, the sprinkling is performed with the mantra: "You have assented; you have given permission. This is the naming of the mantras. (ĀpGs 2.8)
"As before" means:
in the rites for the ancestors (*paitṛka*), everything is performed silently;
elsewhere, there are four sprinklings accompanied by mantras. //7//
The substitution of *sannāma* for *asan-nāma* means "inference" (*ūha*).
For the word "anumanyasva," the substitution is "anvamaṃstha."
The word "prāsāvīt" is the substitute for "prasuve. Prior to the sprinkling of water, the enclosing sticks (paridhis) are thrown into the fire silently.
Before the secondary offerings (upahomas), twenty-one fuel-sticks (samidhs) are added to the fire.
In the first offerings, there is no throwing of the *barhis* grass;
rather, there is the placing of this fuel-stick upon the two smearings.
In the offerings of clarified butter (*ājya*), there is no throwing of the *barhis* grass.
Since the rule "of the two coatings" pertains to the *pākayajña* oblations,
the release of the *praṇītā* waters occurs at the end of the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*).
And the *brahman* priest withdraws by the same way he came at the conclusion of the ritual.

Regarding the phrase "the naming of the mantras" (*mantrasannāma*), the mention of "mantras" is for the purpose of ensuring that the procedure for their naming is performed according to their own specific [rules]; otherwise, one might suspect that even fire (*agni*) could be subject to such naming,
since the word *sannāma* is seen used elsewhere as well.
As it comes together, he either arranges it or strokes it. //9//
The sprinkling of water around the fire is as before;
however, this is the distinction:
in the three [formulas] beginning with "O Aditi, give your consent," the word "anumanyasva" (give your consent) is replaced by "anvamaṃsthāḥ" (you have consented).
In the mantra "devasavitaḥ," the word "prasuva" is replaced by "prāsāvīḥ.
Here, as in the Śrauta ritual, he releases the *praṇītā* waters silently; for these waters, having fulfilled their purpose, require a formal disposal (*pratipatti*).

According to the statement of Bodhāyana, "Having brought [the guest] from the consecrated waters (praṇītā) toward the directions" (Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.4.38), and in accordance with established custom,
the Brāhmaṇa, having been honored according to his capacity with gifts, respect, and so forth, should depart.

In this matter, the established position is as follows: the collection of preliminary (prācya) and subsequent (udīcya) subsidiaries, beginning with "agnim indhe" and ending with "mantrasaṃnāma," is common to all principal *gṛhya* oblations (*pradhānahoma*).

This is because the phrase "having offered the principal oblations according to the instruction" serves as a qualification of the oblations in relation to the preliminary and subsequent items, thereby designating them as primary.
Consequently, in the case of non-oblation rites such as the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) and others, there is simply no occasion for the application of the *tantra* (the common ritual procedure).

But if this is so, for what purpose is there a repeated instruction in various places, such as "from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings"? It is replied: because in other instances it is said, "Or one may offer with the subsequent [verse]" (*Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra* 5.20), or "One may offer to Kāma and Manyu" (*Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra* 1.26.13).

In such passages as these, there is no formal instruction (upadeśa) [to the effect that] "this is the ritual procedure (tantra) for this [specific rite] alone"; rather, the purpose is restrictive (niyamārtha). Why is this so? Because this tantra is taught in connection with offerings consisting solely of clarified butter (ājya-havis), even in the absence of another specific injunction.

As for acts such as the preliminary dedication (upākaraṇa) and the conclusion (samāpana), although there is no explicit teaching of the tantra for them there, one understands from such statements as "one should offer ghee with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras" that they require a ritual procedure; thus, the tantra is established by this very general rule.
The understanding that [the *tantra*] applies to all [rites] arises because the other *Gṛhyasūtras* teach it only for those who follow the *tantra*,
because the teaching follows the system seen in the *Āpastamba-śrautasūtra*, and because of the uncontradicted practice of the learned (*śiṣṭa*).

If this is so, why is there an instruction on the *tantra* (ritual framework) even for a marriage ceremony where the oblations consist of clarified butter (*ājya*) and medicinal herbs (*oṣadha*)? It is said in reply: because the offerings of parched grains (*lāja-homa*) are complete in their own injunctions and thus do not depend on a *tantra*; the instruction on the *tantra* applies only to those [ceremonies] involving offerings of clarified butter, such as the initiation (*upanayana*) and others.
Immediately after the rule "Then, as he sits down there, the bridegroom sits to the north" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 4.9), the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire (upasamādhāna) follow;
however, this is not the case immediately after the rule "Having sat down in their respective places" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 5.10).
The phrase "immediately after this" (*ityasyānantaram*) signifies sequence (*krama*).
Consequently, even in the case of the *sthālīpāka* offering consisting solely of medicinal herbs as the oblation, it serves the purpose of establishing the sequence.

Although, according to the observation in the Śrauta ritual, threshing and other such acts are properly performed immediately after the sprinkling of the vessels (*pātraprokṣaṇa*), [in the present context, the sequence remains as established].
Nevertheless, by the force of this statement, [the procedure] occurs "right before" [the main rite] from the *tantra* [of the sacrifice];

thus, even in the case of the *sthālīpāka* in the northeast, the preparation of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) is performed at that time, and not—as in the *pārvaṇa*—only after the consecration (*pratiṣṭhita*) and the sprinkling of clarified butter (*abhighāraṇa*) within the house. This is precisely for the sake of the correct sequence.

In certain cases— such as the *ājya-homas* prescribed in other ritual manuals (*kalpa*) where there is an extended application (*atideśa*) from non-regular rites (*apārvaṇa*), and which require a ritual framework (*tantra*) as in the injunction "one should offer ghee with the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras"— the general rule "according to the instruction" is intended to ensure the application of this very ritual framework. However, regarding the rites belonging to this [text], such as marriage (*vivāha*) and others, the rule applies only where there is a specific re-injunction (*punarvidhāna*).
The injunction for a *tantra* (common performance) in various rites is for the purpose of restriction, namely that it applies only to the *paṇya-homa* and similar offerings;

however, in the case of ancestral rites (*pitrya*), since there is a specific injunction such as "each [offering] is connected with the ancestors" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 1.18), the establishment of a *tantra* follows from that. //8//
Having thus stated the common Smārta procedure for all domestic (gārhya) oblations,
he now states the optional Śrauta procedure regarding the Pākayajñas—
13. The meaning of the term "Pākayajña."
For worldly people, the term *pākayajña* is used. (ĀpGs 2.9)
The meaning is that "worldly" (*laukika*) refers to those things characterized by worldly memory (*lokasmṛti*). By the word "world" (*loka*), the cultured (*śiṣṭa*) are meant.
The term "cooked sacrifice" (*pākayajña*) is prescribed as a designation for marriage and other such rites.
The word *pāka* signifies "small" or "minor," as in the expression: "One should sacrifice quickly; O Pāka-deva" (*Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra* 20.15).
If, according to the etymology, a sacrifice characterized by the quality of being small were called a *pākayajña*, then this designation would not apply to offerings of clarified butter (*ājya*).
The purpose of that designation is twofold: first, the inclusion of these [rites] within the statement, "We shall explain the sacrifice" (Āpastamba Paribhāṣā-sūtra 1.1);
and second, the attainment of ritual properties (*dharma*) in the statement, "One should sacrifice to Nirṛti with a *pākayajña*" (Āpastamba Śrauta-sūtra 6.31.1). // 10 //

"Lokas" refers to those who perceive the meanings of the Vedas through the Vedas—namely, the learned elders of the three Vedas, the cultured, and the twice-born. Those rites which are performed by these "lokas" are called *laukika* (worldly).
Among those, the term *pākayajña* is well-known as a designation for seven types of rites, beginning with the *aupāsana-homa*.
But this does not apply to the Vedic rites such as marriage and the like, because people do not employ those terms in common usage.
If it is argued that the designation "pākayajña" for these [Vedic rites] is already well-established solely through common usage, [we reply:]...
In that case, the statement "the rule regarding the *pākayajñas* is dependent on the observation of the Brāhmaṇas" is sufficient;

for what purpose is it said, "the word *pākayajña* refers to worldly [rites]"? It is replied: because this is a restatement of a well-established technical term—namely, that a *pākayajña* is a sacrifice accomplished by means of cooked (*pakva*) sacrificial porridge (*caru*)—it follows as a necessary consequence that in the Agnihotra injunction, the *caru* itself is the oblation (*havis*).
This is for the purpose of indicating the restrictive rule that [the oblation] is not ghee and so forth, as it might be in other procedures;
however, Baudhāyana has prescribed ghee as the sacrificial offering (havis) here.
But the Agnihotra oblation does not constitute the havis in this context.
Because there is no authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the ritual rules (*dharma*) of the *agnihotra*,
the five constituent elements [of the rite], such as "he offers twice" (*dvir juhoti*; Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 2.11), arise solely by the force of explicit scriptural injunction (*vacana*).
The deities, however, are precisely those who are to be propitiated by their respective mantras. //10//
In that regard, the ritual procedure is to be observed according to the Brāhmaṇas.
He offers twice, wipes [the vessel] twice, eats twice, moves away, sips water, and licks [the vessel] clean. (ĀpGS 2.11)
In this regard, concerning those *pākayajña* sacrifices, they speak of another procedure called "the inspection by the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇāvekṣa*).
One who inspects the Brāhmaṇa as an authority for himself is "one who inspects the Brāhmaṇa" (*brāhmaṇāvekṣa*); the meaning is that it is "seen in the Brāhmaṇa.
"Procedure" (*vidhi*) refers to the ritual performance (*prayoga*).

The previously mentioned *āghāravat* [rite] has the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as its archetype (*prakṛti*), whereas this one has the *agnihotra* as its archetype and is dependent on the Brāhmaṇa texts. It is stated that there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the two in those cases; this is for the purpose of showing that in those *pākayajñas* where the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the *āghāravat* applies, it is obtained optionally.
Therefore, this rule does not apply to commercial offerings (*paṇyahoma*) and the like.

In that context, by the statement "he offers twice," it should be understood that the procedure for both oblations of the *agnihotra* is prescribed with reference to the principal oblation and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering in *pākayajña* sacrifices.
Furthermore, "he wipes twice" refers to the wiping of the smearings, just as in the *agnihotra*.
The phrase "he eats twice" refers to eating with the fingers.

And as for the phrase "having moved away, he sips water," that which is prescribed there—namely, the third eating, having taken hold of the *barhis* grass, turned toward the north, and moved away, he sips water—that is what is enjoined.
As for the phrase "he licks [the spoon]," it is because "having licked the *sruk* twice... [is stated].
And this has been enjoined as follows:

by whatever procedure the successful accomplishment of the *homa* and other rites is achieved, that much should be understood as being performed even without mantras in the case of the *agnihotra* and similar rituals.
For example, the drawing up [of the ghee] with the *sruva* ladle.
The fuel-sticks of *pālāśa* wood are for the purpose of maintaining the continuity of the oblations;
[the offerings consist of] four portions or five portions.
Regarding that, the procedure is as follows: having kindled the fire and swept around it,
Having strewn [the sacrificial grass] around, having sprinkled water around,
and having consecrated the clarified butter for the oblations of clarified butter;

In cooked oblations (*pakvahoma*), having cleansed the cooking pot (*sthālīpāka*) and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, he takes portions— either fourfold or fivefold— as many times as there are principal offerings (*pradhānāhuti*).
Where there is both [types of] sacrificial food (*havis*), he takes portions of both,
as in the case of the monthly ancestral rite (*māsiśrāddha*).

Then, having placed [the offering] on the sacrificial grass (barhis) to the west of the fire and having added a fuel-stick (*samidh*) made of *palāśa* wood, and having recited all the formulas in succession, he offers the principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) only once.
Having wiped away the smearings as in the morning *agnihotra*, he wipes them off on the sacrificial grass if the rite is performed during the day;
if at night, it is like the evening *agnihotra*.
Then he offers the second oblation for Sviṣṭakṛt, excluding the subsequent oblation: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā! in the case of cooked grain offerings (*sthālīpāka*);
"Whatever [is deficient] in this rite... in the case of oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*).
In the Īśāna sacrifice, however, the rite is performed with the mantra prescribed therein.
Then, having wiped away the smearings as before, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he wipes them on the ground to the south.
Then, having set down the *sruk* ladle, the procedure from the tasting of the residue from the fingers until the final wiping is the same as in the Agnihotra.
Then follows the thorough washing with *darbha* grass, and then the sweeping around and the sprinkling with water.
This ritual procedure known as the *āgnihotrika* is optional in all *pākayajña* sacrifices, being alternated with the *āghāravat* ritual procedure. //11//
Among those *pākayajñas*, in the five beginning with the *pārvaṇa*, the procedure is one that depends upon the *Brāhmaṇa* texts;
it is a procedure that relies directly on the *Brāhmaṇa*, and not one that is to be inferred from worldly custom, as is the case with [the injunction] "having kindled the fire," and so forth.
The meaning is that even this [inference] occurs through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) regarding these [objects];
there is no mutual connection between these two types of cognition,
nor is there any sublation of the memory-based [cognition] by this [inferential one].
Even for a Brāhmaṇa that is directly perceived, its authority is equal to that of Smṛti when it restates a Smṛti rule, according to the logic established in the section on the Kalpasūtras.
For this very reason, [it is said]: "He crosses over all evil; he who performs the Aśvamedha sacrifice crosses over even the murder of a Brāhmaṇa" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 5.3.12).
Thus, by this Vedic text and by the restatement in the *Manusmṛti* (11.74), "Or he should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha," there is an option between the Aśvamedha and the twelve-year penance;
and this matter is clearly stated in the *Baudhāyanīya*.
Regarding this, they cite an example:

Bādari says that the *prakṛti* (archetype) of the *darvīhoma* is the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration); likewise, Ātreya says it is the *agnihotra*; but Kāśakṛtsna maintains its status as an *apūrva* (an independent rite).
Thus [Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.4.44]: "One should not place them together with one another, because there is no instruction [to that effect]" (Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.5.1).
However, the *mantras* for the *homa* and so forth, although belonging to other ritual injunctions (*vidhi*), apply here as well by virtue of their purpose and established usage (*ācāra*).
If this [text] possesses an authority equal to that of the *Smṛtis*, [then it is authoritative].
For what purpose is it said, "not looking at a non-Brahmin"?
This has already been answered: [it concerns] the rule for the Agnihotra, in the event of a lapse, as stated in the *Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* (25.34): "If [the lapse occurs] on account of the Yajus..."
Thus ends the Śrauta expiation;
however, regarding the destruction of that which is Smārta, it is not the case that "if it is unknown or if there is total ruin" (Ai. Brā. 25.34). //10//

Considering that all the principal oblations (*pradhāna-homa*) constitute a single oblation due to their commonality as principal oblations, the Śruti says "he offers twice" with reference to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering; it does not mean, however, that he offers exactly twice. [This is illustrated by the statement:
"Seventeen [animals] dedicated to Prajāpati. (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.3.4)
Thus, because there is no acceptance here of the identity of the deities,

some— taking as many fourfold portions (*caturgṛhīta*) into the ladle as there are principal oblations (*pradhānahoma*), and having recited all the offering-mantras (*homamantra*) in succession— offer them all at once. The [injunction] "he wipes twice," etc., has its meaning evident.
As for the ritual procedure: the spreading of the grass, the consecration of the ladle, the under-layering of ghee, and so forth, do not take place here, because they are not prescribed;
however, the cooking of the sacrificial porridge (caru) certainly exists by virtue of the purpose.

Having filled the ladle with that *caru* sufficient for the principal oblations, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and the consumption, he places it upon the *aparṇa* fire on *darbha* grass; then, taking it up, he offers all the principal oblations in their proper order with their respective mantras. Thereafter, taking the residue from the ladle and wiping it with *darbha* blades, he offers the remainder as the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he again takes the residue and [places it] to the south.

Having wiped [the vessel] on the ground and touched it, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), he should take the smearings with his finger using the ladle, eat them, and rinse for purification.

Having performed this again, he should turn toward the north, move aside, and consume the entire remainder of the oblation with the ladle. Having licked the ladle clean and rinsed, he should wash it with water and *darbha* grass.
Now, one might ask: why is this rule not applicable to the Vaiśvadeva and the domestic (aupāsana) oblations? It is said in reply:

because in those cases, according to the injunction "sprinkling [of water] on both sides" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 7.22), there is an exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) of both rules which serve the same purpose; for this very reason, there is also an absence of the disposal of the remnants of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

Some maintain that because the word *pāka* in the term *pākayajña* signifies "small," marriage ceremonies (*vivāha*) and the like are also called *pākayajñas* in comparison with sacrifices such as the *Soma*, and thus this injunction applies to them as well. That is not correct; for since those [marriages] are for the purpose of purifying humans (*manuṣyasaṃskāra*), they lack primacy, and it is therefore untenable for them to be designated by the word *yajña*, which denotes what is primary. //11//

Since the marriage mantras are recited earlier in the section on the rules for the single fire (*ekāgni-vidhi-kāṇḍa*), he intends to explain marriage first; regarding its timing, he states an exception to the rule concerning the northern solstice (*udagayana*) and other such requirements:
3. Topics concerning Marriage – 1. The Time of Marriage.
All seasons are suitable for marriage, except for the two months of the dewy season (śiśira) and the last month of the summer (nidāgha).
Now follows the procedure for marriage, which takes place prior to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).

Although it should have been stated as "excluding the cold season" (*śiśiraṃ parihāpya*), the expression "the two months of the cold season" (*śaiśirau māsau*) is used in order to indicate the specific months in the phrase "and the last month of summer" (*uttamañca naidāgham*);
otherwise, one might understand it to refer to a single day as well.
The prescription for all [times] is an exception to the northern solstice (*udagayana*).

However, some maintain that the bright fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*) and so forth, which are established by general rule (*paribhāṣā*), remain applicable to marriage just as the prescriptions for spring and so forth apply to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
Others, however, consider this to be an exception even to the bright fortnight and the like.
For them, marriage is not prohibited during the dark fortnight or at night. //12//
All six seasons, each consisting of two months, are the times for marriage;
the meaning is that all twelve months, including those beginning with the dark fortnight (aparapakṣa), are times in their entirety.
By the term "seasons" (*ṛtu*), the months themselves are intended through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

How is it understood that [the prohibition applies] to the seasons? It is said: because of the exclusion of the months, as indicated by the phrase "the two months of the cold season" (*śaiśirau māsau*).
Otherwise, since injunction and exclusion would share the same object, and for the sake of brevity, he would have simply said "having excluded the cold season" (*śiśiraṃ parihāpya*).
The purpose of the rule regarding marriage is the absence of restrictive regulations such as those concerning the auspicious lunar days (pūrvapakṣa) and so forth.

However, in cases such as the initiation ceremony (upanayana), where there is no such reason [for an exception], there is a desire to prescribe [the performance] specifically during the proper season;

in that case, just as the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) serves as a means for the sacrifice by way of being offered into the fire, so too [the specific time] is established by way of the general injunctions regarding the auspicious lunar days and so forth.
Since it is not established that the season (*ṛtu*) is a means for accomplishing ritual action, the beginning of the fortnights and so forth is indeed fixed.
The two months of the winter season (*śiśira*) are Māgha and Phālguna;
and the last month of the summer season (*nidāgha* or *grīṣma*) is Āṣāḍha.

Having excluded and avoided these three months— here, by the superlative suffix *tamap*, the last month of the summer season (*naidāgha*) which is the month of Śrāvaṇa, as well as the second Āṣāḍha following the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*), both of these are also set aside. //12//
All the lunar mansions mentioned as auspicious for meritorious acts [are suitable]. (ĀpGs 2.13)
Since all [other] injunctions involve some form of exclusion, this [injunction] is for the purpose of prescribing auspicious days (*puṇyāha*).

Likewise, there is a prohibition against marriage during the night and the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*). Even so, the mention of the specified [periods] would otherwise be redundant; it is included, however, for the purpose of selecting the specific *muhūrta*s—so that whatever asterisms (*nakṣatra*) are declared auspicious and whatever *muhūrta*s are declared auspicious, all of them may be used for marriage.
"May they be. In that regard, the constellations are to be understood from the science of astronomy (*jyotiḥśāstra*).
*Prātaḥ* (morning), *saṅgava* (forenoon), *madhyandina* (midday), *aparāhṇa* (afternoon), and *sāyāhna* (evening)—these are the *muhūrta*s. //13//

Those lunar mansions (nakṣatras) which are declared meritorious in the science of astrology (jyotiṣa) as being givers of auspicious results— since the mention of "lunar mansions" is intended to be illustrative, it includes lunar days (tithis) and so forth— all those declared meritorious therein are to be collected here. //13//
2. Auspicious rites at the wedding;
likewise, auspicious ceremonies [in general]. (ĀpGs 2.14)
Expressions such as "having fed the Brahmins" and "having caused them to recite benedictions," which are well-known from one's own scriptures;

and auspicious rites such as bathing, wearing unwashed garments, being anointed with fragrances, wearing garlands, and having eaten, which are well-known in the world as part of the barber’s work, such as the application of the sprout (aṅkurārpaṇa), and so forth.
All these are to be understood as such. //14//

At a wedding, one should provide auspicious rites well-established in the conduct of the cultured, such as the sounding of conchs, drums, lutes, and musical instruments; songs by women of good family; the grooming of hair and beards; the wearing of clean, unwashed, and variegated garments; the application of perfumes and ointments; the wearing of fragrant garlands; the movement on foot; and the use of parasols, banners, and the like. //14//
3. The performance of marriage rites is also [determined] by custom; and those who have been initiated should be understood as being excluded from women. ĀpGs 2.15.
Ritual acts devoid of mantras are called *āvṛta*.

In whatever country, village, or family those *āvṛta* rites are well-known, they remain established in that very manner so that they may be understood accordingly; it is not the case that this is so everywhere. //15//
The rites of marriage, whether performed with mantras or without mantras, being indistinguishable in their essential nature,
the bridegrooms should learn them all from women and from members of all social classes (*varṇas*) and perform them.
Among these, those performed with mantras— such as the worship of the *agraha*, the planting of the *aṅkura*, and the binding of the *pratisara*— are established by traditional custom (*ācāra*).

The rites without mantras—such as the offerings to Nāka, Bala, Yakṣa, Bali, Indrāṇī, and so forth—are established according to region, according to caste, according to family, and according to whether one is male or female;
they are not all to be combined everywhere. //15//
They are released with the *invakā* verses, those bridegrooms being welcomed.
Verses praising the lunar mansions have been cited in the section on marriage for the sake of the context regarding suitors:
if the suitors, who are the wooers of the maiden, are urged toward choosing her during the *invakā* [Pleiades] constellation. (16)
They, having obtained those boons, are greeted by those who possess daughters and become successful in their aims;
therefore, in connection with the granting of boons, the lunar mansion named Mūla is praised.
He himself will explain that "the word *invakā* refers to Mṛgaśiras.
Therefore, it is understood that this verse is merely a worldly one well-known from another Smṛti, and not the work of the author of the Sūtra. //17//
In the phrase "inkābhiḥ mṛgaśirasi nakṣatre," the instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative according to Pāṇini 2.3.45 (*lupi*).
Those suitors (*varāḥ*), who are the seekers of brides, are sent forth— that is, dispatched— for the purpose of choosing a maiden when the moon is in the constellation Mṛgaśiras.
They are greeted with joy by those who have daughters and are honored preeminently;
the meaning is that they become ones whose purposes are accomplished. //16//
Thus ends the second section in the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
Third Section. 4. The acquisition of cattle under the asterism Maghā, by means of purchase and so forth: "Cattle are acquired under the Maghās. (ĀpGS 3.1)
If cows are acquired through purchase or other means under the asterism Maghā, and those cows become productive, therefore the Maghā asterism is recommended for the acquisition of cattle. //1//

Based on the statement, "In the Ārṣa [form of marriage], a pair of cattle should be given to the father of the daughter" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 2.11.18), the cattle offered by the bridegrooms in an Ārṣa marriage are accepted from those who have daughters during the Maghā asterism.
What is meant is this: one should perform the Ārṣa marriage only during the Maghā asterism.
It is not like [the case of] Brahmā and others, such that [the name] applies even to other stars. //1//
5. On the two Phalgunī days, the army is arrayed for the purpose of battle;
it is arrayed on the two Phalgunī days. (ĀpGs 3.2)
If an army is arrayed under the two Phalgunī constellations at the time of battle, it will be victorious;
therefore, the two Phalgunīs are recommended for the arraying of an army.
Since there is no distinction specified, this applies to both the prior and the later Phalgunīs.
In all instances, the third case ending is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) according to Pāṇini 2.3.45: "And [the third case ending is used] when *lup* [is applied] to *nakṣatra*. //2//
And here, the bride is led from her own home specifically during the two Phalgunī constellations;

however, she is not led at that very moment [immediately after marriage] as in the case of the Brāhma and other forms of marriage, because of the statement: "Then, her... (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 5.13).

Some, imagining this to be a verse from another Vedic branch (śākhāntarīyā gāthā) because the word *invakā* is explained later in the passage beginning with "by the *invakās*" and ending with "is arrayed by the two *Phalgunīs*," maintain that under the asterism Maghā there is the acquisition of cattle through purchase and the like,
as well as the arraying of an army for battle.
They explain [the phrase] as "because there is no distinction between the two preceding or the two following Phalgunīs," since it would otherwise be irrelevant to the subject at hand. //2//

6. Under the asterism Svāti, one should give away a daughter whom one desires will be dear to her husband; under the asterism Niṣṭyā, one should give away a daughter for whom one desires, "May she be dear [to him]. She indeed becomes dear, and moreover, she does not return [to her father's house]. This rule is based on the authority of the Brāhmaṇa. (ĀpGs 3.3)

If a father should desire a daughter whom he loves, thinking, "May she be dear to her husband," he should give her away under the constellation Niṣṭhā. Given in this manner, she indeed becomes dear to him;
and this is another virtue of this constellation: she does not return again from her father's house seeking wealth.
In her very own house, all her desires are fulfilled.
Others, however, consider this to be a censure;

for since there is the statement that "the rule is to be observed by a Brāhmaṇa," others also follow the rules regarding the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) based on the *Smṛtis* and based on the constellations.
Otherwise, this very same asterism would apply to the *puṃsavana* rite as it does to the *tiṣya* [wedding], and likewise to the wedding itself. //3//
Thinking, "May this daughter be dear to her husband," the father should give her to a suitor under the asterisms of Niṣṭyā or Svāti;
she will indeed be dear to him.
Furthermore, she does not return to her father's house even when afflicted by disease, poverty, or other such misfortunes, nor when seeking [support].
The rule regarding the consultation of Brahmins is that all her purposes are accomplished right in her own home;
here too, as before, there is an option between the nakṣatras mentioned in the Smṛti texts concerning merit. //3//
The word *invakā* refers to the constellation Mṛgaśiras. (ĀpGs 3.4)
The meaning of these two is explained because they are employed in the Veda (chandas).
These [rules] are clearly stated in the Sūtras.
4)–5) The word *niṣṭhyā* [is used] for *svāti*. (ĀpGS 3.5)
At a wedding, there is the ritual slaughter of a cow;
at a wedding, a cow [is sacrificed]. (ĀpGs 3.6)
At the place of the wedding, a cow should be offered by one who has a daughter. //5//
At the place of the wedding, a cow should be brought near.
In the houses, [the offering is] a cow.
And in the houses, a cow is to be sacrificed by that very father who has a daughter;
this is the application of those two. //6//
Likewise, in the house or in the shed, another cow should be brought near. //7//
To the question "For what purpose?", he says: 8. He is worthy of honor with a cow; with that [cow], one should honor the guest as is best. (ĀpGs 3.8)

With the cow that was given at the wedding, he should honor the bridegroom as one would a guest; because of the statement "as a guest," this includes honoring him with the *madhuparka* offering as well, according to the rule:
"A student of the Veda is to be honored with a cow and *madhuparka* on the day [of arrival]" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.8.5).
Because of this statement. //7//
With that cow brought to the place of the wedding—
however, not with the one mentioned immediately above—
he should honor the bridegroom, just as one honors a guest.

The meaning is that one should honor the bridegroom—even if he is merely a student of the Vedas—with a *madhuparka* accompanied by that [offering] which, as a constituent part, functions either as the means for producing the oblation (*havis*) or as the means for its offering. //8//
Whoever is honored by him, he should honor with the other [form].

The teacher who has come together with him who is honored and worthy of worship among these suitors—that [teacher] he should honor with a cow that is obtained in the houses of the others. To the question "In what manner?", [the answer is]: "He should honor him like a guest.
At a wedding, for the sake of the suitor and those accompanying him, there is a separate preparation of food at another fire.
The offering of the omentum (*vapā-homa*) takes place at that very same spot.
In the houses of those who have been humiliated (*apacita*) and their associates, there is a separate preparation of food.
Furthermore, the roasting of the cow’s omentum and its offering are performed specifically on the *aupāsana* fire; such is the manner of performance. 8.
He who is a relative of this bridegroom by virtue of being his father, teacher, or preceptor, and is honored in the world due to his perfection in learning, lineage, and so forth;
or alternatively, he who is honored— that is, venerable— to the bridegroom.
The connection is that one should honor him like a guest with the other [mixture] kept ready in the house.
Both of these *madhuparka* offerings are auxiliary parts of the marriage ceremony,
because of the context.
If, however, it were for the sake of the person who gives the gift, one would have stated: "To the teacher, the officiating priest, the father-in-law, the king, the bridegroom, and the honored guest.
On the contrary, [the text] says: "The guest, the ancestors, and marriage" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 3.10), which mentions only the connection with marriage.

Now, one might ask: since it should have been stated simply that "one should honor [the guest] as one would a guest," for what purpose is it said, "In the case of a marriage, a cow [is given]," and so forth?

It is replied: this is for the purpose of making known that the two objects of worship, being in different locations, constitute separate ritual procedures (*tantra*); otherwise, there would be a single unified procedure (*tantratā*) for those things that could possibly be combined.

And for the purpose of prohibition—lest the singularity of the cow, which might otherwise be applicable here by way of option between the boon (*vara*) and the honor (*apaciti*), should occur due to the observation of the option regarding the singularity of the cow among all the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) in another ritual manual (*kalpa*), as expressed in the rule: "Or [the gift may be] from all, because of the manifestation of a single desire. //9//
9. There are nine occasions for the slaughter of a cow:
these are the occasions for the slaughter of a cow—the guest, the ancestors, and marriage. (ĀpGs 3.10)
The slaughter of a cow (*gorālambha*) occurs only in these three types of affection (*sneha*), and not elsewhere in the *pākayajña* sacrifices.
By the word "guest" (*atithi*), the rite of hospitality (*ātithyakarman*) is designated, as in the passage beginning, “where they show him honor” (*Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra* 13.2).
By the word "father" (*pitṛ*), the *aṣṭakā* rite is designated, as in the passage beginning, “on the following day, with *darbha* grass, [one approaches] the cow” (*Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra* 22.3).
By the word "marriage" (vivāha), that which was mentioned immediately before is understood.
Since the immolation of a cow is prescribed even in other ritual manuals (kalpa) for rites such as the sacrifice to Īśāna,
this restrictive rule is intended to prohibit that.
By speaking thus, other specific details observed in another ritual manual (kalpa) are implicitly permitted. // 9 //
A guest who has arrived and is learned in the Vedas, the ancestors, the *aṣṭakā* rite,
and marriage—
these three occasions constitute the grounds for the ritual involving the immolation of a cow.
This is what is meant:

just as a guest and the ancestors are the causes for the ritual act consisting of the immolation of a cow, so too, by virtue of this very statement, marriage is likewise independent of any other qualification.
For if this sūtra were not explained in this manner, then [the rule] "he says 'not a cow' regarding a cow" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 13.15) would apply.

Because this is already established by these very [rules]: "On the following day, he dedicates the cow with darbha grass" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 22.3) and "In marriage, a cow [is the fee]" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 3.6).
[Otherwise] it would be entirely useless;
therefore, even to those who have not studied the Veda, if they are honored as guests, the Madhuparka should be given without the cow prescribed for the Dharma;
however, to those who have studied the Veda, it should be given together with that [cow].

Some [hold] that these three alone are our basis for the sacrificial cow (go-ālambana), and not others, such as the "Knowledge-Bull" (jñāna-vṛṣi) also known as the "Spear-Bull" (śūla-gava), which [is used] even through conceptual construction (vikalpa) as by others.
By speaking thus, they imply that we also permit the various specific details mentioned in other ritual manuals (kalpa) through conceptual construction. //10//
Now, he states the girls who are to be avoided in marriage:
"In the selection [of a bride], these girls are to be avoided: one who is asleep, one who is weeping..."
One should avoid a girl who has already gone out for the purpose of choosing a husband. (ĀpGS 3.11)
When suitors have arrived for the purpose of choosing a bride, if a girl falls asleep, weeps, or departs from the house,
she should not be chosen;
these are inauspicious signs.
The word "pari" has the sense of absolute negation; [it means] "even though there is fixation of the mind and the eyes. //10//
She who sleeps when suitors have arrived seeking her hand,
she who weeps, or she who goes out from the house— these are [the faults].
One should avoid these two in concealment—that is, one should avoid them absolutely—even when supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is known through signs such as light and so forth;
for it is intended here that sleep and the rest are both indicators of a lack of supernatural power and are [otherwise] powerful states. //11//

One should avoid a girl who has been given away (*dattā*), one who is protected (*guptā*), one who is radiant (*dyotā*), one who is preeminent (*ṛṣabhā*), one who is powerful (*śarabhā*), one who is humble (*vinatā*), one who is deformed (*vikaṭā*), one who is bald (*muṇḍā*), one who is frog-like (*maṇḍūṣikā*), one who is from a mixed caste (*sāṅkārikā*), one who is red-complexioned (*rātā*), one who is a guardian (*pālī*), one who is friendly (*mitrā*), one who is her own younger sister (*svanujā*), and one who brings rain (*varṣakārī*).
*Given away* (*dattā*) means she has been bestowed upon another by word.
*Protected* (*guptā*) means she is being guarded with great effort.
She is either immoral or possesses unwholesome characteristics;
she has a distorted view regarding light and is like a bull.
She has the character of a bull,
she is more beautiful than a śarabha;
men would desire her, and she [desires] them.
*Vinatā* means one whose limbs are bent, or one who is hunchbacked;
*vikaṭā* means one with broad shanks;
*maṇḍā* means one whose hair has been removed.
*Maṇḍūṣikā* means a frog-skin, that is to say, something rough;
others say it refers to a dwarf.
*Sāṃkārikā* is one born in another family or one who has become the offspring of another family.
Or, while she was in the womb, her mother was one who had accumulated bones,
one who was devoted to sexual pleasure (*rati*),
or one who was a protector (*pālī*) of calves and other such creatures.

*Mitrā* means "having friends," "having many friends," or "being herself a friend. *Svanujā* refers to one who has a beautiful sister; she is *svanujā* because she is lovely and beautiful to behold. She is born after a short time following the birth of her elder sister; others say she is born in that very same year.
"Varṣakārī" means one who menstruates excessively; others say it refers to one whose nature is to perspire.
It is said "one should avoid her," so that the term "avoidance" (varaṇa) does not continue to apply here [as it did in the previous verse regarding choosing a bride].
Therefore, there is no formal choosing (varaṇa) of women in the Brāhma and other forms of marriage; yet, even in those cases, these [types of women] are prohibited.
If it were associated with anything at all, there would be the undesirable consequence of an absolute negation [of that thing]. //11//

One should avoid fifteen types of girls, beginning with the "given" (dattā). A "given" girl is one who has been promised to someone by word of mouth, or one who has been formally bestowed through the pouring of water.
She is concealed, covered by garments such as a bodice for the sake of remaining unseen,
or guarded with great effort due to the suspicion of misconduct and the like;
she has glowing, tawny eyes.
Or she may have tawny hair, or an uneven gaze;
"ṛṣabhā" means preeminent.
She whose body, gait, or character is like that of a bull (ṛṣabha), or she who possesses a hump (kakud);
a śarabhā is one whose brilliance has faded.
Or having entirely blue hair,
or formless,
or lusterless.
Some are beautiful, because she is desired by paramours; some are hunchbacked or crooked.
With shapely or unshapely calves,
or with broad calves;
shaven-headed, meaning with hair removed.
Or one who has no hair;
or a *maṇḍūṣikā*, small-bodied,
or an *aruṇadatī*, or one with the skin of a frog.
Others have stunted limbs or burnt limbs;
she is one who, while remaining pregnant, causes her husband to perform the collection of his bones [at the funeral pyre].
Or she has become the daughter of another family; that is to say, she is one whose character is devoted to pleasing her husband and who is fond of playing with balls and such,
or she is one who has bathed after her menses.
Some are *ratiśīlā*, meaning those whose habit is the enjoyment of sense objects;
they are protectors of groves, calves, fields, and so forth, or they are friends (*mitrā*) or close companions (*bahumitrā*). Or they are female friends (*sakhī*).
"She whose younger sister was beautiful" means that her younger sister was beautiful,
but not that she herself had a beautiful younger sister, for there might occasionally be negligence toward a beautiful younger sister.
Some say she was born later in the very same year as her elder brother.

"Varṣakārī" means one who has excessive menses, or one whose menses flow excessively. Although the prohibition is already implied by the general injunction "one should avoid [such women]," the repetition of the word "should avoid" is for the purpose of excluding these [types of women] from all forms of marriage, beginning with the Brāhma rite.

Since there is no other possible destination, even when supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) has been examined, [this is stated] either for the purpose of negating the attainment of a different state or for the sake of providing a definitive conclusion. //12//
Names of constellations, names of rivers, and names of trees are censured [as names for a son]. (ĀpGs 3.13)
And one should avoid all those whose penultimate letters are *ra* or *la* when choosing a bride. (ĀpGS 3.14)
Those whose names are [derived from] constellations (nakṣatra) are called "nakṣatranāmāḥ";
those with river names and tree names— such as Rohiṇī, Gaṅgā, Kareṇu, and so forth—
are likewise forbidden in marriage.
Likewise, all [names] ending in *ra* or *la* as the penultimate letter are of this nature; such is the meaning of the term "name" (*nāman*).
Examples include *karā*, *kālā*, *suvelā*, and so forth.
One should avoid choosing them; the meaning is that one should not even perform their selection. // 12 //
Those whose names are like the name of a constellation are "nakṣatranāmāḥ";
there is an elision of one of the two words "nāma," as in the case of compounds such as *uṣṭramukha* ("camel-faced").
In this way, compounds such as *ikṣvādi* [are explained]; *rohiṇī*, *citrā*, and so forth are names of lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*);
*gaṅgā* and so forth are names of rivers;
*śiṃśupā* and so forth are names of trees.
