Those who are censured are to be avoided. //13//
The meaning is that those whose name has the letter *ra* or the letter *la* as a penultimate (*upadhā*) syllable— for example, *gaurī*, *śālī*, and so forth—

the rest is clear. Here, since their exclusion is already established by the attraction (*anukarṣaṇa*) of the word "despised" (*garhitāḥ*) by means of the particle *ca*, the statement "one should avoid all [such women] in marriage" is redundant.
This is because it is easy to grasp.
Alternatively, those [names] such as Gaurī, Śālī, and so forth, which have *repha* (*r*) or *lakāra* (*l*) as their penultimate letters,
as well as those mentioned in other Smṛtis that likewise have *repha* or *lakāra* as their penultimate letters by way of another classification—
This is for the purpose of making it known that one should avoid all those women who belong to the same *gotra* or the same *pravara*, even if they are unchaste, during the selection of a bride.

However, this must be stated here: although there may be other possibilities and their supernatural signs (*ṛddhi-liṅga*) may be manifest, there is an absolute prohibition regarding those of the same *gotra* and so forth;
but this is not the case for Gaurī and others, as it is for the *guptā* and other such classes.
Some maintain that this verse beginning with "nakṣatranāmā" and so forth was sung in another treatise; they imagine that the words "sarvā varaṇe parivarjayet" are intended to fill out its meter.

They explain it thus: since those whose names begin with asterisms (nakṣatra) and so forth, and who have the letter *ra* or *la* as penultimate letters, are censured, therefore one should avoid all such women in marriage. //14//
11. Examination of Prosperity:
Having placed objects within one's power but concealed from view, one should say, "Touch them. (ĀpGs 3.15)
Various seeds mixed together, soil from a threshing floor, a clod of earth from a field, dung, and a clod of earth from a cemetery—these are the materials for the altar. (ĀpGṛS 3.16)
He will state that "one should marry a woman endowed with auspicious marks" (*lakṣaṇasampannām upayaccheta*).
Since those marks are not yet known therein, the means for their examination is taught.
And this is not an obligatory rule (*nityavidhi*).
Because of the statement "the scope of [her] capacity" (*śaktiviṣaya*), "capacity" (*śakti*) means ability (*sāmarthya*). If it refers to possibility (*saṃbhava*),
the meaning is that it should be done only if the kinsmen of the bride (*vadhūjñātayaḥ*) give their consent, and not otherwise.
How is that to be performed?
It is said: having concealed five substances—about which more will be said—within lumps of clay, and having placed them near the girl, the suitor should say to her: "Touch one of these lumps.
But what are those substances?
Various seeds mixed together, such as rice and barley; dust brought from the sacrificial altar;
and a clod of earth brought from a field rich in crops.
Once [the following are used]: cow dung, and a clod of earth brought from a cremation ground.
Although these do not deviate from being substances among seeds, they are called "substances" because other substances seen in another treatise are also included here.

[The use of] a word with a derivative suffix for the sake of attainment is as follows: "Because she does not give alms from her own house, the gambler's wife [is like] one who has no grain in a barren field" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.5.6). //13//
Power (*śakti*) is capacity;
it is the scope for an object.
In this examination of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), there occurs the possibility of the capacity of those belonging to the opposing side within that scope.

The meaning is: "if the maiden and her [relatives] were to accept this test. Precisely because this concerns power (*śakti*), he says that for this reason this examination of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) is optional (*vaikalpikī*) according to the *Jyotiṣa* and other [texts].
But it is not an integral part of the marriage like the obligatory rites.
Having placed the substances to be mentioned later, concealed within lumps of clay, into a single vessel, and having brought the girl close by, he should say to her: "Touch one of these lumps. (15)
To the question "Which are those?", he says:
various seeds, such as the seeds of rice, barley, and so forth;
they are mixed, having been cast into a single mass.
The dust brought from the Vedic altars of the Soma sacrifice;
a clod of earth brought from a field rich in crops;
these two are well-known and require no further definition. //16//
At the ritual touching of the eastern [waters], there is success according to the respective characteristics.
They declare this to be the highest.
In that regard, by touching seed, one attains prosperity through offspring;
by touching the loose earth of the altar, through sacrifices; and by touching a clod of earth from a field, through wealth and grain.
"With cow dung [one gains] cattle;
with a clod of earth from a cremation ground, death"—such is the meaning according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*).
They "proclaim" the final substance as "supreme," meaning they censure it, that is, they avoid it. //14//
By touching the four [substances] mentioned previously, there is prosperity according to their respective characteristics;
by touching various seeds, there is prosperity of progeny; and by touching the dust of the altar, there is prosperity of sacrifices.
From the field comes the harvest of grain, and from the dung comes livestock;
thus, because of the certainty of prosperity, there is the certainty that the marriage must be performed. //17//
The learned declare that a clod of earth from a cremation ground is the best [for the rite], yet they censure it, because it is a sign of the death of either the wife or the husband. //18//
Regarding the girl to be married, he says:
12. The excellence of the girl to be married. One should marry a girl who is endowed with good family, character, and auspicious marks, and who is free from disease. (ĀpGs 3.19)
The girls who are to be avoided have been described; now those who are to be accepted are described.
By the word "bandhu," one's lineage is meant.
As Āśvalāyana stated: “One should first examine the family, both on the mother’s and the father’s side,” as previously explained (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.5.10).

[She should be] endowed with good character, possessing the conduct of a noble person; endowed with auspicious marks, possessed of the female characteristics, free from disease, and devoid of consumption, epilepsy, and other such ailments. //15//
The term "endowed with" (*sampannām*) is connected to each [of the following]: "endowed with kin," meaning one of noble lineage;
"endowed with virtue," meaning one possessed of qualities such as faith (*āstikya*).

One should marry— that is, take as a wife— a woman endowed with auspicious marks, possessing the female characteristics such as hidden ankles, and free from disease, meaning devoid of incurable ailments such as consumption, epilepsy, and leprosy. //19//
Now he states the qualities of the bridegroom:
13. The qualities of the bridegroom: being endowed with noble lineage, good character, and auspicious marks; being learned and free from disease—this is the excellence of the bridegroom. (ĀpGs 3.20)
"Learned" means one who is perfected in hearing and study.
"Excellence of the groom" refers to excellent qualities.
The meaning is that a daughter should be given to one possessing such qualities. //16//
"Endowed with the characteristics of good conduct and learning" is to be explained as before. "Learned" means one who is accomplished in hearing and study;
for one who lacks knowledge has no entitlement to perform the rites of the twice-born.
And because marriage has as its purpose the acquisition of dharma and other goals;
"free from disease" is as explained before; for even that [disease] would result in non-participation due to incapacity.
Such is the excellence of his fortune;
the meaning is that a daughter should be given to such a bridegroom endowed with these qualities. //20//

Now, regarding the determination of the [proper] place, some state this opinion: "In that place where the binding of the mind and the eyes occurs, there is success; one should not attend to anything else. (ĀpGs 3.21)

Some learned authorities state that for whichever maiden there arises a firm attachment of the mind and the eyes of the groom, prosperity in her case is certain; in such a case, one need not pay heed to the examination of qualities or defects such as whether she has been given away in marriage or not. According to this view, even if a girl is endowed with every excellence, if the mind and eyes are not fixed upon her, she is to be rejected.
Even in that case, those things prohibited by the scriptures must certainly be avoided, such as a woman of the same caste who is born of the same lineage (sagotra). //17//

In whatever maiden the mind and eyes of the bridegroom are intensely bound— that is to say, by the excellence of his attachment, his mind and eyes remain fixed upon her— in the presence of such a wife, there is the fulfillment of dharma and the other goals of life.
Some say that one should not pay heed to the observation of other qualities or defects;
what is meant by this is that here, the sole cause for paying heed is the binding of the mind and the eyes,
and not the qualities known through light and so forth.
Likewise, the mere absence of that [recipient] is the reason for avoidance,
and not defects such as sleep and so forth;
thus, in both views, one must certainly respect the prohibition regarding gifts given to those [unworthy recipients].
This is because of the collection of scriptural statements such as, "one who is not of the same ṛṣi or gotra," and "beyond the fifth on the mother's side and the seventh on the father's side. //21//
Thus has the *Tātparyadarśana* been composed by the noble Itthaṃsudarśana.
In the first chapter, it was composed according to the commentary and according to my own understanding.
Thus ends the third section in the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
The first chapter is completed.
Now begins the second chapter,
the fourth section.
Chapter 4: The Section on Marriage — 1. Sending the Suitor.
He should send forth as suitors his friends who have assembled and are accompanied by those who know the mantras. (ĀpGs 4.1)
Now follows the ritual for choosing a bride (*kanyāvaraṇavidhi*).
It has been stated that [the marriage] is performed under the *invakās* (Pleiades).
On that day or on another auspicious lunar mansion (*puṇyanakṣatra*), having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce blessings, [he should invite] his friends.

He should send out—dispatch—kinsmen who are assembled together, who are conversant with the sacred mantras, and who are perfected in Vedic learning, as suitors for a maiden, saying: "From such-and-such a family, you should choose a maiden for me. Although in such a matter only friends would be expected, they are nevertheless called "kinsmen" so that, in the absence of those conversant with the mantras, one may resort to mere friendship. By the term "conversant with the mantras," only Brāhmaṇas are intended.
Therefore, even for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, Brāhmaṇas alone are the preferred [officiants]. //1//

In the preceding section, the time for sending the suitor (vara), which is utilized for the marriage ceremony, was stated in the passage: "They are sent forth with the Invakās" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 2.16).
Now, he states the procedure for that.
"Friends" are one's own allies;
"assembled" means those who have come together for their respective tasks; "possessing mantras" means possessing both the Mantra and Brāhmaṇa portions [of the Veda].
Because the mention of "mantras" is intended as an illustration— as in the rule *śucīn mantravataḥ* (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.15.11)—
[the word refers to] the suitors who are choosing the bridegrooms.
The "vara" (the suitor) should send or dispatch these even-numbered Brāhmaṇas; so say some. //2//
One should consecrate them from the beginning with two mantras. (ĀpGs 4.2)
As they are departing, he should consecrate them with the two *ṛc*s beginning with "paprasugman," which are recited at the beginning of the traditional collection of mantras (*mantrasamāmnāya*).
Consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) is the utterance of a mantra directed toward a specific object.
Then, having gone to the girl's family, they should say: "We choose your daughter for such-and-such a lineage, for the sake of performing joint duties."
Then they should reply: "Excellent; we shall do so.

In that regard, in the *brāhma* and *daiva* forms of marriage, the formal choosing (*varaṇa*) is omitted because of the absence of a motive and because of the observation of other ritual manuals (*kalpa*) stating, "In these cases, one should not send suitors.
The same applies to the *gāndharva* and *rākṣasa* forms. (2)
As they have set out,
he should consecrate them with two verses from the beginning of the collection of mantras, starting with "prasugmantā.
Consecration (abhimantraṇa) is the recitation of a mantra directed toward [the object].
The procedure for the *anumantraṇa* (subsequent consecration) is likewise; however, the distinction is that [in this case] the mind must be directed toward the substance to be consecrated.
Now, because the ritual manual (sūtra) is incomplete, the sequence is stated:
having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and formed the resolve, "I shall dismiss the chosen ones," he consecrates the chosen ones with the two verses beginning with "prasugmantā."
He should send a messenger with the words: "Please choose a maiden for me from that family.

Then, having gone to the house of the one possessing a daughter, they should carefully examine her to ensure she is free from defects such as being of the same lineage (*sagotra*) and is endowed with virtues such as [having] relatives and so forth.

"Having sons, with our father at their head, we choose your daughter for Viṣṇuśarman of the Gautama gotra, our groom, for the sake of procreation and the performance of joint duties," they should say.
Then the father or other relative should reply, "I shall give her.
Thereupon, having returned, they...
"We are pure and distressed," they should announce to the suitor;
and this [announcement] applies only to the Āsura and Ārṣa forms of marriage,
not to others, because the purpose [of the announcement] is absent in those cases.
Now, on the day before the wedding—specifically on the fifth or third day prior—one should perform the rite of sowing the sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) according to the practice of the learned.
Likewise, [the bridegroom] should observe auspicious rites and receive them from women, thinking, "The wedding is tomorrow" or "The wedding is today. (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 2.14, 15)
Thus have the rites been described; the groom and the bride perform them at the proper time and as is appropriate.
Some say that on the previous day, one should perform the *nāndī-śrāddha* according to another ritual manual (*kalpa*).

Then, the father or other relative should give the maiden to the groom who has arrived at the bride’s family, preceded by the pouring of water, with these words: "This Lakṣmī, born of the Vatsa lineage, I give to Viṣṇuśarman of the Gautama lineage, for the sake of asceticism and for the performance of duties involving offspring."
"I bestow [the bride]"—
however, there is no such bestowal in the cases of the Gāndharva and Rākṣasa marriages, because they do not depend upon the activity of a giver.

Then the bridegroom, having accepted her and established the fire in the wedding place according to the rule, "Wherever the fire may be" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.1.13), goes to that very hall where the maiden resides and receives the honey-mixture (madhuparka) as is fitting and according to the prescribed rite.
In the same way, even one who has committed a grave offense [is purified]. //2//
Regarding what the groom should do immediately thereafter, [the text] says:
2. "The inspection of the girl;
having seen her himself, he should mutter the third [verse]. (ĀpGs 4.3)

Then, once the marriage is settled, having performed the *nāndī-śrāddha* on the preceding day and having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce blessings on the following day, the groom goes to the bride’s family.

Having offered him the *madhuparka*—beginning with the gift of the *kūrca* grass mat and ending with food—he bestows the maiden upon him, saying: "I give her to you for the duties of procreation and shared life.
Then, having personally beheld her, the groom should mutter the third verse.
Regarding the phrase "one who does not kill her brother":
if the word "herself" (*svayam*) were not stated, the meaning would be "having seen a suitor," because that is the subject under discussion;
however, by the inclusion of the word "herself," the meaning becomes "having seen a maiden."
Among those, in the Brāhma marriage there is the formal bestowal preceded by water; however, in the Gāndharva and Rākṣasa marriages, there is no such formal bestowal at all. //3//
Having seen the bride herself, [the groom] should mutter the third verse, "abrātṛghnīm.
Upon seeing her, he closes his eyes. And the muttering is always performed with the fourfold accentuation (cātussvaryeṇa).
But it is not with a single intonation (*ekaśruti*), as in the case of ritual instruments or mantras;
for there is the rule: "A single intonation is used when addressing someone from a distance" (Pāṇini 1.2.33).
And here, the specific qualification "himself" is used so that this recitation may not apply to the suitors who are the subject at hand.
Some [maintain] that he should recite only while looking at the bride herself, and not at the suitors.
And the passage beginning with "having seen for oneself" is applicable without modification to all forms of marriage. //3//
On the fourth day, he should examine it. ĀpGs 4.4.
"Beholding by way of parts" means *samīkṣaṇa* (close inspection).
"With eyes not terrible"—this is the fourth [quarter]. //4//
He should gaze [at her] with this [verse], "aghora-cakṣuḥ.

Having been looked at by the bride, he casts his own gaze [upon her], because of the indicative mark (liṅga) of the mantra: "aghora-cakṣur apighny edhi" ("be one whose gaze is not terrible, nor a destroyer").
Some say that "one should examine" means one should inspect [the bride] limb by limb.

In this regard, while seated on the *darbha* grass mats, the groom and the bride, holding blades of *darbha* grass and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), make this formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "We two must perform our duties, and we must procreate offspring. (4)
3. The cleansing between her eyebrows:

having grasped a blade of *darbha* grass with the thumb and the ring finger, he should cleanse the space between her eyebrows with the following *yajus* formula and then cast it away toward the west. (ĀpGs 4.5)
The *upamadhyamā* is that which is situated near the middle finger; by this finger—that is, by the ring finger—one [performs the action] with the other *yajus* mantra, "Idamaham...
This is the mantra for sweeping (*saṃmārjana*), not the mantra for casting away (*nirāsana*).

"Pratīcīnam" means directed backward. One should strike [the water] repeatedly above the head. Following that, there is the ritual touching of water (*udakopasparśana*). Although the specification "with the ring finger" (*upamadhyamayā*) is already established by its association with the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*), the mention of the qualified term "finger" (*aṅgulyā*) is for the sake of clarity.
The qualification "with the Yajus" is used so that there may be no suspicion that the word "uttareṇa" (to the north) refers to a direction. //5//
The ring finger and the little finger,
but not the index finger,
because the latter is designated as "the slipping one."
With the subsequent Yajus formula, "This [I take] from you...
and so forth; the remainder is clear.
Having cast away the Darbha grass, he should touch water. //5//
When the occasion arises, one should recite the subsequent [verse]. ĀpGs 4.6.

The weeping of the bride and her kinsmen is the cause [for this rite], based on the indicative mark (liṅga) in the verse "the living ones cry out. Regarding this subsequent verse, "the living ones cry out," this recitation (japa) occurs everywhere at the conclusion of the *samāveśana* rite within this marriage ceremony when this specific cause arises.
In the repetition of the *nimitta*, the mantra is repeated. //6//

When the occasion arises that corresponds to the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra—"The living ones are weeping"—that is, when the mother or others, or the maiden herself, has wept due to anxiety over their mutual separation, one should mutter this *ṛc*. //6//

4. For the purpose of bringing water for her bath, he should send out pairs of Brāhmaṇas; he should dispatch those gathered in pairs, accompanied by the mantra, with the following verse, to fetch water. (ĀpGs 4.7)
The fetching of water for the purpose of bathing the bride is performed with the subsequent ṛc, "He has sprinkled away the cruel" (RV 10.85.34).
One should send forth—that is, cause to be brought—the waters accompanied by mantras.
Although the term "auspicious things" (*maṅgalāni*) alone would have sufficed, the mention of "pairs" (*yugma*) is intended because he will later prescribe the bathing with five mantras.
In that case, there is a repetition of the bathing for each mantra;
and since the bathing is performed an odd number of times, the water-pitchers intended for that purpose should also be odd in number,
as should the Brahmins who perform the rite.
Therefore, it is said "in pairs.
By this, for each mantra there is a division of the jars, and for each jar there is a division of the Brahmins; this is established.
In that regard, if there are four jars, the consecration is performed with the fourth jar using the fourth and fifth mantras.
When there are eight [priests], then [the rites are performed] with five [mantras] at each recitation and silently with the others.
The mention of "those who have assembled" regarding the fetching of water is for the purpose of acting together.
The phrase "those possessing mantras" refers to the Brāhmaṇas.
Because it is seen in the mantra: “O Brāhmaṇas, [be seated] for her. //7//
"Paired" means of equal number;
"assembled and accompanied by mantras" is as explained previously.

With the subsequent verse, "He has washed away the cruel," which is recited loudly because it is a *praiṣa* (directive), he should cause [the water] to be sent forth from the waters; he should send forth those who are to bring the water for the purpose of bathing the bridegroom.

And these [waters] are indeed Brāhmaṇa-waters, according to the indicative mark of the mantra: "O Brāhmaṇas, come hither. And those Brāhmaṇas, having removed grass, *avakā* plants, and other such things from those waters in which men have previously not died during bathing and so forth, draw up the water.
This is because of the indicative mark (liṅga) in the mantra: "O you who do not slay heroes. //7//
5. Her bathing, the wearing of new garments, and the fastening of the girdle.
With the following Yajus, having placed a blade of Darbha grass upon its head, he fixes the southern end of the yoke-pin into the hole with the next [verse];

having placed gold within the hole with the following [verse], he bathes it with the five subsequent [verses], covers it with a new garment with the following [verse], and binds it with a yoke-tie with the following [verse]. (ĀpGS 4.8)
Then, having brought water in those [vessels], they prepare a circle for the deceased with *darbha* grass and *śara* grass;

having placed [the fire] upon that circle to the north with the Yajus formula, "The fire of Aryaman," they fix the southern hole of the yoke upon that [fire] with the following verse, "In the hole of the cart," and the outer hole of the southern yoke-halter. Upon that hole, they place gold with the next Ṛc, "May it be well..."
He causes her to bathe with water poured through a golden vessel while reciting the verse "Hiraṇyam asi" and the five subsequent verses beginning with "Hiraṇyavarṇāḥ," one mantra for each bath.
But how is it possible to perform a bathing by means of a vessel that acts as an interposition?
He makes it disappear in such a way that the water flows out.
Then, with the following verse, "O lover of songs, may songs encompass thee," he covers her with a new garment.

Having himself recited the mantra, he causes her to put it on. After covering her and making her sip water, he girds her with a waistband using the following verse, "May [the gods] grant... and so forth.
The specific details pertaining to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, such as "mityā," are intended here. //8//
A *iṇva* made of *darbha* grass—
meaning a ring-shaped object fashioned from *darbha* in the form of a chain—

is placed upon the head of the bride with the subsequent Yajus formula, "The fire of Aryaman," and then the hole of the right yoke-pole is inserted into that *iṇva* with the next verse, "Of the cart."
Having fixed the southern end of the yoke against the outer hole of the southern pole-hole,

and having placed a piece of gold within that hole with the verse "Aśaṃ te hiraṇyam," he bathes [the horse] with the five subsequent ṛcs beginning with "hiranyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ pracakramur hitvā."
And this [concluding act] for the five [priests] occurs only once at the end, because it has been stated: "A single ritual act may consist of many mantras" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 1.47).
Thus it is in all cases, including such rites as the first feeding of solid food and so forth.

Some say that because of the statement "with five," it means "for each mantra"; but that is not so, because this [statement] is intended to preclude the optionality of the two remaining [mantras] after the three.

Otherwise, since there is no mention of an affix denoting the repetition of an action, there would be the undesirable consequence of assuming a repetition of the primary act of bathing for the sake of a subordinate quality, which would involve excessive complexity in the application of the injunction.
Having clothed him with the verse "Around you, O steed, [are] the songs" (RV 9.1.6),
and having caused him to put on a new, unwashed garment, he should cause him to sip water twice.
With the verse, "Desiring good-will," he fastens [the victim] with the yoke-rope;
this is the complete rule.
Some say it is for the purpose of demonstrating the procedure for the preparation of the sacrificial fires. //8//

Then, having taken her by the right hand with the following [verse], and having led her toward the fire, he spreads a mat with its ends pointing north behind the fire; they both sit upon it, the bridegroom to the north. ĀpGs 4.9.
Then, immediately after the donning of the garments, he prepares the fire according to the option beginning with "Wherever the fire [is]";
having either churned it or brought it from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), he then leads the bride toward the fire with the following verse,
"May Pūṣan lead you here."
This is the mantra for bringing [the grass];
however, the grasping of the hand is performed silently.
The mention of "with the tips pointing north" is for the purpose of precluding [the tips] from pointing south. //9//
The word *atha* has the meaning already stated; it serves to prohibit other purposes.
Having taken this bride by the right hand with the following verse, "May Pūṣan lead you from here," etc.
One brings the fire toward oneself, leading it facing the fire;

this is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the mantra, "May he lead. Even though the act of leading is separated [from the mantra], due to its application (*viniyoga*), one spreads a mat with its tips pointing eastward not far behind the fire.
They sit down simultaneously on that mat, with the bridegroom to the north and the bride to the south. //9//
6. The ritual beginning with the kindling of the fire:
After the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he should then consecrate her from the beginning with two verses. (ĀpGs 4.10)
Then, having sat down in this manner, he undertakes the ritual beginning with the kindling of the fire.

Having kindled the fire with [fuel-sticks] whose tips point eastward, and once the rite up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings has been performed, he immediately thereafter rises and addresses the bride as she sits with two verses from the beginning of the third section, namely, "Soma was first... and so forth.
The statement beginning with "the kindling of the fire" (agner upasamādhāna) is for the purpose of establishing the ritual framework (tantra).
The mention of "up to the two portions of clarified butter" (ājyabhāgānta) is for the purpose of indicating the timing for the subsequent rites, such as the consecration (abhimantraṇa) and so forth.
The word "atha" (now/then) is for the purpose of showing a change in state.
"Having performed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings while seated, he stands up and proceeds with the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) and subsequent acts.
Thus says Baudhāyana: "Then, having approached her, [he touches] the region of her heart" (BauGṛ 1.4.1).
And Āśvalāyana says: "Standing and facing east, [he addresses] her who is seated and facing west" (ĀśvGṛ 1.7.3).
The phrase "enām" (her) is used to indicate that one should not fear the consecration of the fire.

Although it would have been sufficient to say "with the following two [verses]," the expression "with the first two" is used for the purpose of demonstrating the arrangement of the sections (*anuvāka*) within the collection of mantras.
Consequently, in such instructions as "one should mutter the remainder at the union," the term refers to the remainder of the specific section. //10//

It has already been stated that this instruction on the ritual manual (*tantra*) is for the purpose of the sequential procedure (*krama*). However, if the offerings of parched grain (*lāja-homa*) were adventitious and devoid of the ritual manual, then that would be a case of following the rules of the *Kramatantra* [inappropriately].
The word "atha" (now) is as before;
some say it is for the purpose of demonstrating the immediate succession of the *pota* established in another kalpa.
The bridegroom should first take hold of this bride and consecrate her with the two verses beginning with "Soma was the first" from the Anuvāka. (10)
7. Taking the Hand. Then, with his right hand lowered, he should take her right hand, which is turned upward. (ĀpGs 4.11)
Then, remaining in that same position, he should take the right hand of her who is seated in that same manner— [her hand] being turned upward—
with his own right hand placed low and slightly bent.
This is the rite of grasping the hand, known as *pāṇigrahaṇa*.
It need not be specified as "with the right," because among actions to be accomplished by a single hand, it is the right hand alone that is conventionally established for such purposes.
If, however, it were not so established, [the specification would be necessary].
Otherwise, there would result a lack of restriction,
as in the case of the initiation ceremony mentioned earlier;
thus, in this instance, the right hand is not specifically prescribed.

What then? This well-known right hand, which is established for all ritual acts, is restated here as being "afflicted by ignorance" (avidāna); the meaning is that with this [hand], the taking of the bride's hand in a low position must be performed here.
And from this very restatement, it is established that the right hand is to be used in every instance. //11//
By this constant rule, the word "he" (saḥ) is connected even with the distant phrase "his right thumb" (abhīvāṅguṣṭham);
otherwise, he would not have used the word "he.
[The word] "to him" (asmai) refers to this bride.
The dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
"With the right hand turned upward" means with the right hand held low;
"with the thumb directed upward" means with the thumb facing above.
The word "ivā" (eva) is a restrictive particle;
one should grasp only the thumb. //11//
Now he states the two types of optional rites:
8. In that regard, there is a distinction based on desire.
If he should desire, "May I give birth only to daughters," he should take hold of only the fingers. (ĀpGs 4.12)
It is the fingers themselves, not the thumb nor the palm.
This is a specific rule connected with desire for that which was previously mentioned;
therefore, here too, there are such particulars as "with the right hand held low," and so forth. //12//
Only the fingers [are used], not the thumb; the rest is as prescribed for the daily rite. //12//
If he should desire, "May I produce only males," he grasps [the hair] over the thumb and over the hairs on the thumb. ĀpGs 4.13.
The word "he should take" (gṛhṇīyāt) is understood as a carry-over [from the preceding rule]. // 13 // // 14 //
He grasps it so that all the hairs, like those on the thumb of the bridegroom, are directed upwards;
the rest is exactly as prescribed for the regular rite.
Therefore, the bride's thumb should also be turned upward. // 13 //
He states the mantras for the previously mentioned obligatory rite and the optional rites: "gṛbhṇāmi te" and so forth, with these four [verses]. (ĀpGs 4.14)
He who does not desire the grasping of the hand should grasp it as if over the thumb or as if over the hairs; here,
the word *abhi* signifies "above," and the word *iva* signifies "slightly."

The meaning is that one should hold it as if holding hair grown on the hand, so that the thumb is slightly touched; "one who desires both [results] should hold the hand with the thumb at the edge of the hair" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.7.5).
Thus says Āśvalāyana. //15//
The connection is "they take";
[this applies] to all of them at the very end. //14//
9. Walking seven steps:
Then he causes her to step forward with her right foot toward the north-eastern fire in either an easterly or northerly direction, saying, "One for food. (ĀpGs 4.15)
Now, having raised this bride up, he causes her to step seven steps with her right foot toward either the eastern or the northern direction from the place north of the fire,
using these mantras beginning with "One for food.
The meaning is that he causes her to set down the steps as they go either eastward or northward.
In this case, having himself taken hold of the foot and recited the mantras, he causes it to be placed down,

just as in the procedure for the placement of the ritual materials (*saṃbhāra*). The phrase "with the right foot" is intended to establish a connection with the right side and to ensure that the action proceeds from the front.

Therefore, the other [offering] follows silently after it. Regarding the statement "here, with these [mantras], one by one for each mantra," namely "To Soma, the knower of birth, svāhā! and so forth, the phrase "one by one for each mantra" need not be stated;
we shall explain how this is so in that very place.
Therefore, their connection here is by way of extraction (*apakarṣa*),
[namely] "with each mantra" through these words "one *iṣa*," and so forth; otherwise, the connection of the mantra with every single word would not be established.

Furthermore, there is a restriction regarding the number of words being seven; just as in the case of "with the three [verses] following this, he circumambulates to the right," where the commencement of the circumambulation occurs at the end of the three, so it should be here as well.
He mutters the insertion "May Viṣṇu follow you" everywhere, because it is recited in both the first and the last [verses]. // 16 //

Then, not far from the fire, beginning from the north, he causes her to take seven steps toward the east or the north, with her right foot, in strides that are either directed eastward or northward, reciting the seven mantras beginning with "One for strength" (*ekamiṣe*), each followed by the appended phrase "May Viṣṇu lead you" (*viṣṇustvānveṣu*). //15//
At the seventh step, he mutters: "A companion. (ĀpGs 4.16)
It has been stated that "he causes her to take seven steps, reciting a mantra for each.

In this context, once the seventh step has been taken, he clasps her foot and mutters the mantras beginning with "sakhe saptapade" (O friend, at our seven steps), which means those mantras that precede the *homamantrebhyaḥ* (the oblation mantras). This is seen in another ritual manual (*kalpa*) as: "having clasped the seventh step. //17//
It is stated that "prior to the oblation" is for the purpose of defining the quantity of the recitation.

When the excellent [step] has been placed on the seventh spot, he mutters the formula beginning with "asakhā saptapadā" and ending with "sūnṛte," employing the fourfold intonation (cātussvaryeṇa) alone. //16//
Thus ends the fourth section in the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
Now begins the fifth section: 10. The principal oblations of the wedding ceremony.

Before the oblation, having circumambulated the fire from left to right and sat down in their respective places, he offers the subsequent oblations while she maintains contact with him, using these mantras one by one: "To Soma, the knower of wives, svāhā! and so forth.
Having completed the recitation, he then circumambulates the fire; the meaning is that he circumambulates it together with her.
In every instance, the circumambulation is performed while holding her by the right hand.
Then they sit down according to their respective places;
that is to say, each sits in the place assigned to him as "the superior one.
Having sat down while the bride has taken hold of him—while she is holding on—he offers the sixteen subsequent principal oblations.
With the formulas "To Agni, the knower of births, svāhā," and so forth, he offers one oblation with each mantra.

Since the act of sitting down is already established by the fact that this is a *darvīhoma*, the word "having sat down" is stated for the purpose of restriction: namely, that he offers the subsequent sixteen [oblations] while sitting, whereas for the others, he must remain standing.
The parched grains (lājāḥ) should be offered while [the sacrificer] remains standing;
for this is seen in many other ritual manuals (kalpa) belonging to the Bodhāyanas, the Bahvṛcas, the Chandogas, the Vājasaneyins, and the Ātharvaṇikas.
Regarding the subsidiary offerings (upahoma), the seating remains exactly as prescribed.
And we shall explain this further:
others, however, desire the oblation (homa) to be performed by the two while they are seated.
The citation of the mantra "To Soma, the knower of births" is for the purpose of indicating the beginning of the oblation mantras; therefore, the recitation mantras (japa-mantras) come before that.
This was stated previously as "prior to the oblation. That the oblation is performed with each mantra individually for the subsequent offerings is established, just as it is in other oblations.
However, it has been stated that the phrase "with these [mantras] one by one" is drawn forward from that previous context.
In that [section], first four mantras are recited ending with the word *svāhā*.
Then follow twelve verses (*ṛc*); at the end of these, the word *svāhā* occurs as an injunction for the oblation—namely, "the offering with the word *svāhā*" (*svāhākārapradāna*). //2//
Having recited "sakhe" (O friend),
before the *homa*— that is, prior to the fire-oblation— he should perform the circumambulation of the fire together with his bride, but no other necessary ritual duty;
this is because of the inclusion of the word "before the *homa*" (*prāg-homāt*).

Then, having sat down in their respective places— meaning without deviating from the positions specified by the rule "the husband sits to the north," and not arbitrarily— and while the bride maintains physical contact with him, [the officiant performs] the subsequent rites consisting of the recitation of the following mantras.
He offers the oblations, that is, the *homa*s. But what are those subsequent mantras, and how does he offer them?
Therefore, he says: there are sixteen mantras beginning with "To Soma, the knower of birth.
Of these, the first four are sacrificial formulas (yajūṃṣi), and the remaining twelve are verses (ṛcaḥ) beginning with "May he release him from here."

With these [mantras], one offers oblations for each mantra, ending with each *svāhā*, and not as in the case of "Svāhā to the sacrifice! Svāhā to speech! Svāhā, place [it] in the wind! (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.1.13), nor as in "O you who have looked down, you have given; svāhā! (Ekāgnikāṇḍa 1.4.4).

By this very *svāhākāra*, the oblation (*homa*) is performed; and the preceding [terms] serve the purpose of indicating the deity, not the act of offering itself. As for the meaning of the root *hu* (to sacrifice), it refers to that which has been enjoined as a deity—whether through a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), a dative case, or the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of a mantra—and which has been relinquished by the sacrificer while designating that deity with the very word ending in the dative case as prescribed.
The offering consists of the casting of the oblation into the prescribed receptacle;
and here, by the indicative power of the mantra, Soma and others are the deities,
and they are not qualified by specific attributes such as being the progenitor of wealth and so forth.
For the status of deities as understood through mantras must be postulated because the performance of the *homa* sacrifice would otherwise be impossible;
and that [postulation] is satisfied by the mere assumption of a deity.
It does not, however, require an unwarranted, heavy, and specific postulation devoid of a basis, which would result in excessive complexity of application (*prayukti-gaurava*).

Nor can the status of being a deity be postulated for the qualified [entities] on the grounds that the recitation of the mantra as the grāhaka (the recipient) would otherwise be untenable; for even if the qualifiers— such as "the head of heaven, the peak"— are connected to the deity's abode by way of praise, those two [the mantra and the qualification] have already served their purpose.

This is because of the technical rule (paribhāṣā) stating: "When it is enjoined that one should offer oblation (havir) and clarified butter (ājya), one should understand 'ājya' to mean ghee (sarpiḥ)" (Āpastamba Paribhāṣā 1.25).

Furthermore, although activities such as gambling (vivāda) and the like do not constitute sacrifices themselves, the ritual duties (yajñadharma) are indeed appropriate there, because they serve to produce in the person about to be authorized for sacrifices the physical fitness required for those sacrifices.
Otherwise,

rules such as "wearing the sacrificial thread and moving to the right" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 2.15), which pertain to rites that are not sacrifices— such as the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) and the *pavamāneṣṭi* sacrifices— would not apply.
The fire, established upon the hearth of the oblation, remains concentrated like a stūpa. //1//
11. The bride’s mounting upon the stone:
then, to the north of the fire, he makes her mount the stone with her right foot, saying, "Mount! (ĀpGS 5.2).
The preparation of the footprint, the placement of the footprint, and the stone—the son of the rock;
and that [stone] has already been installed together with the vessels. //3//
For the sake of clarity. //2//
12. There are twelve oblations of parched grain.
Then, having spread a base of ghee in her joined palms, he pours the parched grain twice and sprinkles it with ghee. (ĀpGs 5.3)
Some say that her uterine brother should scatter parched grains for her.
The word *atha* (now/then) serves to indicate the connection of sequence.
Thus, [the rule applies] "only when it has arisen" and "only when she has arisen.
Therefore, the sequence beginning with the cutting off (*avadāna*) is maintained.
In that context, the procedure for the portions (*avadāna*) pertaining to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) has been demonstrated, not another procedure.
Therefore, here too, for each offering (*pratyabhighāra*), there is a fivefold portion (*pañcāvatta*) for those who follow the fivefold division;
and for the parched grains (*lāja*), the worldly preparation is applied.

The setting down and sprinkling of the vessels occur together with the vessels themselves; however, it has been stated that for the *añjali* (the cupped hands), there is no setting down or similar ritual action. //4//
Because of the statement, "The brother pours the fried grains," the spreading [of the base] and the sprinkling [of clarified butter] belong to the groom alone;
however, according to the other view, everything belongs to him alone. //5//
These [rules] also have their meaning made explicit in the Sūtras:
according to the traditional practice, there is a threefold pouring of parched grain (*lāja*) for the Jamadagnis;
and the *lāja* oblations are not preceded by other rites.

Because of the complete injunction beginning with "Having poured [the butter] into her joined palms," and because there is no extension (atideśa) from the Pārvaṇa rite, the ritual properties of the *pākayajña*—namely, the *agnimukha*, the second libation (*pratyabhighāraṇa*), the *sviṣṭakṛt*, and the smearing and anointing (*lepañjana*)—are simply not applicable here.

Some, because the common ritual manual (*sādhāraṇatantra*) is not obtained through the prescription of the *kṛtsna* [rite] alone, do not even accept the refinement of the joined palms (*añjali-saṃskāra*) and so forth contained within the ritual manual for the offerings of parched grain (*lāja*) and *kiṃśuka* flowers. //3//
"The woman who offers [the oblation]... (ĀpGS 5.5).
The act of offering the oblation belongs to the groom alone;
the bride’s cupped hands serve as the vessel. //6//

The bridegroom offers the parched grains with his joined palms, which are not separated from those of the bride by means of this verse, "This woman," using the *devatīrtha* (the part of the hand sacred to the gods);
he does not offer them from the side,
because there is neither a direct instruction (*upadeśa*) nor an extended application (*atideśa*) for that.

Some [commentators] say: "Having circumambulated the fire clockwise and sat down in their respective places"—this rule regarding the restriction of "respective places" (yathāsthāna), namely that the groom is on the north side and the bride is on the inner side, is not tenable.
Why?
Because in a marriage ceremony, due to the preeminence of the bride, her position on the inner side is established by logic (*nyāyasiddha*).
Furthermore, the preeminence of the bride among women is to be understood precisely from her not being married again;
this has been explained in the sūtra: "When he sits down there, the bridegroom sits facing north" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 4.9).

Therefore, according to the sequential order of the places [of the ritual], this rule is intended solely as a restrictive injunction (*niyama*) for the sitting that is already established by the general technical rules (*paribhāṣā*):
one offers the subsequent sixteen oblations while seated,
but not even the *lāja* oblations.

They argue that, precisely because of this restrictive rule and in accordance with many other *gṛhya* texts, the oblation must be offered by one who remains even while transgressing our own uncontradicted practice.

That is not so; for in the marriage ceremony—which, through the production of the *aupāsana* fire and through the production of bodily consecration (*saṃskāra*), assists the sacrifice to be accomplished by both husband and wife—the primary status characterized by ownership belongs equally to the two.

Furthermore, regarding all enjoined rites, since there is a statement concerning the husband’s performance that "whatever duties are to be performed by you, they are to be done together with this bride," it follows, on the contrary, that women possess no independence.

However, the prohibition against remarriage for these women—even though they are not the primary [wives]—is established solely by the force of the injunction: "Therefore, one woman does not obtain two husbands" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.6.4).
Therefore...

Since there would otherwise result either an absence of restriction regarding the internal positioning according to logic, or its opposite, this injunction is intended as a restrictive rule (*niyamārtha*)—stating that, by restating the act of sitting, the husband alone is the one who should sit in the proper place. Therefore, even the *lāja* oblations must be offered while sitting, in accordance with the rule:
"He offers the *darvihoma* oblations while sitting" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 3.10).

Thus, because all *darvīhoma* offerings are enjoined for us without distinction, and because even though many other *Gṛhya-sūtras* exist, they are not to be incorporated when a matter is already addressed within one's own *sūtra*. //5//
13. Circumambulation of the Fire, etc.:
Having circumambulated the fire to the right with the three following [verses], he causes him to step upon a stone as previously described. (ĀpGS 5.6)
With the three subsequent verses beginning with "tubhyam agre paryavahan," he circumambulates the fire from left to right.
Taking her by the hand, he begins the circumambulation at the end of the three verses;
for it is a rule that "a single ritual act may be accompanied by many mantras."

Since the number three is already established by the plural form "with the subsequent ones" (*uttarābhiḥ*), the explicit mention of "with three" (*tisṛbhiḥ*) is intended so that there may be only a single circumambulation with all three verses together, and not a repetition of the action for each individual mantra. //7//
With the three subsequent verses beginning with "For you, first, they led [the bride] around" (RV 10.85.36–38),
having circumambulated the fire from left to right, he makes her mount [the chariot] in the same manner as previously described, with the verse "Mount this one" (RV 10.85.21).
And the oblation is performed with the following [verse]. (ĀpGs 5.7)
The phrase "as before" is understood here; [he offers] with the following verse, namely, "Aryaman, indeed, the god... //8//
And the oblation of parched grain is performed with the following verse, "Aryaman, the god... (RV 5.4.5).
Again, the circumambulation. (ĀpGs 5.8)
The enema. ĀpGs 5.9.
Furthermore, the circumambulation of the fire must be performed, as well as the placing of the stone.
The word "furthermore" (punar) is intended to indicate the repetition of the action;
by it, [the application of] the next three verses and so forth occurs. //9//
Circumambulation of the fire. //8//
Of the self. //9//
And the oblation is performed with the following verse. (ĀpGṛS 5.10)
With the next verse, "O Aryaman," he [should perform the rite]. //10//
With this verse, "Thou art Aryaman," [he should worship]. //10//
Again, the circumambulation. ĀpGs 5.11.
The word "again" (punar) is as before. //11//

In the five sūtras beginning with "The oblation is performed with the following [verse]," the phrase "as before" is to be supplied as an ellipsis; and the elliptical supplements "the rite is to be performed" and "the rite" are to be added according to the gender of each case. //11//
One undertakes the Jaya and other rites. (ĀpGs 5.12)
By the previous statement regarding the kindling of the fire and so forth, the application of the *tantra* (the ritual framework) was shown.
This present statement, however, is for the purpose of providing instruction on the "raft" (*kola*), so that the *jaya* and other offerings may take place after the circumambulation (*parikramaṇa*).

Otherwise, based on the rule "he offers the *jaya* and others," the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) would occur immediately after the offering of parched grain (*lājā-homa*), and the third circumambulation would follow only after that. //12//

The intended meaning of what has been stated is this: where the injunction is, there alone are the victory and other rites, not elsewhere; and among these, there is no taking hold (anvārambha). //12//
14. Immediately after the untying of the yoke-cord, she is led to her own home by means of a palanquin or similar conveyance.

Having performed the rites up to the sprinkling of water, he unties the yoke-cord with the two following verses; then he should either cause her to be driven away from there himself, or have her carried away. (ĀpGs 5.13)
The mention of "up to the sprinkling" (pariṣecanānta) is an indication for the remainder of the ritual procedure (*tantra*).
Therefore, at the end of the release of the *praṇītā* water, there must also be the release of the *yoktra* (thong).

Although it would have been established by the rule that one "proceeds with the *jaya*-hymns and so forth," the specific mention of "up to the sprinkling" is so that the release of the *yoktra* occurs immediately after that [the *praṇītā* release] and not at the time of departure.
[The release is performed] with the two subsequent [verses], namely "I release you" (*pra tvā muñcāmi*);
because of the scriptural statement that a single ritual action may have multiple mantras,
the release consists of two mantras.

The word "tataḥ" (then) is intended to ensure that there is no fixed rule regarding the time of departure for the unyoking; rather, it means one should set out whenever it is appropriate, whether tomorrow or immediately.
*Pravāhaṇa* is conveying [the body] by means of a chariot or similar vehicle; *prahāraṇa* is conveying it by means of a palanquin or similar vehicle carried by men.
The word "or" (vā) occurs in both instances in order to indicate that both positions are equal.

Otherwise, since the bringing of the chariot is taught here as being virtually perceptible, it would be understood as implying that the human vehicle—which is not so taught—is like the ritual procedure of the Agnihotra;
therefore, the word "or" is used in both cases.
Therefore, even in the case of human eyes, the mantras beginning with "ā rohatām uttarābhiḥ," "uttarayā," and "śaṃta uttarābhiḥ" become established. //13//
"Having performed [the rites] up to the final sprinkling (pariṣecana)" means that, by implication, he completes the remainder of the ritual procedure (tantra).
By that, he also performs the removal of the yoke-pin (śamyāpohana), the disposal of the praṇītā water, and the dismissal of the Brahman priest.
With the two verses beginning with "pra tvā muñcāmi," he unfastens the yoke-strap.
Immediately thereafter, he should cause that bride to mount an elephant or a horse.
One may cause a palanquin, a swing-chair, a chariot, or a man—or even a horse—to carry [the burden].
In both cases, the word *vā* (or) intervenes [between the verb and the object], according to Pāṇini 1.4.28: *avyavāhitāśca*.
The two occurrences of the word "vā" (or) are intended to indicate that these two injunctions are of equal status, and that neither is a mere secondary alternative (*anukalpa*).
Here, although the suffix *ktvā* is present in the word "vimucya," the fact that he says "tataḥ" (then) indicates [the following].
A statement containing the suffix *ktvā* does not necessarily prescribe anteriority of time or identity of agent.
Sometimes it merely prescribes an action alone, restating it as something already established, as in: "Having made the *veda*, having strewn around the fires" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 11.2.15).

For in this case, the act of preparing the Veda does not necessarily precede the strewing [of grass], because it must also be performed among the other acts such as the cleansing of the Veda, the sweeping of the fire-hall, and the smearing of the sacrificial ground. Likewise, here too, after performing the rites up to the final sprinkling, one "unfastens the yoke with two *uttrā* blades," because the sprinkling for the deceased and other such acts must be performed in the interval.
Likewise, regarding the *dadhigharma*, [the text says]: "At this time, having replied, 'The oblation is cooked,' and taking it, he goes to the Āhavanīya fire" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 13.3.4).

In that case as well, the Pratiprasthātṛ is the preparer of the *dadhigharma*, while the Adhvaryu is the performer of the offering; therefore, there is an absence of a common agent (*samānakartṛtva*).

Similarly, in another passage concerning the Aśvamedha, it is stated: "With the words, 'O slayer of Vṛtra, I and you have crossed over the lack of sacrificial fees,' the Brahman priest takes the hand of the sacrificer" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra).

Likewise, in this context: "Having caused [the student] to recite, 'And it has been remembered by me,' having given a choice gift to the teacher, and having raised him up with the words, 'Up! Long-lived one! (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 11.17). //13//
15. There is the perpetual maintenance of the nuptial fire.
Having gathered this fire, they carry it away. (ĀpGs 5.14)
Having placed this marriage fire into the mouth [of the vessel], the men belonging to the couple carry it behind them as they go.
The word "having placed" (samopya) is for the purpose of prohibiting the ritual depositing (*samāropaṇa*) seen in the case of the *śrauta* fires.
By making this prohibition, he shows that in the rule "the fire is to be churned after following [the bride]," the churning is not from the embers as in the *śrauta* rites.
The word "anu" serves the purpose of prohibiting the carrying forward [of the ritual] from the preceding [context]. //14//
Having kindled this *vivāhāgni*, they carry it following the *ukhā* (the cooking-pot). The attendants lead it behind the bride without any interval between them.

The inclusion of the word "this" (*etam*) is for the purpose of ensuring that the *vivāhāgni*—known as the *aupāsana*, which is manifested by its technical name—is always physically carried even during a journey. If "this" were not included, then, for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*), the ordinary worldly fire (*laukikāgni*) used for all purposes would be carried instead.
And for the *aupāsana* fire, there shall be a ritual depositing (*samāropaṇa*) prescribed by another *gṛhya* text in the event of departure.
It is eternal. ĀpGs 5.15.
It should be worn. ĀpGs 5.16.
This nuptial fire is perpetual and eternal; it is to be maintained for the sake of the rites related to one's wife. //15//
From the time of taking the hand in marriage, this fire is perpetual for the purpose of performing all rites characterized by proper conduct; it is not abandoned as long as one lives.
"The fire beginning with the taking of the hand is called the *aupāsana*."
This is because of the statement of Hiraṇyakeśin: "In that [fire], the domestic rites [are performed]" (HirGṛ 26.1, 2).
Therefore, even when the marriage ceremony, together with its ancillaries, has been completed, it is said: "When the rite has concluded, it becomes worldly" (ĀpDhS 4.22).
Thus, it does not exist. //15//

Since "eternal" (*nitya*) is already established, the commencement with the word "to be maintained" (*dhārya*) implies that even at the time of death, the ritual placement (*samāropaṇa*) of the fire either within the self or in the two kindling sticks (*araṇī*), as prescribed in other *Gṛhya* texts, would not be optional. This is just as in the case of the rule, "He offers all expiatory oblations (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) with the *juhū* or the *sruva* ladle" (*Śrauta-sūtra* 2.11.1),
where the rule "the Adhvaryu is the performer" (*Āpastamba-pariśiṣṭa* 1.26) [restricts the agent].
Because of this statement, the Adhvaryu alone is the performer;

the Brahman priest, who is prescribed by the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra in the rule "he makes [the Brahman] offer the expiatory oblation" (Āśva. Śrau. 1.1.16), is not an option even by way of alternative.

And thus, according to the rule "having brought this fire together, they carry it after [the bride]" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 5.14), this is a duty for all [occasions], not only for the departure at a wedding.
Just as the rule prescribed for the departure of the fire-possessor— namely, "having brought these two fires together and having reloaded them"— is intended for all purposes, so too,
even though ritualists do not desire an option (*vikalpa*) in such cases, [the rule applies universally].
Nevertheless, there is evidence for the existence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in this regard:

"The sons born of a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*) who has not been previously married to another, according to the injunctions of the scriptures, have a connection with [the father's] ritual duties and an undivided inheritance from both parents; however, there is fault in sexual intercourse with one who has already been married to another, with one who has not been consecrated by marriage rites, or with a woman of a different caste" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.13.1–3).
Having thus prohibited the taking of a wife from a different caste (*asavarṇadārasaṅgrahaṇa*), the author of the Sūtra himself states: "He [is entitled] to three castes" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.2).

The meaning of the word "three" has been explained by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) as follows: "For he has three wives who are not prohibited according to the statements of other Smṛtis; the number 'three' is for the purpose of establishing his entitlement (*adhikāra*) together with them."
From this sūtra and its commentary, it is understood that the taking of a wife from a different class (asavarṇadārasaṅgraha), though prescribed by other Smṛtis, is not prohibited in every respect;
and this serves as an indicator of the existence of such an option (vikalpa) in other similar cases as well. // 13 //
He states the origin of this domestic fire (*aupāsana*) that has been kindled: "16. When [the wood] has been followed, there is churning;
when it has been followed, it is to be churned. (ĀpGS 5.17)
"Anugata" means "udvāta," that which is produced by churning (*manthana*).
According to this view, even in the case of marriage (*vivāha*), its origin is this very same [process];
and the maintenance (*dhāraṇa*) of both [the fire and the ritual] takes place from the time of marriage onwards.
In that marriage ceremony, churning with the two fire-drills is prescribed; if they have been consumed by fire, it is said that one should churn from the very embers themselves.
In the absence of those, one should touch the fire-drills with ashes and then churn. 16.
If this fire has gone out, it should be produced by friction from those very same kindling woods (*avakṣaṇa*).
If they are not available or are incapable [of producing fire], then one should produce it by rubbing the lower fire-drill (*araṇi*) against the base block (*upaveṣa*). //17//
17. Or it may be brought from the house of a Śrotriya;
or it is to be fetched from the house of a Śrotriya. ĀpGs 5.18.
A Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with learning, conduct, and Vedic study is a Śrotriya; from the cooking fire in his house, [the nuptial fire] is to be taken.
According to this view, even in the case of marriage, this alone is its source. //17//
Alternatively, it may be brought from the house of one who has studied the Vedas;
and this is a settled option:
if the marriage takes place when the fire has been churned, then it is to be produced by churning.
If the fire has been brought [from elsewhere], then it is to be brought back;
or if the fire is lost or stolen, this same procedure for its production applies.
This is because the term "followed" (anugata) is intended to indicate both being lost and being stolen. //18//
He states the expiation:
18. In that case, one of the two spouses shall observe a fast;
and the fast may be observed by either the wife or the husband. (ĀpGs 5.19)
In this case, the connection between the words is established by assuming an ellipsis.
When the fire has gone out, there is fasting for both the wife and the husband, or for either one of them;
the word "ca" (and) serves to indicate the conjunction of fasting for both.
"Of the wife and of the husband":
the word "vā" (or) has the sense of an option regarding either one of them;
that is, "or of either one of those two."
Fasting consists of not eating at both meal-times;
this is well known from tradition. Furthermore, immediately after following [the deceased], the establishment of the fire and the performance of the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblation take place.
[Objection: But surely "the fire-drill has been followed" was the subject under discussion; so why is there this mention of a cause with the word "followed"?
[Response: It is said: the departure of the husband and wife is what is under discussion here, as in the passage, "Then he should cause her to lead it forth."
However, the rule regarding fire is incidental (*prāsaṅgika*);
consequently, the procedure for the fast (*upavāsa*) would also be understood as having no remaining connection [to the main subject].
And in that case, there would be no connection with the incidental [rules] such as "for three nights both [husband and wife] sleep on the ground and observe celibacy" (*brahmacarya*).
However, it is by means of the very context [of the rule] that [the application is established].

Since it would already be established that when both follow [the husband], there is fasting for both or for either one, the separate mention of "of the wife" and "of the husband" is intended to demonstrate that this fire has an absolute connection with the wife. For this very reason, the wife is mentioned first; therefore, in any rite where the wife does not have the status of a co-participant—such as in the acts of bringing forward (upākaraṇa) and concluding (samāpana)—there is no application of this fire in her case.
And in rites such as the subjugation of rivals, even though there is no co-operation with the husband, the engagement with this fire occurs solely due to the connection with the wife. //18//
The fast—meaning the abstention from food—belonging to either time, whether day or night, pertains to either the wife or the husband.
The word "ca" (and) serves to indicate the conjunction of the rites for the production of fire and the expiation.

If the fire goes out before the meal, whether during the day or the night, then, having churned it out or brought it back, one should re-establish it according to the rule "wherever [the fire] is," and [proceed] with the verse, "If it is unknown, or if there is total destruction."

Having performed the *sarvaprāyaścitta* (universal expiation), one should fast for the remainder of that time; if it occurs after a meal, then one should fast for the remainder of that time and for the subsequent period as well. However, in the case of following [a corpse] when it has merely been recognized, the rites such as the production [of fire] and so forth must be performed.
Because the effect must necessarily be performed immediately after the cause.

Others, however, maintain that fasting is obligatory for both husband and wife and is not optional, because their status as owners [of the ritual] is identical, as stated in *Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra* 2.1.4: "And on the parvan days, there is fasting for both."
Thus, because a combination [of options] is observed in the Smṛti tradition,
and since the word "or" (vā) has the sense of "and" (ca),
the sūtra need only have been stated as: "Their fast, or that of either one."
By the very fact of the matter, the fast will apply to both masters as well.

Some, having split the sūtra—*upavāsaścānyatarasya bhāryāyāḥ patyurvānugate*—explain it by assuming a disjointed syntactical connection (*vyavahitānvaya*), [interpreting it as]: "When [the husband] has followed [the wife] into the fire, there is fasting for the wife, for the husband, or for either one.
In this context, however, since the word *anugata* (followed) is mentioned again, such incidental meanings would not be possible without further effort.
However, it is for the purpose of making known that this is indeed the primary meaning of the subject matter. //19//
Or, even if [the impurity] has passed, one should avoid eating with her; one should not fast.
With the following verse, "And come hither, O Agni," one should offer a single oblation.

This oblation does not possess a formal ritual framework (*tantra*); however, the spreading of grass around the fire, the preparation of the clarified butter, and the cleansing of the offering-spoon (*darvī*) do take place.

Since the optionality is already established by the very word "api vā" (or else), this offering is intended to serve as a substitute specifically for the fast (*upavāsa*), so that it may take its place.
Consequently, even in this case, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) with the *sarvaprāyaścitta* oblation.
This same expiation (*prāyaścitta*) should also be understood to apply when the fire is destroyed by theft or other such causes.
Regarding the intentional abandonment of this very fire or its interruption after twelve days, an expiation has been stated in another Smṛti;
in that case as well, the re-establishment of the fire (agnisaṃskāra) is exactly the same. //19//
Alternatively, if the fire has gone out, one should offer clarified butter with the verse "O Agni, come hither" (RV 6.16.41), but one should not fast.
Because of the repeated mention of "gone out," this option does not apply when the fire is lost or carried away;
rather, in those cases, there must be a fast.

Or rather, since the alternative of fasting has already been excluded by this very [preceding] statement, and because it begins with "he shall not fast," this option applies to fasting alone; however, even here, there is indeed an expiation. //20//
19. The specific details regarding travel by chariot:
the *uttarā* is the prop for the chariot. (ĀpGs 5.21)
Now, the specific duties for the departure of the couple are taught.
Regarding the verse beginning with "uttarā satyenottabhitā," the meaning is that the support of the chariot must be performed with this verse as the means of supporting the chariot.
By what [means]? By means of a boon, because he has been authorized. //20//
"Uttarā is supported by truth"—this is the mantra for the support, the means of propping up the chariot. //21//
He yokes the two draft animals with the two [verses] beginning with "vāhā," the right one first.
The two by which the chariot is drawn are the two draft-animals, whether they be horses or oxen.
With the following two [verses], they yoke the sun:
"In the yoking..."
With these two [verses], he yokes— that is, he fastens the yoke-pins;
with "yuñjanti" (they yoke), the southern one, and with "yoge yoge" (in every yoking), the northern one.
Some maintain that there is a conjunction of each [of the two] with both [the preceding and the following]. //21//

That is to say, subsequently [the movement] is to the left; and when facing westward, the statement does not apply. Otherwise, it is established that the completion of the rite occurs in that manner. //22//
With the next two verses, "They yoke the ruddy steed" and "In every yoking," he fastens either the draft-horses or the oxen to the yoke-pole and the shaft;
and of these two, he anoints the right side first—
two verses for each animal.

Not at all; for here, by means of a *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one) that sets aside the *dvandva* (copulative compound) in the expression "with the two subsequent [verses]," both mantras—which are denoted as being in mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*) in relation to the action of joining mentioned alongside them—are employed together, according to the principle:
"Ritual acts consist of a single mantra" (Āpastamba Paribhāṣā-sūtra 1.41).
This is an exception to the rule of *itva*.
[Objection: But in that case, would not the second mantra have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārthatā*)? [Reply:
True; nevertheless—

Based on the statement of the most authoritative commentator that "one [verse] for each pair," it is inferred that when performing the recitation of two mantras together in each single application, this practice pervades all places, times, and performers.
(ĀpGS 5.22) He consecrates the woman as she ascends with the following verses. (ĀpGS 5.23)
Then the bride mounts that yoked chariot.
As she is mounting, he consecrates her with the four verses beginning with "uttarābhiḥ" and "sukiṃśukam.

Because of the use of the plural number here, there would otherwise be the contingency of using three or more verses without restriction; however, by virtue of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, the rule is established that exactly four are to be used.
In the case of a vehicle, all such acts as uplifting [the wheels] and so forth occur;
and it has been stated that for horses, men, and others, rites such as consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) and those pertaining to the duties of husband and wife take place.
Based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra "O good wheel" (*sucakra*), some maintain that the mantras apply only to the chariot.
Others hold that because the mantra is intended for the handing over of the bride, its reference to the chariot is a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). //23//
"She mounts the chariot"— the form *marohantīm* for *ārohantīm* is a Vedic (chāndasa) phenomenon where the nasal (*n*) is elided;
[and the word] "sukiṃśukam."
With these four [verses] beginning with "ityādi," he consecrates [the chariot];
he consecrates the chariot itself as she is mounting it, not the horse or other parts, because that would contradict the grammatical gender in the word *sucakrim*.
Or he consecrates her with the three verses beginning with "ud uttaram" as she mounts the horse and the other animals. //23//
20. The manner of yoking the two draft animals: On the path, he spreads out grass with the subsequent [formula]: blue grass on the southern [track] and red grass on the northern [track]. (ĀpGS 5.24)
The two sūtras concerning "blue and red" refer to both tracks of the chariot;
this is a future designation for those two tracks upon which the two wheels of the chariot are intended to roll.
It is more appropriate to read the word as *vartinyoḥ* (of the two rolling [tracks]).
And thus, the use of the feminine gender in the subsequent passage—"in the south" and "in the north"—is appropriate. The prefix *vi-* has the sense of "obliquely";
he spreads it obliquely.
With the verse beginning "nīlalohita," namely this one [RV 10.85.28]. //24//
Of those two cords, that which is blue he spreads out upon the southern path. //25//
"In the northern one" means on the track of the left wheel;
having grasped the cord simultaneously, he spreads it out all at once with the mantra,
even though there is a difference in location, because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra.
Another says: "The repetition of the mantra is due to the difference in location.
However, the mounting [of the horse] should be understood as being like the *sānnāyya* pot; [the mantra is recited]: "For the non-falling of the sacrifice, I place the two hooves.
There is no spreading of the ritual grass (*sūtra-vyavastaraṇa*) upon the horse and other animals, because of the construction of the chariot. 26.
The term *vartman* means "the two tracks" (*vartanyoḥ*).

Because of the feminine gender in the expression "the blue one on the right" (*nīlaṃ dakṣiṇasyām*), [it refers to] the two future tracks of the chariot; with the verse beginning "The blue and red ones arise" (*nīlalohite bhavataḥ ud*), he spreads out two threads, weaving them across.
And this occurs simultaneously,
as indicated by the dual number in the expression "blue and red exist."
And upon those two cords, he spreads a blue one on the southern cord and a red one on the northern cord. // 24 //
He approaches them with the following verses. ĀpGs 5.25.
He approaches and passes over those [verses] in the Sūtra with the three subsequent Ṛg-verses beginning with "ye vadhvaścandra" (those who [follow] the bride, O Moon);
while proceeding there by chariot, he thus passes over them.

The mantras should be recited even when proceeding on horseback and so forth, because they serve the purpose of going; this is not for the sake of [mere] movement. The restriction to three [mantras] follows from the indicative mark (liṅga) of the mantra.
The commencement of the journey takes place at the end of the three. // 27 //
With the three verses beginning "The moon of the bride," he goes over—that is, passes above—the stretched-out thread. // 25 //
21. Recitation is occasional;
furthermore, one should recite the Uttara [verse] upon passing by a sacred bathing place, a pillar, or a crossroads. (ĀpGs 5.26)

"Passing beyond" (*atītyagamanam*) means "transgression" (*atikrama*); "transgression" itself is "violation" (*vyatikrama*), where the prefix *vi-* is redundant, just as *upāya* is synonymous with *abhyāya*.
The bridegroom should mutter the following verse: "Tāmandasāna... and so forth.
If there is an omission of the *nimitta*, there is a repetition of the recitation (*japa*).
The word "and" (*ca*) is intended to connect [the term] with each instance of recitation;
otherwise, [it would not apply].
When there is a simultaneous transgression of the three [periods], recitation (japa) should be performed, according to the indicative mark of the mantra;
for in that mantra, holy bathing places and the like are not being praised,
but rather the two Aśvins.
Therefore, one should not object that the mention of the other two [senses] in the case of transgression would be useless, nor should one suspect the removal of those words. // 28 //
A *tīrtha* is a sacred bathing place, a holy river, and so forth;
a *sthāṇu* is a post driven into the ground for the purpose of scratching cows;
a *catuṣpatha* is a well-known crossroads.
In the event of transgressing these [rules], one should mutter the verse beginning with "atā mandasāna.
Furthermore, even upon transgressing any one of the rules regarding sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and so forth, the entire verse must be muttered, and not the verse deprived of its other words.
Since direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is stronger than indicative mark (*liṅga*), as in the case of "One worships the Gārhapatya fire with the Aindrī verse.
[Objection: But in this case, the direct statement must be inferred from established practice (*ācāra*); therefore, it is not proper for it to sublate the indicative mark.

It is not so; for in this case, the inferential mark (*liṅga*) is dependent upon the subject matter of the *śoṣi* and other rites prescribed by direct revelation (*śruti*). Indeed, the weakness of an inferable revelation occurs only where it is contradicted by a directly perceived revelation.
Therefore, even an inferable revelation is certainly capable of subverting an inferential mark that is itself dependent on something else.
However, the distinction in the application of words such as *tīrtha* and others is justified by the difference in the employment of mantras when those respective [words] are transposed.
Therefore, even when *tīrtha* is transposed, the words *sthāṇu* and *patha* denote *tīrtha* itself due to their commonality with the location of a foolish person (*durmati*).
Likewise, the other two [words] denote *sthāṇu*.
The other two [mantras] also [apply] to the crossroads.
