Just as in the mantra for gathering the fuel, the words *upaveṣa*, *mekṣaṇa*, and *dhṛṣṭi* refer to the very pieces of wood used for the fuel, because they share the common property of being wood touched by fire;
or as in the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), there is a consecration with the following two [mantras].
"Smelling [the child] on the head, and recitation in the right ear" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 15.1);
because of the commonality of these actions— consecration, smelling, and recitation— as rites for the consecration of a newborn, one says, "I smell [you]."

Furthermore, since the Aśvins are being praised as the primary subjects, and since it is from them that one seeks protection against the affliction arising from the transgression of sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and so forth, the recitation (*japa*) must be performed with the text in its unaltered form.
Moreover, if other words were substituted, there would be the undesirable consequence of breaking the *jagatī* meter.
Logically speaking, a mantra used for recitation is not intended to convey a specific meaning; therefore, neither the sacred fords nor the Aśvins are denoted here with any intentional significance.
Therefore, the recitation of the entire [formula] alone is well-founded;
this same principle applies to the crossing of rivers and desert wastes. //26//
Sixth Section. 22. When crossing a river by boat while on the journey, there is a recitation. He consecrates the boat with the *uttarā* verse. (ĀpGS 6.1)

Now, if on the way there should be a river, a pond, or a lake to be crossed by boat, he addresses the boat with the verse, "May this [boat] carry us to the further shore, for our well-being," meaning he should recite it over it. Standing behind [the boat] and looking at it, the utterance of the mantra is what constitutes the *anumantraṇa* (addressing).
Once the consecration has been performed, the bridegroom and the bride mount it.
If a river must be crossed by boat on the way, then the groom consecrates the boat with the verse, "May this [boat] carry us to the further shore.
Thereupon, both of them ascend it together with the fire. 1.
And while spreading the mats on the boat, the bride must not look about.

Those who lead the boat are "boat-people" (*nāvyāḥ*), namely fishermen; "while crossing" (*tāratī*) means at the time of crossing. Although the feminine gender alone would have sufficed [to indicate a woman], the inclusion of the word *vadhū* (bride) is so that the prohibition against looking may apply specifically to the bride.
"Having crossed by means of that, he should recite [the mantra]" refers specifically to the bridegroom;
the word "and" (ca) is for the purpose of showing that both the bride and the bridegroom cross together.
Thus, they both cross.

Regarding the phrase "and this is another specific feature of the bride," some explain that "nāvyā" refers to waters that are crossed by boat; for them, the use of the masculine gender [in the compound] is untenable. // 2 //
"Nāvya" refers to ships, their navigators, and fishermen;
"tāri" is a Vedic form meaning "crossing over" at the time of crossing.
"Tarantī" means while she is crossing.
The substitution of *śatṛ* [for the present participle suffix] occurs according to Pāṇini 3.2.126: *lakṣaṇahetvoḥ kriyāyāḥ*. [Thus, the meaning is:
"the bride should not see [him]."
By the use of the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that there is a prohibition against the bride seeing the crossing, and that the groom alone should cross together [with the bride]. //2//
Having crossed over, one should recite the Uttara-mantra.
Having crossed over and reached the northern bank, the bridegroom should mutter the verse beginning with "asya pāre.
If it is not a river, then he should also mutter the verse beginning with "yā oṣadhayaḥ," for the author will state later that this applies upon crossing rivers and auspicious landmarks. //3//
Having reached the further shore, one should mutter this very [verse]: "On the further shore of this. //3//
23. An oblation is performed when passing through a cremation ground or similar places.

When passing over a cremation ground, or when a vessel or a chariot is damaged, he kindles the fire and, after the *ājyabhāga* offerings, while she holds on to him, he offers the subsequent oblations; then he proceeds with the *jaya* and following rites, performing everything up to the final sprinkling of water.
(ĀpGS 6.4)

If one transgresses over a cremation ground, or if a vessel, a bowl, or the like, or a chariot is broken or lost, the following oblation shall be performed for such ill omens as these and others of a similar kind;
herein, the ritual procedure beginning with the kindling of the fire is undertaken.
Because of the use of the prefix *adhi*, this [action] occurs only when one goes over the cremation ground;
however, in the case of sacred fords (*tīrtha*) and the like, it occurs even when one passes by them. //4//
He offers the subsequent oblations;
the meaning is that he offers these seven oblations with these subsequent mantras beginning with "yadṛte cid.
The restriction to seven is established by the indicative mark (liṅga) of the mantras.
Having performed the oblation, he proceeds with the remainder of the ritual according to the Jayādi-tantra.
The use of the vessel is performed once;
the śamyā sticks serve the purpose of the enclosing-sticks (paridhi).

The statement beginning with "the kindling of the fire" (agner upasamādhāna) is for the purpose of establishing the ritual framework (tantra); the statement ending with "the two portions of clarified butter" (ājyabhāga) is for the purpose of instructing on the time for the assistant's holding-on (anvārambha);
and the phrase "he proceeds with the Jaya and other offerings" is for the purpose of ensuring the non-cessation of that holding-on.
In this way, one attains victory and the other results exactly as they were established. //5//

This refers to the ritual acts beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the sprinkling of water; immediately following that, he performs the occasional rite (*naimittika*) that has been prescribed.

The meaning is that he does it only once, and not repeatedly. Even if the previously mentioned occasions (*nimitta*) recur due to differences in place or time, this oblation (*homa*) is to be performed only once at the end. //6//
When there is a transgression regarding the cemetery or when one passes over the ground of the cemetery,
or when a vessel— such as a bride’s ornament— is damaged, or when a chariot is wrecked,
he performs the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the sprinkling of water.
It has already been stated that in sacrifices where clarified butter alone is the oblation, there is no *tantra* (common procedure) in the absence of a specific scriptural injunction.

The phrase "ending with the *ājyabhāga*s" is intended to prescribe the time for the commencement of the subsequent rites. These are the seven oblations performed with the formula beginning "without the *vidanti* [verses]" (*yadṛte vidadbhiśriṣaḥ*).
The remainder is clear. //4//
24. When one has crossed [a boundary], a recitation (japa) must be performed.

Upon crossing milky trees or other trees possessing auspicious marks, as well as rivers and deserts, one should recite the subsequent [mantras] according to their respective characteristics. (ĀpGs 6.5)
This refers to milky trees such as the *nyagrodha* and others that are not easily identifiable, as well as other well-known boundary trees that possess distinctive marks (*lakṣaṇa*).
Even with the reading *lakṣmaṇyānām*, the meaning remains the same.

Upon crossing rivers—whether containing water or devoid of it—and across arid wastes and forests, one should recite the two subsequent verses according to their respective characteristics (*liṅga*); that is, upon crossing whichever [terrain] for which a characteristic is observed in a verse, one should mutter that verse. Among these, upon crossing a tree, one should recite: "Those Gandharvas... and so forth.
Regarding the crossing of a river with the mantra "The herbs that... and the crossing of a desert with "Those deserts that...":
both mantras are to be used in both situations according to their respective gender and number, so that it does not happen otherwise.
It remains complete even when crossing a river; likewise, it remains complete even when crossing a desert. //7//

*Kṣīriṇaḥ* are those possessing milky sap, such as the *plakṣa*, *nyagrodha*, and others; *lakṣmaṇyaḥ* are those characterized by specific marks, such as the *durgā*, *tintriṇikā*, *sīmā*, *kadamba*, and so forth;
*nadyaḥ* are the well-known rivers; and *dhanvan* refers to long stretches of wilderness where domestic animals do not dwell.
In the event of transgressing against these, one should mutter the subsequent [mantras] according to their respective characteristics.
The formula "O Gandharvas" is used when crossing trees;
"O Herbs" is used for rivers and deserts.
The statement "according to their respective characteristics" is made so that it may not be like the *jātakarman* rite.
In the phrase "of those yielding milk" (*kṣīriṇām*), etc., the plurality is not intended to be significant,
because it resides in the cause [the material],
just as in the case of the "dual nature of the oblation" (*havir-ubhayatva*). //5//
He causes them to look upon the house with the *uttarā* verse.

Then, having reached his own home and helped her descend from the chariot, he brings that wealth which had come as her dowry into the house; thereafter, with the subsequent ṛc beginning "I cause them to appear" (*saṅkāśayāmi*), he causes her to look at them properly—that is, he makes her examine them.
And the mantra should be applied to this purpose in whatever way is appropriate.

I cause to appear; I show the dowry—the wealth brought from the bride's father’s family—with a benevolent and non-terrible gaze, O Brahman. Not merely with a non-terrible gaze, but with a benevolent one. "Together with my houses" means together with my own home.
That ornament called Viśvarūpa which is fastened upon her—look at that; the plural number is used for the singular.
"May Savitṛ make my husband's face pleasant for me. //8//

With the verse, "I cause the bride to see her excellent home, endowed with kinsmen and wealth," he causes her to see— that is, he shows it to her. Now, although the prefix *sam-* is seen in the sense of "together" in such passages as "having taken portions together from the two milkings" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.20.3),
[it is used here in the sense of "to see"].
Nevertheless, how is it determined that what is intended here is precisely the state of the houses being accompanied by kinsmen and wealth?
It is said: on account of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "to carry [them] as it were to Saṅkāśyā.
And the meaning of the mantra is as stated in the Bhāṣya. //7//
He unyokes the two draft animals with the two northern verses, releasing the right one first.
With the two subsequent [verses], namely "āvāmagan" and "ayaṃ no devassavitā," the unyoking is performed with each mantra individually, as in the case of the yoking. //9//
That is to say, the left [hand] is behind. //10//
With the two verses beginning "āvāmagan," he releases one horse each day. //7//

25. Entering the House: Having spread a red bull’s hide with its neck toward the east and its hair upward in the middle of the house, reciting the next verse, he causes [the bride] to step forward into the house with her right foot. (ĀpGS 6.8)

Having unyoked the two draft-animals, the excellent man himself enters the house where the couple reside; there, in the middle of the dwelling, he spreads a bull's hide with the following verse, "A refuge, a protection," which is red in color. The manner of spreading it is such that the hair is directed toward the north and the neck toward the east.
Having spread [the grass], he then causes her to step forward with his right foot into the house;

he causes the bride to enter. While causing her to step forward, he makes her recite the next verse, "The houses... Although "houses" was already mentioned in the context, it is stated again as "into the houses"—for otherwise, since the chariot had also been the subject of discussion, one might suspect that the mantra applied to the entry into the vehicle rather than the house.
This very point is the indicator that the spreading of the skin takes place within the inner chamber.
Because of the statement "he causes [the sacrificer] to recite while offering," there is a simultaneous connection of the mantra and the ritual act;
the offering does not take place at the end of the mantra. //11//

Then the groom, having first entered his own house, spreads out a skin according to the ritual manual with the mantra "śarma varma," and then, leading the bride into the house by making her step forward with her right foot, he makes her recite the verse "gṛhān bhadrān. //8//
And he does not stand upon the threshold.
The *dehalī* is the wooden plank beneath the door;
others say it is the surrounding platform (*paryantavedikā*). The meaning is that at the time of entering, neither he nor she should step over it.
When the two have prostrated themselves, he leads them toward the fire.

Then, having entered the house, he should eat his meal at that time; thereafter, in whichever house the skin is spread out, there he should place the vessels once for all, using yoke-pins as the enclosing sticks.
And she, upon entering, does not touch the threshold;
some say that by the word "and" (ca), the bridegroom also [does not touch it]. //9//
26. The Entrance Oblation (praveśahoma):

In the northeast part of the house, having performed the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, while she maintains contact with him, he offers the subsequent oblations;

then he proceeds with the *jaya* and following rites. Having performed everything up to the sprinkling of water (*pariṣecana*), they both sit down upon the skin according to the next [verse], with the bridegroom to the north. (ĀpGs 6.10)

The bridegroom alone offers the thirteen principal oblations of the subsequent section, beginning with "āgan goptha," even though there is a conflict with the indicative mark (liṅga), because the injunction (vidhi) is more powerful;
and the indicative mark is not intended to be significant here.

Since mantras serve the purpose of recollecting the deities, it has been stated that the rule "the subsequent [mantra] is the boon" applies as a specific feature in all oblations (*homa*). The injunction "in the north-eastern part of the sacrificial ground" is to be understood as applying to the fire in every instance. //14//
With the following verse, "O cows, be propagated here," they both sit down.
This statement regarding the end of the ritual sprinkling implies that the sitting must be performed immediately thereafter and nothing else;
by this, it is established that the meal takes place beforehand.
Regarding that act of sitting down, the mantra belongs to both [the bride and the groom].
Since there is no connection with the fire here, it is stated that the groom sits facing north;
and they both sit facing the east. //15//
With the thirteen oblations beginning with "They have come" (RV 10.85.18), and with the following verse,
"O cows, be propagated here," they both sit down upon the skin previously spread out.
As before, the latter alone is superior. //10//
27. The giving of fruit to the son of a woman whose sons are living.
28. The restraint of speech for the couple.

Then, having seated the son of that woman whose sons are living upon her lap from among two men, having given the fruits to him with the subsequent Yajus formula, and having recited the subsequent [formula], they both restrain their speech.
Until the stars appear. (ĀpGṛS 6.11)
She who gives birth only to males and not to females is a "puṃśū" (male-bearer). Regarding her, the reading is *puṃsvo jīvaputrāyāḥ*;
the letter *repha* (the visarga) should not be recited, or if it is recited, it should be regarded as a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).

"Jīvaputrā" (one whose sons are living) and "jīvapatyā" (one whose husband is living) should be understood as referring to one whose children are indeed living and have not been lost. Likewise, regarding "auspicious things":
for such a woman of the three higher castes, [the father] should offer a son to this bride with the verse beginning "asomenādityā... (O Ādityas, with Soma...).

Having seated the boy on his lap and having given fruits to him with the subsequent Yajus formula, "May you go forth in well-being," and then having murmured the two subsequent Ṛg-verses, "What is dear here" and "These auspicious ones," both of them, sitting upon that very skin, restrain their speech.
"Until the stars" means until the rising of the constellations;
and the boy, having taken the fruits, goes according to his purpose. //16//

The reading in the *Ṛgveda* is "puṃsvāḥ" (from the root *puṃs-*); she who gives birth only to males and not even to females, and who gives birth [naturally] and is not barren—having become possessed of sons through purchase or other means—is a "puṃsūḥ.
She whose sons are living males is a "jīvaputrā."

Furthermore, because of the rule for the formation of a single remainder (*ekaśeṣa*), "brother and son [are used in the dual] with sister and daughter" (Pāṇini 1.2.68), even in the case where one's daughters are also living and only one son is living, [the term *putrau* would apply].
She too is intended here as one whose son is living, because otherwise the qualification "between two males" would be untenable.

Having seated the son of such a woman on her lap with the verse "The Ādityas [have placed him] with Soma," having given fruits such as plantains to the son with the *yajus* formula "May he stand forth," and having murmured the two *ṛc*s beginning with "May he be dear here through offspring,"—
Both of them restrain their speech until the stars appear, that is, until the rising of the constellations. //11//
29. Showing the Dhruva and Arundhatī to the bride:

When the stars have risen, having gone out toward the eastern or northern direction, he shows her the Dhruva and Arundhatī with the two following mantras, according to their respective characteristics. (ĀpGs 6.12)
Because of the statement "when the stars have risen," their sitting upon that very same hide while restraining speech must take place prior to that; afterwards follows the departure.
Although the rising [of the stars] alone would suffice, the mention of "stars" (*nakṣatra*) is for the sake of clarity.
[The departure is performed] with the two subsequent verses, namely *dhruvakṣitir* and *saprarkṣayaḥ*.
In both cases, the act of seeing the bride is performed with the mantra;
however, while the groom sees her, he first causes her to recite [the verse] "dhruvam" (the Pole Star), and then the subsequent one, "vasvadarundhatīm" (Vasu and Arundhatī).

Then follows the release of speech. Since the seeing according to the respective signs is already established by the indicative power (*liṅga*) of the mantras themselves, the explicit mention of "according to the signs" is for the purpose of allowing an option.
"By means of the two subsequent [verses], he shows Dhruva and Arundhatī according to their respective characteristics (yathāliṅgam).
According to this, in the case of the northern verse, the ritual act for the bride consists of the simultaneous showing of all the Seven Sages, beginning with Kṛttikā, as well as Arundhatī;
or alternatively, it may consist of the showing of Arundhatī alone. //17//

With the two following verses, "The firm-seated, the firm-born" and so forth, according to their respective indicative marks (*liṅga*), he shows the Pole Star (*dhruva*) with the preceding verse together with the seer's name, and Arundhatī with the subsequent one, to the bride.
The phrase "according to their respective indicative marks" is used so that, as in the birth-rite (*jātakarma*), it does not happen that each single verse is applied to both stars.
Some say that [the rule] "according to the gender" does not exist here;
rather, due to the negligence of the reciters, what was seen in another location has been transposed and read here.
With the next two [verses], he shows, respectively, Dhruva and Arundhatī;
or, having divided the Sūtra according to the indicative marks (*yathā-liṅgam*), they explain it as requiring an ellipsis to be supplied:
"With this [verse] beginning with *sapta ṛṣayaḥ prathamām*, he shows the Seven Seers, Kṛttikā, and Arundhatī together."
"Or rather, it applies even while [the substance] is being cooked," this is for the purpose of providing an option; "according to the gender and number [of the original substance]. //12//
In the second chapter, this *Paryadarśana* has been composed by Sudarśanārya according to the commentary and according to his own understanding; let it be accepted.
Thus ends the sixth section in the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
The second chapter is completed.
Now begins the third chapter,
the seventh section.
30. The *sthālīpāka* for Agni. (Its rules:
Now he causes her to sacrifice with the *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Agni. (ĀpGS 7.1)
From the word "atha" (now), it follows that on this very night a *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooked offering) is performed.
It is called *sthālīpāka* because it is cooked in a pot (*sthālī*). The prescription for its deity is: "to Agni."
But will it not be prescribed that "Agni is the deity, with the offering made by the utterance of Svāhā"?
True;
however, there is another [text] regarding that as well: "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second."
Furthermore, if that itself were the injunction regarding the deity, this oblation would have two deities;
consequently, at the time of the pouring out (nirvapaṇa), the formal resolve (saṅkalpa) would have to be made for both of them.
Even though, in reality, the Sviṣṭakṛt sacrifice is subordinate, it is nevertheless enjoined there as if it were primary, in the words: "Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt is the second."
And therefore, an intention would have to be formed for that [offering] as well;
thus, this *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Agni is [regarded as] independent. (It must be stated that it belongs solely to the act of offering to Agni.)

If this expiation applies to the case where the portion has not yet been offered to the deity, then for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, it applies only to the case where the portion has already been offered to the deity. Because of the statement, "He causes her to sacrifice," there is no joint performance of both [offerings] in this ritual act.
This ritual action belongs solely to the bride,
whereas the officiating of the priestly duties belongs to the groom.
Therefore, this preparation of the *sthālīpāka* and the offering of rice and other items as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) belong exclusively to the bride's property.
Regarding this, it is said: "Grant us a share of our household property" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.2.1). // 1 //

Now, one might object: "It should have been stated simply that 'then the wife threshes' and 'having cooked [the rice],' because its status as being dedicated to Agni (Āgneyatva) is established by the subsequent injunction, 'Agni is the deity' (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 7.5)."

Since it has already been prescribed that "he causes her to sacrifice with a *sthālīpāka*" by the injunction "having cooked [the rice]," and since it has also been prescribed that "he causes her to sacrifice" while she is holding on to him by the injunction "while she is holding on," for what purpose is this further section begun with the words, "Then he causes her to sacrifice with an *āgneya* *sthālīpāka*"?
It is said: first of all, a Sūtra composed by a seer (*ṛṣi*) ought not to be meaningless.

Therefore, even that meaning of a Sūtra which is accomplished through ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and other means established by common usage in the world is declared to be the Vedic meaning to be practiced. For example: "Having certainly shown [the star] Arundhatī, immediately thereafter, at the place where one performs the sacrifice with the *sthālīpāka* offering to Agni, there alone he causes his wife to sacrifice; he offers the oblation while the wife holds on to him."
Nor [does it apply] on the full-moon days or during the modifications of the full-moon sacrifice;
thus, by virtue of this extension (*atideśa*), the sūtra is indeed meaningful.
Others claim that because of the statement "he causes [the bridegroom] to sacrifice," someone other than the bridegroom may also be the performer of this *sthālīpāka* sacrifice.

That is not so; for, by virtue of the context, this sacrifice is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the marriage ceremony, and according to the principle "the primary act together with its auxiliaries" (*sāṅgaṃ pradhānam*), the primary act along with its auxiliaries must have a single performer.
Some [hold that] later on there is not only the injunction "Agni is the deity," but also "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second";
therefore, let this *sthālīpāka* not have two deities.
However, the injunction "by means of the Āgneya [offering]" is for the purpose of establishing that it belongs to a single deity alone.
Therefore, for rice and other materials intended for the Āgneya itself, the worldly act of pouring out (nirvāpa) is to be performed as implied by the context.
As for the statement "he causes him to sacrifice this," there is no entitlement for both [the sacrificer and the priest] in this ritual act.
However, it is by the bride alone;
the groom, moreover, stands in the place of the officiating priest (ṛtvij).
Therefore, in the oblation and other rites, the renunciation of the substance proceeds from the woman's own wealth.

That is not so; for if there were a single governing injunction (*adhikāra*), there would be a sublation of the status of marriage as a subsidiary (*aṅga*) understood from the context, because the scripture and its meaning differ according to the difference between the governing injunction and the act to be accomplished.
Furthermore, it would entail the sublation of the fact that the bridegroom is the performer, which is established by custom.
Because there is no contradiction even in [his performing] other priestly functions. // 1 //
The wife husks [the grain]. ĀpGs 7.2.

Immediately after seeing the Arundhatī star, he enters the house and pours out fresh rice or barley intended for the fire-offering— enough as he deems necessary for the oblation and for the feeding of the Brahmins— and sprinkles them with consecrated water while remaining silent;
thereafter, his wife threshes them.

Just as in the case of the mantra "enā patyā" and others, although it would have been sufficient to refer to her by the pronoun "sā" (she) as "sāvahanti," the specific term "patnī" (wife) is used so that it may be understood that this is the wife's duty.
Otherwise, it might be understood as the duty of the sacrificer (yājamāna).
If the bride were considered the sacrificer here, it would follow that the husband must perform the threshing in rites such as the Pārvaṇa. //2//
Regarding the rice and other grains for the *sthālīpāka*:
although one should say "he threshes," because of the additional syllables in the phrase "the wife threshes" (*patnyavahanti*), she should perform only the threshing,
and not even the cooking and so forth.
That and the rest are indeed the choice [of the wife].
Some [hold] that, beginning from the word "wife," the threshing is the work of the wife alone,
and not the work of the sacrificer.

For if she were a co-eligible participant in the husband's ritual duties, then in rites such as the *pārvaṇa*, the threshing would have to be performed by the husband, since he is the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) in those instances.
For this very reason, there is no ritual grasping of the hand (*anvārambha*) in the *pārvaṇa* and similar rites.
[The opponent argues: "It is like [the case of] 'the wife threshes,' because there is no statement such as 'while the wife is holding on'.
[The author replies: Not so; for the qualification of the husband alone has already been refuted. //2//
31. The *sthālīpāka* oblation; the number of its portions (*avadāna*).

Having cooked it, sprinkled clarified butter over it, and removed it [from the fire] toward the east or the north, he sprinkles clarified butter over it once it has been set down. Then, from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, while she maintains contact with him, he offers [portions] from the *sthālīpāka*. (ĀpGS 7.3)

Then the bridegroom washes those [grains] which have been husked and dehusked three times, and cooks them. The mention of the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire is for the purpose of establishing the *tantra* (the ritual framework) and for the purpose of establishing the time; it indicates how the *tantra* is to be undertaken at the end of the sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*), and not before. Therefore, the sprinkling is performed with clarified butter (*ājya*) that has not yet undergone the formal consecration.
Here too, the use of the sacrificial vessels occurs only once;
likewise, the *śamyā* pegs are used [once],
because this rite is a supplement to the marriage ceremony.
"No," say others. //3//
The statement ending with the *ājyabhāga* offerings is for the purpose of instructing on the time for the *anvārambha* (the taking hold);
the mention of "from the *sthālīpāka*" is redundant,
because that [offering] is intended for the *homa*.
Nor should it be said that the *sthālīpāka* is for the purpose of feeding Brahmins, while the *homa* follows from the clarified butter (*ājya*) alone;
for this is because of the injunction for sacrifice and the injunction for the deity.

In that case, this is the method of the Teacher: wherever there are two oblations, namely clarified butter (*ājya*) and vegetable food (*auṣadha*), he provides a qualification for the principal oblation by saying, "from the cooked rice (*sthālīpāka*), from the grain-food (*anna*), from the cake (*apūpa*), [or] from the clarified butter-oblation.
By this, it is established that where no such qualification exists, there is only one oblation.
Therefore, in the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice—
There is an absence of clarified butter (ājya). Consequently, in that case, only the position of a single defilement applies,
because the spreading under (upastaraṇa) and the sprinkling over (abhighāraṇa) are impossible due to the absence of clarified butter.

And in the case of the wedding ceremony, regarding the statement "having sat down according to their respective places," since there is an absence of the qualification "an oblation of clarified butter" (*ājyāhuti*), it is established that only clarified butter is there the substance accompanied by ritual rules (*dharmavat*), whereas the parched grains (*lājā*) are without such rules (*adharmaka*). //4//
Having dismissed [the fire] for the sake of convenience and having re-established it to the west of the original fire,
he pours clarified butter over the established fire.
It has already been stated that even when the sacrificial offering consists of herbs, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is applied here for the sake of establishing the proper sequence.
"At the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, while she has taken hold [of him]";
the taking of hold begins with the *upastaraṇa* and continues until the end of the principal oblations. //3//
There is a single spreading of the underlayer and a single pouring over, and the cutting out of portions is done twice.
By this, the procedure for cutting portions (*avadāna-kalpa*) pertaining to the sacrificial cake (*pauroḍāśika*) is to be understood as demonstrated here;
it also applies to [the formulas] beginning with "mīm" and so forth,
as well as the five-fold portioning (*pañcāvatta*) for those who practice five-fold portioning.
And regarding the re-sprinkling of the oblation, it is like the taking of the fried grains (*lāja*):

although one should say that after spreading [the butter] as a base (*upastīrya*), having taken two portions (*dvir-avadāya*), one sprinkles twice (*dvir-abhighārayati*), the singular mention is intended to indicate that the spreading and the sprinkling are for the purpose of accomplishing the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*).
Therefore, in the absence of the fourfold portion, there is also an absence of both the spreading and the sprinkling.
As in such cases as: "One should offer by striking [the ladle] once" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 7.7), and "With a handful of curds alone" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 22.10), and so forth. //5//
The under-layering (upastaraṇa) should be performed once with the homa-spoon, the *sruva*-ladle, or another ladle; thereafter, two portions of the sacrificial oblation (*caru*) are to be taken.
For the Jamadagnis, three portions are to be taken.
There is a single sprinkling [of clarified butter].
Then follows a second sprinkling of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) for the sake of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering;
this is because it serves to demonstrate the rule for the portions to be cut off in the *iṣṭi* sacrifice, and also because of established practice. //4//
He states the deity:
32. The rule for its deity is as follows:
Agni is the deity, with the offering made by the utterance of *svāhā*. (ĀpGs 7.5)
Because there is a duality of primary factors, this is a restatement of what is already established, intended for what follows:
Agni alone is the deity of the preceding oblation, who was enjoined by the word "āgneyena"; another [deity] is enjoined for the subsequent one. //6//
That in which the offering is made with the utterance of "svāhā" is called *svāhākārapradāna*;
it is the oblation (*homa*) of the *sthālīpāka*.
Because no distinction is specified, it applies both to the preceding and the subsequent [rites].

In that context, due to its connection with the utterance *svāhā*, the word for the deity ends in the dative case—as in "Svāhā to Agni" (*agnaye svāhā*) and "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" (*agnaye sviṣṭakṛte svāhā*).
[The rule states: "That which enjoins the act of *juhote* (offering) is characterized by the offering of *svāhā*. (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 3.4).

Since this is already established, the present statement is intended to prohibit certain other alternatives: namely, the injunction that "in some other ritual procedures (*kalpāntara*), the offering is prescribed with a mantra, saying 'One should sacrifice with *amuṣmai svāhā*, or with a *ṛc* addressed to that deity," as well as the rule that "having recited the *puronuvākyā*, one should sacrifice with the *yājyā*.
Even so, in the case of the *sthālīpāka*, one should simply say, "He sacrifices from the *sthālīpāka* with 'To Agni, svāhā'," and for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, "To Sviṣṭakṛt, svāhā."

However, this statement is intended to prohibit the use of mantras in cases where deities are prescribed according to the rules extended from the *pārvaṇa* rite— such as in the rule "the deities are as taught"— by specifying that "in the case of the full moon [rite], the full moon [deity]" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 7.28). Therefore, in those instances where the deity of the *sthālīpāka* is specifically enjoined, the oblation (*homa*) is performed using the word for the deity itself.
It is established that [the rite] is not performed with a mantra dedicated to that deity. //7//
This is a restatement of a technical rule (*paribhāṣā*) intended to specify the particular fire (*agni*) enjoined as "Agni is the deity.
If it is asked, "How is it specified? [the answer is: that fire is the deity if the offering is made with the utterance *svāhā*.
The meaning is: "if it is joined with the fourth case-ending (caturthī-vibhakti) appropriate for [the word] *svāhākāra*.

Now, one might ask: when it could simply have been said, "He offers to Agni while she is being touched," why is this more prolix expression taught—"Agni is the deity, with the offering made by means of *svāhākāra*"? It is replied: the word (*śabda*) is the deity, not the object (*artha*).
Even the object assists in the sacrifice only through the very word that denotes it, ending in the fourth case as prescribed.

Because the meaning [of "devatā"] cannot be pointed out, and because no other secondary benefit (*upakāra*) can be easily defined, the Mīmāṃsaka view is not intended here; it is for this very reason that he states "the deity" in order to make known his own position.
If it is asked, "How so?"—it is because the word *agni*, which ends in the nominative case and is unfit for use as an object of action, is employed [in the mantra].
Now, one might object: even if Ṛtu were the deity, since the vowel *u* is [already] expressed by the word itself, there would be no difference in the performance of the rite.
Not so; for it is not merely the utterance of the word ending in the dative case that must be performed, but the mental visualization (dhyāna) of the referent as well.
Regarding this, the established principle is stated in the Nirukta (8.3.7): "But the settled rule is that they belong to Agni."
Such is the statement of the author of the Nirukta.
In other ritual manuals (kalpa), an alternative is prescribed: "One should offer with the formula 'Svāhā to such-and-such,' or with a verse addressed to that deity.
Let there be no such option for us.
This [sūtra] is intended to mean that at the Pārvaṇa rites and their derivatives, one should offer only with the formula "Svāhā to such-and-such. //5//
In that regard, there is the position of simultaneous striking;
or alternatively, one may offer the oblation after having struck [the grain] all at once. ĀpGs 7.6.
With the same ladle as that used for the *homa*, one should offer [the oblation] after scooping it up once;
in this view, it is established that there is no under-sprinkling (*upastaraṇa*) nor over-sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*).
Some, however, perform these.
The statement "one should offer" is intended to ensure that [the procedure] applies even to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. //8//
Alternatively, having taken a single portion from the *sthālīpāka* with a ladle, one should offer it;
however, unlike the previous cases, there is no fourfold or fivefold division (*caturavatta* or *pañcāvatta*), because *darvihoma* offerings are not preceded by such rules.
Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second [deity].
Agni Sviṣṭakṛt becomes the second by way of being a deity.
The mention of "second" is for the purpose of making known that he possesses the same ritual properties as the preceding one.
Therefore, by that [rule], in the case of "the principal oblations according to the instruction" and so forth, there is also the inclusion of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering;
likewise, there is the application of both the rules "having taken up [the material] once, he should sacrifice" and "the offering is made with the utterance of *svāhā*. //9//
"Deity" is the understood subject. A second oblation is to be performed from the remainder of the *sthālīpāka*;
the meaning is that Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the deity for that [oblation].
Even though the sense is already established by the second [word],
the purpose for employing the term "without a second" (*advitīya*) will be explained in the passage: "The Lord of the Assembly is without a second" (*Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra* 8.2).
Some [hold that] this indicates that [the subsequent offerings] possess the same characteristics as the preceding *homa*.

And if that were the case, then in the rule "having offered the principal oblations according to the instruction," it would follow that one should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* and then the *jaya* offerings and so forth. // 7 //
Regarding this, he states the rule for the cutting of portions:
34. In that regard, there is the procedure beginning with the under-layering;
there is one under-layering and two cuttings, followed by two pourings over. (ĀpGS 7.8)
In this case as well, the procedure for the portions of the *paukaja*, *āśika*, and *sviṣṭakṛt* offerings should be understood as demonstrated:
"By that [method], one who takes five cuttings (*pañcāvattin*) makes each subsequent portion larger;
he does not pour clarified butter over the oblation" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.21.3, 4, 5).
Thus, these specific distinctions should also be understood here. //10//
The spreading of the underlayer (upastaraṇa), the cutting of the portion (avadāna), and the double sprinkling (abhighāraṇa) should be performed once;
however, for the Jamadagnis, there is a double cutting of the portion. The cutting of the portion from the deity's share is superior.

Nor is there a second pouring over the oblation (pratyabhighāraṇa), because this is for the purpose of demonstrating the rule for the portions taken for the iṣṭi and the sviṣṭakṛt offerings, and also because of established practice. //8//
The cutting-off portion is from the middle of the eastern [quarter]. ĀpGs 7.9.
This means "of the preceding principal oblation.
This statement is for the sake of the view that there is an interruption (*upaghāta*).
However, in the case of the fourfold portioning (*caturavatta*), it is already established because it belongs to the *pauroḍāśika* section.

But would it not be for the purpose of prohibiting those two specific locations— namely, "the second from the first half" and "the third from the second half"— even in that case? If this were so, then the rule "of the subsequent [portion] for the subsequent [deity]" regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering need not be commenced,
as there would be no distinction [between the cases].
Therefore, in the case of the four-fold portioning (caturavatta), the rule is indeed that pertaining to the sacrificial cake (pauroḍāśika);
however, this statement is for the purpose of the alternative involving accidental damage (upaghāta).
The portioning (avadāna) for the preceding deity must be made from the middle of the oblation (havis).
This undertaking is intended solely for the sake of the view that there is no damage [to the oblation].

However, in the case of the four-fold portioning (caturavatta), by the force of demonstrating the ritual procedure pertaining to the iṣṭi sacrifice, the portioning consists of a measure equal to the joint of the thumb taken from the middle.
"One cuts transversely from the front half for one who offers twice; lengthwise for a second [portion]; and for one who offers five times, a third from the rear half. (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.18.9).

Since this establishes the locations for the portions (*avadāna*), it demonstrates that under the view of "striking" (*upaghāta*), the ritual duties such as spreading the butter (*upastaraṇa*) and so forth do not apply to the twice-offering portion. //9//
The fire-oblation (homa) is performed in the center. (ĀpGS 7.10)
The middle [portion] is the junction of the Āghāra libations.
Here too, it should be understood that the place for the oblation is shown to be exactly that of the Pauroḍāśika [section].
Therefore, even though there are multiple oblations, [the rule] "each preceding one is joined with the following" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.19.9) applies.
Such specific details as these also apply here. //12//
Homa is the act of throwing [an oblation] into the fire.
In the center of the sacrificial fire, at the junction of the two *āghāra* libations,
when there is a plurality of principal offerings (*pradhānāhuti*), one should recite each preceding *sāṃhitā* formula first (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.19.9).
And so it is;
however, this [verse] has the meaning of both sides. //10//
From the second half [of the portion], [he eats] of the northern one. ĀpGs 7.11.
This undertaking also has the purpose of refuting the position that [the soul] is subject to injury. //13//
The cutting for the subsequent Sviṣṭakṛt offering must be made from the northern half of the sacrificial oblation;
this also serves the same purpose as the "unintentional injury" (upaghāta) alternative mentioned previously. //11//
The oblation is offered in the north-eastern quarter. (ĀpGs 7.12)
Here too, the ritual procedure (dharma) of the *pauroḍāśika* *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is to be understood.
By that [procedure], the specific rule "not joined with the others" (*asaṃsaktām itarābhiḥ*) from Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.21.6 applies here as well.

If the mention of the *homa* (oblation) were being relied upon, then the phrase "the northern half and the eastern half" might also be construed with the subsequent statement, "like the *prastara* [grass-bundle] at the two smearings. //14//
The oblation for the Sviṣṭakṛt is offered in the eastern part of the northern half of the fire.
Since this [specification] is also intended as an illustration, it is also the case that [the offering] is "not mixed with other oblations" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.21.6). //12//
He states the disposal of the two ladles used for the spreading of the oblation and so forth, as well as of the sacrificial grass spread for the purpose of using the vessels:
"Having silently thrown the two smeared [ladles] into the fire like the *prastara* [bunch of grass], he throws the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) [into the fire]. (ĀpGS 7.13)

Taking some of that sacrificial grass (*barhis*) upon which the oblation and the clarified butter (*ājya*) are established, he silently wipes the two smears of food and clarified butter from it as he did with the *prastara* bundle;
then, just like the *prastara*, he silently casts it into the fire.
Precisely because this is prescribed as a disposal (*pratipatti*), the spreading of the *barhis* takes place behind the fire.
And there is the placing of the oblation-materials (*havis*) therein; this is made clear in another ritual manual (*kalpa*):
"Having sprinkled the cooked oblations with clarified butter, having moved them northward, one should place them upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*)."
Some consider the anointing to be performed from the grass strewn around the fire;
because of the statement "like the *prastara*," the anointing takes place in three places.
In that regard, according to the view of the fourfold portion (*caturavatta*), [the anointing] is of the tip of that [grass-bundle] with which the oblations are offered.

By means of that [ladle], the spreading of the base (upastaraṇa) and the sprinkling (abhighāraṇa) are performed; in it, the anointing of the middle portion takes place, and in the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), the anointing of the root portion occurs.

However, according to the view of the "minor offense" (upaghāta) rite, since there is no ladle for the purpose of spreading and sprinkling, the anointing of the middle portion is done in the vessel for clarified butter, and that of the root portion in the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (carusthālī).
It is also said: "Having taken away a blade of grass from that which has been anointed.
Likewise, he himself performs the placing [of the oblation] upon that [grass] by means of which the offering is made, as well as the duties of the Āgnīdhra priest. //15//

Having silently dipped the two ladles—which are smeared with remnants—into the water strewn upon the sacrificial grass for the purpose of cleansing the vessels (just as one does with the *prastara* bundle), he throws them into the fire in the same manner.
This is also intended as an illustration;
therefore, he performs everything from the application of collyrium up to the pouring out of the remnants silently, just as in the Śrauta ritual.
But is it not the case that the analogy of the *prastara* (grass-bundle) is inappropriate here?
For it is impossible to smear the tips, middle, and roots of the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) onto two offering-spoons (*darvī*) in the manner of the *prastara*.
It is replied: the tip is smeared on the homa-spoon.
In the other case, according to the rule "anyāllopau vivṛddhir vā" (Āpiśali 4.13), [the form] is *tridvivī* from *madhyamūlī*. Thus, there are two forms.
In the view that "it is not for another purpose," the root [of the grass] is used only once for the purpose of the *upastaraṇa* (spreading) and so forth,
while the middle and the tip are used for the purpose of the *homa* (offering).
Others, however, place the *ājyasthālī* (clarified butter pot) in the position of the *dhruvā* in all three views.

This is because [the rule] is for the purpose of applying the ointment to the vessel used for the collyrium; furthermore, it is seen in the passage: "Either ending with the *iḍā* at the Āhavanīya fire, or ending with the *śaṃyu* formula at the Gārhapatya fire" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 3.14.6), as well as in: "The root [of the grass] is in the butter-pot" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 3.14.7).

In this case, however, the dual number in the word *lepayoḥ* refers to the two types of smearing— the clarified butter (*ājya*) and the medicinal herbs (*auṣadha*)— and not, as previously [assumed], to the duality of the two underlayers (*āghāra*).

Some say that "ointment" refers to something taken from the fire upon which the sacrificial oblation and clarified butter are placed according to another ritual manual (*kalpa*), or from the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) or the surrounding strew (*paristaraṇa*).

That is not correct; because the placement of the sacrificial grass mentioned in another ritual manual is merely optional, the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), which has a fixed sequence as a permanent requirement, is not thereby dispensed with.
Because it is a subordinate element of the fire, he says:
"The subsequent sprinkling is established. (ĀpGS 7.14)
The meaning is that the *Jayā* and other rites from the *Ānā* [Tantra] should be performed here as well, according to their established procedure.
And how are they established? From the statement, "He performs the supplementary oblation" (*upajuhoti*).
After the principal oblations (pradhānahoma), the throwing-in of the sacrificial grass (barhis) occurs subsequent to the secondary oblations (upahoma);
otherwise, because of the instruction that it follows immediately after the principal oblations, the throwing-in would have to take place prior to the secondary oblations. //16//
In this context, the word "having performed" (kṛtvā) is to be supplied.
The meaning is: "having performed the sprinkling around (pariṣecana), having completed the ritual up to the final sprinkling around.
For what purpose is this?
This is for the purpose of establishing that after the sprinkling (pariṣecana), only the rites beginning with the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas are to be performed, and no others.
Others, however, reading the single rule as "the subsequent sprinkling is established" (siddham uttaraṃ pariṣecanam), explain it thus:

by this, in the case of the *sthālīpāka*, after the principal oblations (*pradhānahoma*), while the remainder of the ritual procedure (*tantraśeṣa*) is generally applicable, only the sprinkling is established here, and everything else remains unestablished.
"Therefore, the omission of the subordinate offerings (upahoma) is enjoined here"; thus, [the statement] "it is the answer to those [arguments]" is redundant. //17//
This is clear.
Therefore, "the liberation through the consecrated water" (*praṇītāvimoka*) is also [established].
Some say that the two words "siddham uttaram" constitute a single sentence.
The *Siddhamāvikṛta* is the supplement to the subsequent *Tantra*, beginning with the *Jayā* offerings and so forth.

Although these have been extracted and taught here [in this section], they are [to be performed] according to the instruction: "Having offered the principal oblations, one offers the *Jayā* and *Abhyātāna* offerings" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 2.7).
Thus, because the order of the Śruti is more authoritative, [the act] must occur immediately after the Sviṣṭakṛt offering, which possesses properties equal to those of the principal rite.
Likewise, the phrase "the sprinkling around" (pariṣecana) is also intended to prescribe immediate succession;
that is, having performed everything up to the sprinkling around, one should indeed proceed to the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas.

That is not so; for it would require the assumption of a major fault in the form of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*), which contradicts the well-established coreferential connection (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the honored [deity] in the phrase "the final sprinkling is established.

Likewise, because there is no such scriptural statement, the *jaya* offerings and so forth do not even exist here, let alone any discussion regarding the relative strength or weakness of their sequence.

Likewise, since the answer to "sprinkling" (pariṣecana) is already established by this [preceding statement], which lacks any further expectancy for a connection, the supply of the word "having done" (kṛtvā) is groundless.
Furthermore, immediate sequence (ānantarya), being obtained from the order of the text, is certainly not something to be enjoined.
Therefore, it is better to hold that this sūtra is intended solely for the purpose of removing the aforementioned doubt. //14//
35. From the remainder of the *sthālīpāka*, there is the feeding of Brahmins. With that [food] mixed with clarified butter (*sarpiṣmat*), he should feed a Brahmin. (ĀpGs 7.15)
The mention of "containing clarified butter" (*sarpiṣmat*) is for the sake of emphasis, since it already contains clarified butter due to the prior sprinkling;
the meaning is that one should pour a copious amount of common clarified butter over it.
He who sits to the south—that Brāhmaṇa here—should be fed by the bride or the groom. (18)
With that remainder of the oblation, mixed with ghee— that is, sprinkled with abundant clarified butter—
he should feed a Brāhmaṇa seated on Darbha grass to his right, because such a person is the subject under discussion here.
But here, the suffix *matup* in the word *sarpiṣmatā* expresses an excellence [of the clarified butter].
Furthermore, by the force of the injunction "one should feed," it follows that the *ruk* (the sacrificial post) must be sufficient for both the oblation and the feeding of the Brahmins. //15//
36. The giving of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the cooked rice offering (sthālīpāka): he gives a bull to that person who is honored by him. (ĀpGs 7.16)
To that teacher who is honored and revered by this groom, the bride gives a bull as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the *sthālīpāka* offering.

Since the fee, which should have been brought from her own family and given to the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) or the groom, cannot be given or received between husband and wife due to the absence of mutual gifting and acceptance, it is therefore directed toward the teacher.
Therefore, he becomes excluded [from the sacrifice].

And this principle is seen in the *Dharmaśāstra*: after stating, "A father shall not perform the sacrifice for his son, nor a son for his father," it continues, "They should give the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the teacher" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.6.15).
Now, this sūtra appears to be improper;
for by stating, "He who is honored by him [should be honored] with the other [verse]" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 3.9), it is understood that someone other than the bridegroom is the giver.
And because there is no other [agent] here;

for even though a wife exists, nevertheless, since she too— through her consent— is accepted as an agent in the relinquishing of wealth during rites that require joint authority when the husband is away on a journey.
Now, because of the statement here, "He causes her to sacrifice," the bride becomes the sacrificer (*yajamānā*). She gives [her] woman's property (*strīdhana*) for the honor of the groom (*vara*).
And by that, the groom, having become the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), is honored.
Nor can it be said that the gift is for the bridegroom alone, because there would otherwise be an absence of mutual giving between the wife and her husband;

this is not so, for since this [gift] occurs within the single jurisdiction of the giver (the bridegroom), its status as an integral part of the marriage— already established by being intertwined with both sides of the marriage— is sublated.

Because there is a distinction between the scripture and its subject matter based on the difference between the qualification (*adhikāra*) and the goal to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Now, if it is argued that the bride herself is consecrated by this primary rite, the sacrifice, solely for the sake of establishing a marriage in which both possess the qualification, then the statement that "the qualification belongs to the bride alone" is a mere assertion; thus, the expenditure of the woman's property is in vain.
Therefore, a sūtra should be explained in such a way that it remains consistent with its context.
To this, it is replied: in that case, it is explained either by supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) or by modifying the construction (*vipariṇāma*):
"He gives a bull to that one who is honored and worthy of worship by him (the giver) himself."

Alternatively, the performer of this *sthālīpāka* sacrifice gives a bull to those who are honored (*apacita*) by him— that is, to the performers of this specific sacrifice— and not to the performers of other *sthālīpāka* sacrifices, because those others are not previously established (*apūrva*).
Alternatively, the genitive case "of this" (*asya*) is transformed into the nominative "this one" (*ayam*).
Thus, he who is honored in the world for his excellence in learning, lineage, and so forth—this very person, as the performer of the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice, gives the bull.
In any case, however, there is no giving of a bull even in other modified forms of the *sthālīpāka*. //16//
37. The Pārvaṇa Sthālīpāka: From this point forward, on the festival days (parvan), it should be performed by those who have fasted, with the exception of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). (ĀpGs 7.17)

Therefore, after this *sthālīpāka* and excluding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the two householders—having observed the fast in the manner prescribed by the rule, "On the *parvan* days, there is fasting for both" (*Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra* 2.1.4)—should perform the *sthālīpāka* on the *parvan* days, that is, on the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and new moon (*amāvāsyā*) nights, according to the very same procedure for the *āgneya-sthālīpāka*.
This is an extension of the ritual procedure: the *sthālīpāka* is to be performed on the *parvan* days.

And for that [rite], there is a ritual procedure (kalpa) not explicitly taught in the scripture, such as "he causes him to sacrifice with a *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Agni" and "he gives a bull to him.

Here, because of the use of the dual number in the phrase "by the two who have fasted," both [the husband and wife] are qualified [to perform the rite]; however, in that other case, only the wife is [qualified].
Furthermore, the distinction here is simply that no sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is required.

In that context, regarding the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha], the specific features associated with the occasion of marriage— such as using vessels only once, the *śamyā* wooden pins, and so forth— are not to be performed. Furthermore, the *anvārambha* (the ritual touching of the wife) is also not to be performed, because it is an act belonging specifically to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
And here, since both are the sacrificers,
let there then be another officiating priest, while the act of taking hold remains for both.
That too is not the case, because of an indicative mark (*jñāpaka*).
In that this [text] prescribes the *anvārambha* (the taking hold) in connection with the heart, it indicates that there is no *anvārambha* in the *pārvaṇa* and other such rites.
Otherwise, the *anvārambha* (the formal commencement) would already be established by the extension (*atideśa*) from the *pārvaṇa* rite.

In such passages as "From the taking of the hand [of the bride] onwards, there is the vow of the two householders," it is intended that the marriage rite is to be performed with all its constituent parts (*sāṅga*).

Therefore, once the marriage rite is completed at the end of the *saṃveśana* (the ritual cohabitation), there follows the engagement in the duties of a householder, such as the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*).
The state of being established in the *pārvaṇa* [rite] would exist even prior to the lying down;
however, the commencement occurs upon the arrival of the *parvan* after the cooking of food.
To that end, he says: "from this point onward."
And its commencement is on the full moon day, not on the new moon day,
because that is seen to be the case for the two Vedic rites,
and because these two [rites] take the place of those.
The Chandogas also recite: "If the new moon (amāvāsyā) occurs first, one should perform that [rite] after having sacrificed with the full moon (paurṇamāsa).
Some say that one should wait without having performed the full moon sacrifice" (Khādira Gṛhya Sūtra 2.1.2).

Since it was already established by the rule "there is fasting for both on the parvan days," the specific statement "by those who have fasted" (upoṣitābhyām) is intended to apply to this particular ritual.
This is for the purpose of demonstrating that both [husband and wife] have the entitlement [to perform the rite].
Even so, one should simply say "by both," rather than "by those who have fasted.

Therefore, since it follows from the context that on the *parvan* days there is a fast for both, the text—having first introduced the fast and then restated it partially—demonstrates the entitlement of the two by means of the dual number in the phrase "by those who have fasted" (*upoṣitābhyām*).
Therefore, the *sthālīpāka* is prepared on the very day of the sacrifice.
On the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight], the ritual is performed on the preceding day.
Thus says Āśvalāyana: "Now follows the *parvan* *sthālīpāka*."
"For him, there is fasting for the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and the binding together of the sacrificial fuel (idhma) and the grass (barhis)" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.10.1–3).

When it is stated that "it should be performed by both on the festival days," then the *sthālīpāka* offering and the fast should occur only on the festival days, because the two injunctions are identical in their direction.

Therefore, the injunction is that after this *sthālīpāka*, husband and wife— who have observed the fast according to the rule, "After the *sthālīpāka*, on the *parvan* days both shall fast" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.1.4)— should perform a *homa* of this same nature, similar to the *sthālīpāka*, on the *parvan* days, namely the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) and new moon (*amāvāsyā*) days, as well as on the second lunar days, excluding the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) and excluding the gift of a bull (*ṛṣabhadāna*).

In the Dharmaśāstra, however, the statement "on the following day, the *sthālīpāka* [is performed]" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.1.10) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of connecting it with duties such as fasting;
and here, the similarity is based on the totality of factors such as the substance and the deity.

As in "This very [sacrifice] among the Revatī verses" (Tāṇḍya Brāhmaṇa 17.8.1), or as in "He performs the Agnihotra for a month"; in those cases, however, by means of the two words "this very" and "Agnihotra,"...
But here, the distinction lies in the phrase "by this very word.
Now, one might object: there is no extended application (*atideśa*) in the case of ladle-oblations (*darvīhoma*), because they are original rites (*apūrva*).
True; there is no [extension] by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of an injunction, but who can prevent extension based on a direct statement (*vacana*)?
Some say: "This is not an extension of *dharma*."
Because, as in the case of the Saurya and other sacrifices, there is no instruction regarding the oblation or the deity, therefore there is only the extension (atideśa) of the ritual procedure;
[the rite is performed] on the following day, the Anvaṣṭakā.
"The ritual procedure for that [monthly śrāddha] has been explained by the statement 'as it is said' regarding the monthly śrāddha"—
this is not so;
for even when the oblation and the deity are not explicitly mentioned, the extension of ritual properties (dharmātideśa) is observed in such cases as "he performs the Agnihotra for a month."

Others, however, maintain that by the principle "when one thing has both [characteristics], there is a distinctness of conjunction" (Jaimini Sūtra 4.3.5), this is an injunction for connecting the very same *sthālīpāka* under discussion with a different context, namely: "it should be performed thus on the festival days."
This also is not the case; for if that were so, the Sūtra would have said, "This is to be done," rather than "But this is not to be done.
Furthermore, there would also be the undertaking of the preceding sections.
For it is precisely because the ritual action under discussion possesses all its constituent properties (*dharma*) that the acceptance of another injunction regarding its performance is possible.

However, regarding the extension of properties (*dharmātideśa*), it has already been stated by the Commentator himself—when he declared that the sūtra "Then with the Āgneya [offering]" is for the purpose of a specific extension—that there is no *anvārambha* (the wife's joining of hands) in such cases.
Furthermore, in this context, the statement "from this point upward" is intended to signify the commencement of the festival (*parva*) even during the midst of the wedding ceremony.
Although the statement "from this point forward" is made without further specification,
the commencement nevertheless takes place on the full moon day alone,
because the unity of time entails the unity of purpose.
And because we see the commencement [of the rite] by way of displacement (*sthānāpatti*),
this is clearly evident among the Chāndogas:
"If the new moon day should fall earlier, one should perform the full moon sacrifice and then perform that [new moon sacrifice]."
"One should desire [to perform] the Full Moon sacrifice even while not performing it," so says one [teacher].

Therefore, if the Full Moon day should arrive before the *sthālīpāka* (the cooked-rice offering), then the commencement of the festival (*parva*) takes place even in the midst of the wedding ceremony.
The commencement of the monthly śrāddha, however, takes place at the end of the fourth oblation during the dark fortnight,
according to the practice of the learned and the statement of Bodhāyana.
Furthermore, it is improper to begin another ritual action in the midst of one already underway;
the same applies to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, as it is stated:
"Upon the employment of those mantras, there is sleeping on the ground for twelve days" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.3.13).
Having observed such vows together with his wife, he should commence [the rite] on an auspicious day. //17//
Some say, however, that the full vessel is the sacrificial fee. ĀpGs 7.18.
The word *pātra* is of both genders.
They say that a vessel full of a hundred handfuls of grain is a "full vessel" (*pūrṇapātra*).
And this sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is to be given to the Brahman priest. //21//
A "full vessel" (*pūrṇapātra*) is any vessel filled with grain or similar substances. Alternatively: "Eight handfuls make one *kiñcit*; four *kiñcit* make one *puṣkala*."

According to the statement, "And four *puṣkala*s are declared to be a full measure (*pūrṇamātra*)," one hundred and twenty-eight handfuls of grain constitute a full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*). Furthermore,
the word *pātra* is of both genders.
By the word "tu" (but), this option applies to the [other] festival days, but not to the gift of a bull. // 18 //
38. The *aupāsana* oblation:
from this time forward, he should offer these two oblations every evening and morning with his hand, using either rice grains or barley. (ĀpGs 7.19)
After this *sthālīpāka*, one should offer these two oblations with either rice grains or barley.
The phrase "after this" (*ata ūrdhvam*) has the same significance as in the *Pārvaṇa* [śrāddha]; therefore, the commencement of the rite takes place on that very night.
Therefore, after that, the evening meal of the husband and wife is called these two oblations;
this is for the purpose of establishing that these are indeed the two Agnihotra oblations offered by one who has maintained the sacred fires.
Consequently, the ritual requirements (dharmas) pertaining to those [Agnihotra oblations] apply here as well.

This is as in the case of [the rules] such as "a fuel-stick of *Butea monosperma* (apālāśī) two finger-breadths long from the root" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 6.10.4), and regarding the times for kindling the fire and the oblation;
and this has been stated in the *Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra*: "The times for kindling the fire and the oblation are explained by those of the *Agnihotra*" (*Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra* 1.9.5), and so forth.
"Hastening" is a rejection of the ladle;
because there is no fault in the ritual procedure (*tantra*), it constitutes a new rule (*apūrva*).
However, the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*) certainly takes place.
However, the ritual sprinkling is prescribed right here. //22//
The phrase "in the evening and in the morning" is an elliptical expression for the four times of the *agnihotra* sacrifice;
this is because the domestic fire offering (*aupāsana-homa*) imitates the *agnihotra*.
"After that" means after the marriage ceremony, up to the conclusion of the *sthālīpāka* offering.
Since marriage itself is the primary subject under discussion here, [the reference] is not "after the parvan" because that is merely a proximate context;
for pronouns do not naturally refer back to a contextual subject that is merely incidental.
Regarding the phrase "until the end of the *sthālīpāka*," this means having performed the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice;
for there is the statement, "from this point onward.
And its commencement must take place immediately thereafter, provided that nine *nāḍikās* (twenty-four minutes) of the night have not yet elapsed.
If it has passed, then on the following day, at the very time of commencing the Agnihotra in the evening;
here, by the rule beginning with "with the hand," the entire procedure is prescribed. Because of the prescription "with the hand," the use of the ladle (*darvī*) and other implements is excluded.
Because of the injunction regarding the cooking [of the oblation] with *tāṃjula* and *yavārvā*,
and because of the restrictive enumeration (*parisaṅkhyāna*) that "there is sprinkling on both sides," the rules of the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] apply.
The same explanation holds for the *vaiśvadeva* as well.

Because of the qualification "these," the meaning here is that the second oblation also stands in the place of the *sviṣṭakṛt* and is thus an auxiliary (*aṅga*). Therefore, if one forgets this [second oblation], it need not be offered again once the ritual action has been completed; rather, only the general expiation (*sarvaprāyaścitta*) is to be performed. //19//
39. Regarding that, the rule for the deities is as follows:
the deity is the same as that of the *sthālīpāka* offering. (ĀpGs 7.20)
The deity itself is the sacrificial object (*daivata*).
"Svāhā to Agni" is the first oblation;
"Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt" is the subsequent one. //23//
This phrase, "these two oblations," is a restatement (anuvāda) of what has already been established, intended to indicate an option regarding the first oblation;

just as it is said in the case of the Pātnīvata sacrifice: "One does not perform the *anuvaṣaṭkāra*," or "Alternatively, one may perform the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* in a low voice" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 13.14.9, 10). //20//
Some say that the first oblation in the morning belongs to Sūrya. (ĀpGS 7.21)
The *saurī* [offering] has the sun as its deity;
either the first oblation is "To Sūrya, svāhā! or it is otherwise the same.
In that regard, one may proceed according to one's desire; however, once the procedure has commenced, one is bound by its rules. // 24 //
According to some, the first oblation at the morning fire-offering belongs to Saurī, whose deity is the Sun, with the formula: "Svāhā to the Sun! (sūryāya svāhā). //21//
The sprinkling on both sides is as described previously.
The sprinkling (pariṣecana) for this oblation must be performed both before and after;
as it was prescribed previously: "He sprinkles around the fire as before, with the sprinkling. // 25 //

In both of these offerings, there is sprinkling (pariṣecana) before and after, as prescribed previously: "He sprinkles around the fire" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 2.3), and "The sprinkling is as before; you have given your consent" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 2.8).
In the seven types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), there is no lightning or rain.
"This very inquiry is fulfilled in the Agnihotra itself;
moreover, they say it is fulfilled in all sacrificial rites. (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.10.9)
In this context, and in the passage "This [rite] constitutes the touching [of water] in all sacrifices" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 4.1.7),
the word "all" does not refer back to everything generally, but rather refers specifically to the śrauta sacrifices under discussion;
for this very reason, [the text states] "he offers twice" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 2.11).

Having thus enumerated [the causes] by means of such statements as "because of the complete prescription," lightning and rain do not occur even in the case of the prescription for the fire-cause. //22//
40. There are forty-four modifications of the Pārvaṇa rite.
By means of the Pārvaṇa, other rites—those beginning with the Ācāra—that are included in the Gṛhya-sūtras, are explained. (ĀpGs 7.23)
That which occurs on the *parvan* days is *pārvaṇa*.
By means of that *pārvaṇa* *sthālīpāka*, all other rites— those which are handed down from traditional practice (*ācāra*) and are known— are explained as being distinct from this *pārvaṇa* rite.

This too is an extension of the ritual procedure (*kalpātideśa*). The meaning is that this very procedure of the *Pārvaṇa* sacrifice—beginning with "In this manner from now on" and ending with "the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)"—is the procedure for all *pākayajñas*. In that regard, fasting does not occur except at the *Pārvaṇa*.

Because it is prescribed in a different context through the connection with the *parvan* (the new- or full-moon day), and because the phrase "by those two who have fasted" (*upoṣitābhyām*) is not itself an injunction; [one might object]:

"But since these duties are taught in this marriage rite (*vaivāhika*), and the *pārvaṇa* rites are extended from that very source, then the extension of other rites should also be made from that same source."

The extension [of the ritual rules] by analogy (*atideśa*) from the *pārvaṇa* [śrāddha] is for the purpose of adopting this specific rule: "With the exception of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the full vessel (*pūrṇapātra*) is the fee," as some maintain.
The statement "other than these" is intended to include only those of the same class;
therefore, this extension applies only to *sthālīpākas* and animal sacrifices characterized by cooked food, and not to those characterized by clarified butter (*ājya*).
Some maintain that even in this case,
because of the mention of "actions" (karmāṇi), it is only the actions themselves that are explained as being subject to the *pārvaṇa* [ritual], and not the properties of time or the agent.

Therefore, in the case of the *pākayajña* for Nirṛti [as stated in Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.26], there is neither the requirement of the presence of the wife (*patnīvatva*) nor the restriction to the full-moon and new-moon days (*parvan*);
furthermore, fasting is required in rites such as the *hṛdayasaṃsarga*.

Because of the statement "they have been explained," it is the explanation itself [of these rites] by means of the *pārvaṇa* rite, and not a relationship of archetype (*prakṛti*) and modification (*vikṛti*).
Therefore, even for one who has not previously performed the *pārvaṇa*, when the proper time arrives, the procedure for the *sarpabali* and other such rites occurs.

Because of the statement that "those beginning with the Ācāra [Kalpa] are included," this instruction applies even to those things not taught in this specific treatise but seen in other treatises that possess the quality of being "cooked" (i.e., fully prepared), such as the case where carus intended for optional rites (kāmya) are substituted by carus for the six oblations, and so forth. //26//
By means of the *sthālīpāka* performed on the new- and full-moon days (*pārvaṇa*) or at marriage (*vaivāhika*).

"Other than this" means other rites such as the *sarpa-bali* and so forth, which are adopted from established custom (*ācāra*); these rites have been explained, and the meaning is that this transfer of ritual rules (*dharma-atideśa*) applies to them.

If it is asked, "How can the *sthālīpāka* performed at marriage be designated by the term *pārvaṇa*?"—the answer is that it is indeed *pārvaṇa* because it occurs on the *parvan* days, as stated in the rule:
"It should be performed on the *parvan* days by the couple who have fasted" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 7.17). Thus, it is *nitya*.

And since this [rite] is related to that *pārvaṇa* as its archetype (*prakṛti*), when the suffix *aṇ* is applied to the word *pārvaṇa* according to Pāṇini’s sūtra 4.3.120 (*tasyedam*), the form *pārvama* arises. Although this is also the archetype for other ritual acts, [it is specifically designated here].
Nevertheless, it is more appropriate to designate this [rite] specifically as being connected to the *pārvaṇa* (the full-moon sacrifice),
just as in this ritual there is an extension (*atideśa*) of both the material and the deity;
whereas in other rituals, there is an extension of only the other properties.

If it is objected: "Even so, since the *pārvaṇa* [rite], which is understood quickly and is eternal, can serve as the archetype (*prakṛti*), why is it said that the *vaivāhika* [rite], which is understood with delay, is the archetype?"—we reply: No, because the instruction on ritual duties (*dharma*) is complete only in the *vaivāhika*, whereas such completeness is absent in the other.
And this principle is well-established: he whose instruction of dharma is abundant is the model for others;
for a beggar ought not to go begging from other beggars.
Therefore, it is logical that only the marriage rite is the model.
Furthermore, that this marriage rite is designated by the term *pārvaṇa* is quite explicit in the *Dharmaśāstra*:
"On the *parvan* days, there is fasting for both;
*aupavasta* means eating at another time."
And they should eat their fill of food;
whatever may be dear to them both, that they should eat on this day,

otherwise, the *sviṣṭakṛt*, being a subordinate part of the offering, would occur only at the end of that specific offering.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "and thus to Agni," this restriction—similar to that of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering—is for the purpose of ensuring that the fire is the mouth [of the sacrifice] even before the principal offerings from both [the *āghāra*s].
Some maintain that the single sūtra ends with the words, "The deities [are worshipped] according to the instruction, [ending with] Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.
