Its meaning is as follows: since it is made known in Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 7.70—that "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second"—that Sviṣṭakṛt possesses the same ritual characteristics as the principal oblation (*pradhāna-homa*), it would follow that in modified rites (*vikṛti*) where the principal oblations of the *pārvaṇa* are omitted, this [Sviṣṭakṛt] would also be omitted.
By this sūtra, "sa mā bhūt," having restated [the rule] "the deities as they are described," the combination of that [deity] with Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is enjoined for them.
Thus, the single word "antareṇa" constitutes a separate sūtra, like [the sūtras] "antarā tvāṣṭreṇa" and so forth.

The meaning is that, by virtue of the context, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is obligatory in all modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) among the modified principal offerings and the *jaya* offerings and so forth;

otherwise, there would be an omission of it in some cases, as [the Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 9.4] states: "Having offered the subsequent oblations from the *sthālīpāka*, one proceeds to the *jaya* offerings and so forth."
Regarding the claim that this constitutes an *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification),

that is not so; for when two words ending in the accusative case— namely "agniṃ" and "sviṣṭakṛtam"— which are mutually expectant in their syntactic division, can form a single sentence through connection with the word "antareṇa" (between), it is improper to assume a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).
Furthermore, because the statement "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second [offering]" is intended for another purpose;
nevertheless, if the Sviṣṭakṛt were to possess the same status as the primary rite (pradhāna), then even upon its omission, the expiation for the omission of the primary rite itself would apply.

Likewise, since it is possible for the word "without" (*antareṇa*) to be construed with the aforementioned scriptural connection as already stated, it is not proper to construe it with an implied connection to something irrelevant. Furthermore, this [construal] is redundant; for in our own system, by the very injunction of the simultaneous performance (*samuccaya*) of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, even the threefold *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusionary specification) is thereby refuted.
Because its non-elision is established by virtue of its being eternal everywhere. //25//
Hospitality must be rendered without alteration.

The meaning is that when a cow is offered as a guest-sacrifice (*ātithya*), and it is said, "It is not a cow, it speaks as a cow," this *ātithya* is a primary modified rite (*apūrva vikṛta*); therefore, the *parvan* duties are not to be performed at the offering of its omentum (*vapā-homa*).
This itself is the indicator that this extension (*atideśa*) does not apply only to *sthālīpāka* offerings;
rather, it applies to all animals characterized by cooked flesh.

Therefore, in the case of the Aṣṭakā rites and in the animal sacrifices performed for specific desires as seen in other scriptural traditions, the ritual details of the Pārvaṇa sacrifice are established by extension.
That ritual for which a guest is the occasion is *ātithya*;
this means the sacrifice involving the immolation of a cow.
That [ritual] should remain unmodified, exactly as it has been taught.
In this case, even the general rule beginning with "having kindled the fire" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 1.12) does not apply as a governing framework,
let alone the Pārvaṇa rite.
This is according to the principle stated in Jaimini Sūtra 8.1.5: "Because the entire procedure is prescribed, the *yajati* [offering] possesses an *apūrva* (transcendental result).

And the "entire procedure" is as follows: "Having cooked its omentum (*vapā*), and having spread a base of clarified butter and poured a libation over it, one offers it with the subsequent [verse] using a middle or a single raised leaf of the *palāśa* tree.
This [citation] is intended merely as an illustration.
Therefore, following the offering of the omentum (vapā), the offerings of *kuṃśuka* grass, mustard seeds, and husks (*phalīkaraṇa*), and so forth, are also indeed *apūrva*;
for the nature of their complete injunction is identical.

Now, one might object: since there is a statement of the ritualists that "the principal [offering] is not [performed] in a fire [that has not been consecrated]," the *vaiśvadeva* and *bali* offerings must at least be subsidiary parts (*aṅga*).
Regarding the oblations in the fire, those which occur between the Āgneya and the Sviṣṭakṛt offerings are indeed the principal ones.

Anticipating the objection that these two [the Āgneya and Sviṣṭakṛt] might be considered subsidiary because they share common features with the snake-offering (sarpabali) and others, he says: "The Vaiśvadeva."
In the Vaiśvadeva [offering], the Viśvedevas [are the deities]. (ĀpGs 7.27)

When it is enjoined, "O noble ones, being purified, [perform] the Vaiśvadeva," this instruction regarding the deities in the rite called Vaiśvadeva is for the purpose of formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*) at the time of pouring out the oblation.
However, those deities which are mentioned there by means of the six initial mantras, such as "to Agni" and so forth, are the deities at the time of the actual offering.

Having thus resolved with the words "to all the Viśvedevas," the householder should prepare cooked food in his own home; from that very cooked food, he should perform the *homa* oblations and *bali* offerings for each respective deity. Such are the originative injunctions (*utpatti-vidhi*) for the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), beginning with the daily *bhūtabali*.
The injunction for their performance, however, is "the noble ones, being purified," and so forth.

Therefore, the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) are not to be performed separately; rather, the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is included therein: that which is offered into the fire is the sacrifice to the gods (devayajña); that which is the offering of bali-oblations is the sacrifice to the beings (bhūtayajña).
That which is offered to the south with the characteristic marks of the ancestors is the *pitṛyajña*;
that which consists of "what is to be given first" and so forth is the *manuṣyayajña*.
Regarding this, the commentator on the mantras has stated that in the *vaiśvadeva* rite, the second oblation is "to Soma, svāhā."

And there is no contradiction with the statement "not by these first six," because that [rule] refers to the principal deities, whereas the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering belongs to the ritual procedure (*tantra*).

Now, why is the complete ritual procedure for the Vaiśvadeva not taught here? It is said: if it were taught here, that procedure would not apply to all *caranas* (Vedic schools), yet this is desired. Therefore, its teaching is placed among the *sāmayācārika* (conventional) rules common to all *caranas*.
Now, why was that instruction from the deity not given right there?
The purpose of the instruction here in this *Gṛhya-sūtra* is so that the *vaiśvadeva* rite may also be taught within it.
Therefore, for our own tradition, that very *vaiśvadeva* ritual procedure is prescribed, whereas it is not enjoined in other *dharma-śāstras*.
And the application of the general rule (paribhāṣā) beginning with "by one wearing the sacred thread (yajñopavītin), [moving] from left to right (pradakṣiṇam)" and so forth, also occurs. //29//
"Vaiśvadeva" is the name of the ritual;
and its basis for application is that all (viśve) the gods (devāḥ) are worshipped here.
And here, since the divinity of those established by the wording of the mantras cannot be something to be enjoined,

all six oblations beginning with the Āgneya, as well as the bali-offerings— even those not intended for Agni— are exclusively primary acts; not even one among them is a subsidiary (aṅga), which is another name for a subordinate element.

Such is the meaning of the Sūtra. The intended sense is this: if the primary [subject] were not fire, but rather only a subordinate element (śeṣa), then it would have been observed in the third chapter, which defines such subordinate elements.
However, this is neither seen [in other texts] nor is it observed to have been stated by the author of the Sūtra;
rather, in the case of the Puṇḍarīka-pitṛyajña, Āpastamba has declared that both the offering of gold and the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) are primary.
"If one's father is living, he should not perform the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa);
having performed [the rites] up to the oblation (āhoma), he should desist," so says Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 1.9.8.
For if the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) were a subsidiary part (aṅga),
then when the principal oblation (homa) is performed, that [offering] would also have to be performed; there would be no cessation [of the ritual].

Therefore, in this case, the cessation characterized by non-commencement applies specifically to the principal act of offering the rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*), just as in the case of [the rule] "one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice shall not eat" (*nāsomayājī saṃvṛśet*) and so forth.
Kātyāyana, however, maintains that on the contrary, the offering of the rice-balls itself is the principal act.

He states that the oblation (homa) is an ancillary part of that [rite]: "For one whose father is living, it ends with the oblation, or there is no commencement at all" (Kātyāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.1.24, 25).
Likewise, for the Sarpa and Īśāna offerings as well, the oblations and the bali-offerings constitute the primary elements.
However, in the case of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), the primary element exists even without fire.
Although this [rite] is a subsidiary part of the Soma sacrifice, its status as the primary element is relative to its own constituent parts.
In the same way, for the Rākṣasa sacrifice and the ass-sacrifice, the primary offering is made in a non-consecrated fire (anagni),
according to the scriptural statement; however, regarding the omentum (vapā), there is an oblation in the consecrated fire (agni) based on the authoritative teaching.

Because of the separate mention of the *vapā* (omentum) in the rule, "If the *vapā*, the sacrificial oblation (*havis*), or the portioning (*avadāna*) should be spilled" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 9.18.15),
there are likewise many other primary offerings even when not performed with fire.
"Or, in the *aupāsana* or *pacana* fire, one should offer oblations with the hand using each of the first six mantras" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.3.17).
By this restrictive injunction (*parisaṅkhyā*), and because this *vaiśvadeva* is a modification of the non-*pārvaṇa* [rites],
it is not a constituent part (*aṅga*) in rites such as the *sarpa-bali*, which are modifications of the *pārvaṇa*.

Furthermore, even among the Vaiśvadeva mantras, primacy belongs to these two— "Svāhā to Agni" and "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt"— because they are specifically prescribed. Now, one might object that even the Vaiśvadeva mantras do not have a direct, explicit recitation.
How is this understood?

It is stated that [it is understood] because there is a sequential application through such sūtras as, "With the first six, mantra by mantra; with the other two, the seventh and eighth, [one worships] the fire" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.3.16, 20); thus, it is understood that there is a traditional recitation [of these mantras].
And that recitation [of the Veda] is prior to the marriage mantras, according to the statement of the Commentator (Bhāṣyakāra).
Consequently, it should be understood that for both the Brahmayajña and the Pārāyaṇa as well, the study of these very [mantras] follows this same sequence.

Regarding their absolute primacy, the purpose is as follows: even if one of these [rites] has not been performed, once the ritual application is completed, it must be carried out with its ancillaries and accompanied by an expiation prior to eating;
however, if eating has already taken place, only the expiation for the omission of the *pākayajña* is required.
Some maintain that in the *vaiśvadeva*, the Viśvedevas are prescribed as the deities at the time of the pouring-out [of the oblation] for the sake of the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*).
It is like the sacrifice to Īśāna.
However, those deities which are prescribed in the Dharmaśāstra through the application of mantras (mantraviniyoga) are the deities at the time of offering.
And here, the instruction regarding the deities is for the purpose of obtaining the general rules (gārhyaparibhāṣā) pertaining to the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
In that regard, the instruction for him is for the purpose of performing all [the rites].
Furthermore, this Vaiśvadeva is not distinct from the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña);
such are the originative injunctions (utpattividhi) for the five great sacrifices.
The passage beginning with "O noble ones, being purified, [perform the rites] for the Viśvedevas" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.3.1) is the injunction regarding performance (*prayogavidhi*).
In that context, whatever is performed in the fire is the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*).

That which is the offering of oblations is the sacrifice to beings (bhūtayajña); that which is performed to the south with a formula containing the word "father" is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña);
and that which is the giving of the first portion is the sacrifice to men (manuṣyayajña). Thus it is said.

That is not so; for in our own view, it would be improper to set aside all the gods enjoined by the Śruti through mere words and then give the sacrificial oblation intended for them to other deities merely on the basis of the wording of the mantras.
However, in the case of the offering to Īśāna, the terms *bhava*, *śarva*, and so forth, are indeed designations of Īśāna himself.
Furthermore, because the author of the Sūtras maintains that the purpose (artha) itself constitutes the deity,
it is appropriate to perform the offering with mantras such as "for Bhava.
As for the giving of portions from this *sthālīpāka* to Mīḍhuṣī and Jayanta, that too is like the *Abhyudayeṣṭi* sacrifice and similar rites, or like the *savanīya-puroḍāśa* offerings.

This is appropriate because of the scriptural injunctions: "Having prepared three portions of boiled rice, having sprinkled them with the subsequent [mantras], and having offered oblations from each portion of boiled rice with the subsequent [mantras]" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 20.4), which, by removing the previous deities from two parts of the *sthālīpāka* and prescribing different deities for them, establishes this.
Furthermore, it is not the case that the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice is not distinct from the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*).
Since a difference in ritual action is understood from the fact that they occur in different contexts and have distinct names,
it is not reasonable to deny a proven difference on the grounds that their performance would be difficult to establish when the actions are distinct;
for in the Bhāṣya, the performance of the Vaiśvadeva and of those [rites] is established as being entirely separate.

Now, the commentary on the ritual application (*prayoga-bhāṣya*) is stated with slight variation: the rite of the *vaiśvadeva* is described here incidentally along with the five great sacrifices (*pañca-mahāyajña*).

At the conclusion of the marriage ceremony, following the recitation for the consummation (*samāveśana-japa*), once the wedding is finished and the *vaiśvadeva* mantras have been employed, there is the vow: "For twelve days, one should sleep on the ground" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.3.13).

Because there is no difference in their ownership [of the sacrifice], the husband, having performed [the preliminary rites] together with his wife, should— on an auspicious day— begin with the procedure starting from "O noble ones, being purified,

you shall be the preparers of the food for the Vaiśvadeva," and once the food is prepared, the wife or whoever prepares the food, while standing, should announce to the owner, "It is ready" (*bhūtam*).
The master should reply, "Subhūti, that food was excellent; let it not go to waste.
Then, whether on the journey or at home, fire should be kindled in the place where the Vaiśvadeva oblation is offered;
there he kindles it according to the procedure prescribed in the Dharmaśāstras.
The same applies elsewhere, such as in the *aupāsana* oblations and other rites.
Now, from whatever food is to be eaten by the householder, he sets aside in one vessel the sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) intended for the oblation;
in a second [vessel], he places that which is not sacrificial food (*ahaviṣya*), mixed with raw salt, pungent condiments, and inferior grains.
On the third [day], he should set aside sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) for the purpose of the sacrifice to the gods;
on the fourth, having taken portions from all [the food], for the sake of the foremost [ancestors];
and on the fifth, having likewise taken portions from all, for the purpose of the sacrifice to humans, provided that the gratification of Brahmins is possible.
This is because of the statement: "One should give to human beings according to one's ability" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.12.15).

Then, having performed the sprinkling (pariṣecana), one should offer six oblations from the food prepared first—measuring only a thumb-joint in size—with the mantras beginning with "Svāhā to Agni," and then perform the subsequent sprinkling.

Then, having removed the hot ashes toward the north, he offers non-sacrificial food (*ahaviṣya*) into that [fire] with the utterance *svāhā*; for there is this scriptural injunction: "That which is not prepared in one's fire, and the first portion of which is not offered, must not be eaten" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.15.13).

Then, having mixed the remainder of the six oblations with the remainder of the *mahāvaiśvadeva* offering, and having offered the *bali* ending with the *raudra* portion according to the procedure prescribed in the *Dharmaśāstras* using food mixed with soup, and having given the first portion to a Brāhmaṇa, he should perform the *devayajña*—which, because it is taught by the Brāhmaṇas, is explained as being like the *apārvaṇa* [offering] and possesses the ritual requirements for the *sannipāta* [conjunction].
Having made the formal resolve (*āgūrya*), "I shall sacrifice with the *devayajña*," [he recites]: "Thou art lightning."
From food prepared on the *aupāsana* fire or the cooking fire;
in its absence, from sacrificial food such as rice, barley, and so forth,
down to wood.

One should offer with the hand, saying "Svāhā to the gods," because the offering with the hand is observed for both the *aupāsana-homa* and the *vaiśvadeva*, which share the same procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
And the sprinkling around [the fire] is performed with the mantra on both occasions.
This is precisely because those two have been observed [in the texts].
"Thou art rain" (vṛṣṭir asi);
in the *vaṣaṭkāra* oblations, there is the instruction: "lightning and rain."

Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), having said, "I shall sacrifice with the Pitṛyajña," and having recited the *vidyudāsī* mantra, he should offer a portion the size of a sacrificial oblation (*āhuti*) from the cooked rice prepared on pure ground, using his thumb and forefinger together, saying: "Svadhā be to the ancestors! (*pitṛbhyaḥ svadhāstu*).
"You are rain.
This is the instruction regarding the procedure for the *bali* offering to the ancestors (*pitrya*).

Now, since the *bali* offering is equivalent to a *homa*, one should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (*yajñopavītī*) and, having said, "I shall sacrifice with the *bhūta-yajña*," [recite] "Vud-yut."
On clean ground alone, one should offer [the food] with the hand, saying, "May this be for the beings.
The instruction is that rain is [offered] according to the procedure for the bali-offering.

Now, since giving is equal to the fire-oblation (homa), one who wears the sacred thread (yajñopavītī) should say, "I shall sacrifice with the human sacrifice (manuṣyayajña)," and then perform the satiation of Brahmins as prescribed by rule,
or the giving of what has been intended for donation.
The instruction is that rain, giving, and command constitute [the forms of] teaching.
However, one should first perform the *brahmayajña*, having offered the *agnihotra* or the *aupāsana* fire sacrifice.
This is because of the scriptural statement, "When the sun has risen" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.11).
The ritual for that [Brahmayajña] is stated as: "One who is about to perform the sacrifice of Brahman" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.11).
In the place prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa and so forth, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules.

However, there is a specific distinction regarding this ācamana: beginning with "having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (*dakṣiṇata upavīya*) and ending with "having touched [the lips] once" (*sakṛdupaspṛśya*; Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 2.11), if a deficiency occurs, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is the oblation (*homa*) performed with the formulas "If [there is a deficiency] in the Yajus" (*yadi yajuṣṭaḥ*) and "Bhuvaḥ svāhā."
Beginning with "having sprinkled the left hand with the right hand," when the remainder has been performed imperfectly, the expiation is "if it is unknown.
Now, the sequence is stated: having said, "I shall sacrifice with the Brahma-sacrifice," [the recitation of] the *vidyut* [verses], and the sipping of water (*ācamana*).

Having performed the rites beginning with the preparation of the seat and ending with the recitation of the Sāvitrī, one should undertake the study of the Veda starting from its beginning, chapter by chapter, until the entire Veda is completed; for it is stated:
"Having commenced the term of study on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.9.1).

This study is to be conducted in whatever manner and sequence the chapters are traditionally taught, including the necessary textual supplements indicated at the outset, such as those known as *anuṣaṅga* and *prakhyā*.
Repeating [the recitation] again and again, one should study with speech and mind as much as possible and as much as one's strength allows.
Having performed the concluding verse (*paridhānīyā*), [one says]: "You are rain."
In this manner, day by day, beginning from the Kṛtānta section until the Veda is completed together with the section on the rules for the single fire (Ekāgnividhi),
having studied the whole and having studied the Vaiśvadeva mantras, one should then study the two sections beginning with "prasugmantā.
This is because such an application is observed.
"The rule for the single fire is the section on the Vaiśvadeva; such is the established tradition."
And because of this statement:

"If one is a student of multiple Vedic branches (*śākhā*), then by this very rule he should study a second [branch] again; if there should be an interruption of study (*anadhyāya*) during the sequential study of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāman* Vedas, then he should recite a single verse (*ṛc*), a single sacrificial formula (*yajus*), or a single chant (*sāman*), beginning from the very end."
When it is the turn of the Brāhmaṇa, he should then utter: "I offer bhūr-bhuvaḥ-suvaḥ, truth, and austerity into faith.
In this manner, one should perform the Brahma-sacrifice for as long as one lives.
At the conclusion of the Manuṣya-yajña, one should make all [beings] partakers of the Vaiśvadeva offering. (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.9.5)
When all [the guests], ending with the wife, have eaten according to these and other injunctions,
one should scrape the remnants from the vessels used for cooking and serving and pour them out toward the north on a clean spot for Rudra as the recipient,
saying: "Svāhā to Rudra!"
The inclusion [of the formula] as if it were obligatory,
because it is a rite of performance:
"In this way, indeed, it becomes auspicious" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.4.23).
This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), according to the principle:
"In the case of substances, purificatory acts, and rituals, [the mention of results] is for the sake of another" (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 4.3.1).

Or rather, it is the fruit [of the ritual], because the author of the Sūtra has taught: "He who performs these [rites] constantly, without distraction, according to the instruction, attains heaven and prosperity" (ĀpDh 2.4.9).
Thus, except for the Mahāyatrās, having performed the rites ending with the Raudra offering in the evening, one should perform the Vaihāyasa Bhūtabali in the open air.

Others say: because of the connection of the particle *eva* with a word separated from it in the rule "only at night with the last [verse]" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.4.8), the evening [offering] must be performed while [the fire] is still in the air.
Now, as an incidental discussion, he teaches the deity for the offering of the snake-sacrifice and its subsequent dismissal:
"The full-moon [offering] is that which is performed on the full-moon day. (ĀpGS 7.28)

Regarding the injunction, “On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, when the sun has set, [one should perform] the *sthālīpāka*,” and so forth: the deity for that rite enjoined on the full moon day is the Full Moon itself.
Who is she? She is the one for whom that rite is performed; [this is indicated by the mantra]: “Svāhā to the full moon of Śrāvaṇa.
In this manner, the oblation is offered from the *sthālīpāka*.
Then, according to the instruction, one offers fuel-sticks of *kiṃśuka* wood and oblations of clarified butter;
then the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering from the *sthālīpāka*;
then the *jayā* and subsequent offerings.
If the phrase "in which [the rite] is performed" were not stated, the oblation would be offered simply with the words "To the Full Moon, Svāhā! (paurṇamāsyai svāhā). //30//
On whichever full moon day—whether the Śrāvaṇī or the Mārgaśīrṣī—the *sthālīpāka* is performed as the occasion, that very full moon is its deity.
This is the meaning: in the *sarpabali*, there is an oblation of the *sthālīpāka* with the formula, "Svāhā to the Śrāvaṇī full moon."
But at the pouring out [of the water], [he offers] with the formula: "To the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, svāhā! //28//
Thus ends the seventh section in the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
The Eighth Section. 43. The Commencement.
Regarding both the commencement and the completion [of the Vedic study], the seer (ṛṣi) who is known [for that particular section] is the one to be honored. (ĀpGS 8.1)
The second is Sadasaspati. ĀpGs 8.2.
The commencement (*upākaraṇa*) is of two kinds: the commencement of a *kāṇḍa* and the commencement of a chapter (*adhyāya*).
Likewise is the conclusion (*samāpana*).
Furthermore, it is seen in another passage: “At the commencement of a *kāṇḍa*, one is without a mother; at the conclusion of a *kāṇḍa*, one is without a father” (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.11.1–2).
The commencement of the term (*adhyāyopākaraṇa*) is well known from the rule: "Having commenced the term on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa.
Likewise, the conclusion is prescribed: "One should cease [studying] on the full moon day of Taiṣa or under the asterism Rohiṇī" (ĀpDhS 1.9.20).
Regarding both types of commencement and conclusion, it is understood from the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇī* that the seer (*ṛṣi*) of the section is the deity there, by virtue of being the seer of the *kāṇḍa*.
In that context, the Lord of the Assembly (Sadasaspati) is the second [deity]. Having offered to the Ṛṣi of the section (kāṇḍa-ṛṣi), one should offer to the Lord of the Assembly; this is the meaning.
In that regard, the sections (kāṇḍas) are those dedicated to Prajāpati, Soma, Agni, and the Viśvedevas.

Prajāpati, Soma, Agni, and the Viśvedevas are the *kāṇḍarṣis* (section-seers) for those mixed sections known as the *Sārasvata*. As Baudhāyana says: "The *Pauroḍāśika*, the *Yājamāna*, the *Hotṛs*, the *Hautra*, and the *Pitṛmedha*—these, together with their *Brāhmaṇas* and *Anubrāhmaṇas*, belong to Prajāpati."

The Āgrayaṇa, the cups (grahas), the sacrificial gifts (dākṣiṇāni), the Samiṣṭayajus offerings, the Avabhṛtha offerings, the Vājapeya, the Śukriyas, and the Soma-pressings (savas)—these, together with their Brāhmaṇas and Anubrāhmaṇas, belong to the Soma-sacrifices.

The Agnyādheya, the Punarādheya, the Agnihotra, the Agnyupasthāna, the Agnicayana, the Sāvitra, the Nāciketa, the Cāturhotriya, the Vaiśvasṛja, and the Āruṇa—these, together with their Brāhmaṇas and Anubrāhmaṇas, belong to the Āgneya rites.
The Rājasūya, the Paśubandha, the Iṣṭis, the Nakṣatreṣṭis, the Divaśyenayas, the Apāghās, the Satrāyaṇa, and the Upahomas [are likewise included].
"The *sūktas*, the *upānuvākyās*, the *yājyās*, the *Aśvamedha*, the *Puruṣamedha*, the *Sautrāmaṇī*, the *Acchidra* rites, the *Paśuhautra*, and the *Upaniṣads*— these,
together with their *Brāhmaṇas* and *Anubrāhmaṇas*, are the *Vaiśvadeva* sections" (Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 3.1.21–24). Furthermore,
our own two *Gṛhya-mantra-praśnas* should also be regarded as the section named *Ekāgni-kāṇḍa* within the *Vaiśvadeva-kāṇḍa*.
In that regard, at the commencement of a *kāṇḍa*, an oblation is offered to the seer (*ṛṣi*) of that *kāṇḍa* with the formula: "To Prajāpati, the seer of the *kāṇḍa*, svāhā!

Thereafter, for the purpose of the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) accompanied by mantras as they occur in sequence, the mantra beginning with "sadasaspatimadbhutam" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.7.8.4), which was previously recited in the section on marriage (*vivāhaprakaraṇa*), is presented here in this place;
this sūtra is stated in this context specifically to demonstrate its application (*viniyoga*).
Otherwise, it would have had to be stated immediately after the initiation (*upanayana*).
Thus, upon the completion of each respective [section], there is an oblation to the corresponding *kāṇḍarṣi*;
the second [oblation] is for Sadasaspati.
Victory and the rest do not occur,
because there is no means of attainment;
some, however, offer oblations by relying on other sūtras.

These are the four Vedic observances (*vedavrata*): those which are the introductory rites (*upākaraṇa*) for each *kāṇḍa* are the observances, and those which are the concluding rites (*samāpana*) are the dismissals of the observances (*vratavisarjana*).
However, at the commencement of the study of a chapter (*adhyāya*), there is an oblation (*homa*) to all the seers (*ṛṣi*) of the *kāṇḍas*, followed by one to Sadasaspati.
Furthermore, the *jayā* and other [oblations] may or may not take place.

In that regard, since the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) and conclusion (*samāpana*) of the *kāṇḍas* must occur during the northern course of the sun and so forth, one should perform the commencement of the *Prājāpatya-kāṇḍa* immediately after the initiation (*upanayana*). Having performed the commencement on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the study of the *Prājāpatya-kāṇḍa* follows.

The ritual abandonment (*utsarga*) takes place in the month of Taiṣya. There, at the conclusion of the *prājāpatya* section after this much time has elapsed, that abandonment occurs; then follows the introductory rite (*upākaraṇa*) for the *saumya* [sacrifice].
Then, until the upākarman at the beginning of the [next] semester, the memorization and study of the *prājāpatya* section should take place during the bright fortnights,
while the study of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) should take place during the dark fortnights. The upākarman ceremony is performed on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa.
Now follows the study of the Saumya-kāṇḍa. The suspension of study occurs on the full moon day of Taiṣa; likewise, the completion of the kāṇḍa.
The same applies to the other two [Vedas].

In all cases, after the formal dismissal (*utsarjana*), the primary rule is that one should perform the *dāraṇa* recitation, the recitation of the ancillaries (*aṅga*), and the fire-oblation (*homa*) for the portion previously undertaken.

Now, for those who study the *Sārasvata-pāṭha*, immediately following the initiation (*upanayana*), they should perform the four Vedic vows (*vedavrata*) in succession; then, having performed the commencement of the term (*upākarma*) at the proper time, they should engage in the study according to the specific recensional text.
The ritual of relinquishment (*utsarga*) takes place on the full moon day of the month of Taiṣya.
As before, there is the holding of the Veda, the study of the Vedas, the study of the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), and the re-commencement (*upākaraṇa*) and so forth.
However, in the first *kalpa*, some do not perform the ritual of relinquishment.
Having studied [the Veda] after the opening ceremony (*upākaraṇa*), they perform the opening ceremony again;
others, however, having concluded their studies (*utsṛjya*), study again at some time or other, and they observe the Vedic vows (*vedavrata*) whenever they may.
Their source must be sought.
In all these views, however, there is a separate introductory rite (*upākaraṇa*) and a concluding rite (*utsarjana*) for the *Śukriyas*.

The procedure therein is as follows: beginning with the full-moon day or the northern solstice, up until the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, one offers oblations with the formulas "To Soma, the Ṛṣi of the section, svāhā" and "To Sadasaspati," and then proceeds from the end of the *jaya* and other rites up to the touching of the *madantī* water, and so forth.
It is practiced;
likewise, the same application [of the rule] holds here as well for the phrase "having emitted," as before. //1//

Here, for the sake of clarifying the subject matter, the nature of the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) and conclusion (*samāpana*) of the chapter, as well as of the sections (*kāṇḍas*) known as the Prājāpatya, Saumya, Āgneya, and Vaiśvadeva, and of the vows associated with those respective sections, is stated. Among these, the commencement of the chapter is the beginning of the study of the chapters, preceded by the performance of the prescribed oblations on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa. And the conclusion is—
For him, on the full moon day of the month of Taiṣya and so forth, the formal commencement (*utsarga*) of study is preceded by a fire-oblation (*homa*).

However, the preliminary rite for the sections (*kāṇḍopākaraṇa*)—which is the beginning of the study of those respective sections at the time prescribed by the sequence—is likewise preceded by a fire-oblation. And their completion (*samāpana*)—the formal conclusion (*utsarga*) upon the completion of the study of each respective section—is also preceded by a fire-oblation.
Those very [rites] that constitute the commencement and completion of the *kāṇḍas* are themselves the observances (*vrata*s);
there is no distinction,
because all the observances of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) are auxiliary to the study [of the Veda].
However, regarding the study of the *Sārasvata* recension, because the *kāṇḍas* are intermingled, it is impossible to study them according to the sequence of the *kāṇḍas*;

therefore, one should perform the initiatory rites (*upākaraṇa*) for each *vrata* individually during the northern course of the sun, just as one does for a *kāṇḍa*, observe them for a year, and then formally conclude them (*utsṛjet*) according to the rules.
And there are exactly four *vedavrata*s.

But it does not refer to the Vedic vow called *sāvitrasammita* mentioned in other *gṛhya* texts, because the two sections (*kāṇḍas*) known as *savitrasammita* do not exist [in this context]. [The sequence is: *caula*, *upanayana*,...
And because of the statement of Gautama: "There are four Vedic vows" (GauDhS 8.15).
Likewise, for the sake of clarifying the subject matter, the *Prayoga-bhāṣya* is written with only slight variations.
According to the instruction following the tradition of Āpastamba, the ritual procedure for the commencement of the study of the Vedas (*adhyāyopākaraṇa*) and other rites is described.
Regarding that, on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, the teacher, having performed breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) together with his pupils, [proceeds].

Having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), "I shall commence the meditation," and having bathed according to the rules in a great river with the sacred grass (pavitra) in hand, he should satiate the nine seers (ṛṣis): "I satiate Prajāpati, the seer of the section; I satiate Soma, the seer of the section."
I satiate Agni, the seer of the section; I satiate the Viśvedevas, the seers of the section;
I satiate the deities of the Saṃhitās and the Upaniṣads.
I satiate the sacrificial deities who are the Upaniṣads; I satiate the Varuṇian deities who are the Upaniṣads;
I satiate Brahmā, the Self-existent.
"I satisfy the Lord of the Assembly"—with these words [he offers].

Then, from the taking of fuel for the fire until the end of the "mouth of the fire" (agnimukha) rite, while the students hold on to him, he offers nine oblations of clarified butter: "To Prajāpati, the seer of the section, svāhā!
To Soma, the seer of the section, svāhā!"
Svāhā to Agni, the seer of the section!
Svāhā to the Viśvedevas, the seers of the sections!
Svāhā to the deities of the Saṃhitās, the Upaniṣads!
Svāhā to the sacrificial deities, the Upaniṣads! Svāhā to the Varuṇa-related deities, the Upaniṣads!
Svāhā to the self-existent Brahman!
With this verse, "sadasaspatim," he offers the ninth *āghuti* oblation.
Then, seated upon *darbha* grass with *darbha* blades held in their hands, the students, led by the teacher, should recite the first four sections (*anuvākas*) of the Veda from the beginning.
Then follows the *jaya* and subsequent rites up to the final sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), ending with the satiation of the Brahmins (*brāhmaṇatarpaṇa*).
In the same way, regarding the *utsarga*,
there is nothing more than this, even by incorporating other Smṛtis; rather, it follows the Sūtra of Āpastamba.
Likewise, the study of the recitations (*anuvāka*) of the Veda is performed with the *nādita* [intonation].
However, the *jaya* and other [rituals] do take place.
With the exception of the *saumya* [rite], at the commencement and conclusion of a *kāṇḍa*, there are no *sūkta-upahoma*, *devatopasthāna*, *jaya*, and so forth.
The *sūktajaya* and other rites belong specifically to the *saumya* [oblation];
thus, following the opinion of Āpastamba, some perform them exactly as prescribed.
Then, having bathed as before for the Prājāpatya vow, there is the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for [the deities] excluding Soma, Agni, and the Viśvedevas.
At the conclusion of the *agnimukha* rite, while the practitioner has taken hold of him, he offers oblations: "To Prajāpati, the seer of the *kāṇḍa*, svāhā!
O Prajāpati, none other than you [has encompassed] these... (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.8.1.2).

With this hymn, he offers six oblations verse by verse; four additional oblations with the verses beginning with "sāṃhitībhyaḥ" and so forth; and [an oblation] to Sadasaspati with the verse "sadasaspatim".
"O Agni, Lord of Vows, from the Seers of the Sections, I shall perform the vow belonging to Prajāpati;
may I be able to do so, and may it be successful for me.
O Vāyu, Lord of Vows..."
"O Āditya, lord of vows; O lord of vows among vows, from the *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis:
I shall perform the vow pertaining to Prajāpati; may I be able to do so, and may it be successful for me."
With these four [verses], according to the respective deities;
then follows the *jaya* offerings and so forth, as well as the satiation of the Brāhmaṇas.

In the same way, the procedure for the *samāvartana* is performed at the completion of each year. In that context, the specific difference in the attendance mantras (*upasthāna-mantra*) is: "I have practiced; I was able; I have succeeded. Some, because the shaving of hair and beard is observed in the *saumya* [sacrifice], desire it to be performed in the *prājāpatya* and other rites as well.
In the same way, it is so in the Āgneya and Vāśvadeva [sections]:
"To Agni, the seer of the section, svāhā!";
"O Agni, lead us" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.8.2).
The hymn consists of three ṛcs.
Regarding the Āgneya [rite], the specific modification is: "O Agni, Lord of Vows, from the seers of the Kāṇḍas, I shall perform the Āgneya vow. [And:
"Svāhā to all the gods, the seers of the Kāṇḍas!"
"May all the unassailable ones come to us" (Tai.
Brā. 2.8.6.3)—this is a hymn (*sūkta*) consisting of six verses.
Regarding the Vaiśvadeva vow, the specific instruction is: "I shall perform the Vaiśvadeva vow."
Regarding the commencement and conclusion of the *kāṇḍa* of Soma, as prescribed in the *Śukriyakalpa*,
it is stated here as follows: having performed the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) as before, from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *agnimukha* rite,
[one offers] "Svāhā to Soma, the seer of the *kāṇva*."
Having offered the six-verse hymn beginning with "Somo dhenu" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.8.3.1),
as well as the subsidiary oblations and to Sadasaspati;

Having performed the preliminary rites as before, having touched the *madantī* water, and having performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the first section (*anuvāka*), he places four fuel-sticks of *udumbara* wood, anointed with clarified butter, into the fire with the verses beginning with "The earth is the fuel" (*pṛthivī samit*, Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 7.4.2).
Then follows the worship of the deities with the formulas beginning, "O Agni, lord of vows, I shall observe the Saubhya vow for the sake of the seers of the Kāṇḍas.

From that point onward, having caused [the student] to recite either by joining the initial words of the Śukriya mantra and Brāhmaṇa sections or by making him utter them, he proceeds to the Jaya and subsequent rites.

Having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), having touched the *madantī* water, and having performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the final Anuvāka, he should then perform the closing of the eyes (*saṃmīlana*) and so forth according to the Sūtra.
On the following day, [he recites]: "The birds, fair-winged... (*avayaḥ suparṇāḥ*, Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 7.42.3).
Thus, at the conclusion of the worship of the Sun, there is the feeding of Brāhmaṇas.
Now, the rule for his private recitation (*svādhyāya*) has been stated precisely in the *Śukriyakalpa*. The same applies to the conclusion of the study.

The specific difference, however, is that the mantras for placing the fuel-sticks (*samid*) and for the worship (*upasthāna*)—beginning with "O Heaven, O Fuel-stick, O Āditya, O Lord of Vows"—are repeated.
Having performed the propitiatory rite (*śānti*) with the final section (*anuvāka*), having given a gift to the teacher, having had his hair and beard shaved, and having fed the Brahmins;
[there is no recitation of the *prabhṛti* verses here].

Now, the Sūtra is challenged: "But surely, since it is stated that 'the seer who is known for the opening and the completion [of a section]'—and thus whoever among Prajāpati and the others is traditionally recited in the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇī* as the seer of a *kāṇḍa* is the deity—this Sūtra is indeed redundant. [The response is:
"In the introductory rites (*upākaraṇa*) of the *kāṇḍas*, one should offer these [oblations] before the verse addressed to Sadasaspati."
And one should offer oblations at the conclusion of each section; this is the eternal Vedic injunction.
Thus, since the status of the *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis and deities is established by the *Kāṇḍānukramaṇī*,
it is true that for this very reason the four beginning with Prajāpati are the deities of the principal oblations (*pradhāna-homa*),
while the four beginning with Sāṃhitya and ending with Svayambhu are the deities of the subsidiary oblations (*upahoma*).

Therefore, these four follow through both the commencement and the completion of all sections, because auxiliary elements (aṅga) must follow their primary (pradhāna); such is the intent of the sūtra, and it does not aim to enjoin [these] as deities (devatā). //1//
Is it not the case that the Lord of the Assembly is the ninth [chapter] for the commencement and completion of the study of the *adhyāyas*,
and the sixth for the commencement and completion of the *kāṇḍas*?
Thus, although this is indeed "without a second," for what reason is it called "the second"?
This is for the purpose that this Sadasaspati may take the place of the second Sviṣṭakṛt;
and it is for this very reason that it was stated previously: "Agni Sviṣṭakṛt is the second" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 7.7).
In the rites of the introductory and concluding offerings where clarified butter is the oblation, there is no Sviṣṭakṛt at all.
How is the rule for the Sadasaspati [offering] established in its place?
This application is prescribed by that very statement,
just as the second oblation in the Agnihotra is prescribed by the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, the oblation for him is offered in the northeastern quarter of the fire.

In the event of forgetting this, there is the expiation for the omission of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. Since it is clear that the oblation should be performed with the verse "sadasaspatimadbhutam" according to both the indicative mark (*liṅga*) and the sequence (*krama*), the author of the Sūtra shows no concern [for other details]. Some say: "The one who is the *kāṇḍa-ṛṣi* at the commencement and the conclusion [of the section]..."
A second Sadasaspati is recognized for him;
this mantra, "Sadasaspati," is employed after the Kāṇḍarṣi,
but not in the marriage ceremony.

"Just as the two verses beginning with 'uddīpyasva' [are recited], the recitation in the midst of the marriage ceremony is for the purpose of the injunction for study"— thus, under the guise of indicating the subject matter of the *sadasaspati* mantra, [the author] implies that since the ritual procedure (*prayogakalpa*) for these two rites is well-known elsewhere but not established here, it must necessarily be adopted.
In this treatise, the purpose of this sūtra is its internal inclusion [within the ritual], and from that follows the commencement of the action.

This is not so; for although the word *sadasaspati* occurring in the sūtra can refer to the deity in its primary sense, it is improper to use it as a secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the mantra by first indicating the opening of the mantra (*mantrapratīka*) and then using that indicated opening to indicate the mantra itself.

Because the application of these two in this very context is well-established by the method already stated, and because there would be the futility of internalizing that which is established elsewhere. //2//

Based on the statement in the Dharmaśāstra, "That which is not offered in the fire must not be eaten" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.15.13), even for the sake of maintaining the body, the meal of a twice-born person must consist only of the remnants of the Vaiśvadeva offering.

Furthermore, according to the statement, "If the fire is not offered for four nights, it becomes a worldly fire," the fire intended for all sacrificial rites would become a worldly fire if the Agnihotra is not performed.

Furthermore, even when there is an affliction such as fever, because the Vaiśvadeva, Agnihotra, and other rites—or the expiatory oblations for them—must necessarily be performed, it follows that even if another officiant is unavailable, both [husband and wife] may perform it in some manner, even if they are uninitiated women and even with a deficiency in mantras or ancillary details. Likewise, regarding the Vaiśvadeva in the context of Śrāddhas and other rites, it is stated: "Now, for the householder, there are oblations and offerings of whatever food he eats" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.3.12).
Based on this statement,

since there is a possibility that even an oblation (*havis*) mixed with *suvarcaka*, barley-alkali (*yavakṣāra*), salt, inferior food, and *kośadhānya*— also known as *māṣa* and other grains excluding sesame— might be used in the *homa*,
he speaks [the following verse] in order to prohibit both of these:
In the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice, the performer and the substances are both prohibited.

They declare that the offering of food mixed with alkaline or saline substances, or with inferior food, should not be performed by a woman or by one who has not been initiated. (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 8.3)

In the section concerning *pākayajña* sacrifices, this prohibition applies everywhere: even among those things such as faith and so forth, the learned avoid—meaning they shun—inferior grains, pulses such as *māṣa*, black grains, and chickpeas or *kodrava*. [It is also said: "A woman should not offer the oblation."
It is not for one who has not been initiated;
nor is there a sacrifice with alkaline salt [permitted]. Although this prohibition is already established by the preceding rule, this present prohibition is for the sake of what follows.

Furthermore: "From the taking of the hand [of the bride] onwards, one should personally perform the domestic rites (*gṛhya*), or else the wife, or the son, or the daughter, or the pupil" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.9.1).
Thus, by the statement of Āśvalāyana, there is a prohibition against the apprehension that women and others might perform the *aupāsana* oblation. //2//

The learned (śiṣṭas) reject—that is, they avoid—the mere performance of a *homa* (oblation), whether it be *śrauta* or *smārta*, by one who is neither initiated (*anupeta*) nor invested with the sacred thread (*anupanīta*). Therefore, the ellipsis of the sentence is: "for that very reason, one should not offer oblations with those two [wives]. By using the general term "*homa*," it is made known that the learned avoid both [types of] *śrauta-homa* as well when performed by a woman or one who is uninitiated; thus, this is an exception to the scope of the *gṛhya* (domestic) rites.
The passage beginning with "kṣāra" (alkaline substances) and so forth is almost entirely self-explanatory.

As for the statement in the *Dharmaśāstra*, "There is no offering of alkaline substances or salt; likewise, there is none of food mixed with inferior grains" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.15.14, 15), that refers to [the case where one should offer] after having pushed aside the hot ashes toward the north, as stated in: "Having pushed aside the hot ashes toward the north, one should offer therein" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.15.16).

Thus, this is a restatement for the purpose of prescribing [the rule]. Furthermore, as for the statement in that same [text], "A woman shall not offer oblations, nor one who has not been initiated" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.15.17,
18), it refers to the fact that substances such as alkaline salts are offered just as [they would be] into hot ashes.
Likewise, in that case as well, it is to prohibit the offering by one who has not been initiated or by a woman. //3//
He states an exception to this prohibition:
"The optional offerings and oblations are to be performed according to the instruction. (ĀpGS 8.4)
This prohibition regarding women and others is not to be observed in the case of optional rites (*kāmya-karma*); these must be performed exactly as instructed.
Likewise, the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) must be given exactly as instructed.
"Whatever merchandise he may have in his house for the sake of success" is an example of an optional rite.

Thus, regarding the passage beginning with "when of what is to be eaten" (*yadaśanīyasya*) and so forth, since the prohibition of women and others enjoined for the *homa* does not apply by extension (*prasaṅga*) to the *bali* offerings, this serves as an indicator (*jñāpaka*) that the ritual properties (*dharma*) of the *homa* extend to the *bali*s.
Consequently, rules such as "with the other [hand]" and "having bent the right knee" (*dakṣiṇaṃ jānvācya*) and so forth also apply to the *bali*s.

Since it was already established by the rule "not in the case of optional sacrifices (kāmya) or offerings (bali)," the statement "according to the instruction" (yathopadeśam) indicates that their performance proceeds solely from the instruction itself—whether by one's own scripture or another scripture—and not as a substitute (pratinidhi). //3//
In whatever manner those vehicles have been taught, they remain exactly so;
there is no avoidance of alkaline substances and the like therein, as indicated by the rule:
"Whatever may be the merchandise in his house" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 23.5).
Because this instruction is qualified by the word "household" (*gṛha*),
if the avoidance of pungent substances and the like were intended there, then he would have said simply, "whatever may be his merchandise."
Likewise, the offerings (bali) are exactly as prescribed;
however, there is no prohibition against salt and the like, for it is stated: "They should be made with [the food] mixed with broth" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.3.19).

This is because of the force of the introductory statement (*ityārambhasāmarthyāt*). Otherwise, by the very rule, "The *homa*s and *bali* offerings [are to be made] from what is to be eaten by the householder," the rites would have to be performed with food mixed with vegetables, meat, and soups, excluding only salted items (*kṣāra*) and the like. Furthermore, in this context, the doubt regarding the prohibition of salted items and so forth—which might arise for the *bali* offerings as well due to their association with the *homa* in the phrase "the *homa*s and *bali* from what is to be eaten"—is here precluded.
Some hold that because of the very injunction stating "the optional offerings and the *balis* according to the instruction," the characteristics of the *homa* apply to the *balis* as well;
for them, the utterance of *svāhā* would be unavoidable when pouring out roasted barley flour (*saktu*) during the *sarpabali*. (4)
45. The expiation for the fire taken for the sake of a *homa* spontaneously catching fire:
in every case where the fire has spontaneously caught fire, one should place two fuel-sticks upon it with the following two verses. (ĀpGs 8.5)

In all *pākayajña* sacrifices, when the fire has ignited itself—meaning, without human effort such as blowing or fanning—and when this occasion has arrived, one should place two fuel-sticks (*samidh*) into the fire with the two following verses: "Flame up! and "Do not harm us! Since this is enjoined by the verb "he places," there is no utterance of *svāhā*.
Because of the use of the word "everywhere" (sarvatra), this rule applies to all *pākayajña* sacrifices;
otherwise, due to the context, it would apply only to the marriage ceremony.
"Everywhere" means in any fire—whether worldly (*laukika*), Vedic (*vaidika*), or domestic (*gārhya*).

Others say [it applies] "at times when there is a single ritual action. Others say it applies "in all cases, in all rituals characterized by various modes of conduct," meaning "always, even at times when there is no ritual action."
When the fire has ignited itself, or when the *aupāsana* fire has been kindled without effort,
one should place fuel sticks upon it with the two subsequent *ṛc*s beginning with "O Jātavedas, shine forth!
One should place a single fuel stick for each verse.

Because there is a distinction of actions when there is a distinction in the means of accomplishment inherent [to them], the utterance *svāhā* is not prescribed for those acts enjoined by the root *juhoti*, such as "he places" (*ādadhāti*) or "he strikes" (*praharati*).
Even in the case of the throwing of the *prastara* grass-bundle, it is stated: "He does not utter *svāhā*" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 3.6.7).
This is for the purpose of showing that the prohibition [of *svāhā*] applies even in cases such as "he places" (*ādadhāti*) and so forth.

Others, however, maintain that the prohibition "he does not utter *svāhā*" indicates that the utterance of *svāhā* occurs even in those acts like "placing" which are enjoined by the verb "to offer" (*juhoti*). //5//
"May the goddess of fortune who has entered me depart from me," or [he may say]. (ĀpGS 8.6)
"With these two *yajus* formulas, one should place these two kindling-sticks (*samidh*) upon the fire"—this is the alternative regarding the mantras. //5//
With the two verses beginning "uddīpyasva," the two Yajus-mantras beginning with "āpanma" are optionally substituted. //6//
46. Not forgetting the wedding day: "One should recognize this as the day on which one brings home a wife. (ĀpGs 8.7)
One should recognize this day and this lunar mansion; one should not forget them. On whatever day—that is, under whichever lunar mansion—one brings home a wife, she is brought from that family.
The meaning is that the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) under which the taking of the hand was performed must not be forgotten.
By the word "āvahataḥ" (of the one who has brought [the bride] home), the initial taking of the hand is intended.
The purpose of the instruction regarding non-forgetfulness is that there is a specific ritual act to be performed every year under that same lunar mansion.
What, then, is this?
It is that which has been taught in the *Sāmayācārika* [sections] beginning with: "And whatever may be dear to these two" (*Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra* 2.1.7).
And this is not a mandatory rule (*vidhi*).

If it were a specific modification (*viśeṣa*) of the *pārvaṇa* rite, then the statement "its procedure is explained by [the rules of] the *pārvaṇa*" would be inconsistent. Alternatively, why is that very rule not taught here?
It is said: In this instruction, because of the context, [the ritual] would be understood as being subsidiary to marriage;
consequently, even the *śamyā* and other such items would become duties of marriage. However, the instruction there is for the purpose of all [Vedic] schools (*caraṇa*). 6.

One should understand that the day on which he performs the rites beginning with the entry into the house and ending with the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice is to be taken as the starting point; from that day forward, for three nights, both [the husband and wife] must sleep on the ground and observe other such rules.
Some say: "He should not forget the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) under which the wedding took place.
According to the *Dharmaśāstra*: "On the following day, the *sthālīpāka* is performed" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.1.10).
This is for the purpose of performing the rites taught here every year.
Now, regarding these rites taught here, how is it that their instruction there [in the other texts] does not result in their being merely subsidiary parts of marriage,
and how is it that they may instead serve the purpose of all Vedic schools?
And because of the very context [of the preceding], it might be argued that starting from the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice, the rule "for three nights both lie on the ground" and so forth will apply.
That is not so; for the injunction has already been set aside by the mention of a different rite as previously stated in the passage "by means of the *pārvaṇa*" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 7.2.3). //7//
47. At the wedding, the rule for the couple’s celibacy is as follows:
for three nights both shall sleep on the ground, observe celibacy, and abstain from pungent and salty foods. (ĀpGs 8.8)
Starting from the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice, for three nights both husband and wife should sleep on the ground and not on beds or similar furniture;
they must observe celibacy by abstaining from sexual intercourse,
and they must avoid pungent and salty foods in their diet.
In this context, the avoidance of alkaline and salty foods does not apply on the journey prior to the cooking of the *sthālīpāka* offering;
however, celibacy (*brahmacarya*) applies even there.
Since the ritual of entering the marriage bed is prescribed for the fourth day, this mention of celibacy is intended to ensure firmness.
Although the two share a bed, nevertheless, effort must be made to avoid sexual intercourse. //7//

For both husband and wife, beginning from the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice, there shall be sleeping on the ground for three nights, and not on a bed or similar furniture; nor shall they sleep on separate beds.
Because of the mention of "both," there would likewise be the characteristic of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) consisting in the avoidance of the eight limbs of sexual intercourse. Furthermore,
Bṛhaspati has stated that sexual intercourse itself possesses eight limbs:
"Remembering, chanting, playing, looking, speaking in secret,
forming intentions, making resolutions, and the actual performance of the act."
The wise declare this eightfold sexual union.
Thus [it is said].
And this [mantra] is to be recited even on the road before the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice, according to the rule: "One should recite the remainder at the *samāveśana*" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 8.10).
Because the sequence is established later on;

for this very reason, in this sutra, since there is only one bed, the prohibition is intended to show that even sexual intercourse— which would otherwise be unavoidable— must be avoided with the utmost effort.

In the same way, there should be the avoidance of alkaline substances and salt; by the use of the word "and" (ca), the avoidance of honey, meat, tooth-cleaning sticks, collyrium, oil-massage, ointments, and wearing greasy substances is also implied.
Alternatively, the seven items beginning with honey are prohibited by the very term *brahmacarya* (celibacy).
The word "ca" (and), however, serves only to include what has been stated;
in all cases, it is precisely for three nights. //8//
48. Between those two as they sleep, a staff is placed. Between their beds, a staff smeared with fragrant paste stands, encircled by a cloth or a thread. (ĀpGs 8.9)

Between the two, the husband and wife, in the middle of the bed, a staff made from a milky-sap tree, smeared with fragrant perfume and adorned with flowers, should be placed, wrapped with a cloth or a thread, so that there may be no mutual contact between them. //8//

For those two, husband and wife, who are established in their vow, as long as the bed is not separated for three nights— that is, within that very interval, in the midst of it— [the practice is performed], but not after the three nights, nor even within a separate bed or a single bed [after that time];
for the pronoun "of those two" (tayoḥ) refers back to the subjects under discussion.
The staff, smeared with fragrance and anointed with sandalwood—
since "fragrance" is intended to include [other ornaments], it should also be adorned with flowers—
and wrapped with a cloth or a thread, it should stand, that is, it should be set up.
And in this staff, the Gandharva Viśvāvasu is to be meditated upon, because of the indicative mark of the mantra: "Arise from here, O Viśvāvasu.
For this very reason, this staff is made of Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, or Plakṣa wood.
This is because of the explanatory passage (arthavāda): "These indeed are the dwellings of the Gandharvas and Apsarases" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.4.8). //9//
49. The concluding oblation of the wedding and the entering together (*samāveśana*).

On the fourth day, during the latter part of the night, having raised her up with the two subsequent [verses], having washed her, and having set her down, [the rite proceeds] from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings.

When she has taken hold of him, he offers the subsequent oblations; having performed the rites beginning with the *jayas* up to the final sprinkling of water, he seats her to the west of the fire facing east. Having poured the remainder of the clarified butter upon her head with the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, he makes them look at each other with the next two verses according to their respective characteristics. Then, having wiped their hearts with the remainder of the clarified butter using the following verse, he mutters the next three verses.
One should recite the remainder at the time of entering [the house]. ĀpGs 8.10.

The third part of the night is the latter part of the night (*apararātra*). [The laying down of the staff] is performed with the two verses beginning with *udīrṣva* and *ātaḥ*. This is a prescription for the laying down [of the staff] which has already been established [by general rule], so that the laying down of the staff on that same bed might not occur again. //9//

He offers the seven principal oblations of the *uttarāḥ* [section], beginning with "O Agni, the expiation" (*agne prāyaścitte*). Among these, in the first four mantras, the phrase "Thou art the expiation of the gods" (*tvaṃ devānāṃ prāyaścittiḥ*) is to be supplied as an *anuṣaṅga*. The remaining mantras are three in number.

The phrase "the portion of clarified butter" (ājyabhāga) is an instruction regarding the time for the ritual grasping; and the statement "one proceeds with the Jaya and other offerings" indicates the cessation of that [grasping]. //10//

Having completed the remainder of the ritual procedure, he then seats her to the west of the fire, behind the fire, facing east. Taking a portion from the remnant of the clarified butter (*ājya*) remaining in the ladle, he pours it onto the head of the bride with each of the *vyāhṛtis*— preceded by the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*—
reciting one mantra for each pouring.
Then, with the two subsequent verses beginning with "I have seen you" (*apaśyaṃ tvā*), they should look at each other simultaneously according to their respective marks—
the bride with the first verse and the groom with the second.

Then the groom anoints the hearts of both the bride and the groom with the subsequent verse, "May they anoint together" (*samañjantu*), using that same remnant of clarified butter taken up once, reciting the mantra only once.
Then he recites the next three verses beginning with "O Prajāpati, [this] body" (*prajāpate tanvam*).
Then he should recite the remainder of the section— the rest of the *anuvāka* beginning with "Climb up, O wide one" (*ārohoru*)— at the time of entering together during the *samāveśana* ceremony.
And the immersion (*samāveśana*) necessarily occurs during that very same latter part of the night;
this alone is the mantra-empowered immersion, and no others.
The statement ending with the ritual sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) is for the purpose of immediate succession.
This very ritual action should take place at the conclusion of the sprinkling;
therefore, the meal occurs beforehand. //11//
Regarding the fourth [night], the reading "in the latter part of the night" (*apararātre*) is explained as follows:

in the fourth night—that is, in the latter part of the fourth day-and-night, specifically in the third division of the night—he should raise that staff with the two verses beginning with "Arise, O man! (*udīrṣvāta*), wash it with water, set it down elsewhere from the bed, and proceed with the ritual procedure (*tantra*) beginning with the kindling of the fire.
When the *ājyabhāga* offerings have been completed, while the bride holds onto [the sacrificer], he offers the seven subsequent oblations beginning with "O Agni, atonement... (*agne prāyaścitta*).
In that context, the phrase "Thou art of the gods" (*tvaṃ devānām*) and so forth is to be appended to the second and third offerings as well.
Then, omitting the holding-on-to, after the *jaya* and other rites up to the releasing of the *praṇītā* waters have been performed, he causes the bride to sit to the west of the fire, facing east.
Taking clarified butter from the remnants of the oblation, he pours it once at the end of all [the mantras] upon her head with the *vyāhṛtis* preceded by *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā*.
Some say [he does so] for each individual mantra.
Then, with the two subsequent verses beginning with "I beheld you with my mind" (*apaśyaṃ tvā manasā*), he performs the rite according to the respective characteristics of each.
The bride [anoints] with the first [verse] and the groom with the subsequent one;

having looked at each other simultaneously, he anoints their heart-regions simultaneously with the remainder of the clarified butter using two blades of *visraṃsinī* grass with their thumbs, while reciting the verse "May they unite" (*asamañjantu*) from the subsequent [section], because of the dual-number indicative mark in the mantra: "May our hearts and waters be united" (*samāpo hṛdayāni nau*).

Then, having recited the next three verses beginning with "O Prajāpati, [guard] my body" (Prajāpate tanvaṃ me), he should recite the remainder of the section, beginning with "Climb onto the thighs" (ārohorum), at the time of *samāveśana*— that is, at the moment of entering together;
for *samāveśana* is the act of lying down with the bride for the purpose of sexual intercourse,
as indicated by the characteristic mark of the word "thighs."
And this rule for the sequential recitation (*krama-japa*) is based on entering [the practice] out of attachment to the purpose of the marriage rite,
just as the prescription of milk and so forth is based on the vow associated with the sequence of meals.
Some, however, maintain that even in the absence of attachment, entry into this sequence for the sake of the ritual act is indeed mandatory.
However, during the intervals between the *samāveśana* rites, this recitation does not apply precisely because it is not for the purpose of a ritual act (*akarmārthatvāt*).
Baudhāyana, however, has stated that there is an option (*vikalpa*) [regarding its performance] (Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.7.12).

If, within this very sequence, the approach to the wife during her fertile period (*ṛtugamana*) should also be performed by chance, then first the recitation beginning with "ārohorum" and so forth is to be performed.
Then, there is the consecration with the mantras beginning with "aviṣṇuryonim. //10//
Or another person may address him with the following mantra. (ĀpGS 8.11)
Or someone other than the Brahman priest should consecrate the bride and groom with the remainder of the section as they are about to come together;
the groom himself should not mutter the *vara* formula.
In that regard, whatever...
The bridegroom has previously caused the bride’s garment to be put on; at the conclusion of the vow, having removed that and put on another garment, the bride touches it.
Because a fault is seen in touching with the hand, [the bridegroom] does so while reciting these verses beginning with "Go away, O Śābalya.
However, during the performance of the vow, because of the intervention of the staff, there is no contact with the body.

On the following day, he should give a boon to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the Sūryā hymn with these four verses beginning with "tadvāsaḥ śvobhūte parādehi śāvalyam. As [Āpastamba] will state: "With the subsequent verses, one should give the bride's garment to one who knows this" (ĀpGṛ 9.11).
Āśvalāyana also says: "One should give the bride's garment to one who knows the Sūryā hymn."
"Food for the Brahmins" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.8.13, 14). //12//
This is for the sake of clarity;
and this [is so] because, even in the face of a contradiction with an indicative mark (liṅga), the Śruti is more powerful—such as in the passage beginning, "I placed the embryo. //11//

50. Instruction regarding a menstruating woman during her first period: When she has become "one wearing soiled clothes" (*malavadvāsas*), he then instructs her in the acts forbidden by the Brāhmaṇas, namely those beginning with the words, "Her who wears soiled clothes" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.5.1). (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 8.12)
"Malavadvāsāḥ" is a designation for a woman in her menses.
The inclusion of the word "yat" (when) is intended to indicate that this applies even after marriage;
otherwise, it would apply only during the period of the marriage ceremony itself.
This follows from the context.
Furthermore, the instruction is given once during the first menstrual period;
that alone serves all purposes.
As in the case of the initiation of a Brahmin,
if the word "this" (*enām*) were not mentioned, it would be understood that someone else instructs them both,
because of the context [of the phrase] "or another [instructs] these two."

It is said that "these are forbidden by the Brāhmaṇas" in order to make it known that things such as sleeping or sitting on high beds, which are forbidden by worldly convention, are to be understood from the world itself.
By the use of the word "actions" (karmāṇi), there is merely an indication of those actions through different words; it is not an injunction based on a statement from the Brāhmaṇa texts.
The expression “these” (etāni) serves to include both those things that have been prohibited, such as “a woman in her courses,” and those that have been prescribed.

By means of this, there is an instruction regarding even those two things that were previously enjoined: “For three nights one should observe a vow, or drink [the water] with the joined palms” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.1).
And thus, in the phrase "those forbidden by Brāhmaṇas," the mention of "forbidden" (pratiṣiddha) is an elliptical indication (upalakṣaṇa).

In that regard, in the verse beginning "Her who has soiled garments" (yāṃ malavadvāsasam), there is a prohibition against sexual union prior to her ritual bath; in the verse beginning "Her who [goes] to the forest" (yām araṇyam), there is a prohibition regarding the location.
Even regarding one who has bathed, there is a prohibition against going with her face turned away, expressed as "she who is turned away" (*parācī*);

there is a prohibition against bathing during the three nights [of impurity], expressed as "she who bathes" (*yā snātī*); and there is a prohibition against anointing, expressed as "she who anoints" (*yābhyajyate*).
"Whatever [is used] for scraping," refers to the comb or similar instrument for scraping the head;
"whatever [is used] for the eyes," refers to collyrium for the eyes;
"whatever [is used] for the teeth," refers to the tooth-cleansing stick.
‘Yā nakhāni’ refers to the instrument for clipping nails;
‘yā kṛṇatti’ refers to the work of spinning cotton and the like;
‘yā rajjum’ refers to the act of making rope.
"By means of a leaf" refers to eating with a leaf;
"by means of a *kharva*" refers to a vessel that is broken in one part,
for *kharva* means something partially mutilated.
The rule regarding time for these prohibitions is expressed in the passage beginning with "for three nights.
The injunction concerning the vessel for eating is found in the passage beginning with "or he may drink with his cupped hands," and so forth.
A woman whose garment is stained by blood—whether that blood has flowed out at the appointed time or is otherwise impure—is one who wears a *malavadvāsas* (a soiled garment).
The meaning is "during her menses.
Because it is a conventional term (*rūḍha-śabda*), even if she happens to be wearing clean clothes by chance, if she should be in her menses,
then the husband alone instructs her— using common parlance— in those actions prohibited for Brahmins.

To the question "Which are those prohibited by the Brāhmaṇa?", he says: "Those [acts] regarding her who is clad in soiled garments"— namely, "They cohabit with her who is clad in soiled garments" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.1.6)— these are the acts enjoined by the Brāhmaṇa.
The meaning is that all these [rules] as well [apply]. Now, for the sake of easy comprehension, they are stated in sequence: sexual intercourse is not permitted before bathing;
nor is it permitted in the forest even after bathing.
That very same [period of impurity] applies even if she has bathed, or if she is turned away, or if she is unwilling.
If the three nights are not yet complete, there is no bathing;
there is no anointing with oil.
One should not scratch the head with a comb or similar object;
one should not apply collyrium to the eyes; and one should not clean the teeth.
One should not cut nails; one should not produce threads from cotton and the like; nor should one make ropes.
Thus, these are the eleven [vessels].
Now, the vessel for food may be the hollowed palms or one that is not *kharva*;
*kharva* means small.
Whether it be broken or burnt, that which is other than these is "not deficient" (*akharva*). Furthermore,
in this context, it is not clearly distinguished in the Bhāṣya whether these prohibitions against sexual intercourse and so forth are injunctions for the performance of non-sexual acts and the like.

However, according to the principle of logic (*nyāya*), because of the scriptural injunction "one should observe the vow for three nights" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.1), rules such as "one should not look at the sun rising or setting" are merely injunctions regarding formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), similar to the regulations for the *prājāpatya* penance. //12//
5. The Seasonal Union. After she has bathed following the appearance of her menses, he addresses her during the seasonal union with the subsequent [verses]. (ĀpGS 8.13)
Regarding the entry [of the husband] during the fertile period (ṛtu) of the copper-colored woman: when that act is to be performed,
he should consecrate it with the thirteen subsequent verses beginning with "Viṣṇur yonim."
"At the appearance of the menses, there is a consecration with mantras;
it is not like the instruction [given] at the very first period.
The word 'bathed' (snātā) is for the purpose of reviving all those things prohibited by the Brāhmaṇas."
The meaning is that she has bathed and performed the auspicious rites;
by this, the application of collyrium and ointment is also included. //14//
Thus ends the eighth section in the Anākula commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra composed by Śrī Harihara Datta.
Of the *rajas*, that is, of the blood;
this is due to its origin from the time of conception (*prādurbhāva*) and its subsequent exit (*nirgama*),
and not because of impurity or similar defects.

"Having bathed" refers to his wife having bathed after the completion of three nights. "At the time of entering for the season" refers to the time of approaching her during the period of her menses; as it is said: "The menstrual period of women is traditionally held to be sixteen nights" (Manu Smṛti 3.46).
Thus, according to the statement of Manu;
he consecrates [the girl] with the thirteen subsequent verses beginning with "May Viṣṇu prepare the womb" (RV 10.184.1).

Since the appearance of the menses occurs here and because of the injunction that she has "bathed," she must indeed bathe on the fourth day for the sake of purification by means of this [rite]. //13//

Ninth Section: 2. The Time for Approaching the Wife during Her Season. They teach that approaching the wife during her season, beginning from the fourth day up to the sixteenth, on each successive even night, leads to the birth of offspring and the highest good. (ĀpGs 9.1)
The accusative case in *ṣoḍaśīm* is used in the sense of the ablative;
thus, it means "until the sixteenth.
The prefix *ā-* here denotes inclusion (*abhividhi*).
Beginning from the manifestation of the menses, the fourth and sixteenth nights are taken [as the primary times],
because of the context.
All nights from the fourth up to the sixteenth are the times for approaching one's wife during her fertile period (*ṛtugamana*).
In that regard also, one should know that each subsequent even night brings greater spiritual welfare (*niḥśreyasa*).

Because of the statement "approaching during the fertile period" (*ṛtugamana*), this instruction applies even when the first approach occurs during the wedding ceremony, as it is prompted by the occasion of the fertile period.
On the fourth night, however, the approach must take place specifically during the latter part of the night.
And in that case, one should recite the remainder during the act of union;
