furthermore, the instruction "one should consecrate with the following [verses]" indicates that there is a cumulative application of the mantras for approaching [the wife].
Among those, first are the mantras for approaching during the fertile period.
Next are the mantras for entering [the state];
others say they are reversed. //1//
The reading "caturthī-prabhṛti" contains a long vowel for the sake of the meter. It means starting from the fourth night up to the sixteenth;
here, the root *aṅ* is used in the sense of inclusion (*abhi-vi-dhi*).
And the second [case-ending] has the sense of the fifth;
that is to say, up until the sixteenth day.
Regarding "each subsequent even night," this refers to engaging in sexual intercourse during the fertile period (*ṛtu*) when cohabitation is performed on each successive even night.
Manu and others teach that the ultimate welfare of progeny—that is, of sons—consists in the attainment of desired qualities such as longevity and so forth.
What is meant is this: when one approaches one's wife during the fertile period (ṛtu) for thirteen nights, provided there is an excess of semen, sons are born.
And in each successive pair [of signs], those good qualities become increasingly superior in their progressive order. //1//

Although the explanation of other rites in the section on consecrated acts (*saṃskārakāṇḍa*) is out of place here, the subsequent collection of sūtras is commenced until the end of the chapter, following the sequence of the recitation of the mantras:

1. When one who has set out for the purpose of acquiring wealth encounters an ill omen in the midst of the journey, such as sneezing, a recitation (*japa*) must be performed. Upon sneezing or coughing while on a journey for wealth, one should touch water and recite the subsequent [mantras] according to their indicative marks (*liṅga*). (ĀpGS 9.2)
One who has set out on a journey is *prādhva*.
"Purpose" (*artha*) means a motive;
whoever has set out on a journey with some purpose whatsoever [is so called].

When that person who is intent upon his purpose encounters an ill omen, such as sneezing or coughing, he should perform an expiation by touching water and reciting these two subsequent verses: "The call after" and "the call around."
*Paritaḥ kṣavaḥ* means a sneeze caused by people standing all around;
likewise for *parikāsanam*.
*Upasparśanam* is contact with the hand.
It may be either bathing or sipping water.
In that regard, one should perform whichever act one considers makes one pure;
the phrase "according to the specific mark" is inappropriate.
Because of the presence of the characteristics of sneezing (*parikṣava*) and coughing (*parikāsa*).

Now, if it is argued that in the preceding verse the word *parikṣava* is a modified form (*ekatośavikṛta*) and thus constitutes the characteristic, even so, in the subsequent [verse] there is no characteristic of coughing at all.
Therefore, it should be explained in this way: when even one of these two causes is present, the recitation (*japa*) of these two mantras must be performed.
And in other ill omens perceived through the signs of mantras, such as *anuhava* and so forth;
therein, calling from behind is *anuhava*,
and calling from all sides is *parihava*.
Slander is defamation;
it is described as reviling. A bad dream is well known.
"Durudita" refers to "short life" and so forth;
"anuhūta" and "parihūta" refer to the inauspicious speech of a bird;
"aśākuna" means that which has become an unfavorable omen.
Regarding the deer, the jackal, and so forth:
"akṣṇayā sṛtam" means moving diagonally, such as by going from left to right and so on. Upon the occurrence of even one of these omens, the recitation of both mantras must be performed.
And in the case of *parikṣava* and *parikāsana*, even though there is an absence of gender markers,
the word *parikṣava* does not possess the gender marker of *kṣavadhu*,
because of the difference in form.
However, a single bodily defect may also occur even in one who is sneezing;
that [defect], when caused by something else, would have to be discussed in another context.
Here, the purpose of the statement is so that this penance applies even to one going for the sake of marriage, should these specific causes occur.
In other contexts, however, those [mantras] heard [in the Veda] function only after marriage;
this one, however, by virtue of the statement "for one traveling on business," serves all purposes.
Furthermore, these two mantras are recited here for the sake of the context of marriage and for the purpose of regulating the place of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*). //2//
*Artha* means purpose;
*dharma-artha* refers to those things that assist it.
One who has set out upon a well-known path with wealth as his objective is "one on a journey for the sake of wealth" (*arthaprādhva*).
However, having set out toward a nearby place for the purpose of bathing, the *brahmayajña* water-offering, or sacrificial fodder and the like,
if an ill omen occurs— such as sneezing, coughing, belching, or spitting— he should touch water; "touching water" (*upasparśana*) here refers to sipping water (*ācamana*).

Or, having performed merely the touching according to his satisfaction, he should mutter the former [verse], "anuhavam," upon sneezing, and the latter, "parihavam," upon coughing, each according to its respective sign;
and when muttering these two, he should indeed employ the fourfold tone (*cātussvaryam*).

And here, by the phrase "according to the characteristic mark," he makes this known: by the first [verse], only the act of spitting out (*parikṣava*) is to be manifested through the transposition of syllables; but by the second, it is the act of spitting out itself that is manifested through ellipsis (*adhyāhṛta*).
And just as these two *ṛc*s reveal, with their primary intent, only the act of spitting out, so it is here.

When the author of the Bhāṣya has explained it in this way, some [hold that] "according to the indicative mark" (yathāliṅgam) means that the recitation of these two [mantras] occurs not only during sneezing and belching, but also during other ill omens recognized by the indicative marks of the mantras, such as the *anuhava* and so forth. //2//

In that very case, there is a recitation upon seeing a variegated tree or similar objects. Likewise, with the following [verses], one should recite according to their respective characteristics: "the variegated lord of the forest," "the flow of dung," "the whistling wind," and "the bird. (ĀpGS 9.3)
By the word "thus" (evam), and by the phrases "when the purpose is primary," "having touched water," and "he should mutter," these [preceding requirements] are expected to apply.
And thus, according to the gender and number [of the object], for the sake of clarity:

*citriya* means "well-known. Having reached a well-known tree that is afflicted or worn out, and having touched water, he consecrates it with this verse: "May there be fire. He should stand near the dung-pile with the words: "Lead us, O Lord, once for all."
"Sigasi" means "you are a winnowing-fan wind. A wind produced by a cloth that has been brought into contact with oneself is a "sigvāta" (winnowing-fan wind).
Although one would expect the long vowel at the end—[yielding *sigāsi na asi*]—the short vowel is used here according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).

One should address the bird with auspicious words using this verse: "O bird, sing like an Udgātṛ priest. However, if it utters an inauspicious sound, the previously mentioned recitation (japa) should be performed;
some authorities maintain that this [verse] should also be used in that same situation. //3//
By the word "evam" (thus), the phrase "having touched water, facing the goal" is drawn forward.
Here, because the instrumental case is seen in the subsequent [verses], one consecrates the trees and so forth with the respective mantras according to their gender;
however, one does not recite them silently as was done previously.
"Citriya" means that which is well-known in the world,
or that which has piling as its root; "vanaspatim" refers to one who possesses fruit even without flowers.
Since this is intended as an illustration, one also consecrates a tree of this kind with the mantra "ārātte agniḥ";
and with "namaśśakṛtsade," one [consecrates] the stream once and the continuity once.
"Sigasinasi" refers to the wind from a fan (*siga*).
"Siga-vāta" is the wind from a cloth fan (*sica*);
whether produced by another or having touched one's own body, it is inauspicious.
With the verse "O bird, like a Udgātṛ," he [addresses] a bird that utters an inauspicious sound, based on the indicative mark (liṅga) of the mantra: "Be well-disposed toward us."
Some say it is for auspicious speech;
however, regarding the sight of the inauspicious, the recitation (japa) has been described in the previous sūtra. //3//
3. A rite that generates mutual affection between a husband and wife:

when there is union of their hearts, having practiced celibacy for at least three nights in water, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (mess of rice), and having performed the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, while she maintains physical contact with him, he offers the subsequent oblations from the *sthālīpāka*;
then he proceeds with the *jaya* and following offerings, and having completed the rites up to the final sprinkling of water (*pariṣecana*).
Having fed an even number of Brahmins, at least two, with that [food] mixed with clarified butter, he should cause them to pronounce words of success. (ĀpGs 9.4)

If the mind of the bridegroom should not be won over by the bride, then, for one desiring success in that matter, this rite must be performed by the bride’s father or others who are engaged in austerity, without the knowledge of the bridegroom,
because its purpose is subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*).
And it should be performed in the *aupāsana* fire.

This was stated previously: since the prescription of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) has a visible purpose, one should perform as much austerity (*tapas*) as one considers necessary for the accomplishment of the goal. Furthermore, this rite takes place under the asterism Punarvasu, according to the statement: "And this ritual occurs under the two Punarvasus."
What, then, is that ritual action?
It is the cooking of a sacrificial mess (sthālīpāka) and the worship of the sacred texts.
All rites are to be performed like those of the *parvan* [full-moon or new-moon sacrifices].
However, because they are taught in the section on marriage (*vivāha-prakaraṇa*), there is a single use of the sacrificial vessels and the *śamyā* sticks;
furthermore, there is no fixed rule regarding the time.

And its conclusion within the section on marriage (vivāhaprakaraṇa) is to be understood from the fact that the gift of the garment (vāsodāna), which is a subsidiary part of it, is taught subsequently;
and it is for this very purpose that its teaching occurs later. //4//
There are seven principal oblations beginning with "prātar agnim" (the morning fire),
followed by the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering,
and then the *jaya* and subsequent rites. //5//
Since the rules of the *pārvaṇa* sacrifice are extended [to this rite], it would follow that only a single Brahmin is to be fed; therefore, the plural number is prescribed.
Consequently, a large *sthālīpāka* (pot-offering) must be prepared.

The mention of "containing clarified butter" (*sarpiṣmat*) is for the purpose of restriction, meaning that after the sprinkling of water (*pariṣecana*), the offerings of the *pārvaṇa* rites must indeed contain clarified butter.
Therefore, the statement "the full vessel (pūrṇapātra) is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā)" does not apply here.
He should cause those who have eaten to recite for success; "recitation" refers to the utterance: "May there be the fulfillment of our intentions.
The mention of the conclusion with the sprinkling around (pariṣecana) is for the purpose of restricting the agent.

How so? Since the one who is the performer of the *homa* must himself perform the feeding of the Brahmins and the recitation for success (*siddhivācana*), the bride is the performer of whatever subsequent rites follow, such as the scattering of grain (*parikiraṇa*) and so forth. //6//

Because of the governing rule, "For both the wife and the husband, there is sleeping on the ground for three nights," and because of the feminine designation "while she [the bride] holds on" used here,

one who desires the union of hearts— the mutual affection of the two minds— the father, brother, or other relative of the bride who seeks her welfare, even if he is sinless, [should remain so] for no less than three nights.

Having practiced celibacy (brahmacarya) to the satisfaction of his mind, he performs the rites beginning with the cooking of the *sthālīpāka* in the *aupāsana* fire and ending with the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*).

While she holds on to him, having taken a portion from the *sthālīpāka*, he offers the principal oblations verse by verse with the seven mantras beginning with "In the morning [I worship] Agni," and then proceeds with the *jaya* and subsequent offerings.

Immediately thereafter, having completed the remainder of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering according to the *pārvaṇa* rite, he should feed an even number of Brahmins—at least two, or more than two—as available, using the remnant of the oblation mixed with clarified butter. Once they have eaten, he should cause them to pronounce the word "Success" (*siddhi*), saying: "May there be the attainment of the fruit of this rite."

Therefore, the phrase "containing clarified butter" (*sarpiṣmatā*) is a restatement of what is already established by the *pārvaṇa* rite, intended to enjoin [the use of] "two sticks" (*yugimān*). //4//

4. The rite for subjugating the husband (*pativaśyakaraṃ karma*): [The scattering of *yava* grains over the *pāṭhā* herb; tying it to both one's own hands; and embracing the husband with those two hands.

On the day following [the full moon], under the asterism Tiṣya, he scatters the *pāṭhā* with twenty-one *yava* grains, saying: “If you belong to Varuṇa, I redeem you from Varuṇa; if you belong to Soma, I redeem you from Soma. (ĀpGS 9.5)

Thinking, "Whatever rite is to be performed tomorrow shall be accomplished under the constellation Tiṣya," the father or another officiating priest, acting as the sacrificer, performs the ritual on the preceding day at the conclusion of the recitation for success (*siddhivācanā*). Then, having gone to the place where the bride stands near the *pāṭhā* plant,
he scatters twenty-one barley grains— three times seven— around that *pāṭhā* while reciting the two verses beginning with "thou art belonging to Varuṇa" (*vāruṇy asi*).
"Trissaptaiḥ" is a Vedic designation for a specific type of herb; however, the followers of the Atharvaveda read it as "pāśā. //7//

The ritual acts beginning with the recitation of the *pāṭha* and ending with the taking of the husband’s hand are performed on the previous day, because it is understood that "on the following day, Tiṣya shall be present. This means that when the asterism Tiṣya (Puṣya) is joined with Punarvasū on the preceding day, the father or other relative performs the rite up to the recitation for success (*siddhivācanā*).
Immediately thereafter, the bride goes to the place where the *pāṭha* is located and, with twenty-one barley grains, [recites] "If you belong to Varuṇa... three times over seven [grains].
With these two [verses], he scatters; that is, he sows around.
"With thrice-seven" is a Vedic form. //5//

On the following day, having caused her to rise with the next [verse] and having consecrated her with the three subsequent verses, she should tie [the plant] covered by the next verse to her hands. At the time of going to bed, she should embrace her husband with her arms, using the verse containing the word *upadhāna*.

Having performed the scattering of grain and fasted, then on the following day, she causes that *pāṭhā* plant to be dug up; having dug it with a spade, she extracts it with the next *ṛc*, namely, "I dig this [plant]" (*imāṃ khanāmī*).
Then she should consecrate it with the three subsequent *ṛks*, beginning with "O thou with upward leaves" (*uttānaparṇe*).
Having cut its root into two pieces, she ties them to her hands with the following verse, "I am...

(RV 10.85.46). The meaning is that they are to be concealed in such a way that her husband does not see them. The mantra is repeated for both [hands]. Having tied them, she should then embrace her husband at the time of going to bed at night.

Regarding the statement "with the verse containing the mark of the lower layer (*upadhānaliṅgā*)", namely with this verse "Come hither, O you who are placed" (*upa te 'dha*), although it could have been simply stated as "with the following [verse]," the specific mention of "containing the mark of the lower layer" is for the purpose of prescribing a particular rule for the enclosing (*parigraha*).
Just as in the case of two roots, one is placed below and the other serves as a cover above, so too should the enclosing be performed. //8//

On the following day, the bride herself, having dug up that *pāṭhā* plant with a wooden tool while reciting the verse "I dig this one," and having consecrated it with the three verses beginning with "O you with upward-turned leaves," she should cut its root into two pieces,

hide them from her husband by some means, tie them to her own hands while reciting the verse "I am the conqueror" twice, and at the time of going to bed at night, she should embrace her husband with her arms while reciting the verse "Upon you [I place] my dwelling," which contains the characteristic mark of a pillow.
And the communication by means of the signs of the test (upadhāna) is an auxiliary part of the ritual action.
Some say that one should grasp the two hands at the base of the *pāṭha* in such a way that one hand serves as a support and the other as a cover. //6//
He becomes submissive. ĀpGs 9.7.

If the wife does not take pleasure in her husband, then this ritual act does not come to fruition; it is for the purpose of demonstrating this that the husband is essential to the wife, but the wife is not essential to the husband. //9//
This is clear (*tāsarthadarśanam*);
because of the masculine designation "vaśya," the term *vadhū* here refers to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). //7//
He states its connection with another sphere of application:
"The rite for the subduing of rivals;
and [the rite] for the subduing of rivals. (ĀpGs 9.8)
This rite is not merely a means for the union of the hearts of both [the husband and wife]; what then?
It is also a means for subduing co-wives, meaning that even a rival wife can be subdued by this.
This is also the case in this alternative view.
The *aupāsana* fire itself is that which was established for her through her marriage; it is this fire that displaces the *saptanī*.
Depending on the specific type of marriage, the fires are thus combined.
Accordingly, it is stated regarding the *rājasūya*: “That [fire] is substituted for the *aupāsana*” (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 18.16.14).
Likewise, the contact with fire is prescribed in the Baudhāyana [text], and even after that contact, it occurs in that very same [fire].
Just as a rival wife being superseded does not know [of the change],
some desire a second marriage in the very same fire as the first.
For them also, it is that very same action. //10//
That by which a co-wife is oppressed is "sapatnībādhanam";
this ritual act is also called *sapatnībādhanam*.
Furthermore, it is appropriate that this constitutes a separate section of authority (*adhikārāntaram*).

Since this ritual is intended for the purpose that even one whose heart is united with one wife does not, out of greed, harm another wife who is her co-wife—even in matters such as religious duties dependent upon her—how much more, then, would he surely harm her by neglecting those very duties? //8//
Now he states another rite for subduing co-wives:
6. When his wife or others are afflicted by consumption, there is a rite to bring about its cessation.
With this very desire, one should always worship the Sun with the subsequent Anuvāka. (ĀpGs 9.9)
With this very desire for the subduing of co-wives, he constantly worships the Sun every day with the following Anuvāka beginning with “ud asau sūryo agāt” (Up has risen yonder sun);
the particle *eva* (constantly) serves to emphasize the daily recurrence. //11//

In this very rite for the subjugation of a rival wife, the bride worships the sun every day before eating with the *anuvāka* beginning "The sun has risen there" (*udagāt sūryaḥ*), until she attains her desire. The inclusion of the word "always" (*sadā*) indicates that even though the desire for the subjugation of a rival wife is already established [by the context], this constitutes a separate ritual act. //9//

One who is devoted to celibacy, having rubbed the limbs of another woman afflicted by consumption or any other disease with the roots of the *puṣkara-saṃvarta* plant while reciting the subsequent [mantras] according to their respective characteristics, should cast them away toward the west. (ĀpGs 9.10)

Yakṣma is the disease of rājayakṣma, or consumption. Having recognized that his wife or another woman of his own household, such as a mother and so forth, has been seized by this, he should prepare this medicine.
What is it?
It is said: [the lotus] is joined with the *brahmacarya* (celibacy/virtue) by means of the roots of the *puṣkara*; that is, by means of its roots which are circular in shape.
Others say "by means of the *saṃvarta*-roots.
According to the lexicographers (*naighaṇṭuka*), *saṃvartikā* means a nine-petaled [flower].

With the subsequent mantras beginning with “From your two eyes, from your two nostrils,” he should touch her limbs—the eyes and so forth—according to their respective characteristics (*liṅga*). He should then cast [the grass] away toward the west in such a manner.
Because of the expression according to the characteristics, both the touching and the casting away are performed for each mantra individually.
The rubbing is performed with each root individually, because the plural number refers to all [the roots] collectively;
for the intestines and so forth are included therein.
The sweeping is performed outside that area. //12//

Desiring her welfare, one who is endowed with the aforementioned characteristics of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) should [treat] a bride afflicted by pulmonary consumption (*rājayakṣman*), or another afflicted by pulmonary consumption or other diseases such as leprosy (*kuṣṭha*),
using the petals and roots of the *puṣkara* (lotus) with the six mantras beginning with "In your two eyes" (*akṣībhyāṃ te*), according to their respective indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Having touched the limbs, beginning with the eyes, which have been explained in the Bhāṣya, one should cast them out toward the west with each respective mantra.
The intended meaning is: "By this medicine, one shall become free from disease."

Some say that when a wife or another female relative, such as a mother, is afflicted by consumption, one should [treat her] with lotus roots that are circular in shape, according to the *Saṃvarta* tradition. //10//
7. The gift of the bride’s garment:
one who knows this should give the bride’s garment with the following verses. (ĀpGS 9.11)
That garment which was worn at the time of the wedding,
he should give to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the meanings of the mantras recited in this section; to him [he should give it].

Some consider this to be a medicinal remnant because it follows immediately after [the preceding rule]. For them, the qualification "in her husband's dwelling" is intended to preclude the giving of clothing to another woman who is afflicted with consumption.

The phrase "one who knows this" means one who performs the medical rites (*bhaiṣajyakarma*). In the mantras, such as "go away to the other [world]," there is seen a censure of touching the bride's garment worn at the time of marriage, as well as the giving of that garment to a Brāhmaṇa who knows the *Sūryā* hymn.
This is made explicit in another ritual manual (*kalpa*): "One who has completed his vow should give the bride's garment to one who knows the *Sūryā*" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.8.13).
Therefore, its status as a remnant of medicine is untenable.
As for what was further stated— that it is because of the immediate [offense]—
the reason for that has already been explained.
How so? Because the section concerning marriage would otherwise end in this manner. //13//
The dwelling of the bride for whom this medicine is prepared is [the place where] it is done.
To one who knows this—meaning to him who understands the meaning of the mantras—one should give with the four verses beginning with "aparā dehi.

Some say that at the time of marriage, having removed the garment with which the bride was covered, one should, while not touching it, offer it on the fifth day with the verses beginning with "aparā dehi" to one who has completed his vows, who knows this, and who knows Sūryā.

One should give these meaningful mantras to him who knows them. He should not touch [the disciple], nor should he say, "This is cruel," or "This is bitter. Furthermore, since this instruction is to be given immediately after the formal entry (*samāveśana*), it is intended for the rite of union with the Heart (*hṛdayasaṃsarga*) and for the purpose of communicating the command (*śamyājñāpana*).

This is not tenable, because the gift of clothing, by abandoning the proximate ritual act, would result in the knowledge of the purpose of marriage occurring only after a very long interval; furthermore, such a practice does not exist among us. //11//
Thus, by the noble Sudarśana, through the sole support of bold resolve, this ocean of the third chapter—whose meaning is extremely profound—has been crossed over with great difficulty. (1)
O wise ones, please forgive whatever has been left unsaid or poorly expressed here due to the dullness of my intellect or my learning, by virtue of my inclination toward the true path. //2//
Thus ends the ninth section in the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
The third chapter is completed.
Now begins the fourth chapter;
here begins the tenth section.
Chapter 6: On the Initiation (Upanayana). Section 1: The Time for Initiation. We shall now explain the initiation ceremony. (ĀpGs 10.1)
The rite by which a boy is led to a teacher is called *upanayana*; it is a Vedic sacrament (*puruṣasaṃskāra*) for a person.

Although the qualification for *upanayana* is already established by the statement to be made later—"One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the sixth year after conception"—the formal declaration is made here for the purpose of indicating its primary importance, as in such passages as "We shall explain the establishment of the sacred fires" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra 5.1.1).
How, then, is initiation (upanayana) of primary importance?
Because one who has not been initiated lacks the qualification for all rites, whether based on Śruti or Smṛti;
whereas regarding initiation itself, one who has not been consecrated by the rites beginning with the impregnation (garbhādhāna) lacks the qualification.
Since the duties of a religious student (*brahmacāri-dharma*) are mentioned in the *Sāmayācārika* [section], they would apply to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) as well;
however, this ritual procedure (*kalpa*) is intended for our own [tradition] alone.
Therefore, there is instruction regarding them here. //1//
*Upanayana* is the name of a ritual action;
it is so called because in this rite there is the leading (*nayanam*) of the boy to the presence of the teacher (*ācārya*),
just like the word *paṅkaja* ("mud-born") and others.

The prefix *vi-* has the sense of "extensive" (*vistara-artha*); the prefix *ā-* has the sense of "partial" (*lava-artha*). Here, because the root *cakṣiṅ*, which means "clear speech," undergoes the substitution of *khyāñ*, the form [of the verb] is *vyākhyāsyāmi*.

And thus the meaning is this: we shall describe the rite called *upanayana*—which is elaborated according to the statements of the optional ritual manuals (*kalpa*), supported by powerful authorities, and expressed through unique terminology.
This declaration is intended to secure the attention of the audience.
Some [hold] that even for one who has not been consecrated by the preceding rites such as *niṣeka* due to obstacles from fate or other causes, the *upanayana* certainly takes place.

However, this declaration is made for the purpose of making known the primacy of the initiation (*upanayana*), [showing] that the subsequent rites— both *śrauta* and *smārta*— are not for one who has not been consecrated by initiation. Furthermore, in order to make known the distinction that eligibility for the rites taught in the *Gṛhya-sūtras* belongs only to the householder and not to the student (*brahmacārin*), the marriage ceremony is taught without a formal declaration,
whereas the instruction on the ritual procedure for initiation is performed with a formal declaration.

And the absence of instruction regarding this [initiation] in the legal treatise (dharmaśāstra) at the passage "the initiation of one who desires knowledge" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.1.9) is intended to preclude its application to all Vedic schools (caraṇas). //1//
One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year from conception.

The year in which one has been in the womb and dwells therein is designated by the word "womb" (*garbha*); those years of whom this is the eighth are "those for whom the womb is the eighth" (*garbhāṣṭamāni*).
The plural number is used because years differ according to the solar and other reckonings.
Another says: from birth onwards, the seventh year is followed by the womb as the eighth.
Therefore, the initiation ceremony (upanayana) is enjoined for all seven years;

among those, because of unfitness during the first four years and due to the contradiction with other sacraments such as the tonsure (caula), the initiation is to take place during the three years beginning with the fifth.

In this regard, there would be no distinction such as that the optional initiation (*upanayana*) occurs in the sixth or seventh year, while the obligatory one occurs in the eighth; rather, it would have to be obligatory in all cases. Furthermore, when the fifth or sixth year is current, how could the "eighth year from conception" (*garbhavarṣa*) possibly occur?
For "completeness" (*pūraṇatva*) is not possible when there are no items to be completed.
Therefore, while residing in the seventh [month], the eighth year of gestation occurs.
Consequently, the plural number is not intended to be significant.
Or rather, the resolution previously stated applies;
however, the optional initiation (*kāmyopanayana*) is obtained through another injunction.
The reading "upanayīta" follows the Vedic scripture, for the verbal root here takes the *śap* affix.

Since the rule regarding the eighth year from conception is established as pertaining specifically to the Brāhmaṇa due to the specific instruction for the Rājanya and Vaiśya, the injunction for the Brāhmaṇa is merely a restatement of what is already heard in the Śruti.

If the phrase "one should initiate him again" were not stated, the previous mention of initiation would serve only to establish the subject matter; it would not convey that purpose which is to be accomplished therein. //2//
The phrase "in the eighth years from conception" is the ellipsis [to be supplied],
based on the statement of Gautama: "The count of years begins from conception" (GauDhS 2.7).
By the word "garbha" (womb), that in which the embryo develops is indicated.
Those years of the seven [stages] beginning with birth, of which the eighth is such [a year], are the "garbhāṣṭama" years.
Among those [seven], one should initiate a Brāhmaṇa.

Thus, although initiation would have been applicable even during the seven stages beginning with birth, it is nevertheless not performed during the first three because they are already occupied by the prenatal sacraments ending with the tonsure (caula).

Even in the fourth case, it is certainly not so; because of the boy’s incapacity for performing the vows (*vrata*), the plural number pertaining here to the subject to be enjoined (*upādeya*)— according to the *kapiñjala-nyāya* (the maxim of the partridges)— is restricted to only three [years], namely the sixth, seventh, and eighth, beginning from conception.

[This is] by implication, through a distinction in application. Now, one might object: since the rule regarding the eighth month from conception is established by implication for the Brāhmaṇa alone—because the specific mention of "Rājanya" and "Vaiśya" later on [in the text] excludes others—it is unnecessary to state "the Brāhmaṇa. Likewise, it is unnecessary to say "he should initiate him," because the topic under discussion is the initiation ceremony, as indicated by the statement, "We shall explain the initiation. [Response: This is not so. The purpose of stating "the Brāhmaṇa" is to indicate that this rule applies even when the eighth month falls during the period of impurity (*sūtakakāla*). the prescription here is for the sake of restricting [the practice] to specific castes (*varṇa*).

By stating, "Let there be no application here of time-periods seen in other treatises," he makes this known: even a time-period seen in another treatise may optionally apply to the *caula* and other rites. //3//
In both cases, according to the *kapiñjala-nyāya*, the meaning of the plural number is precisely three. //3//

The restatement [of this] is for the purpose of prescribing such [rules], and so forth. //4//
2. At the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), there is the shaving of the hair in all directions.

Having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce blessings, and having fed the boy, he mixes warm water with cold water with the first *yajus* of the [first] section; having poured the warm water into the cold, he moistens the boy's head with the following [verse].
Now follows the rule for the initiation: on the previous day, the *nāndī-śrāddha* is performed.
Then, when the next day has dawned, having fed the Brahmins, he causes them to pronounce blessings with the words, "May there be oil-cake for himself and prosperity.
Then he should feed the boy.
Such is the ritual procedure for the father and others until this point.
Then the teacher mixes warm and cold water with the first *yajus* of the subsequent section, namely,
"O wind, with warmth," while mixing he pours the warm water into the cold.
[He does not moisten the head] with cold [water] when it is hot.
Then, with those waters, he moistens the boy's head with the verse "May the waters moisten," which is the next ṛc.
Although it would have been sufficient to say "with the next yajus," it is stated as "with the first yajus of the section" for the purpose of providing a specific designation.
By the phrase "with that hot [water], O Vāyu, with water," there is the inclusion of this entire section (anuvāka).

Otherwise, there would be doubt as to whether it refers to the section or to the mantras. Since the result would already be established by the words "the hot [should be poured] into the cold," the explicit mention of "mixing" (saṃsṛjet) is for the purpose of demonstrating its applicability to all cases.

He mixes together the substances used for the bathing of himself and the barber; and this is clearly understood from other [sources]: one should instruct the barber, saying, "Performing the service with cold and warm water, do not cause pain, but make him well.

By the phrase "having fed the Brāhmaṇas," that *śrāddha* which is prescribed in the Dharmaśāstra by the rule, "In all rites, one should feed those who are pure and accompanied by mantras" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.15.11), is intended.

That which is well known as the *nāndī-śrāddha* or the *abhyudaya-śrāddha* is precisely what is being discussed here; and that should be performed according to the procedure established in other *smṛtis*.
However, its recitation here again is for the purpose of performing [the rites] according to the order of the text;
otherwise, because the constituent elements (padārthas) would possess a fixed sequence, they would end up at the very conclusion, as in the case of marriage and other such rites.
This same principle applies even to the pronouncement of blessings prescribed by the Dharmaśāstras.
And the procedure for the pronouncement of blessings is as stated in the Bhāṣya.
Some say that the *nāndī-śrāddha* should be performed on the previous day, based on custom and other Smṛti texts.
And on the following day, there is the feeding of Brahmins, specifically for the purpose of having those who have finished eating recite blessings;

for it is said that at the conclusion of all rites, one should feed those who know the mantras, according to the injunction: "In all ritual acts, one should feed those who are pure and conversant with the mantras."

And in this case, prior to the prince’s meal, there is the wearing of the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) with the mantra beginning, "The sacred thread is the supreme purifier," because of the statement in the Dharmaśāstra: "One should wear the sacred thread during meals, ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and Vedic study."
"Some say [it occurs] even before the placing of the fuel-sticks."
And the child's meal is served without alkaline salts, salt, and the like;
furthermore, there is a double sipping of water (ācamana) at the beginning and at the end. Some perform this [rite] for the mother and father at the conclusion.
From this point onward, he is called the Teacher (ācārya).
With the first Yajus of the Anuvāka, namely "O Vāyu, with heat," he mixes the hot and cold waters;
and while mixing them, he pours the hot into the cold, not by means of a fixed rule.

And here, the mention of the *anuvākas* is for the purpose of making known that only those *gṛhya* mantras which are actually recited [in the *Gṛhyasūtra*] are intended, and not those found in the *Kalpasūtras*.
The purpose of this is stated to be that these [mantras] are to be studied during the *brahmayajña* and other such rites.
Then, with those waters, he moistens the head of the boy with the mantra: "May the waters moisten [you]."
Starting from the east and proceeding clockwise, it moistens [the ground] up to the edge.
Having placed three blades of darbha grass between each, he scatters [the soil] toward each of the directions with the four subsequent formulas, one mantra for each direction. ĀpGs 10.6.
"Pravapati" means he first shaves; that is to say, he begins the shaving.
By this it is stated that the teacher performs the shaving with the mantra first, and afterwards the barber.

The procedure there is as follows: having placed three *darbha* blades upon the boy's head in the eastern direction, he cuts them with the razor using the mantra, "With that wherewith [the gods] shaved."

In place of the word *asau*, one should take his name in the nominative case; for example: "This one here is Yajñadatta Śarmā. Thus, in every instance where *asau* is employed, the name must be specified.
Having cut them off, he throws the hair onto a ball of cow-dung mixed with barley for an ox.
Then, having touched water, he does the same toward the southern direction with the verse, "With which, O Pūṣan," and toward the western direction with the verse, "With which, more."
In the north, [he recites] "With that by which, O Pūṣan...
Here, the name is taken in the vocative case; thus: "With that I shave you, O Yajñadatta Śarman, for the sake of long life. //5//
Then, having placed three darbha blades between [the head and the razor] in each direction with the four mantras beginning with "yenāvapat" (RV 10.85.39–42), he shaves the hair.
Because of the word "pra-" [in the mantra], the act of smoothing the hair is also performed by the teacher alone.
In that regard, in the first mantra, the name of the boy is to be inserted in place of the word "asau," such as "Viṣṇuśarman."
But in the fourth [case], it is by means of perfect awakening. //6//
The mother or a student (brahmacārī) standing to the south addresses him with the next [verse] as he shaves.

When the shaving has been performed by the teacher in this manner for each direction, the barber shaves his hair while using water that has already been used for the purpose. As the barber is shaving him, the teacher addresses him with the next verse, "yat kṣureṇa" (ĀpGS 10.8).

Sitting to the south, the mother of the boy, or some female ascetic (*brahmacarī*), addresses the teacher as he shaves with the mantra beginning, "Whatever [hair] with the razor... Why is the *sūtra* worded in this way? It is said:

because in the case of an address using the second-person singular form—"Do not deprive this boy of his life"—there would be a contradiction, since the act of shaving is performed by the teacher (*ācārya*) who is the agent, whereas the address is directed toward him.
Because there is no subject under discussion other than the mother and the celibate student (brahmacārin). //7//
The plucked-out hair is deposited at the root of an Udumbara tree.

Having placed barley-grains upon a lump of cow-dung from an ox, he winds the hair around it and deposits it at the root of an Udumbara tree or upon a bunch of Darbha grass, with the next [verse]. (ĀpGS 10.8)
Then the boy’s mother, or some celibate student, sits down to his right, prepares a lump of bull-dung in a certain vessel, places barley grains upon that lump, and gathers the hair—
seizing it so that none falls to the ground— and having thus gathered all the hair, [he applies it] to an udumbara branch.

He places [the hair] at the root of a tree or in a clump of *darbha* grass with the following verse, "Having shaved the hair... (*āptvāya keśān*). If it is his mother, she causes him to recite that concluding mantra.

Since the initiation (*upanayana*) is the subject under discussion, the mother or the religious student (*brahmacārī*), having shaved the hair with the verse "Having shorn the hair," performs the rites beginning with the ball of cow-dung from the ox, according to the instruction.
Some say: the teacher begins the shaving first;
then the barber, while performing the preliminary rite with water already mixed together, shaves the hair.
And while he is shaving, the teacher addresses him with the following verse.
As for the statement, "The mother [stands] to the south," its meaning has already been explained.
Furthermore, this shaving is not completed by the barber, because there is no scriptural injunction to that effect.

And because there is no impossibility in that assumption; for the prefix *pra-* indicates a falling away (*vipāta*) understood through another means of knowledge, and because it is logical that the one who performs the recitation (*anumantraṇa*) should be the very same person mentioned in the statement itself, according to the distinction of the stated sūtras regarding the *mātrā* and so forth. //8//
4. The placing of the bathed boy upon a stone:

After the bath, from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, having caused him to place a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood with the following [verse], he makes him step upon the stone to the north of the fire with his right foot, saying, "Step upon [it]. (ĀpGS 10.9)
“Having bathed the boy, dressed him in clean garments, and bound his topknot, he fastens the sacred thread upon him with the mantra: ‘The sacred thread is the supreme purifier.
Then, having thus invested him with the sacred thread, he leads him to the place of sacrifice,” so says Baudhāyana. (Baudhāyanagṛhyasūtra 2.5)
The statement regarding the bath serves as an indicator for all of that.
Thereafter, the teacher proceeds with the ritual procedure beginning with the kindling of the fire;
the production of the fire is like that of a marriage.
The *śamyā* sticks serve the purpose of the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*).
The vessels are employed only once.
The sacrificial garment, the girdle, and so forth are also placed down together.
Then, at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he causes the boy to take up a fuel-stick (*samidh*) of *palāśa* wood with the following verse, "O God, giver of life" (*āyurdā deva*).
The boy places the fuel-stick on the fire while reciting the mantra;
the teacher directs him and makes him recite the mantra.
And since he causes him to recite this here,
there is no contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, because the deity is the object to be addressed.
Others, however, maintain that the application of the mantra belongs to the teacher alone.
Having caused him to place a fuel-stick on the fire, he establishes a stone placed to the north of the fire with his right foot, using the mantra: "Mount this [stone].
This mantra belongs only to the Ācārya, because the boy is the one addressed by it.
Then the teacher, having released the mantra, takes hold of the nurse’s foot with both hands and causes it to be placed upon a stone. //8//
Then he proceeds with the ritual procedure beginning with the kindling of the fire.
At the time of arranging the vessels, he sets down together the stone, the garment, the girdle, the antelope skin, the staff, the *kuśa* grass, and the broom;
some say that the ladle and other implements should also be set down together.
When the *ājyabhāga* offerings have been completed, he causes the bathed boy, holding a *pālāśa* fuel-stick in his hand, to offer it with the verse, "O God, giver of life.
At the end of the mantra, he should say, "Place [it].
This is the mantra for the offering.
Some say that the teacher should cause [the father] to recite the *ādadhāna-mantra*.
For them, there would be a contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "May we lead him to old age.
Now, if it were for the purpose of causing the recitation, the mantra might be uttered for the sake of addressing the boy, just as the mantra for placing the stone is used [in another rite].
It is not for the purpose of denoting the deity;
if it is argued that a single utterance lacks the capacity to denote both [the substance and the deity],
we say no, because in the case of "O Agni, whose back is anointed with ghee" (*ghṛtapṛṣṭo agne*), it is the deity alone who is the object of denotation.
Therefore it has been said: "Having uttered the mantra, one should say, 'Place [the fuel]! Offer the oblation!
The remainder is clear. //9//

5. The donning of the garment for the boy: having consecrated the garment—whether it be one that has been worn or one newly cut—with the two following [verses], and having caused him to put it on with the three following [verses], he consecrates the garment once it has been put on with the next [verse]. (ĀpGs 10.10)
On the very same day, that for which there is the act of weaving and the act of sewing is called *sadyaḥkṛttotam* (woven and sewn on the same day).
One should consecrate such a garment with the two subsequent *ṛc*s beginning with "revatīstvā" (RV 10.85.46–47).
Then, one causes it to be put on with the three subsequent verses beginning with "yā akṛntan" (RV 10.85.28–30).
The mantras belong to the teacher alone.
According to the statement "one [is for each]," the putting on of the garment occurs at the end of the three [mantras].
Then, the teacher consecrates that boy who has put it on with the following verse: "parīdaṃ vāsaḥ" (RV 10.85.28). //9//

not on another day even if it were auspicious. Some [commentators] say it refers to that for which both the act of spinning the thread and the act of weaving occurred on one and the same day.
Regarding the phrase "that which has been freshly cut":

having consecrated such [a garment] with the two verses beginning "O Revatīs, you," and having caused it to be put on with these three verses beginning "Those who cut," he consecrates the boy who has put it on with this verse, "This garment around. 6. Wearing the girdle of muñja grass and the skin.
Having wound a triple-stranded girdle of muñja grass three times around him from left to right with the next two verses, he should place a deerskin over his left shoulder with the following verse.
Then, with the two subsequent verses beginning "This [girdle] wards off ill-spoken words," he thrice girds the boy with the triple-stranded girdle made of muñja grass.
Having himself uttered the mantra, the teacher causes the boy to recite it.
According to the indicative mark of the mantra, the triple-stranded girdle is made of muñja grass.
The *trivṛt* consists of three strands;
the long vowel in the reading *trivṛtām* is a Vedic (chāndasa) usage. Then, he makes the deer skin his upper garment with the following verse.

[he should wear] a girdle made of muñja grass,
which is triple-stranded.

He winds the girdle three times from left to right with the two verses beginning "This [girdle] from ill-spoken words...
and "Threefold..."; and when possible, they should be wound from right to left.

Having performed the upper garment as prescribed in the Dharmaśāstra and so forth, he puts it on with the verse, "The eye of Mitra" (mitrasya cakṣuḥ). //11//
