Having initiated him, he mutters into his right ear: "O you of good offspring!"—the muttering ends with the words, "O you who are well-nourished, [may you be] among those who nourish. (11)
With the verse "By the northern one we have come together" (RV 10.85.20), and with the verse "From the ocean the wave...
(RV 10.85.1), he sprinkles [it] three times; here, the dative case in *asmai* is used in the sense of the genitive.
Once with the mantra, twice silently;
[this is done] with the ten subsequent mantras beginning with "Agni has grasped your hand."
At the end of all [the mantras], there is a single grasping of the hand.
With the eleven [mantras] beginning with "I entrust you to Agni," he entrusts [the student] to the deities whose names are recognized from the indicative marks (*liṅga*) for the sake of protection.
Consequently, if the entrusting were done only once, then due to the transgression of the rule, the *sarvaprāyaścitta* expiation must be offered.

And among all words that are not [proper] names, the name is to be uttered in the vocative case. With the subsequent Yajus formula, "I initiate you with the impulse of the god Savitṛ," he brings [the boy] near to himself;
and the utterance of the name is likewise in the vocative case.
Some youths, holding in their left hands the water brought by the teacher in their joined palms,
sprinkle themselves three times with their right hands;
however, the teacher sprinkles them.
And the elision of the *ṇic* suffix is to be understood;
furthermore, they explain that the mention of "taking by the hand" (*hastagrahaṇam*) implies "at every recitation" (*pratimantram*), as it depends upon various alternative interpretations. //12//
Thus ends the tenth section in the Gṛhyatātparyadarśana composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
Eleventh Section: 8. Questions and Answers between the Teacher and the Boy.
"I have come for the life of a student (*brahmacarya*)," the boy says. (ĀpGs 11.1)
The statement "the mantra ending with 'impelled by Savitṛ' says" is for the purpose of its high-pitched (uccaiḥ) recitation. //1//
It is manifest. //1//
The response of the youth to the question of another. ĀpGs 11.2.
The four mantras beginning with "Who indeed are you? are for the purpose of providing answers to questions.

In that context, the meaning is "starting from where it was asked" regarding the ritual action. The form *praṣṭam* [for *praśnam*] is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*) characterized by the absence of *saṃprasāraṇa*.
Or it may be a textual corruption;
that which is the response belongs to the youth.
Among the words beginning with "asau," the youth indicates his name by means of the nominative case.
The teacher, having awakened, asked for the boy’s name. "What is your name? the teacher asked.
"I am named Yajñaśarman," the boy replied.

"Under whom do you practice the holy life (brahmacarya)? asks the teacher. "I am the student of Prāṇa, Yajñaśarman," replies the boy. The word "says" (āha) is used in the loud register because it follows from the preceding rule. //2//
*Praṣṭam* means "that which is to be asked";
the form, however, is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
In the four mantras beginning with "Who are you by name? (*ko nāmāsi*), which serve as questions and answers, *praṣṭam* refers to the other, namely the teacher.
As for the response of the youth, the application is as follows: "What is your name? asks the teacher.
"Are you named Viṣṇuśarman? the boy should reply.
Likewise, "Whose student (*brahmacārin*) are you, Viṣṇuśarman?"
"Thus said the teacher.
"I am the brahmacārin of Prāṇa," said the boy. //2//
The other recites the remainder. (ĀpGs 11.3)
After the response to the question, the other teacher recites the remainder of the section, beginning with "This is your [portion] in the sun" (eṣa te dve sūrye). //3//

The teacher recites the remainder—the portion of the section beginning with "O God Viṣṇuśarman, this [is for you]" and ending with "wander along, O Viṣṇuśarman"—because of the injunction to recite the prayer for personal blessing contained in the verse "O Lord of paths, of the paths. //3//
9. The recitation of mantras containing blessings for oneself is performed by the boy; he causes him to recite those mantras containing blessings for oneself. (ĀpGs 11.4)
At that very point, he causes the boy to recite the remaining benedictions beginning with "O Lord of the paths, [protect] the paths," and so forth. //4//
In that mantra where the fruit of the benediction (āśīḥ-phala) pertains to oneself, it is a mantra containing a benediction directed toward the self (*pratyag-āśīḥ*).
The singular number is used with reference to the class [of such mantras].
Beginning from "adhvanām" up to the completion of the initiation (*upanayana*), those mantras containing benedictions for oneself are "yoge," and so forth.
He causes all of them to recite [the formulas] for the boy. //4//
10. There are the principal oblations for the initiation (*upanayana*), as well as the *jaya* and other offerings.
It has been stated that [the ritual] concludes with the *ājyabhāga* offerings. (ĀpGS 11.5)
Then, having caused him to offer the subsequent oblations, he proceeds with the *jaya* and following rites.
The ritual procedure up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings has already been explained.
Now, at this point, he causes this boy to offer eleven principal oblations with the verses beginning with "In every union" (*yoge yoge*).
The boy offers these with the subsequent mantras.
The teacher employs that [rite] by means of the recitation of the mantra.
Regarding the second and fourth mantras as well, the youth himself is the speaker,
because they are intended to designate the deity.
Another says: because of the contradiction in gender, the Teacher is the speaker and Kumāra is the Hotṛ;
since there is the statement "having caused [the offerings] to be offered in the principal homas," the Teacher alone is the performer in the subsidiary offerings. //5//
Lest this be considered a mere restatement, it is explained by supplying the necessary predicate.
Beginning with the words "not only of the paths," he causes [the student] to recite the mantras that contain blessings directed toward oneself (*pratyagāśis*).

Having spoken up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, those mantras containing blessings for oneself which were previously mentioned in connection with the girdling of the waist and other rites—beginning with "This [girdle] from ill-spoken words"—he himself speaks and causes them to be recited.
The statement "it has been said" refers to the general class [of rites].

However, this must be explained here: in those purificatory rites (*saṃskārakriyā*) where the boy is the primary object, such as the girding with the belt (*mekhalā-parivyayaṇa*) and others, there are mantras containing internal blessings (*pratyagāśis*).

Having performed those actions which are enjoined as instruments by those mantras—whose application is indicated by the *codaka* (transferred injunctions)—he subsequently causes [the boy] to recite them.
This is because the mantras of the self-initiation (svataḥ-karaṇa) must be recited by the performers themselves, who have become subordinate to the ritual action;

furthermore, in this context, the youth is the primary object of the rite as the one to be consecrated (saṃskārya). However, in cases such as the fire-oblations (homa), where [the youth] is indeed subordinate, [the mantra is recited by another].
There is no state of being modified;
in that case, he simply causes them to recite those benedictory formulas.
Some [hold] that even in the rites such as the girdling (parivyayaṇa) and others, the mantra belongs to the boy alone.
But the other merely causes [the text] to be recited. //5//
In this sequence— and not immediately after the *ājyabhāga* offerings due to the general statement, "the principal oblations according to the instruction"—
one [offers] to this boy (*kumāra*).

At the *uttarā* [section], while making [the bride] recite the eleven verses beginning with "yoge yoge," he causes her to recite those containing blessings directed toward himself (*pratyagāśis*). Having taken her hand, he causes her to sacrifice [with the oblation] at each mantra.

Among these, because of the contradiction in the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the second and fourth [mantras], "O Agni, this [person] for long life" and "Agni, grant him long life further," he himself should recite them, just as in the case of "O God, giver of life, [grant] old age."
He does not have him recite this.
Some [hold] that because these two also serve the purpose of expressing a pair, they should be uttered by the boy alone;
thereafter, the teacher proceeds with the *jaya*, *abhyātāna*, and *rāṣṭrabhṛt* formulas, as established by the general rule.
Consequently, there is neither the recitation of the private benedictions (*pratyagāśis*) such as "May Agni, the lord of beings, protect us from all sides," nor the *havana* offering. //6//
11. The seating of the teacher on a grass mat:

having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling of water, he places a grass mat with its tips pointing north behind the fire; upon that, the teacher sits down with the [following] Yajus formula. (ĀpGS 11.7)
With the subsequent Yajus formula, "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom," he performs the sprinkling around;
this statement at the end [of the rite] is for the purpose of indicating immediate sequence.
Some perform the vow called Sāvitra at this time, while others recite the Sāvitrī at the end of the three nights.
Both of these are undesirable to the Teacher;
because of the expression "having deposited," the Teacher alone is the agent of the depositing,
not the student.
Since this is already established by the context alone, the statement "the one who initiates" (upanetā) is for the sake of what follows:
so that [the direction] "sitting facing west in front" refers to being in front of the initiator (upanetṛ), and not in front of the fire;
likewise, in the phrase "with his right hand [touching] the right foot," it is the foot of the initiator, not that of the student (māṇavaka). //6//
The seat is made of *kūrca* grass;
[he prepares it] with the northern *yajus*, namely, "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom. The one who initiates him is the *ācārya*.
The remainder is clear. //7//
12. The boy’s request to the teacher for instruction in the Gāyatrī:
Sitting to the east facing west, the boy, having grasped the teacher’s right foot with his own right hand, says, "Sir, please recite the Sāvitrī. (ĀpGS 11.8)

"In darbha grass, having sat down," according to another Gṛhya text; the mention of "with the right [hand]" is intended so that this alternative—namely, that both [hands] should grasp both [feet]—may not apply here.
By this, the specific rule "he should grasp [the feet] including the ankles" becomes applicable. //7//
Seated facing east in front of the teacher, the boy, having grasped and held the teacher’s right foot with his own right hand, requests him, saying: "O Sir, please recite the Sāvitrī to me. (8)
13. The instruction on the Gāyatrī: He recites for him, "That [splendor] of Savitṛ... (RV 3.62.10). ĀpGs 11.9.
Then, he should offer the entire remainder of the sacrificial cake from the back half.
Because of the statement "tasmāt" (therefore), there is a recitation for the purpose of favoring the boy.
By this, the boy is favored throughout all three recitations. The prefix *anu* is intended to indicate favor (*anugraha*).
Out of favor, he says, "He recites after [the teacher]. Therefore, if the boy is unable to speak for that long, he causes him to recite according to his capacity.
Having first spoken himself according to the rule, he first recites by quarters, making a pause at each quarter-verse.
The second [verse] is the half-verse;
thereafter, he recites all [the verses].

It should be stated that "the latter" refers to the instruction "tat savituḥ," which is the designation for the Sāvitrī in the contexts of the Sāvitrī [rites]; [according to Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.27.1], one should offer a thousand pieces of fuel with the Sāvitrī.
This is so that only this [specific verse] may be taken in the case of the *dityā* and other [rituals],
and not just any verse addressed to the deity Savitṛ; for this purpose,
the word "from there" (*tataḥ*) is used, indicating that on this day the recitation consists of this much alone.
By these statements, it is meant that if [the student] does not grasp [the lesson], there shall be teaching at another time. //8//

For the sake of that boy’s grasping [the mantra], the teacher recites this verse, "Tat savitur vareṇyam. In this context, although the request was made in general terms— "Recite a verse having Savitṛ as its deity"—

the specific rule that "he recites 'Tat savituḥ'" indicates that the word *sāvitrī*, even though it is etymological (*yaugika*), refers specifically to the verse "Tat savitur vareṇyam," just like words such as *dhenu* (cow) or *paṅkaja* (lotus).
Thus, its application is restricted to this very [verse] alone, and not to others such as "ā satyena rajasā" and so forth.
Consequently, in the Dharmaśāstra, it is stated: "The Sāvitrī [should be recited] with each breath-control (prāṇāyāma)" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 1.26.15).
In such passages as "One should offer a thousand fuel-sticks with the Sāvitrī" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.27.1), there is the understanding that this very verse is intended, and not any other. //9//
How does he recite? To this he says:
having paused at every foot, foot by foot; having paused at every half-verse, half-verse by half-verse.
Therefore, "all" means the entire [text] without end;
and since the recitation of the whole here serves an invisible (transcendental) purpose, it is recited in its entirety for this boy who is unable to grasp [it all at once]. //10//
Now, he states a specific rule regarding that very recitation:
"One should recite the *vyāhṛtis* expanded at the beginning or at the end of the quarters, and likewise at the two halves; however, the last one [should be recited] in its entirety. (ĀpGS 11.11)

In that regard, there is a specific rule for the recitation and counter-recitation: during the first recitation, the three *vyāhṛtis* should be uttered in sequence at the beginning or at the end of each of the three quarters of the verse. //9//

In the second recitation, two *vyāhṛtis* should be spoken in sequence, either at the beginning or at the end of the half-verses; thereafter, the last one remains, namely *suvaḥ*. One should recite that last one in its entirety during the final recitation.
In this regard, the application is as follows: the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*) should be uttered first.
"The *oṃkāra* is the door to the Self; therefore, one who is about to study the Veda [should utter it]" (*Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra* 1.13.6).
According to this statement:
*Oṃ bhūḥ tat savitur vareṇyam* / *Oṃ bhuvaḥ bhargo devasya dhīmahi*.

Oṃ suvaḥ! May that which impels our thoughts [be established]. Oṃ bhūḥ! We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ. Oṃ bhuvaḥ! May that which impels our thoughts [be established].
Oṃ Peace! We meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; may he impel our thoughts.

He recites each of the *vyāhṛtis* in all three [sections], either at the beginning of each quarter-verse (*pāda*) or at the ends of the quarters. Likewise, when pausing at the half-verse (*ardhaca*), even in the performance, he recites one [of the *vyāhṛtis*] either at the beginning or at the end of each half-verse.
But the supreme *vyāhṛti*, which is undifferentiated, [is recited] at the beginning and at the end of the whole;
"of the whole" (*kṛtsnāyām*) is read with the sense of the genitive case.
The actual application, however, is: first he recites the *praṇava*.

This is because of the Vedic revelation: "The Brāhmaṇa, about to recite [the Veda], says 'Oṃ'" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.8), and because of the statement in the Dharmaśāstra: "'The syllable Oṃ is the gate to heaven; therefore, one who is about to study the Veda should commence with this' (1.136)."
Oṃ bhūḥ; that excellent splendor of Savitṛ. Oṃ bhūḥ; may we meditate upon the radiance of the divine. Oṃ suvaḥ; may he impel our thoughts.
Oṃ bhuvaḥ! We meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine;
Oṃ bhuvaḥ! May he who impels our thoughts inspire us.
"Oṃ suvaḥ; we meditate upon that excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ, who may impel our intellects.
In the alternative view where [the syllables] are at the ends, the application is: "Oṃ, bhūḥ—that excellent splendor of Savitṛ; Oṃ, bhuvaḥ—we meditate upon the splendor of the divine."
Oṃ! May he who impels our thoughts [toward the truth] [bestow] heaven.
Oṃ, we meditate upon that most excellent splendor of the divine Savitṛ; Bhūḥ! Oṃ, may he who shall impel our intellects [grant it]; Bhuvaḥ!
Oṃ tat! We meditate upon the excellence of that divine Savitṛ; may he impel our thoughts. Suvaḥ! Thus. //11//
O youth, with the subsequent mantra, he touches his upper lip.
Then, sitting right there, the youth touches his own upper lip with the northern mantra,
"Vṛdham asau saubhya," and touches water.
Because there are two lips, the word "upper" (uttara) serves as a specification.
The mention of the *mantra* is for the purpose of preventing the suspicion that the word "subsequent" (*uttara*) refers to a direction.
In the mantra, by the term "this one" (*asau*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is denoted, neither the teacher nor the student;
therefore, no mention of a name should be made. //11//

With this mantra, "O gentle one, he has grown," spoken by the teacher, the boy touches his own upper lip; the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is used according to Vedic usage. Furthermore, in the word *asāvi*, there is no mention of the boy's name.
Because they are designated as "prāṇa" (vital breaths);
for there is the scriptural injunction: "Having touched the lips, which have the dark-red [inner] edge as their limit, one should sip water" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.16.10).
However, the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) must be performed. //12//
The ears with the subsequent [formula]. ĀpGs 11.13.
With the subsequent mantra, "You are the guides of Brahman," [he touches them] once;
because of the dual number in the word "ears" (*karṇau*), the touching is performed sequentially. //12//
With both hands simultaneously, he touches his own two ears, according to the northern [text] by the indicative mark of the dual number in the mantra: "O two, you are the yoke-pins of Brahman. //13//
14. Taking up the staff: he takes up the staff with the following [verse]. ĀpGs 11.14.
With the following mantra, "O you of good fame, [make me] of good fame," [he should touch it]. //13//
By the subsequent [verse], "O you of good fame," and so forth. //14//
Now, by means of three sūtras according to the order of castes, he states the rule regarding the qualities of the staffs—15.
The prescription of specific staffs based on the distinction of caste:

the staff of a Brāhmaṇa is made of Palāśa wood; that of a Rājanya is from the trunk of a Nyagrodha tree and not pointing downward; and that of a Vaiśya is made of Bādara or Udumbara wood. (ĀpGs 11.15)

Since this is already established by the specific injunctions for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, the mention of the Brāhmaṇa is intended so that this rule [regarding the staff] may also apply when connected with a caste.
Consequently, the option "the staff is made of wood" applies to the Brāhmaṇa as well;
otherwise, it would apply only to the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, on the grounds that the injunction regarding the connection with a caste was made specifically for them.
A modification of the *nyagrodha* tree is *naiyyagrodha*.
That which is born on a trunk is *skandhaja*.
That whose tip is directed downwards is *avāṅagra*.
The reading "ṅkāra" is a Vedic (Chāndasa) form. //15//
That which is a modification (*vikāra*) of the *badarī* is called *bādara*; because it belongs to the class of trees, the *udumbara* is a tree, not copper. //16//
"Pālāśa" is a derivative of the palāśa tree; the analysis of the compound is the same for the subsequent terms as well. "Skandhaja" means that which is born on the trunk (skandha).
*Avāṅgraḥ*: that staff whose tip (*agra*) is directed downwards (*avācīna*). //15//
Some teachers instruct that the staff should be made of wood, without regard for its specific color or species.
"Vārkṣa" means a modification of a tree;
"of a sacrificial tree," according to another ritual manual (kalpa). The former rule is connected with [the term] "forest-grown" (vaṇasaṃyukta).
This [initiation], however, is common to all and is not connected with any particular caste.

And here, the rule of punishment pertaining to conventional conduct (*sāmayācārika*)— which applies to all *caraṇas* (Vedic schools)— is restated for the purpose of introducing the mantras in the case of the *naiyyagrodha* and other [trees].
Otherwise, the taking [of the fuel-sticks] would occur with the mantra for the *pālāśa* alone, while the others would be taken silently;

for the term "Suśravaḥ" is a designation specifically for the *pālāśa*. As it is said: "The gods, O Brahman, were conversing; the Parṇa tree overheard it, saying, 'I am indeed Suśravaḥ by name'" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.5.7).

Although the rule would have been established by the mere statement "the staff is made of wood," the inclusion of the phrase "not joined with a vowel" is for the purpose of showing the non-confusion between the two alternative options—that if a ritual procedure (*kalpa*) involving a combination of vowels has been commenced, that very same procedure must be carried out until the return ceremony (*asamāvartana*). //17//
*Vārkṣaḥ* means a modification of a *māñjiya* tree, but not of bamboo, rattan, or the like.
They teach that by the conjunction with the vowel *a*, it applies without distinction to all letters.

In this regard, although there is a conflict with the indicative mark (*liṅga*)— since the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), "He heard it on that leaf; his name was Suśravas" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.5.7), indicates that the word *suśravas* in the mantra denotes the *pālāśa* tree, and thus this mantra would apply to the taking up of staffs made of *nyagrodha* wood and others as well— nevertheless, due to the superior authority of the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), "He takes up the staff with the following [mantra]," [the mantra applies only to the *pālāśa* staff].
By this very [rule], setting aside the general indicative mark (*liṅga*), all penalties are prescribed; furthermore,

there is a restatement in the Dharmaśāstra such as "the penalty for a Brāhmaṇa is non-laziness" (ĀpDh 1.2.38), and likewise, "he shall observe the student's life according to the three Vedas" (ĀpDh 1.1.28).

Thus, even when performing the expiation for the lapse of the time for initiation (*upanayana*), [the wearing of the staff] is for the purpose of each specific caste (*varṇa*) wearing its respective staff.

Some [hold that] this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of all the staffs prescribed for all [castes] in that very context; and even though all are mentioned there, [this rule] is for the purpose of prescribing this specific mantra by means of the *Śruti*. //16//
16. The recitation of the *Smṛti* and so forth, and the worship of the Sun (*ādityopasthāna*).

Having caused [the student] to recite "And this has been remembered by me," and having given a gift (*vara*) to the teacher, he makes him rise with the words "O long-lived one! and worships the Sun with the following verses. (ĀpGS 11.17)
Then, having taken up the staff and remaining seated right there, the youth recites the proclamation of his vow beginning with "And this has been remembered by me.
Thereafter, he gives a gift to the teacher.
Then, with the mantra "O Long-lived One," he should rise; with the subsequent mantras beginning with "That eye" and ending with "O Sūrya, for the sake of seeing," he worships the sun.
The youth alone is the performer of the four ritual items beginning with the proclamation of the vow (*vrata-saṃkīrtana*).
However, the statement of the reason [for this] is not intended to apply in both cases—namely, "having made him recite" and "having made him rise.
If that were intended, then the preceptor (*ācārya*) alone would be the performer in the case of the granting of boons (*vara-dāna*) and the worship (*upasthāna*).
Therefore, this is a restatement of the operation of the cause, which is established by implication. //18//
Then the teacher makes the boy recite this collection of mantras beginning with "asmāñca me. Among them, eight mantras have identical endings, while the ninth is the remainder.

Since it would follow from the very fact that they contain blessings directed toward oneself (*pratyagāśiṣṭva*) that the teacher should cause him to recite them, the explicit statement "having caused him to recite" is made again for the purpose of ensuring there is no interval between the act of causing the recitation and the granting of the boon.
Then the youth gives a choice cow to the teacher, the Ācārya, saying, "O Guru, I give you a boon.
Regarding the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*), it is said: "The cow is indeed the boon" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 4.11.4).
Because it has been stated thus;

however, the Teacher, having set aside [the offering] seventeen times, recited the tenth section of the Hotṛs beginning with "Of the god... and ending with "...O Goddess, on the right," and having joined it with "May I attain immortality through this cow for Rudra," [he recited] "May Aṅgīras, lying supine, accept you" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.10).
He accepts [the gift] in this manner, as prescribed by the Śruti;
for there is a statement in the Dharmaśāstra: "The initiation (upanayana) of one seeking knowledge is a purificatory rite (saṃskāra) according to the Śruti" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.1.9).
Then, having raised the boy with the words "O long-lived one," he causes him to recite this [verse].
Thereupon, the boy worships the sun with the ten mantras beginning with "That eye, beneficial to the gods," which have been recited by the teacher.
Here, regarding the suffix *ktvā* in the word "vācayitvā" (having caused to recite), [the rule applies].

The intention lies merely in the performance of the action, and not even in the identity of the agent; for this has been made known [by the rule]: "Having released the cord from her, he should then drive her forward" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 5.13).
In this context, or rather, there is a connection by way of mediation:

having caused the teacher to recite the *Smṛti* and so forth, and having made him rise with the words "O long-lived one," [the teacher] should perform the rite beginning with "Whomever he may desire" and so on.
The boy, however, having given a gift to the teacher, worships the sun with the subsequent [mantras].
Some [hold] that even the four items, beginning with the recitation of the *smṛti*, have Kumāra as their agent;

however, in the phrase "having made him recite and having made him rise," the sense of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is not intended to be significant. Otherwise, because the agents would be different, the granting of the boon and the ritual attendance (*upasthāna*) would have to be performed by the teacher (*ācārya*), and likewise the taking of the staff (*gurugrahaṇa*) in the *caula* and other rites would be for the purpose of granting a boon to the Brahman priest. //17//
Now he states the optional rite:
17. The optional procedure for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
[Regarding] whom one might desire: "May this person not [be... (or "May this person [be...]").
Thinking, "May it not be cut," he should take hold of him by the right hand with the following verse. (ĀpGS 11.18)
Whatever he desires for the pupil, the teacher should bring about; why so?

Thinking, "May this one not be severed from me, may he not be separated, but remain entirely dependent on me until his final return," at that time he should take him by the right hand with the following verse, "In whom all beings... and so forth, while clearly pronouncing the pupil's name.
This injunction is optional, not obligatory;
this itself is the indicator that one need not remain in the proximity of the teacher alone until the completion of one's studies. //19//

If one should desire that this boy "may not be cut off from me nor separated [from me] until his return [from study]," then, having addressed him with the verse beginning "In whom all beings... (RV 10.82.6) and having called him by name, he should take him by the right hand. This applies if the teacher is a master of the four Vedas, a knower of all the Śāstras, and capable of both teaching and explaining them. //18//
They maintain this fire for three days. (ĀpGs 11.19)
The father and others maintain this initiation fire for three days, ensuring it does not go out. //20//
This is clear. //19//
18. The rule for the observances of the religious life (brahmacarya) includes the avoidance of alkaline salts and salt. ĀpGs 11.20.
The avoidance of alkaline salts and salt in his food shall last for three days.
For this religious student (*brahmacārin*), there is a perpetual prohibition based on conventional practice;
however, this present rule is connected specifically to a period of three days.
There is an option regarding these two;
however, the prohibition of honey and so forth is always merely conventional (sāmayācārika). //21//
There is also the avoidance of alkaline substances (*kṣāra*) and salt (*lavaṇa*) for three days.

Here, because of the restrictive rule (*niyama*) "for three days," the prohibition of both alkaline substances and salt is established by the Dharmaśāstra statement: "Just as [one avoids] alkaline substances, salt, honey, and meat" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.4.6).
After three days, [the impurity] lasts for a fortnight; however, in the case of honey and other such substances, it is always [immediate]. //20//
19. Regarding the placing of the fuel-sticks:
having wiped around [the fire] with the verse "pari tvā," one should place the fuel-sticks upon it with the subsequent mantras. (ĀpGs 11.21)
Having wiped that *upanayana* fire all around with the mantra "pari tve" and having sprinkled water all over it,

the religious student (*brahmacārī*) should daily place fuel-sticks (*samidh*) upon it, one by one with each of the twelve mantras beginning with "agnaye samidham," both evening and morning (ĀpDh 1.4.14–16).
The specific rule regarding this should be understood as conventional (sāmayācārika), as it is said:
"Some say that the worship of the fire is to be performed only in the evening" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.4.17).
However, this instruction is intended for the purpose of commencing [the rite] at this particular time.
Therefore, the rite begins in the morning with the placing of fuel and concludes in the evening; in the other fortnight, it begins in the evening itself, and not at any other time.
In that regard, one may proceed according to one's desire.

Although that [obligation] is established by the very context (*adhikāra*), the explicit statement "in that" is intended so that even after three days have passed, the placing of fuel-sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) shall take place in that very fire of initiation (*upanayana-agni*).
By this, its perpetual maintenance (*nitya-dhāraṇa*) is also established as an optional alternative.
At the end, he also places four fuel-sticks with the *vyāhṛtis*;
this should be understood as a remedial rite (*prāyaścitta*), and because it is seen in other ritual manuals (*kalpa*).
The worship [of the fire] is performed with the verses beginning "O Agni, that splendor which is yours," and according to established custom, there is the smearing with ashes. //22//
Having wiped around the fire with the mantra "paritvāgne" and having swept around it,
he should place one fuel-stick for each of the twelve subsequent mantras beginning with "agnaye samidhamāhārṣam" into that initiation fire (upanayanāgni) for as long as it is maintained;
and again at the end, there is a silent sweeping around.
Immediately thereafter, both [should perform] the sprinkling all around in silence,
according to another Smṛti and established custom.
And this placing of fuel-sticks (samid-ādhāna) should be performed after first kindling the fire with wooden sticks;
for there is a statement in the Dharmaśāstra: "Having kindled the fire and swept around it, one should place the fuel-sticks" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.4.16).
The injunction "having swept around [the fire] with the formula *paritve ti*, he should wipe it all around" applies to a fire that has not been carried around.

Likewise, in the Dharmaśāstra, the statement "one should sweep around the kindled fire with the hand, not with a broom" (*Āpastamba Dharmasūtra* 1.4.18) is a restatement for the sake of a specific quality (*guṇārtha*). //21//

Having thus described the worship of the fire, including the placing of fuel sticks along with the prescribed ritual procedures, he now states another quality related to the qualification for that very [rite]:
"In the same way, even in other cases, one should always fetch fuel from the forest and so forth. (ĀpGS 11.22)

Just as the offering of fuel-wood for this initiation fire is enjoined as a constant duty under the view that it is to be maintained perpetually, so too, under the view that it is to be maintained for three days, the meaning is that this rite must be performed even in another fire after the three days have passed. //23//
By the mention of "forest," there is a prohibition of cultivated fruit-bearing trees.
By the expression "having brought," there is a prohibition of those [fruits] brought by others. "Edhāḥ" means pieces of wood.
The inclusion of the word "edha" (fuel) is for the purpose of removing the suspicion that it refers to the fetching of fire.
Among the rules of customary conduct (*sāmayācārika*), there is a prescription that a student (*brahmacārin*) must fetch fuel for the sake of his teacher;
however, this [present rule] is for one's own sake. 24.

According to the rule thus stated, from the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) until the return home (*samāvartana*), the placing of fuel sticks (*samid-ādhāna*) must be performed daily, both evening and morning, or at least in the evening;
and this may also be done for three days after that, even in an ordinary worldly fire (*laukika agni*).

However, the omission of the obligatory (*nitya*) fuel-offering (*samidādhāna*) does not occur simply because the fire of initiation (*upanayana*) has been extinguished; rather, one must fetch fuel from the forest and offer it. Furthermore, regarding this, the *Dharmaśāstra* states: "In the evening and in the morning, according to the instruction," and "Some say that the worship of the fire is only in the evening" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.4.16, 17).
Thus, this is a restatement (anuvāda) for the purpose of an optional injunction.
Some [hold] that the instruction here regarding the kindling of the sacrificial fuel (samitsamindhana) which is normally obligatory, is intended for its commencement at this specific time;
consequently, this rite begins in the morning and concludes in the evening.
Regarding the position that it must be performed only in the evening, however, the commencement occurs only in the evening and not at any other time;
in that case, one may proceed according to one's preference.
Likewise, whether in that [evening] or on another [occasion], because of the commencement [of the rite], there is an option for maintaining the fire of initiation even beyond three days.
And in that very place, there is the placing of fuel-sticks. //22//
With the following verse, he instructs her. (ĀpGs 11.23)

"Thou art a student of sacred knowledge," meaning thou hast entered the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya-āśrama*). Therefore, do not act, speak, or eat according to thy own will.
"Very well," is the reply.
"Drink water; without my permission, drink only water and nothing else."
As before, give the response in every case: "Perform your duties, such as service to the teacher.

such is the absence of sleep here."

"be dependent upon the teacher" means that having abandoned even the authority of one's mother and father, one should remain under the control of the teacher.

"O Brahmacārin, do not be one who acts according to his whims, speaks as he pleases, or eats whatever he desires."
"Having been permitted by me, drink only water;
however, maintain your hunger.
Perform service: perform service for my sake even if not told by me."
Do not sleep; be one who rises first and goes to rest last, for it has been said: "They say of him that he does not sleep" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.4.28).
"Do not sleep during the day," he said;
"go on your alms-round, even if you are eating through invitations and the like, continue to practice the mendicant's life for our sake."
"Be dependent upon the teacher;
do not perform acts such as officiating at sacrifices without my permission.
In this context, the verb form *āsīta* is a Vedic (Chāndasa) usage of the suffix *liṅ*.
The form *suṣupthāḥ* is also used.
In all instructions, the boy should be made to give the reply, "Certainly," or "I shall do so.
And at the conclusion of the instruction, he should go for alms.
Then, handing him an unfilled vessel, he says: "Beg from your mother first" (Baudhāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 2.5.40). This concludes the ritual concerning the *pālāśa* leaf.
Having caused her to put on another garment, he gives her the fourth garment with the following [verse].

Now, when the three nights have passed, on the fourth night—the word "fourth" being used in the sense of the seventh—he does what? The teacher takes away that garment which was worn by the boy, which was freshly cut and woven, and put on him; he takes it with the following verse, namely, with “yasya te prathamavāsyaṃ.”
Having put on another garment,

in this context, "the fourth" does not intend to refer to the night.
What then? It is the aggregate of day and night.
Among those, regarding the shaving [of the head] during the day, there is the restriction: "during the northern course of the sun, during the bright fortnight, on a day.

Having cast those that are ruined into the waters, other [implements] should be held, accompanied by the appropriate mantras. //26//
The accusative case in "caturthīm" is used in the sense of the locative;

that is, on the fourth night, specifically on the day of the fourth day-and-night, because of the rule: "during the northern course of the sun, during the bright fortnight, and on a day" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 1.2).

At the time of the initiation ceremony, the teacher, having removed seven times the garment that was put on [the student], takes possession of it with this very mantra, "That which is your first garment," and not with the Sāvitrī verse.
In this matter, because a specific injunction is more powerful [than a general one],

the view of the Teacher [Upavarṣa] is that, based on the indicative mark (liṅga) in the passage "The gods, indeed, caused Varuṇa to sacrifice" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.2.5), there is no injunction for accepting gifts in non-sacrificial contexts.
This garment, or another one, must be put on by the boy;
he, however, should give it with the words, "O Guru, I give you this garment. And this garment, having been worn according to the mantra for three days, must be put on [again].

Now, the commentary on the *pālāśa* rite is written:

Faith with the hymn "By faith the fire is kindled" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.8.8), and the goddess Medhā with [the hymn] "The goddess Medhā" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 4.41).
With this *anuvāka*, he [attains] wisdom.

In this fourth chapter, the *Tātparyadarśana* has been composed by Sudarśanārya according to the commentary and according to his own understanding; let it be accepted.
Well-composed speech is difficult to find, and the meaning of such speech is very hard to grasp;

Now begins the seventh chapter on the *upākarma* and *utsarjana* rites, specifically the section concerning the *upākarma* and *utsarjana*.
1. The Rule for the Time of the Upākarma.
Now, therefore, we shall explain the rites of the commencement (upākaraṇa) and the conclusion (utsarjana). //1//
Now, the word "atha" (now/then) at the beginning is for the purpose of auspiciousness, as it marks the commencement of a new section.
The two words "ataḥ" (hence) indicate the reason;
because it is impossible to employ these [two terms] without an explanation, therefore we shall explain them. //1//
When the herbs have grown during the fortnight of Śravaṇā, or on the full moon day of the month of Hasta, the commencement of the study of the Veda (adhyāyopākarma) takes place. //2//
"In the fortnight of Śravaṇa" means the first fortnight (the waxing moon) of the month of Śrāvaṇa.

"When the herbs have grown" means when they have sprouted due to the rains; the meaning is that the commencement of the term (*upākaraṇa*)—that is, the beginning of the *upākarma* ceremony—should be performed on the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa under the asterism Hasta.
Because of the statement, "when the herbs have grown," [the rite] takes place on the full moon of Proṣṭhapadā even when the herbs have not yet grown.
And so it is stated in another ritual manual (kalpa): "on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, or of Proṣṭhapadā, or of Āṣāḍhā. //2//

2. The oblation to the Kāṇḍa-ṛṣis and others: After the kindling of the fire and the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings have been performed, while [the sacrificer] has taken hold [of the hand of the teacher], he offers to the Kāṇḍa-ṛṣis: having offered to Sadasaspati, to Savitṛ, to the Ṛgveda, to the Yajurveda, to the Sāmaveda, and to the Atharvaṇaveda, some say that the *upahoma* offerings for the Veda-oblations follow after the offering to Sadasaspati. 3.

Thus the time for the preparatory rite (*upākaraṇa*) has been stated. Now follows the ritual procedure (*prayoga*): one undertakes the main ritual sequence (*tantra*) beginning with the kindling of the fire.
And the fire is to be brought from the house of one learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).
Or rather, it is the *manthya* fire,
and not the *aupāsana*, because here there is no co-partnership among many [priests],
and because there is no co-partnership with the wife; thus, there is the application of the formula here.
This ritual, connected with the Vedas, is for the purpose of purifying knowledge.
Therein, at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, while the pupils hold on to him [the teacher], he offers the principal oblations to the five *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis:
Prajāpati, Soma, Agni, Viśvedevas, and Brahmā Svayaṃbhū. These are the five *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis.
In that regard, there is an oblation with the formula, "To Prajāpati, svāhā!
Others say it is with the formula, "To Prajāpati, the seer of the section, svāhā!
With the verse, "The wonderful Lord of the Assembly," he makes an oblation to Sadasaspati.
With the verse "tatsavitur," one offers an oblation to Sāvitrī, because it is seen so in another ritual manual (kalpa).
Then there are four Vedic oblations: to the Ṛgveda, to the Yajurveda, to the Sāmaveda, and to the Atharvaṇaveda.
Then follow the subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*);
the meaning is that one proceeds with the *jaya*-offerings and so forth.
Some teachers maintain that the offering to Sadasaspati should be made after the Vedic oblations (*vedāhuti*). //3//

3–4. Of the first three *anuvākas*, one should study either the first and the last, or all three. Having performed the rites up to the sprinkling of water (*pariṣecana*), they should recite the three *anuvākas* from the beginning.

Having completed the remainder of the *tantra*, they should study the first three *anuvākas* of the Veda: "For food thee, for strength thee," "May the waters moisten [thee]," and "While digging up. He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Anumati; a cow is the sacrificial fee.

These are the first four *anuvākas* of the sections dedicated to Prajāpati, Soma, Agni, and Viśvedevas. "'Together indeed [were] the gods and the Asuras'—this is from the Self-existent (*svayaṃbhū*)."
Or, the study of these five sections (anuvākas). //4//
Or rather, the first and the last *anuvākas*. 5.
Or alternatively, they should study the first and last sections (anuvākas) of the Veda, namely: "For food, thee! and "Bhṛgu Vāruṇi. //5//
They should study after having observed a period of three days or one day of fasting. //6//
From the day on which the *upākaraṇa* (commencement) is performed, they should study with a break for either three days or one day in the forest;
that is to say, there is no study for three days or one day once the *upākaraṇa* has been performed.
In this regard, if it is the commencement of a *kāṇḍa*, it is one day; if it is the commencement of a *pārāyaṇa*, it is three days.
The statement "they should study" is intended so that, after the introductory rite (upākaraṇa), there may be a mandatory period of study for three days thereafter. //6//
Chapter Seven: On the Opening Rite.
The study should be conducted in the same manner as the introductory ceremony (*upākaraṇa*) was performed.

If, after making offerings to all the *kāṇḍa*-ṛṣis, the commencement of the first three sections (*anuvāka*) at the beginning of the Veda—or of the first and last sections—was made, then the study should be carried out chapter by chapter (*yathādhyāyam*). However, if the commencement of all the *kāṇḍas* was made, then it should be studied according to the *kāṇḍas*.
However, for one who is unable to study the entire Veda in the forest—having omitted the *anuvākyās*—before the *utsarjana* ceremony, there is a separate *upākaraṇa* for each *kāṇḍa*.

In that case, for that specific *kāṇḍa*, there is only one *ṛṣi*, namely Sadasaspati; the *Sāvitrī*, the *vedāhuti*s, and the *upahoma*s [are performed]; at the end of the *pariṣecana*, there is a day of non-study (*anadhyāya*) for one day for an *anuvāka* of that very *kāṇḍa*; and the study is that of that very *kāṇḍa*.
This is the time for the *utsarga*.
The ritual of release (utsarga) takes place under the asterism Rohiṇī during the month of Taiṣa, or on the full moon day. //8//

Having thus commenced [the study], avoiding the days when Vedic study is forbidden, one who studies the Veda or a *kāṇḍa* in the forest— omitting the *anuvākyās*— must perform the ritual conclusion (*utsarga*) under the asterism Rohiṇī, or on the full moon day of the month of Taiṣa. In that rite, there is also an oblation (*homa*).
How does it come about?
Because the procedure is identical to that of the *upākaraṇa*, one proceeds with the rite being performed after having offered the oblation in the house, just as in the case of the *upākaraṇa*.
However, according to the Hiraṇyakeśins, the oblation is performed at the edge of the water after the *tarpaṇa* (water libation). //8//
5. Therein, the preparation of seats for the sages who are to be gratified is as follows:

having gone out toward the eastern or northern direction together with his retinue to a place where there are waters that are pleasant, easy to enter, clear, and abounding in shells, he goes to their edge and performs ablutions with fragrant waters, with the *abliṅga* verses, with the *vāruṇī* verses, and with the *hiraṇyavarṇā* verses.

Having purified themselves with the *pāvamānī* verses, they enter the water and, while submerged, perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) with the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn. Having emerged, sipped water, and stood up, they hand darbha grass to one another and prepare their seats upon darbha grass with the tips pointing eastward in a clean place. //9//
"Accompanied by his retinue and disciples": this means that in whatever place he sees water in the eastern direction;
"pleasant" means pleasant to the touch; "easy to enter" means having good landing places (*sutīrtha*).
Those [streams] which have reeds (*avaka*) are called *avakinyaḥ*, and likewise those with conch-shells (*śaṅkhinyaḥ*); having gone to their vicinity and performed ablutions (*abhiṣeka*) with jars,

he then [performs them] with the verse beginning "O fragrant one" (*surabhimati*), with the *adhrigu* formula, with the *ābliṅga* verses, with the three verses beginning "O Waters, you are most healing" (*āpo hi ṣṭhā mayo bhuvaḥ*), with the Vāruṇī verses, and with the verses beginning "Release us from sin" (*avate heḍaḥ*), "Lift up the highest [bond]" (*ud uttamam*), "This prayer to Varuṇa" (*imaṃ me varuṇa*), and "That I implore of thee" (*tat tvā yāmi*).

Having purified himself with the four *pāvamānī* verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ" (Hiraṇyavarṇīyās) and with this entire section beginning "pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ," and having sprinkled [the water], the ritual action is repeated for each mantra; according to others, it is repeated for every quarter-verse (*pratipāda*).

Then, having entered the water and submerged within it, he performs three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) while reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* triplet—"Ṛtaṃ ca satyaṃ ca"—which was revealed by Aghamarṣaṇa.
In all cases, this is done together with his attendants (*sagaṇa*).
Having immersed himself in the water, he mutters this Anuvāka once; that constitutes one breath-restraint.

Having thus recited it three times and having crossed over [the water], and having put on unwashed clothes that have not been worn before—according to the instruction of other domestic manuals—and having sipped water and stood up, two [students] together hand darbha grass to one another;
then, in a pure place at the very edge of the water, having prepared separate altars (sthaṇḍila), they arrange seats with darbha grass pointing eastward. 9.
To whom? To the gods, the ancestors, and the seers;
to Brahmā, Prajāpati, Bṛhaspati, Agni, Vāyu, Sūrya, Candramas, the constellations, the seasons, the year, King Indra, King Soma, King Yama, King Vaiśravaṇa, the Vasus, the Rudras, and the Ādityas.
"To all the gods, to the Sādhyas, to the Maruts, to the Ṛbhus, to the Bhṛgus, and to the Aṅgirases"—thus for the groups of gods.
"Hosts of gods" (devagaṇa) means both the gods and their respective groups;
here, the ten deities beginning with Brahmā and the five kings beginning with Indra [are intended].
The ten groups of deities beginning with the Vasus [are intended];
because of the statement "they arrange them all," the phrase "I arrange" is connected to every instance.
Thus: "I arrange for Brahmā; I arrange for Prajāpati."
These twenty-five seats are arranged with their ends toward the north;
and the libation for them is performed using the part of the hand sacred to the gods.
The hosts of gods and the hosts of seers are to be gratified.
Now, as for the seers: Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Gautama, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa—these are the seven seers.

to the south, for Agastya; and above Kaśyapa, for Arundhatī.
Because it is seen in another Gṛhya text. //11//
Then they fashion [the vessels] with as many as one hundred and eight teeth. //12//
Immediately after that, as many as there are who have a single altar-limit (ekavedyanta) or a common altar-limit (samānavedyanta)—
namely, the Seven Seers (saptarṣis)— for them they prepare [the portions].
Who, then, are they? They are the sages beginning with Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana.

This is what is meant: [the lineage] from Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana to Jītūkarṇya, to Tarukṣa, to Tṛṇībindu, to Somaśuṣmin, to Somaśuṣka, to Varmin, to Sanadvāja, to Bṛhaduktha, to Vāmadeva, to Vācaratna, and to Haritayajvan.

"To Udameyas, Gautama, Ṛṇañjaya, Kṛtñjaya, Babhru, Tryaruṇa, Tridhātu, Trivarṣa, Śibinta, Parāśara, Vasiṣṭha, Indra, Mṛtyu, Karta, Tvaṣṭṛ, Dhātṛ, Savitṛ, Bhṛtaśravas, Sāvitrī, and to the Vedas"— thus [he offers] separately.
These thirty-four sages, beginning with Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, together with the four Vedas, make thirty-eight, ending with the single Veda. These are [placed] along with the seven sages.
Some, however, maintain that the Atharvāṅgirasas, the Itihāsas, the Purāṇas, the Sādhyas, the gods, and all living beings are also included by the term "Veda."
Because it is seen to be so in another Kalpa. //12//
Having arranged their sacred threads over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta), [he offered] to Vaiśampāyana, to Paiṅgi, to Tittiri, to Ukha, to Ātreya, to Padakāra,
to Kauṇḍinya the author of the Vṛtti, and to Baudhāyana the author of the Pravacana.
To Āpastamba, the author of the Sūtras; to Bharadvāja, the author of the Sūtras;
to Satyāṣāḍha Hiraṇyakeśin;
"I offer [this] to the teachers who are perpetual celibates, and to the forest-dwellers whose wives are devoted to a single husband. //13//

Then, all of them having arranged their sacred threads over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*), they prepared seats for the twelve [sages] beginning with Vaiśampāyana to the south of the gods, specifically for Agastya.
There, on ground sloping toward the south, they arranged [the seats] with the tips of the grass pointing southward and the ends facing west;
such is another ritual tradition (*kalpāntara*). 13.
14. The preparation of seats for the ancestors who are to be satiated;
then, they arrange [the offerings] separately for the paternal ancestors and for the maternal ancestors, each according to their respective lineage.

The meaning is that they prepare [the offerings] for all those on both sides, each according to their own respective ancestors—namely, the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, as well as the maternal grandfather and the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather of the mother.
The phrases "having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder" (*prācīnāvītāni kṛtvā*) and "to the south" (*dakṣiṇataḥ*) carry over from the previous context.
In that regard, the preparation is performed by uttering the names of the ancestors and so forth individually, such as "for Rudraśarman" and "for Viṣṇuśarman."
Others prescribe [the formula] simply as "to the fathers.
Why, then, is it said "according to their respective [relations]"?
It is for the purpose of making known a specific method here as well—just like the offering of rice balls—for those whose fathers are still living. //14//
Having put on their sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*), they satisfy the gods and the seers in those very places and in that same sequence with those very names;
however, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), they satisfy those beginning with Vaiśampāyana down to their maternal great-grandfather, saying:
"I satisfy so-and-so; I satisfy so-and-so; I satisfy so-and-so. (15)
Now, a distinction is observed in another ritual manual: "Homage to this one, homage to that one" with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps;
"Svāhā to this one, Svāhā to that one" with food; and "I satisfy this one, I satisfy that one" with fruit and water (Bhāradvāja Gṛhyasūtra 3.11; Sāṅkhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.10.5, 6, 7). //15//
Or they gaze intently at one another. //16//
It attains this form:
*abhipsyā* means longing.
Here, in the rite of dismissal (*utsarjana*), the joint engagement of the disciples and the preceptor in rites such as bathing and so forth is enjoined.

Because the plural number is used everywhere—[as in] "having performed the consecrations (abhiṣeka), they prepare the seats"—therein this optional distinction is taught: either they consecrate one another, or two by two, having come together, they solicit one another for the sake of engaging in sexual intercourse, and not all together. In the reading *adhītsanta*, this is a form derived from the root *ṛdh*.
And by the power of the prefix, that very same meaning [is conveyed].
However, for those who insert only the letter *t* after the word *adhi* and not even the *ra* and *repha*, the verbal root [for them] has the meaning of "desiring" (*mārga*). //16//
8. Their satiation [of the ancestors] is performed in due order.
9. The study [of the Veda] is as before.
Having performed the rites for the sacrificial cord, they should recite the first three sections (anuvākas). 17.
The method of study has been explained by [the rules for] the Upākaraṇa ceremony. //17//
Or, the first and last [verses] of each section (kāṇḍa) may be used instead. //18//
This alternative view has also been explained in the section on the preparatory rites (upākaraṇa). //18//
10. The planting of *dūrvā* grass near water:
with the two verses beginning "Growing forth from joint to joint," they plant *dūrvā* grass in the vicinity of the water.
Then, having brought a clump of *dūrvā* grass together with its roots, he plants it near water.
He buries it so that the *dūrvā* may sprout, reciting the two verses beginning with "From joint to joint it springs up.
Since the word "dūrvā" is heard in the singular there, only one person—the principal officiant—buries it, while the others should touch him from behind.
Others arise for each individual person. // 19 //
11. Agitating the water, running on the ground after emerging from the water, and plunging into the waters—they thus make it an ocean. //20//
Then, having entered the waters, they turn them into an ocean;
the meaning is that they agitate it like the ocean, the *udadhi*. //20//
He explains how that is so:
"Surrounding it on all sides, they become wavy. //21//
The meaning is that they act so as to surround it on all sides with many [beings] and completely block it, just as waves arise there;
in this manner, they do so three times. //21//
Having lifted it up, they run toward the goal line until they reach the water. //22//
Having emerged and crossed over, they run toward the hermitages of those who have attained [liberation], running toward the eastern or northern direction;
such is liberation. //22//

12. The feeding of the Brahmins: Having returned and having fed the Brahmins with parched barley flour and boiled rice, beginning with the recitation of the *abhidhāna* and so forth, he causes them to pronounce blessings. //23//
"Having returned" means having entered his own house;

"of the master" refers to those [rituals] such as the *Puṇyāha* (day of merit), after which he causes [the officiants] to recite, "May it be a day of merit! May there be well-being! May there be success! //23//
Likewise, at the conclusion of the Pārāyaṇa, the rites beginning with the Kaṇḍādi are performed, excluding the planting of dūrvā grass and the running with curd. //24//

Just as the *utsarga* (formal conclusion) is enjoined when this annual term (*vārṣika*) is completed, so too must it be performed upon the completion of the *pārāyaṇa* (recitation of the entire Veda).

In that regard, the following are to be avoided: not studying the *kāṇḍa* [of the Veda] immediately thereafter, the planting of *dūrvā* grass, the making of a water-pot (*udhikaraṇa*), and the driving of cattle (*ājijhāvana*). //24//
Having returned, he undertakes the ritual acts such as the feeding of Brahmins. //25//

Some maintain that because of the mention of "sections" (*kāṇḍa*) and so forth, the study during the *pārāyaṇa* recitation must be according to the sections alone, and not of the text as a conflated whole.
Others, however, hold that since the mention of "sections" and so forth is illustrative (*upalakṣaṇa*), there is a prohibition against the study of *anuvākas* of every kind.
And they say that in the case of the *pārāyaṇa*, the study may be performed according to one's preference. //25//
In this very manner, one should daily satisfy the gods, the sages, and the ancestors with water. //26//
Because of the statement "with waters," the daily libation (*tarpaṇa*) is performed with water alone.
Consequently, in the rite of offering (*utsarga-karman*), there is also the application of the previously mentioned items such as perfumes (*gandha*) and so forth.
The daily libation occurs after the knowledge of Brahman.
Because it is seen in another kalpa. //26//
Thus ends the chapter on the Upākarma and Utsarjana rites in the Anākulā commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra.
Now begins the fifth chapter,
the twelfth section.

8. Samāvartana—In the preceding section, the initiation (*upanayana*) was explained. Regarding the one who has been initiated, the *Dharmaśāstra* states: "Now follows the rule for studentship" (*atha brahmacaryavidhiḥ*, Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.2.18).
Beginning with these words, the dharmas have been taught. Furthermore,

regarding the rules for the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) and conclusion (*samāpana*) of the *adhyāya*, *kāṇṇḍa*, and *vrata* observances, the passage "At the commencement and at the conclusion, the seer (*ṛṣi*) who is known [for each]" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 8.1) has already been fully explained therein.
Then, having brought either this Veda or the vows, or indeed both, to completion.

Having explained the ritual known as *snāna*— also synonymous with *samāvartana*— which is to be performed by one who has completed his duties through the practice of the meaning of such injunctions as *(Yājñavalkya-smṛti 1.51)* and has returned from the teacher’s house, some [commentators] state that because these two [procedures] are not well-known in this ritual manual (*kalpa*) at the points mentioned in *Āpastamba-gṛhya-sūtra* 8.1, namely "at the commencement and at the conclusion," [the following applies].
Claiming that one must necessarily rely on what is well-established elsewhere,
they explain the section on vows (vratapaṭala) beginning with "Now, therefore, we shall explain the commencement and conclusion [of the vow]" immediately after the initiation (upanayana).
This is not so; for the commentator has already fully explained both these injunctions in the very passage, "At the commencement and at the completion" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 8.1),
and because the study of the Vrata-paṭala is subject to dispute.
And because there is no occasion for such a discussion in the Bhāṣya.
1. The rule for entering the cow-pen before sunrise:

Having studied the Veda and being about to perform the ceremonial bath (snāna), he enters the cow-pen before sunrise and remains there, having blocked the entrance with a hide with the hair side inward. (ĀpGS 12.1)

Having been thus initiated and having lived the life of a religious student (*brahmacarya*), having studied the Vedas along with their six auxiliary sciences (*ṣaḍaṅga*), if he desires to seek another stage of life (*āśrama*) other than that of the teacher's family, his ritual bath (*snāna*) is performed according to rule; this is called "the bath," meaning he shall perform that bath which is the "return ceremony" (*samāvartana*). "Before sunrise" refers to the rising of the sun.
On account of the scriptural vision: "The sun does not depart from this day";
*vrajam* means a cow-pen;
*antaḥ* means within.
With the skin of any deer whatsoever that has its hair on the inner side;
the mention of "seat" is for the purpose of prohibiting [using it] for departing.
The singular number in "a hide" (*vedam*) is not intended to be restrictive.
"Having studied the Veda"—meaning one, two, or all three Vedas, having mastered them both in terms of their verbal recitation and their meaning.
The mention of "one who is about to bathe" (snāsyann) is intended so that there may be no further duty for the lifelong student (naiṣṭhika). //1//
The Veda is characterized by the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas.
The singular number is used with reference to the genus (jāti), as in the passage:
"Having studied the Vedas—whether all of them, two of them, or even one—in due order."
This is according to the statement of Manu:
"Having studied"— meaning having mastered through both recitation and comprehension— the Veda along with its six auxiliary limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and its Mīmāṃsā.
And the injunction "having studied" is for the purpose of illustrating the statement: "Having brought the Veda or the vows to completion, or indeed having attained fearlessness."

One who is about to bathe—that is, one who is about to perform the rite called "bathing"—should enter the cow-pen, which is enclosed, before sunrise, that is, prior to the rising of the sun; the rest of the passage has a clear meaning. //1//
On this day, the sun shall not scorch him.
While he is performing this rite on this day,
the sun shall never scorch him;
therefore, even his urine, excrement, and so forth, should be discharged right there in the cow-pen, even in the shade.
By the mention of the sun, there is no prohibition of the heat of fire. //2//
The meaning is that on this day, until sunset, he shall not go outside the pavilion even for the purpose of voiding urine or excrement. //2//
2. The shaving is like the initiation (*upanayana*).

At midday, after the kindling of the fire and the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings have been performed, he places a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood upon the fire with the following verse. Then, having sat down to the west of the fire on a mat of *kaṭa* grass or *erakā* grass, he consecrates the razor with the following verse and hands it to the barber with the following *yajus*. [Then] of the waters...
From the reintegration [of the body] up to the depositing of the hair, the procedure is the same.
Then, on that day at midday, the ritual procedure is commenced,
beginning with the kindling of the fire and so forth,
up to the placement of the wooden pins (śamyā).
The performer himself, and not the preceptor, performs the recitation of the *pābhāṇi* formulas together with the razor and other implements.
The mention of the limit up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings is for the purpose of indicating the time for the subsequent rites beginning with the placing of the fuel-sticks (*samidādhāna*).

Even though the performance of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is already established by this very [preceding rule], the mention of "laying the fire" (*upasamādhāna*) and so forth indicates that the commencement of the *tantra* and the restriction to midday apply only to the main part,
not to the entire rite.
[This is done] with the following verse, namely, "imaṃ stomam" (RV 10.75.1).
There is no utterance of *svāhā*, because there is an absence of an injunction to offer (*juhoti*).
A "mat" (*kaṭa*) is well known; it is a grass that has *erakā* as its constituent material.
Others say [the mantra is] "kaśipū.
Having consecrated the razor with the following verse, "atryāyuṣam," [he should proceed].
With the subsequent Yajus formula, "Thou art named Śiva," the barber—

the shaver, not the teacher— hands him the razor. Then, the ritual beginning with "Warm [water], bring the cold [water]" and ending with the placing of the hair, including the mixing of the waters and so forth, is the same as in the initiation ceremony (upanayana).
What? The ellipsis is "he causes to be made. By whom does he cause it to be made?
By the teacher (ācārya), even though he has departed from the teacher's household.
Nevertheless, at the time of the ritual bath and at the time of the wedding, the teacher should assemble [the relatives], because of the force of the word "together" (*samāna*); for it is said:
"He who is honored by him, him [he honors] with the other" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 3.9).

And because it is seen [in scripture] thus; and it is clearly stated in the *Āśvalāyanagṛhyasūtra*: "Now, one who is returning [from his teacher's house] prepares these [items]" (*āśva.gṛ.* 3.7.1), and so forth.
Others, however, desire that he should return home directly to the teacher's family.

There, having performed the ritual of parting the hair (*saṃsarjana*) on the head, having taken a razor from the barber, having shaved [the hair] in each direction, and having given it back to him, he consecrates the one shaving with the following verse.
Thus ends the ritual duty of the teacher. 3.

One should perform the ritual action such that the principal offerings consist of clarified butter (ājya), just as they do at midday. However, in this case, there is an instruction regarding the ritual manual because the oblation has clarified butter as its principal substance.
Furthermore, the phrase "at the end of the ājyabhāga offerings" is intended to indicate the proper sequence.
When the division of the clarified butter (ājyabhāga) has been performed, there is only the placing of the fuel-sticks (samidādhāna), and not the performance of other ritual purposes as well;
and here, in the preparation of the vessels, the ladles and other implements are placed in pairs.
The razor, the *kaṭa*, and so forth are used only once; the *śamyā* pieces are for the purpose of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Some say that the ladle (*darvī*) and other such items are also used only once.
"Pālāśī" means made from parts of the Palāśa tree, using the verse "imaṃ stomam" as the subsequent [formula].
"Kaṭaḥ" is the well-known mat made of grass.
"Erakā" is the grass that serves as the material for the mat, known by the name *paṅktikaṭa*.
Some [say]:

with the verse "kaśipv" and with the following two verses, namely "āyusam," and with the subsequent Yajus formula "aśivo nāmāsi," he hands that razor to some Brahmin who knows the mantras and acts as the barber (vaptṛ).
Some say that here too the teacher begins the shaving, while the barber merely provides him with the razor;
that is incorrect.
In this case, because there is no officiating Ācārya present, and because the barber is not learned in the mantras;

therefore, beginning with the first Yajus of the Anuvāka, [the text continues]: "Having tied the hair upon that [post], he places it at the root of an Udumbara tree or at a clump of Darbha grass with the following [verse]" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 10.8).
Thus far, [the procedure] is the same as that for the initiation ceremony; the word "it is" is to be understood as the ellipsis. //3//
3. The giving of the girdle to the religious student (brahmacārin).
Having sat down at the rear half of the cow-pen and loosened the girdle, he hands the girdle to the religious student. (ĀpGs 12.4)

Then, having had his hair, beard, and nails trimmed, and having sat down on the hindquarters—that is, the rear half—of a cow-pen, he loosens and unties his girdle and gives it to some student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*). //4//
Then, having sat down in the rear half of Vraja, that is, in its hind part, with his hair and other features disheveled, he performs [the following] acts. //4//
4. He places her upon a clump of darbha grass;
with the following Yajus formula, he conceals her at the root of an udumbara tree or within a clump of darbha grass. (ĀpGs 12.5)

He covers [it] with the subsequent *yajus* formula beginning with "This I conceal from so-and-so, the son of so-and-so," and so forth; in those instances where the word "this" (*idam*) occurs, there is the insertion of the name: "This I conceal the evil of Yajñaśarman, the son of Gārgya; may Yajñaśarman be superior to his enemies."

Now, if it should be "of Yajñaśarman, Gārgyāyaṇa," at this time there is also the discarding of the staff and the antelope skin. That student, however, hides that girdle in the place prescribed by the Sūtra, making it invisible, [saying]: "Here I hide the sin of Viṣṇuśarman Gautama; may Viṣṇuśarman be superior."
With this Yajus mantra, "dviṣadbhyaḥ," the name and lineage of the bather (snātṛ) should be taken here. //5//

5. He bathes with water prepared according to the preceding rules, and cleans his teeth with an udumbara twig; having bathed with the subsequent waters, he cleans his teeth with an udumbara twig. ĀpGs 12.6.
"Thus prepared" means mixed together as before, that is to say, with water both cold and warm.

In that mixing, there is an omission of the mantra; [the mixing is done] with the *ṛg* verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and those beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇāḥ. Among these, the verses beginning with "yāsu jātaḥ" are to be understood.
And there is an ablution for each mantra.
He cleanses his teeth with a twig; he removes the impurity from his teeth.
With the following verse, "Arrange yourselves for the sake of food," he does so.
With water prepared in this manner— mixed silently with cold and warm water—
the mantra for mixing is not employed because it would contradict the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra "May he shave the hair" and because of the restrictive particle *eva*.
[The shaving is performed] with the subsequent six verses and with the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
He bathes and consecrates him;
and this is done only once at the end of the six [verses]. Some, however, say it is done verse by verse.
That is not so; for it has been stated that it is improper to assume a repetition of the principal act for the sake of a subordinate quality.
Now, with a piece of Udumbara wood, he removes the impurity from the teeth with the mantra: "For the sake of food, cleanse yourselves. (6)
Having covered [him] with bathing substances, he bathes again;
he puts on a new inner garment and applies sandalwood unguent.
The tying of the jewel upon the necks, the tying of the jujube-stone (*bādara-maṇi*) upon the right hand,
and the wearing of the upper garment.
Having been covered with bathing powder, he bathes. ĀpGs 12.7.

Having put on an inner garment with the next *yajus* verse, having offered *sarvasurabhi* sandalwood paste to the deities with the following verses, and having anointed himself with it using the subsequent verse, he should take a golden amulet together with its case and thread, and having immersed it three times clockwise in a water-pot with the next verse, he should tie it around his neck with the following verse. In the same manner, except for the mantra, he should tie a *bādara* (jujube) amulet on his left hand; then [he puts on] the new upper garment.
The wearing of the garment is the same, with the mantra "O wealthy ones, come hither. (ĀpGS 12.8)

Then, having been rubbed with bathing powders such as *klītaka* and other substances suitable for bathing, and thus having his impurities removed, he bathes again with those very same waters. Then, with the subsequent *yajus* mantra, "Thou art the body of Soma," he puts on a new (*ahata*) lower garment (*antara-vāsa*);
that which covers the waist is called the *antara*.
That by which the outer garment (*nīvi*) is covered or the sacred thread (*upavīta*) is made is called *itara*.
Having put on another garment between those two, he applies ointment with the fourth [verse].
With what? With sandalwood.
Of what kind? "Possessing all fragrances" (*sarvasurabhi*): that in which all fragrant substances are present is *sarvasurabhi*.
Regarding the reading *sārvasurabhiṇā*, the derivation of the form must be sought [elsewhere].

Therein, first he offers to the deities with the three subsequent mantras beginning with "Obeisance to the planet" (*namo grahāya*). Then, with the following mantra, "The fragrance of the Apsarases," he anoints himself.
"A Brāhmaṇa should first anoint his face; a Rājanya, his arms..."
"The Vaiśya [should wear it] on the stomach," says Āśvalāyana (Āśvalāyanagṛhyasūtra 3.7.10–12).
Then he fastens the amulet and ties it around his neck.
And that jewel is made of gold;
it is set with lapis lazuli and other gems,
and strung upon a thread of fine silk.
The meaning is "together with the cord.
He causes that amulet to float three times in a vessel of water with the next verse, "This herb...
The mantra is recited only once.
Then, with the following verse, "Thou art the bond, O Lord," he binds it around the necks.
This word "grīvā" (necks) refers to the vessels (dhamanīs); though plural in form, it is applied to the throat because of its connection [to them].
In this ṛc, the earth is praised.
Therefore, this herb must be called *trāyamāṇā*;
the elision of the letter *s* is due to Vedic usage.
Then, having likewise prepared a cord from the seed of the *badarī* tree, he causes it to float three times clockwise in a vessel of water and ties it on his left hand.
In both the floating and the binding, there is a prohibition of the use of mantras;
because of the repeated mention of the "jewel" (maṇi), its placement [on the body] does not occur,
but it remains threaded on a string.
Having tied on the jewel, he then puts on an upper garment that is indeed new.
In this regard, the ritual procedure beginning with "The Revatīs... should be understood as being identical to that of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).

Although the rite would be established by the words "with these [verses] beginning 'The Revatīs... or simply by the word "with the subsequent [verses]," the explicit statement of its identity is for the purpose of applying it to the performance of one who has already undergone initiation.
With those two [mantras] beginning with "uttarābhyām," he consecrates [the garment]; this constitutes the teacher's ritual action, ending with the consecration of the one who has put it on. //7//
Having rubbed his body with bathing accessories such as *klītaka* and *madhūka* powder, he bathes with bathing substances such as ground *āmalaka* and other ingredients. //7//

With the sacrificial formula (yajus), "Thou art the body of Soma," he puts on the inner garment— the *antara-vāsa*, meaning the undergarment or innermost clothing. By this rule, the wearing of an inner garment is prescribed as a constant requirement for the *snātaka* from this point forward.
Furthermore, the *yajuḥ* is solely for the purpose of ritual action, because it is recited with the syllable *ma*.
Therefore, the connection is made with the distant [word] "anulimpati" (he anoints), as in: "he anoints with sandalwood perfumed by all fragrant substances, such as musk and the like."
How does one anoint?
To this he says: "With the subsequent [mantras]," and so forth;
"Homage to Graha," etc.

Having first offered sandalwood to the deities with these three mantras beginning with "ityādi," he subsequently anoints himself with the verse, "The fragrance which is among the Apsarases. Furthermore, the anointing is performed first on the face.
According to the *Āśvalāyanagṛhya* (3.7.10), "The Brāhmaṇa should first smear [the food] on his face"; furthermore, the offering to the deities is performed with the word "namaḥ" (salutation),
and not with the concluding part of a mantra.
Because even the act of salutation has the purpose of offering;
what kind of jewel? One made of gold, a transformation of gold.

It is encased on both sides with gold, diamonds, lapis lazuli, and so forth, and strung upon a thread. Having recited once the verse, "O herb, thou art the protector," one should continuously swirl it three times clockwise in a vessel of water.
Then, having tied that gem around the neck with the subsequent mantra beginning with "Thou art a bond-breaker" and ending with "for merit," which concludes with three pauses, [one should wear it].
Having silently caused a jujube fruit made from jujube seeds, along with a cord and a jewel, to float three times clockwise in a vessel of water,
he silently ties them to his left hand. He puts on an unwashed upper garment as his lower garment as well.
But not the upper garment;
that is the same as the [act of] leading [the student] forward.
He puts it on himself.
In this case, due to the absence of a preceptor,

one consecrates the garment to be worn with the two verses beginning "May Revatī clothe you," puts it on with the three verses beginning "Those who cut [the cloth]," and then follows it with the mantra "This garment around."

Furthermore, by the force of the statement, "He performs [the rite] similarly with the mantra, 'Revatīstve,'" there is indeed a sublation of the gender (liṅga) of the word *yuṣmad* contained in the mantra.
Alternatively, another learned Brāhmaṇa performs it similarly with the mantra, "Revatīstve.
