But why, moreover, is it that by the phrase "an unwashed upper garment" (*ahatam uttaraṃ vāsaḥ*), only the lower garment (*paridhāna*) is meant, and not the upper robe (*uttarīya*)?

It is said: because of the statement, "The [rites] beginning with 'O you who cry out' are the same as the initiation ceremony" (*Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra* 1.20.4), and because at the initiation ceremony, one understands that the garment for the purpose of wearing is [obtained] from the rule, "Having clothed him with three [verses], he clothes him around with the next [verse]" (*Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra* 10.10),
and because of the injunction for the previous [ceremony], "A new, unwashed garment."

However, because of statements in the Dharmaśāstras such as "the upper garment must always be worn over" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.4.21), a cloth for the upper body is already established here as well.
Some, however, maintain that only the upper garment is prescribed here, and not the lower garment.

Because of the statement "the subsequent [rite]," and because the teacher himself performs the same procedure as the initiation ceremony beginning with "May the Revatīs favor you," that is not so; for [he does so] after having clothed [the student].

This is precisely because it is illogical to say "it has been worn. Likewise, this bath is performed after one has returned from the teacher's family; in that case, there is no possibility at all for the teacher to be the agent [of wearing it]. //8//
At the end of the garment, having tied the two earrings and placed them on a ladle superior to that [ordinary one], he performs the principal oblations, the *jaya* offerings, and so forth.

Having tied them to the fringe of the garment, placed them in the ladle, and poured clarified butter over them while reciting the subsequent [mantras], he offers the remaining oblations and proceeds with the *jaya* offerings and the rest. (ĀpGS 12.9)

Having tied two golden ear-ornaments (*karṇālaṅkāra*) onto the fringe of that northern garment and placed them on a ladle (*darvī*), he offers the eight principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) with clarified butter (*ājya*).
The meaning is that while causing the clarified butter to be poured over the two ear-ornaments as they are being brought forward, he performs the offering.
Alternatively, the reading is *abhyānayan*.
In this view, the drawing toward oneself is performed with the left hand;
"abhyānāyam" is appropriate as a form derived from the suffix *ṇamul*,
meaning "having drawn toward oneself" or "having brought near."
In every respect, the principal oblation (pradhānahoma) is performed with clarified butter poured over the two pravarta-sticks;
the recitation of the Jaya and other formulas follows after removing the pravarta-sticks for the purpose of concluding the rite as it has been accomplished. //8//
Having tied two golden earrings to the fringe of that aforementioned cloth by means of a ladle and placed them at its tip, [the text says] "with clarified butter.
This is a restatement of what is already established by the general rule (*paribhāṣā*) for the purpose of prescribing the act of heating (*abhyānayana*).
The reading "abhyānāyam" is a variant form containing a suffix with the sense of the gerundive (*ṇamul*).

Then, having poured clarified butter over the two fire-sticks (*araṇi*) which have been placed by his own left hand, and having offered with that very butter the eight principal oblations (*pradhāna-āhuti*) beginning with "āyuṣyaṃ varcasyam," he then removes a portion from the tip [of the ladle] with the *darvī* and proceeds with the *jaya*-oblations and so forth as is well known.
Because of the etymological derivation from "indicating" (*sūcana*), a rule (*sūtra*) everywhere involves the prescription of multiple meanings;
thus, even a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) is not a fault, as stated in the passage "having kindled the fire" (*agnim idhvā*, Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 1.12).
Some maintain that the reading should be "blowing [the fire] with the left hand" (*savyena hastena abhyānāyan*) or "blowing [it] with the other hand" (*anyena abhyānāyan*). //9//
The tying of those two earrings:
having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling, he should tie them on the right ear with these [verses], and on the left ear with these [same verses]. (ĀpGs 12.10)
The statement ending with the final sprinkling (pariṣecana) is for the sake of continuity;
therefore, there is no eating on that day.
"With these very oblations" means with the mantras intended for the oblations.

Because of the statement, a single action should be performed with many mantras, and the mantra containing the *svāhākāra* should be employed. If it were said simply "and on the left," there would be a distributive application of the mantras;
therefore, it is stated again, "with these [mantras]. (9)
Immediately after the sprinkling, with these same eight verses beginning with "āyuṣyaṃ varcasyam," he should tie one earring on the right ear and fasten it;
likewise, with those same verses, he should do the same for the other one on the left ear.

And here, since the *homamantras* themselves are enjoined by the *śruti*—inferred through their similarity to the words of the *sūtra* as being the means for tying (*ābandhana*)—the tying is also manifested by them through secondary figurative usage (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*). Just as in the case of the *aindrī*, the feminine gender designation in the phrase "tathaitābhiḥ" [is used] because of the plurality of the *ṛcs*, like the expression "a village of Brahmins.

Nor is there any contradiction here in assigning those mantras intended for the *homa* to the purpose of tying, just as one might say, "This cow belongs to Devadatta," or "This cow belongs to Yajñadatta."

Because, as in the case of the statement "he scatters the husks with the potsherd of the sacrificial cake" (*puroḍāśakapālena tuṣān upavapati*), the application [of the mantra] is possible through indication (*lakṣaṇā*) based on its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*), even without obscuring the form already enjoined; furthermore, it has been stated in the *Āgneyī-adhikaraṇa* that even multiple meanings are not improper in the case of *ṛc*-mantras.

Some [hold] that by the word "with these" (*etābhiḥ*), the mantras intended for the oblations are indicated because they refer back to the oblations under discussion, just as in the expression "he worships with the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses of the ancestors."

It is not so; for in the previous instance, it is better to understand the mantras under discussion by means of indication (lakṣaṇā) through the phrase "subsequent oblations," rather than resorting to indication here in this sentence as well.
9. Wearing a garland on the head, applying collyrium to the eyes,
and looking into a mirror.
The removal of sandals, and the carrying of an umbrella and a staff;

likewise, with the following [terms], according to their respective characteristics: a garland on the head, the application of collyrium, looking into a mirror, sandals, an umbrella, and a staff. (ĀpGs 12.11)
In this manner, with the subsequent mantras as well, one should employ the six substances, beginning with the garland, according to their respective characteristics and as appropriate.
Therein, the binding of the garland upon the head is performed with the two [mantras] beginning "O auspicious one, [place] the head";
for it is stated according to their respective characteristics that [the binding is done] with these two [beginning] "I bind this [garland] upon him."
"Srajaḥ" is the genitive singular,
not the nominative or accusative plural;
this is because of the singular forms "imām" and "tām."
Because of the statement "on the head," it does not apply to two swords.
"Not [if] addressed to Mālā.
If they should say [it] to Mālā:
Thus says Āśvalāyana.
Then, with the two verses beginning "The collyrium from Trikakud," he should apply collyrium to his eyes;
in that rite, the application to the right eye comes first, using both mantras.
Then, by those same two [mantras], [he anoints] the left [eye].

Although there is a dual number in the mantra "With that I anoint the left," nevertheless, by the force of the extension (*atideśa*) expressed as "in this manner" (*evam*), there is a repetition of the action, just as in the case of the binding of the two forearms.
And there is a repetition of the mantra;
in that case, as with the *sānnāyya* vessels, there is a dual number, as in: "I place the two *ukhā* pans of the sacrifice whose essence has not yet been exhausted."
Then follows the looking into the mirror with the verse, "Whatever luster is mine...
If "looking" were not explicitly stated, it would imply merely taking up [the mirror] at this time;
[as the text says later], "This, indeed, he takes up again."
Because of this indicative mark (liṅga), there is the inclusion of the act of looking.
Thereafter, he puts on the two sandals with the Yajus formula, "You two are the unestablished.
As in the case of applying collyrium, there is a repetition of the action and a repetition of the mantra.
Then, taking an umbrella, he covers himself with it while reciting the Yajus formula, "Thou art the refuge of Prajāpati.
With the Yajus formula, "By the impulse of the god Savitṛ... he takes up a staff;
according to Āśvalāyana, it should be made of bamboo.

Just as in the middle of the ritual procedure the two arms are bound with mantras, so too one should bind the six items beginning with the garland (*sraj*) with the subsequent mantras, according to their respective characteristics and in accordance with the indications of the mantras; such is the completion of the sentence as appropriate.
In that regard, one should bind the garland on the head with this single mantra: "O auspicious one, [bind] the head."

The phrase "yām āharat" is for the purpose of providing an option, as it is said that "rites [performed] with a single mantra are optional"; the remaining [phrases] are also for the purpose of providing options (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 1.4.1; 4.12).
This is because of the technical rule (paribhāṣā):
"The word *sraj* [is used] in the sense of the accusative singular";
thus, [in the mantra] "O auspicious one, ascend to my head," [the word *srajam* is understood].
This is because of the singular number and masculine gender in such phrases as "yām āharat" (whom he brought),
or else because of the genitive singular.
That being the case, the remainder [of the sense] is that the binding of the garland must be performed.

Likewise, by the single formula "the collyrium from Trikakud," which is uttered only once, the application of collyrium produced from the mountain Trikakud must be performed simultaneously upon both eyes.
Here too, the four sacrificial formulas (yajūṃṣi) beginning with "In me, O mountain" are intended solely for the purpose of providing options (vikalpa).
Nor should collyrium be applied to the eyes alternately, because that would contradict the dual number in the word "vām" (of you two).
In the same manner, one should perform the inspection of the mirror with this [verse]: "Whatever luster of mine has departed... and so forth.
In the same manner, he puts on the two shoes simultaneously with the Yajus formula,
"You two are supports," because of the dual number indicated in the word "supports.
Likewise, having silently taken up the umbrella, he covers himself with it using the Yajus formula, "You are the shelter of Prajāpati."
In the same manner, he takes up the bamboo staff with the Yajus formula beginning with "devasya tvā" and so forth;
such is the meaning of these six substances.
Some maintain that the binding of the garland is performed with both [verses]: "O auspicious one, ascend my head" and "Yama has brought it."

Likewise, by the force of the statement, "With the two [verses] beginning 'When the ointment' and 'Upon me, O mountain, the man,' [the ointment is applied] to both eyes, repeated for each, in sequence to the right and left eye"; and consequently,
even the gender [indicated] in the word "to the left" (*vām*) in the verse "With that [ointment] to the left" must be set aside by the force of the injunction.

Just as there is the mark of the dual number in the single *sānnāyya* pot with the words "I place the two *ukhā*s," so too the explanation regarding the removal of the sandals is like that of the ointment (*añjana*).
That is incorrect, because [the rule states] "those [acts] have a single mantra" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 1.41).
Because this contradicts such technical rules (*paribhāṣā*) as [Pāṇini 1.4.2],
and because the rule "in the same way with the subsequent [words] according to their gender" remains applicable even under the previous interpretation;
furthermore, even if the reading "mayi parvate pūruṣam" were joined together (*praśliṣṭa*), there would still be no syntactic expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*) once the division is made.
And because a split in the sentence is understood. //11//
10. Restraint of speech, worship of the directions, and worship of the lunar mansions and the moon; he restrains his speech until the appearance of the stars. (ĀpGS 12.12)

When the stars have risen, having gone out toward the eastern or northern direction, he should worship the directions with the second half-verse, and then the stars and the moon with the following verse. (ĀpGS 12.13)

Then, with the latter half of the verse beginning "The goddesses, the six earths" (*devīṣṣaḍurvī*), facing east with palms joined in reverence, he brings all the directions to mind; having turned clockwise at the end of the mantra, he gazes around them.
This is because of the gender [of the word] in the phrase "the six earths" (*ṣaḍurvīḥ*), which indicates that there are indeed six directions.
The four [directions] beginning with the east, as well as the upward and downward directions;
then, with the subsequent half-verse beginning with "May we not be abandoned by them," he worships the constellations together with the moon. //11//
And this has been explained. //12//

Having worshipped the directions, with the downward direction as the sixth, by means of the second half-verse beginning with "The six gods, the wide ones" (devāṣṣaḍurvīḥ), he worships the lunar mansions and the moon by means of the second half-verse beginning with "May we not be abandoned" (mā hāsmahi).
And on the strength of the Vedic text, one must supply the word "lunar mansions" (nakṣatrāṇi) in the phrase "may we not be abandoned," for they are indeed objects to be illuminated. //13//
11. Conversation with a friend and going as one pleases; having conversed with a benefactor, one departs according to the purpose. (ĀpGs 12.14)

Having conversed with that *rāti*—his kinsman—asking, "What should I do? Which stage of life (*āśrama*) should I adopt?", he goes along with that *rāti*; the meaning is that he returns to an unestablished stage of life.

Since this is already established by the rule, "Having understood [the rules], whatever he may desire, let him undertake that" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.21.5), the repetition is for the purpose of ensuring that even for one who has renounced the world (*pravrajita*), the ritual of the bath (*snāna-karma*) should extend at least as far as the conversation. //12//

Based on the etymological derivation that *rāti* (a friend) is "one who causes delight," one should converse with him with confidence; having deliberated upon and determined matters such as dharma in accordance with one's own power and capacity, one proceeds toward the true goal— that is, whatever purpose, whether dharma or liberation, has been resolved as the objective to be accomplished together with that friend.
He enters a stage of life corresponding to that, whether it be the householder's stage or the state of silence [of a forest-dweller].

And thus, even for one who goes forth from the stage of studentship (*brahmacarya*) itself, he should go forth only after having performed the ceremonial bath (*snāna*) which concludes with the formal conversation. //14//
Thus ends the twelfth section in the Gṛhyatātparyadarśana composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
Thirteenth Section: 9. Madhuparka—1.
The one worthy of honor is seated upon a grass mat (kūrca).
Now, this is another [rite]: having silently bathed at a sacred ford (tīrtha), he silently places a fuel-stick (samidh) on the fire. ĀpGs 13.1.
The ritual of bathing (*snānakarma*), which is both weightier and primary, has been explained.
Now, this other procedure for bathing, which is lighter and secondary, is being explained.
What is it? One bathes silently in water that reaches the ground at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
[He offers] with water that has not been drawn up and is cool;
and he places the fuel-stick silently, not with a mantra.
The fuel-stick is made of *pālāśa* wood;
in this ritual procedure, only this much is to be done,
and nothing else, such as "go before sunrise" and so forth.

However, the shaving and so forth are worldly and non-dharmic. The procedure for that is as follows: having had his hair, beard, nails, and body hair shaved; having removed his mat, staff, and deerskin; having silently bathed at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*); having cleaned his teeth with a stick made of *udumbara* wood; and being covered with bathing garments, he bathes once more.
Having put on two unwashed garments, sipped water, kindled the fire, and strewn grass around it, he places a fuel-stick of *palāśa* wood into the fire while meditating upon Agni in his mind;
then he takes up the ornaments, beginning with the jewel, as they are available, performing everything silently. 1.
Now, another procedure is stated—
the word "is said" being understood as the ellipsis— at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), such as a meritorious river and so forth.

The fuel-stick should be made of *pālāśa* wood, because there is no contradiction [with other authorities], and because of the restrictive particle "eva" (only), nothing else whatsoever is to be performed in this rite.
Now, one might ask: why is it not accepted that in the previous rite itself, the bathing and the placing of the fuel-stick are of an entirely different nature and optional?
It is said: because it would result in the redundancy of the particle *eva*;
because bathing and the placing of fuel (*samid-ādhāna*) are mentioned here in reverse order; and because this sūtra consists of many syllables.

For if this [option] were intended as an alternative within that very preceding rule, then he would have composed the sūtra with far fewer words, such as: "Having placed a fuel-stick of *pālāśa* wood with the next [verse], or silently; having bathed with the six [verses] beginning with those [already] prescribed, or silently at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*)."

Furthermore, this is not the established style observed among the authors of the Sūtras—namely, that after stating the primary rite together with its constituent parts, one subsequently describes the various optional variations by means of a Sūtra beginning with "atha" (now).
This very same principle applies to the explanation of the passage: "Now, furthermore, he offers curd with his joined palms" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 22.10).
As for the ritual procedure: having discarded the marks of a student such as the girdle and so forth, and having silently bathed at a sacred ford (tīrtha),
put on another garment and so on, and having fetched fire from the house of one learned in the Vedas, he should kindle it according to the rule, "Wherever [one finds] fire."
There, meditating upon Prajāpati in his mind, he silently places the fuel-stick on the fire.
Some say that he also performs other non-conflicting acts, such as shaving the hair and beard, silently. //1//
Wherever they offer him honor, he sits upon a grass mat (kūrca) just as before. (ĀpGS 13.2)
By either of the two [vows] mentioned, one becomes a *snātaka*.
At this time, his relatives should perform an honoring ceremony for him, because of the statement: "The study of the Veda, a cow, the *madhuparka*, and a day of rest."
"One should offer the *arghya* after having announced [the intention]"—this is another ritual procedure (*kalpāntara*).
The Kauṣītakins record the announcement in a formal recitation (*nigada*), saying: "O you who have well-performed the vow-bath, we shall offer the *arghya* to you."

"‘A seat, water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, the honey-mixture, and a cow— one should announce each of these three times’— thus says Āśvalāyana (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.21.6).
In that regard, in whatever place his kinsmen pay him this honor,"
There, he sits upon the *kūrca* offered by them, just as the teacher [did] previously during the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
The meaning is that, having taken the *kūrca* offered and placed it with its tips pointing north, he sits upon it with the mantra, "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom" (*rāṣṭrabhṛd asi*). //2//

In whatever house of a householder who is engaged in his own duty, the members of that household perform for this *snātaka*—who has arrived for the sake of hospitality—the honor (*apaciti*) known as the *madhuparka*;
and because it occurs in a subordinate element (*anupādeya*), the plural number is not intended to be significant.
For this very reason, the singular number is used later on when he says, "he [should offer]... (*prāha*).
When a seat of grass (kūrca) has been offered by them there in that house, he sits upon it;

the meaning is that he should sit in the same manner as the teacher sat previously during the initiation ceremony, with the Yajus formula: "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom" (rāṣṭrabhṛdasi). //2//
2. The mantra for the seating of the King and the Stapati:
in the same way, with the following two [mantras], the King and the Stapati [are seated] according to their respective characteristics. (ĀpGs 13.3)

In this manner, the king and the sthapati sit upon the *kūrca* just as a *snātaka* Brāhmaṇa does; they sit according to their respective characteristics (*yathāliṅga*) on the teacher’s throne (*ācāryāsandī*).
Thus, being honored, the king and the sthapati sit down according to their respective characteristics with the two subsequent *yajus* formulas.
In that regard, a Kṣatriya who has been consecrated as the sovereign of a kingdom for the sake of kingship possesses the insignia of universal sovereignty (*sāmrājya*).
He alone is the lord of people (*janādhipati*).
One who has been consecrated for the office of a master builder is a *sthapati*.
Its characteristic mark is its predominance (*ādhipatya*).

Although it would have been established by the two subsequent [words] as "the king" and "the chieftain," the expression "according to the characteristic mark" (*yathāliṅga*) is stated for the purpose of making known that the application [of the mantra] occurs according to the characteristic mark of the first mantra, and likewise for the two subsequent ones.
Therefore, the first mantra belongs to the Brāhmaṇa alone,
because of the indicative mark "the teacher (ācārya) [is] Sandī," and because it has been stated that the Brāhmaṇa is remembered as the teacher.
Therefore, for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, there is only the silent sitting [of the bridegroom].
In that regard, honor is shown to the king with the formula: “To the teacher, to the officiating priest, to the father-in-law, to the king.
However, the lord [the king] receives honor as a father-in-law. //3//

Just as the Brāhmaṇa, having sat down with the mantra, is worthy of honor, so too the King and the Stapati should sit according to their respective marks: the King with the mantra "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom, the throne of the Sovereign," and the Stapati with "Thou art the sustainer of the kingdom, the throne of the Overlord. This is the meaning.
And the king must be a Kṣatriya alone;
one of another caste, even if he performs the protection of subjects, is not [the king]. Now, is it not the case that the application of the word "king" to a Kṣatriya is peculiar to the Āndhras?

But since the wives [of the sacrificer] perform tasks such as protecting the offspring, how can it be that the king is exclusively a Kṣatriya by setting aside the application of the word *ārya* which has greater force? It is not so;

for it was established in the *Aveṣṭyadhikaraṇa* that it is appropriate to regard the specific traditional rule (*smaraṇa*) "the word *rājan* [is used] except before *ase*" in the *gaṇapāṭha* of the venerable Pāṇini—the most excellent of Āryas—as being rooted in the usage of the Andhra region.
And the *sthapati*, though belonging to another caste, attained great sovereignty; others say the *sthapati* was a Vaiśya, while some maintain he was indeed a Kṣatriya consecrated for kingship. //3//
3. The offering of water for the feet: "The waters are for the feet," he says. (ĀpGS 13.4)
Then the giver of the honey-mixture, having brought forward water for the washing of the feet, says: "The waters are for the feet. //4//
Then the host, having taken up water for the purpose of washing the guest's feet, says, "The waters are for the feet.
This statement of confirmation is for the purpose of indicating that the guest should now perform whatever task follows immediately.
The same purpose applies to [the statements] such as "The waters are for hospitality" (*arhaṇīyā āpaḥ*) and so forth. //4//

4. After the feet have been washed, he should extend his feet; having consecrated them with the following [verse], he should offer the right foot to a Brāhmaṇa and the left foot to a Śūdra. (ĀpGS 13.5)

Then, while being honored, he consecrates those waters with the following verse, "O waters, you who wash the feet," and should first extend—the right foot—to a non-Brāhmaṇa who is washing them; the left foot [should be extended] to a Śūdra.
For a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, there is no fixed rule, because the masculine gender is not intended to be significant.
The same applies to women as well;
"the woman washes [him], the man sprinkles [him]"— this is another ritual option.
"The wife and the sacrificer run along the shanks"—this is a specific rule regarding the sacrifice.

Although it was already established by the context that "the waters are for the feet," the explicit mention of "feet" (pāda) is for the purpose of ensuring that the suffix *pratyaya* does not apply to the word "foot" (*pāda*) in subsequent passages;
consequently, the touching of the feet by the person who washes them does not take place. //5//
Then the worshipper, having consecrated those waters with the mantra, "O waters, you are for washing the feet," should first hand over his right foot to a Brāhmaṇa who is to wash it;
however, if it is a Śūdra, he should first hand over the left.
In this matter, only a Brāhmaṇa or a Śūdra may be the washer.
But not for a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, because they are not mentioned [in this context].
Others, however, maintain that one should give the first quarter [of the fee] to a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya without restriction. //5//
5. There is the touching of the one who has washed [the feet] and the self-touching.
Having touched the one who has washed [the feet], he should touch himself with the following Yajus formula. (ĀpGS 13.6)
Likewise, there is another ritual procedure: "He should touch the hands of the one who has washed with his own hand" (Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.2).
With the subsequent Yajus formula, "May greatness [be] in me," he performs the touching toward the west.
And that occurs in the region of the heart,
for that is the seat of the self.

Then, having washed his feet and touched the hand of the one who washed them, he should touch himself at the region of the heart with the Yajus formula, "In me is greatness," touching it with his hand in reverse order; then follows the sipping of water.
6. The offering of the water for the feet: Having taken up two bunches of grass, he says, "O waters fit for honoring, [come] in this earthen vessel. (ĀpGS 13.7)
Then the giver, having taken up the water brought in an earthen vessel with two bunches of *kūrca* grass, grasping it from below and above, says, "The waters worthy of honor," and thus offers them;
according to another ritual manual, they should be joined with flowers and unhusked rice grains. //7//

Then the host, having brought water for the guest-offering together with flowers and unbroken grains into an earthen vessel, and having grasped it from below and above with two bundles of grass (*kūrca*), says: "The waters worthy of honor. // 7 //
7. Having brought a portion of that [water] into the reverent cupped hands (añjali), he should consecrate it with the following [verse];
while the portion is being brought into the cupped hands, he should mutter the subsequent Yajus formula. (ĀpGs 13.8)
Having offered the water worthy of honor with the verse beginning "āma āgan," he consecrates it with the following verse.
Then, while being honored, the guest forms a hollowed palm (añjali); the giver then takes a portion of that water and pours it into his joined palms.
While that [milk] is being brought, he who is being honored should mutter the subsequent Yajus formula: "Thou art the milking of Virāj. //8//

Then the worshipper, having consecrated those waters with the verse "ā māgan," should mutter the Yajus formula "avirājo dohīsi" while a small portion of them is being poured by the giver into his own joined palms. //8//
He consecrates the remainder being poured forward with the following verse. (ĀpGS 13.9)
Then the giver leads the remainder of that water toward the eastern direction.
As it is being led, he, being honored, consecrates it with the following verse, "To the ocean you... (*samudraṃ va*).
At this time, he should give a pair of garments, a pair of earrings, a cow, a garland, and whatever else serves for the purpose of adornment—all of that.
Others say [it refers to] the end of the meal;
all of that should be understood as being indicated by the word *apaciti*. //9//

Then, as the remainder of those [portions] is being led forward by the giver, the one worthy of honor (pūjya) consecrates it with the verse, "The ocean for you" (*samudraṃ vaḥ*). Some say that at this time, or at the conclusion of the meal, ornaments such as a pair of garments and earrings should be given to the one worthy of honor;
otherwise, he would not truly be honored.
And this is indeed understood by us as well through the word *apaciti*. //9//
8. The offering of the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*).
Having mixed together curd and honey, having covered it with a large bronze vessel, and having grasped it with two bunches of *kūrca* grass, he announces, "The honey-mixture! (ĀpGS 13.10).

He offers the madhuparka with a large, wide-mouthed bronze vessel; there is also a connection [in the text] stating that he covers it with a wide-mouthed bronze vessel. By this, the requirement for both vessels to be made of bronze is established.
The word "iti" denotes a manner; for example, "curd and honey" or "milk and honey. //10//
Having mixed these two— curd and honey— in some vessel according to the rule of injunction, and having covered it with a larger, broad bronze vessel,
the rest is clear.
Others, however, hold that the mention of bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) as the lid is for the sake of illustration; by that, other [vessels] made of bell-metal are also intended. //10//
9. The ingredients for the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*):
some say it consists of *trivṛt* and ghee. (ĀpGS 13.11)
The combination of three substances is *trivṛt*:
the two previously mentioned, either curd and honey or milk and honey, with ghee as the third. //11//
The combination of three substances is expressed by the word *trivṛt*.
According to that view mentioned previously, curd, honey, and ghee are to be mixed together. //11//
Some say that parched grains and barley meal constitute the *pāṅkta* offering. ĀpGS 13.12.
The collection of five substances is called *pāṅkta*:
curd, honey, clarified butter, parched grain, and flour. //12//
Here too, the collection of five is "pāṅkta";
the rest is as before. //12//

10. The consumption of the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*): Having mixed it with the two subsequent *ṛc*-verses, he sips water with the two *yajus*-formulas; having consumed it three times with the subsequent [verse] before and after [the mixture], he should give it to one who is worthy of compassion. (ĀpGS 13.13)
Then, having consecrated that madhuparka with the two subsequent verses, "trayyai vidyāyai" and "āmāgan," he receives it while being honored.
Since the consecration and reception of the water for the feet (pādya) and other items is observed [in the ritual], there is likewise the consecration and reception of the madhuparka.
He does not accept it with a consecratory formula. Then he consumes it three times with the verse beginning "That which is in honey," once with the mantra and twice silently.

Then, before and after the consumption [of the Madhuparka], he sips water in due order with the two *yajus* formulas recited immediately following [the main ritual], namely, "Thou art the under-layer of immortality" (*amṛtopastaraṇam asi*) and "Thou art the covering of immortality" (*amṛtopidhānam asi*). The procedure there is as follows: having sipped the water for the under-layer with the formula "Thou art the under-layer of immortality," he consumes the Madhuparka with its mantra; then, having sipped water again, he consumes it twice more silently; finally, he sips the water for the covering with the formula "Thou art the covering of immortality. Afterward, there is a sip of water for the sake of purification.

The remainder—the remnant of the consumption of the *madhuparka*—he should give to one who is to be shown compassion, that is, to one who is to be favored, such as a son or a brother who has returned from his studies (*samāvṛtta*).
He too consumes it.

Regarding the consumption of Soma, the consumption of *madhuparka*, and eating, the learned (*śiṣṭas*) remember that there is no state of being "impure from food" (*ucchiṣṭatā*) in the midst of these acts. 13.
Then the one worthy of worship, having accepted the *madhuparka* and removed the covering vessel, consecrates it with the two verses, "From the threefold knowledge... and "...O glory, thou hast come.
With the Yajus formula, "Thou art the under-layer of immortality," he drinks water prior to the consumption [of the *madhuparka*].
Then, having sipped water, he eats [the honey] three times with the verse, "That which is the essence of honey," twice silently;
then [he drinks the water] with, "Thou art the covering of immortality."

Thus, with this Yajus formula, he may also drink water afterwards. Having sipped [water], he should give the remainder to one who is to be shown compassion, one who is to be favored— such as a son, a disciple, or one who has returned home from his studies— but not to a student (brahmacārin).
Because of the prohibition: "And one should not give him leavings that are contrary to the Vedic injunctions" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.4.5).
Now, one might object: "In this case, after the under-layering (upastaraṇa), an ācamana for the sake of purification should not be performed in the middle."
Because there is no statement [to that effect] from us,
it is not so even according to logic;
for, like eating, the action is a single unit ending with the closing [of the vessel].
Otherwise, even for a Bhoja, the rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) would result in being required after every morsel of food.

If it is argued that this must be performed due to the force of a custom (ācāra) that pervades all places, times, and agents, we say no; for it is difficult for people of later times to determine whether this practice possesses the characteristics previously described or not.

To this it is replied: This is not a valid objection, because since the rules for sipping water (*ācamana*) are observed in the *Gṛhyasūtras* of Bodhāyana and others immediately after the spreading of the seat (*upastaraṇa*), it is quite easy for us to determine that our own practice is universal, pervading all regions and so forth.

And this has been stated in the passage, "Now, the rites beginning with those of conduct" (*Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra* 1.1), where the word *gārhya* (pertaining to domestic rites) is used instead of the specific term *sva* (one's own).

The term "from conduct" (*ācārāt*) is to be explained as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the mention of domestic rites (*gārhya-karma*); thus, even the conduct of our own people regarding matters taught in other *Gṛhyasūtras* and similar texts is rooted in the Veda alone.
However, with regard to eating, there is no necessity of performing the sipping of water (*ācamana*) at every single mouthful.
In some cases, however, there is no sipping of water because of the absence of an explicit scriptural statement and the absence of such a practice.
Regarding the drinking of Soma, on the other hand, because of the scriptural statement, "They do not become impure by means of Soma," there is no sipping of water even at the conclusion.
Moreover, this sipping of water (ācamana),

like the tying of the top-knot (śikhābandhana) and other such acts, is a purifier of the performer; and the experts in logic maintain that even if not explicitly stated, that which is required for the completion of the rite must be supplied from another source.
Therefore, in this context, the sipping of water (ācamana) must indeed be performed immediately after the spreading of the base (upastaraṇa).

Some [teachers], such as Baudhāyana and others, argue that because the spreading and covering (upastaraṇa-apidhāna), as well as the offering of the waters intended for those purposes, are taught separately, and because the rule for sipping is prescribed after the spreading, it is understood that the spreading and so forth constitute separate rites due to their being external members; thus, for them, it is appropriate that the sipping occurs even before the consumption [of the food].

"But for us, since there is no such instruction, and because [the acts] from spreading the seat to covering [the food] are, by virtue of being internal, a single action like eating, it is not proper to perform the sipping of water (ācamana) in the middle for the sake of purification.
Do not say so; for even for us, there is a separate instruction for the two instances of sipping water through a different scriptural statement: "He sips water with two Yajus-formulas."
Precisely because of this separate instruction, the non-perception of water for those purposes is also implied.
Therefore, since there is no disparity between our [view] and theirs regarding the instruction, the ritual rinsing (ācamana) is indeed equal in its application and security. 13.
If the recipient of the madhuparka is a king or a chief architect (sthapati), he must give a gift to the officiating priest;
indeed, immediately upon receiving it, the king or the chief architect gives it to the priest. (ĀpGs 13.14)
By the use of the word "eva" (only), it is indicated that he should give [the remainder] to the domestic priest without having consumed it himself;
he [the priest], in turn, consumes it according to the prescribed rule. //14//
The king and the *sthapati*, having received the *madhuparka*, should hand it over to the domestic priest (*purohita*) immediately;
by the use of the word "immediately" (*eva*), it is indicated that no consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) is to be performed [by them].
However, the rites beginning with the consecration and ending with the consumption are to be performed by the domestic priest alone.
The ritual up to the consumption [of the remains] belongs to the domestic priest alone; furthermore, the subsequent rites belong to the king and others alone. //14//
12. Announcement regarding the cow: by saying "gauh," he refers to a cow. (ĀpGS 13.15)
Then, having sipped water and sat down, he presents a cow, saying, "A cow!
And it is a female cow,
as seen in the statement, "The cow is the giver of wealth."
Or rather, he may even become a male. For it is heard [in scripture]: "Just as here on earth, when a human king arrives, or another worthy guest, they slaughter a bull or a cow."

For this very purpose, the word "cow" (gām) is used here so that there may be the cognition of the mere genus of cow; otherwise, it would have been sufficient to say simply "having taken a cow" (gaur iti pragṛhya), as is the case with the water for the feet and other such items. (AiBrā 1.3.4) [15]
When the consumption has been performed, the giver says "gauḥ" regarding the cow;
and because of the feminine gender indication in the statement "gauḥ dhenur bhavyā," the word "go" refers to a female.
And this statement is for the purpose of ascertaining the intention of the venerable one: "Should this cow be slaughtered or should it be released?"
And he should communicate his own intention to the donor. //15//
Having cooked the omentum of that [cow], he performs an oblation with a *palāśa* leaf from it;

having consecrated it with the following [verse] and having cooked its omentum, he offers it—with clarified butter spread beneath and poured over it—using either the middle or the end leaf of a *palāśa*, while reciting the subsequent [verse]. (ĀpGS 13.16)

The word "should permit" (anujānīyāt) is to be supplied [to the text], because it is seen to be so in another ritual manual (kalpa). One who intends to cause [the mantra] "oṃ" to be uttered should say, "please permit."
When the cow has been designated, he should worship it while consecrating it with the verse following [the previous one], namely, "Thou art a cow, with sin destroyed.
If he desires its slaughter, he should obtain permission;
for although only a single half-verse is traditionally recited, nevertheless, because of the feminine gender designation, this is indeed a *ṛc* in the *gāyatrī* meter.
In that [formula], in place of the word "amuṣya," the name of the giver should be specified, as in "and of me, Yajñaśarman. //16//

Then, when the giver has been permitted by him [the recipient] due to their lack of connection, he performs the immolation of that cow according to worldly custom; having extracted the omentum (*vapā*) and grasped it with the two *vapāśrapaṇī* spoons, he cooks it either on the *aupāsana* fire or on a cooking fire.

Having spread an underlayer of clarified butter and poured a final sprinkling over it, he offers it into that same fire with the middle or the last leaf of a *palāśa* branch, using the subsequent verse, "May Agni eat it.
The phrase "having spread an underlayer and poured a final sprinkling" means that he performs the acts of spreading the underlayer (*upastaraṇa*) and pouring the final sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*).
Having offered it, they then prepare the meat together with the cooked food and present it to him.
Because of the statement, "hospitality is unaltered," this rule applies even when the preliminary spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the final sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) are not otherwise applicable.

Although the offering could have been established by the mere mention of "with a *palāśa* leaf," the specific mention of "with the middle one" or "with the last one" is so that an oblation might not be made with a leaf from a two-leaved *palāśa* stalk.
Alternatively, the meaning of the conceptualization of non-existence is [taught] by the first [verse], its absence by the middle, and [its further absence] by the last. //17//
If the Pratīhītṛ desires the animal to be slaughtered, then he consecrates the cow with this verse ending without a pause: "The cow is free from blemish and has its evil struck away.
In place of the word "amuṣya," he takes the name of the person to be honored, such as "Viṣṇuśarman."
Then he should sit comfortably.
The ritual for the donor alone extends up to the offering of the omentum (vapāhoma).
Furthermore, the suffix -ktavatu in the word "abhimantrya" (having consecrated) serves solely to indicate the performance of the action itself.
But it does not have the sense of having a common agent. Therefore, having performed the ritual slaughter of this [animal] and having extracted the omentum,
Having cooked it,

and having spread a base of ordinary clarified butter with a middle-sized or small leaf of the *palāśa* tree, he takes a single portion of the entire omentum, sprinkles it with ghee, and offers it into the fire with his own hand using that very leaf, while reciting the mantra: "May Agni consume [this]."

And in that regard, the statement "with either the middle or the last [portion]" is for the purpose of prohibiting two portions, or for the purpose of excluding the option of non-existence. One should feed the guest rice together with the remaining consecrated portions of the offering. Furthermore, this method of slaughter (*saṃjñapana*) must be abandoned now, as it is recorded among the practices of the Kali age. //16//
14. The procedure to be performed on the occasion of the release of the cows:
if he should release them, he should mutter the next [verse] in a low voice and say aloud, "Om, he releases. (ĀpGs 13.17)
Now, if he releases a cow, when it is said, "This cow is being honored," he mutters the four subsequent mantras, beginning with "May she prosper in non-sacrifice," in a low voice (*upāṃśu*).
Having muttered them, he gives the command aloud, "Om, release her!
And the giver, having released her, prepares other meat.
However, according to another ritual manual (*kalpāntara*), "the *madhuparka* consists of no meat" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.24.28).

In that case, regarding the seizing of the bull, the [verses] addressed to the Earth, Dhenu, Ambikā, and the Rudras are omitted because of a contradiction in gender; others, however, say this is not so.

Since the mantra is accomplished by mere recitation (*japa*), the mention of "whispering" (*upāṃśu*) is for the purpose of restriction: only the four subsequent mantras are to be recited in a whisper,
not the *praṇava*.
A contingency arises from observing other treatises:
"as loud as the *praṇava*" or "above the *praṇava*."
Therefore, this alternative view of Bādarāyaṇa alone becomes established.
Even though there is no explicit mention of "impulsion" (prasava) here, impulsion must be understood precisely because of the statement "by means of the utterances" (vāgbhiḥ). //18//
If the one to be honored should desire that the cow being released be let loose,
this *liṅ* suffix is used for the purpose of expressing a wish (*kāmapravedana*).

In that case, having muttered the three subsequent mantras beginning with "May the sacrifice increase" (*yajño vardhatām*) in a low voice (*upāṃśu*), he should then loudly proclaim, "Om, release her!"— this is the remainder of the instruction.
Some say that the four mantras beginning with "yajña" refer to this cow; and even in the view where she is released, she belongs to the enjoyer alone. // 17 //
15. The offering of food: Having consecrated the food with the whispered [mantras] followed by the subsequent ones, he says aloud, "Oṃ, it is prepared. (ĀpGs 13.18)
Then, having brought food containing meat, he says to him, "It is ready" (*bhūtam*).
According to another ritual manual (*kalpa*), when the food is prepared, he says, "It is ready" (*bhūtam*). (Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.2.55).
And [it is offered] during our Vaiśvadeva rite;
therefore, the announcement is simply "bhūta" (beings).
Having consecrated that food silently with the five subsequent mantras beginning with "bhūta," he gives the command loudly: "Oṃ kalpayata! (Arrange it!)

The attendants who have been dispatched should serve the meal; he should say, "Feed four Brahmins of various lineages," and when they have eaten, he should have food brought to him—this is another ritual procedure. (Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.2.19)
Then the giver, having honored the prepared food with the mantra "bhūtam," should announce it—that is, present it—to the recipient.
Why is this so? Because it is seen [prescribed] in the Vaiśvadeva rite: "Standing over the prepared food, one should announce 'bhūtam' to the owner" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.3.10).
In the very section on the *madhuparka*, it is stated: "Standing by the cooked food, he says, 'It is well-prepared (*bhūta*)'; and also from another ritual manual (*kalpa*).
Thus, the eater, having consecrated the food thus offered with the five subsequent mantras beginning with "It is well-prepared (*subhūtam*") while whispering (*upāṃśu*), [should eat].
"Oṃ kalpayata," [he says] loudly;
here too, "I would authorize" is the ellipsis.
Then follows the meal.
Because the offering of food has a visible purpose, and because it is so established by custom. //18//

16. The honey-mixture (madhuparka) is to be offered to the teacher, the officiating priest, the father-in-law, and the king; this should be done for those who have come to visit after the lapse of a year. ĀpGs 13.19.
The *ācāryas* and the others are well known.

For these four, after they have been sent away and have remained for a full year, and have come to the house by way of the *ātiśyena* [route], this act of honoring—beginning with the *kūrca* [seat] and ending with the meal—must be performed.
By whom? By the householder.
For when a household has been established, the regular duties are heard of, according to the scriptural statement: "The fire-sacrifice and guests [are required].
Regarding this, some say:
This [gift] is to be made for the teacher, the officiating priest, the father-in-law, and the king;
this constitutes one rule.
Furthermore, it is also to be made for those who wait upon him after a year has passed.
Therefore, after the wedding, an honoring should be performed by inviting the teacher and the father-in-law;
likewise, for the officiating priest after the ritual, and for the king after his consecration.
Then, when one year has passed from those very [days] that have arrived, it is what must be performed by the Brahmin. //20//

Regarding this rite of honoring— beginning with the *kūrca* grass mat and ending with the meal— which is prescribed to be performed by a householder for a *snātaka* who has arrived on the very day of his bath: that must be performed repeatedly for teachers and others who visit his home after the lapse of a year or more,
and not just once as in the case of a *snātaka*.
Nor [should one do so] within a year.
Here, the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "api" (also).
Now, it may be objected that according to the *Dharmaśāstra*: "One who has studied the Veda [is worthy of honor], as is one who offers a cow and the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*)."

An *ācārya*, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a graduate (*snātaka*), or a king who is not unrighteous—[to these] a cow and the *madhuparka* [are to be offered]. The *madhuparka* is curd mixed with honey, or milk mixed with honey; it is so called because it is offered to an *ācārya*, an officiating priest, a father-in-law, or a king who has come as a guest within the course of a year.
Regarding the rule "water is [the substitute] for what is absent" (*āpa.dha.* 2.8.5–9),

the *madhuparka* is prescribed along with a cow intended as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the *snātaka*, the teacher (*ācārya*), the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), the sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), the father-in-law (*śvaśura*), and the king.
For what purpose is it prescribed here once again?

It is stated: here, the mention of the *trivṛt* and *pāṅkta* [mixtures] prescribed by rule is for the purpose of obtaining them when they are being given to a non-Vedic scholar and to a father-in-law during that *gomadhuparka* ceremony.

As for the repeated statement in that very same context, "the cow and the *madhuparka," it means that these should be performed again and again for the teacher, the officiating priest, the Vedic scholar, the father-in-law, and the king, even if they have approached repeatedly within a year.
But for the sake of the *snātaka*, the Vedic student, and the guest, it is only once; such is the meaning. //19//
To Citra, who speaks but once, [be there obeisance].

One should not perform the *prativatsaram* (annual rite) repeatedly in the Kali age because of the prohibition against the slaughter of cows; having said "May the sacrifice increase," and so forth, one should mutter [the mantra]. This refers to the omission of the intermediate mantras.

To the teacher (*pravaktṛ*) of the Veda and the meaning of the Veda—who is wonderful, renowned, and whose doubts have been dispelled—to such a person who has appeared before one, this act of honoring (*apacitikarma*) should be performed once.

"Not every year" (na pratisaṃvatsaram) //21// The "expounder" (pravaktā) is one who speaks pre-eminently by means of grammar, logic, and epistemology; that is to say, one who is a correct utterer of words and an interpreter based on valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).

The meaning is that "vivid illumination" (citraḥ prakāśaḥ) is well-known in the world; this is a qualification of the speaker alone. To him, this [teaching] should be imparted all at once, free from hesitation. Furthermore, this speaker is not merely one who has studied the Vedas.
For he is indeed the master of the cows;
he who studies the Veda with its six auxiliary limbs and understands their meaning is a "Vedādhyāya" (one who has mastered the Veda).
Now, it may be objected: "In the *sāmayācārika* [section], the rules for the cow-offering (*gomadhaparka*) have not been taught;
how, then, should it be performed?
It is said in reply: "The Mīmāṃsakas hold that a name serves as the indicator of its specific ritual rules."

Therefore, the very same rules taught for the domestic rite known as *madhuparka*— as established by the tradition of the ritualists (*yājñika*)— are extended by the name "madhuparka" to this [present] rite in the passage "the madhuparka with cows," just as in the case of "he performs the *agnihotra* for a month.
[The *madhuparka* consists of] curd-mash and honey-mash.

In this context (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 6.32.5), however, there is no extension [of the rule] because the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) lacks the requirement for a specific substance as does the ritual act itself.
And here, regarding the study of the Veda and the honoring of guests, this is the distinction:

"Because of the direct injunction that 'the madhuparka consists of curds mixed with honey,' the threefold nature (*trivṛttva*) and the fivefold nature (*pāṅktatva*) obtained through extended application (*atideśa*) are set aside" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.8.8).

This is the established meaning here: for a teacher, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), one who has studied the Vedas, a father-in-law, and a king, the domestic *madhuparka*—whether according to the rules of the Gṛhya-sūtras or customary practice (*sāmayācārika*)—must be performed using more than one cow as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Furthermore, it must be performed repeatedly for those who arrive after a year has passed.
For a father-in-law who is not a Vedic scholar, the rule prescribed by the *Gṛhya-sūtras* applies, provided he brings an extra cow;
for Vedic scholars who are guests or honored persons, it is declared by Dharma that they should be given a cow along with [other gifts].

However, for two non-Vedic scholars who are honored persons, or for a *snātaka*, the rule prescribed by the *Gṛhya-sūtras* or declared by Dharma applies even if no cow is given, provided he has arrived on the very day of his ceremonial bath (*snāna*).
And for the sake of illumination, one who speaks without a cow is blameworthy;
however, for others besides the four beginning with the teacher (ācārya), it is only once. Some here say that there is a formal split in the rule (yogavibhāga).
Regarding the phrase "to the teacher and the others": this rite is to be performed for these four; this constitutes one grammatical rule (*yoga*).
Consequently, immediately after the wedding, an offering must be made even if the teacher and the father-in-law have been invited.
Otherwise, even for those who have been away for a year, it would not be accomplished even once.
Furthermore, honor must be rendered to the officiating priest at every ritual act,
and to the consecrated king as a matter of absolute necessity.

Likewise, there is another rule: "to those who attend repeatedly before a year has passed. This distinction is clear in the *Sāmayācārikas*, where, having first prescribed the [offering of] cow and *madhuparka* for each day, it continues: "for those who come repeatedly, however, one should offer a single cow and *madhuparka* at the end of the year. Thus, the distinction between the two cases is established. Furthermore, this is the meaning of the word "repeatedly" (*punaḥ-punaḥ*). For example, when it is said, "he studies repeatedly," it means he studies again and again; it does not mean that he studies the same thing over and over. The fourteenth section:
The sacraments beginning with marriage have been explained according to the sequence of the transmission of the mantras.
Immediately following, the sacraments beginning with the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) are now explained in that same sequence.
10. Sīmantonnayana (Parting the Hair).
1. The Time for Sīmantonnayana:
The Sīmantonnayana rite is performed during the first pregnancy in the fourth month. (ĀpGs 14.1)

The *sīmanta* is a specific mark in the middle of the hair; that rite in which it is raised is called the *sīmantonnayana*, a ritual for the consecration of the fetus. That should be performed in the fourth month [of pregnancy].
This is the consecration of the receptacle (ādhāra) resulting from the first rule;
and when the receptacle has been consecrated, all the embryos deposited therein become consecrated as well. //1//
"Sāmantonnayana" is the name of this ritual;
the remainder of the sentence is "we shall explain that rite in which the *sīmanta* (parting of the hair) of a pregnant woman is raised.
And that [is performed] in the first pregnancy.
But it is not for every single embryo;
rather, the rite of parting the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) is a consecration (*saṃskāra*) intended for the womb itself.
Because it is a consecration of the woman, once performed, it consecrates all embryos [conceived thereafter].
"Every fourth month": the elision of the vowel [in *caturthe*] is Vedic, according to the traditional rule that "the Sūtras are like the Vedas. //1//
2. Therein, the principal oblations, the *jaya* oblations, and so forth [are performed].

Having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce blessings, and having performed the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he offers the subsequent oblations while she maintains contact with him; then he proceeds with the *jaya* oblations and the rest. (ĀpGS 14.2)
On that occasion, on the preceding day, the *nāndī-śrāddha* is performed.

Then, on that very day, having fed the Brahmins and having had them pronounce blessings after they have eaten, he proceeds with the rites beginning from the kindling of the fire. He prepares the vessels once; the porcupine quills and other items are used together with the *śamyā*-sticks.

There are eight principal oblations: four with the mantra "May Dhātṛ grant us wealth" (*dhātā dadātu no rayim*) and four with the mantra "He who [knows] you with a longing heart" (*yas tvā hṛdā kīriṇā*). //3//

In this rite, the injunction regarding the feeding of Brahmins and the pronouncement of blessings is for the sake of establishing the sequence, just as in the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). However, at the time of placing the vessels, items such as the porcupine quill (*śalalī*) and so forth should be placed only once according to their purpose; likewise, the *śamyā* pegs are used in the sense of enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
The subsequent [verses] are eight: the four beginning with "May Dhātṛ grant us wealth," and the four beginning with "He who [loves] you with a humble heart.
The rest is easy to understand. //2//
The parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) is performed with a three-spotted porcupine quill.

Having completed the rites up to the sprinkling of water around the fire, he seats the wife to the west of the fire facing east. With a three-spotted porcupine quill, three tufts of *darbha* grass, and a bunch of *śalālu* fruit, he parts her hair upwards with the *vyāhṛtis* and the two following verses.
(ĀpGS 14.3)
Facing east, she [the cow] faces eastward while he himself faces westward.
In three places she is variegated—*enī*, *śvetī*, and *treṇī*;
the elision of the vowel *i* is a Vedic archaism.
And it is called *ṇatva*. The hair-needle of the porcupine (*śalalīśalyaka*) is called the "stalk with branches" (*saviśākhā nāḍīpuñjīla*).
There are three bunches of *darbha* grass.
A fresh cluster of *udumbara* fruits is called a *śalāṭu-glapsa*;
others say it is a *piśāca-udumbara*.
Having taken these substances together, he performs the parting of the hair with them, drawing it upward, using the [three] formulas "bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ," the two subsequent ones,
and the two [verses] beginning with "rākām aham" and "yās te rāke."
At the end of the three [oblations], there is a single pouring out.
In this collection of mantras, the recitation of the *vyāhṛtis* need not be performed;
the understanding is already established by the word "with the *vyāhṛtis*" alone.
Just as in cases such as "having recited the vyāhṛtis" and "the distributed vyāhṛtis," so too,
since the vyāhṛtis are already established, their recitation here is for the purpose of the traditional collection (samāmnāya).

Furthermore, if the recitation were not present, and it were merely stated "with the *vyāhṛtis* and with the two subsequent [mantras]," then it would follow that they are to be taken from the *yajamāna-samāmnāya*— namely, the two mantras beginning with "ucchuṣmo agne"—
because that recension is well-known.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the two mantras, "I invoke Rākā" and "O Rākā, those which are yours," are also principal oblations, as there is no distinction [between them and the others].
Therefore, the Vyāhṛtis are recited here so that they may be included from this very collection (samāmnāya). //4//
The bride faces the east, being oriented toward the east;
he himself, however, faces west.
She is called *treṇī* because she possesses these three white [substances].
Alternatively, *treṇī* means white (*enī*) in three places;
the form *treṇī* is Vedic.
*Śalyaloman* refers to hair shaped like a thorn-needle (*śallīsūcī*).
*Treṇī* is a qualifier for *śalalī*.
A *darbha-puñjīla* is a stalk of *darbha* grass with its branches.
*Śalālu* refers to the *goṣṭhodumbara* tree.
*Karapatrodumbara* and *piśācodumbara* are synonymous.
*Glapsa* means a cluster or bunch.
"Piśācodumbara" means a particular cluster of young fruits of the *udumbara* tree.
With these substances taken together, she raises [the hair] upward from the parting (*sīmanta*) on the head, drawing a line across the middle of the head.
By which mantras?
[He should worship] with these mantras: "bhūrbhuvaḥsuvaḥ," "ārākāmaṃ suhavām," and "yāste rāke sumatayaḥ.
The word "ca" (and) is intended to indicate that there are many other mantras [to be used]. //3//
ĀpGs 14.4: Regarding the two lute-players, for the purpose of the lute-song, he instructs them:
"Sing!"—thus he instructs the two lute-players.
He who sings a verse with a lute is a "lute-singer" (*savīṇagāthī*). Both of them have already been brought forward; he instructs and directs them, saying, "Sing!"
The two sing;
in that case, there is a restriction regarding the Ṛg-verses. //5//
"Sing the verse with the lute," thus [he says]; they are called *vīṇāgāthin* (lute-singers). "Sing!"—thus he instructs and gives the command. //4//
Of the two northern [altars], the eastern one belongs to the Sālvas, and the other to the Brāhmaṇas.

Of the two subsequent verses, the one beginning with "yā pūrvā'yogandharī" is the *gāthā* for the *sīmantakarma* (parting-of-the-hair ceremony) of the Sālvas; the meaning is that this verse is to be sung by those residing in the Sālva country.
That region is situated on the bank of the Yamunā.
And there, Vaiśyas are the most numerous;
their king is Yaugandhari.
The other [verse], "Soma alone is our king," refers not to all Brāhmaṇas, but specifically to the Sālvas. //7//
The two lute-players should sing the two subsequent verses.
To the question, "Of which [verses], and which verse? he says: "The former," etc.
"Yaugandhari was in the east"—
this is a verse belonging to the three social classes (varṇas) of the Sālva country,
as indicated by the general designation "Sālavī."

For Brāhmaṇas residing in other regions, the chanting should be performed on the verse: "Soma alone is our king. However, for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, the chanting must be performed on the verse seen in the Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra (1.12.7), which is applicable to all castes: "May Soma alone be our king; may he protect our human progeny."
But it is not the absence of singing, because there is an injunction for the command "sing both" without distinction; some say that this applies even to the Brāhmaṇas of the Sālvas. //5//
5. The naming of the river situated nearby;
and the designation of the river in which they dwell. (ĀpGS 14.6)
In the second mantra, in place of the word *asau* (that one), the name of the river should be indicated in the vocative case;
the meaning is "in which [river] they dwell and upon which they depend.
For example: *tīreṇa kāveri tava*.
For all Kṣatriyas, however, the singing occurs upon a verse seen in another Kalpa that pertains to all social classes (*sārvavarṇikī*):
“Soma alone is our king,” so say the human subjects,
“seated with their wheels turned back.”
Here too, the mention of the river is in the vocative case. //8//
In the mantra "Soma eva no rājā," instead of the word "asau" (that one), there occurs a reference to a river by means of its vocative case, such as "Kāveri" or "Vegavati.
If it is asked, "Of which river?"— this is a locative of proximity (*samīpa-saptamī*), meaning "in which [river] they dwell."
The meaning is that it is the instruction of her in whose vicinity they dwell. //6//
6. The tying of barley sprouts, and then the restraint of speech: having tied together barley that has begun to sprout, he restrains his speech until the appearance of the stars. (ĀpGS 14.7)
She ties sprouts that have grown and budded, fastened with threads, upon the head of the bride;
she alone restrains her speech.
Such is the instruction, and they do not desire food for her on this day.
And barley should be sown even earlier, so that it has sprouted by this time. //9//
Having tied barley grains that have sprouted and are strung on a thread, he binds them upon the head of the bride.
Why "on the head"? Because of established custom (ācāra). //7//
7. After the rising of the stars, the touching of the calf and the release of speech [are performed].
When the stars have risen, having gone out toward the east or the north, having touched the calf and having murmured the *vyāhṛtis*, he should release his speech. (ĀpGs 14.8)
The calf is both male and female;
the *vyāhṛtis* in their entirety are to be understood from the *Yājamāna-samāmnāya*. //10//
This is for the sake of clarity.
Here, some students read "yacchataḥ" and "avisṛjataḥ" in the dual number.
According to that view, both the husband and wife perform the five ritual acts, beginning with the restraint of speech.
Some [hold that] everything from the tying of the barley-grain and so forth belongs to the bride alone, and not to the husband. //8//
11. Puṃsuvana (the rite for ensuring the birth of a male child) — 1. Its time: The puṃsuvana is performed when the embryo has become manifest, under the asterism Tiṣya. (ĀpGs 14.9)
That rite by which a male child is produced is called *puṃsuvana*;
the substitution of *uvaṅ* is Vedic, as seen in the mantra: "Thou art the producer of males" (*puṃsuvanamasīti*).
Āśvalāyana, however, prescribed it as a mere subsidiary rite (*guṇa*):
"It should be performed when the fetus has become manifest;
and the manifestation of the fetus occurs in the third or fourth month."
Even when [the *puṃsavana*] is performed in the fourth month, it must take place before the *sīmanta* ceremony,
because the [former] is the antecedent rite.
As for the purpose of its instruction later [in the sequence], we shall explain that.
That which is to be done under the asterism Tiṣya is called *taiṣyam*.
Here, the third case ending is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) according to the rule "when [the suffix] *lup* is elided after [a word denoting] an asterism" (*nakṣatre ca lupi*). //11//
*Puṃsavana* is also the name of a ritual; that rite by which, as its cause, a pregnant woman gives birth to a male child is *puṃsavana*.
The word "is explained" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
And here, the substitution of *ovaṅ* is Vedic;
Āśvalāyana, however, employed the form with its [proper] quality as "puṃsavanam.
When the fetus has become manifest—that is, when it is certain that a fetus exists—[the rite is performed].

And the *vyakti* (manifestation) occurs in the third or fourth month, because both alternatives are seen in the *Bahvṛca* and other *Smṛti* texts. If the *puṃsavana* is to take place in the fourth month, then the *sīmantonnayana* must be performed first.
Why is this so? Because even if the *puṃsavana* is performed later, there is no transgression of the prescribed time for it.
Furthermore, because the sequence [of the ritual] is intended to follow the order of the mantra-transmission (*mantrāmnāya*) and the instructional sūtra (*sūtropadeśa*).
Some maintain that, as in the third month, it should also be performed in the fourth month, on the grounds that the "sign" (*nimitta*) occurs prior to the *sīmanta* ceremony.
This [rite], like the *sīmanta*, is to be performed only during the first pregnancy.
But it does not apply to every single embryo;
it would be like the logic of grinding what has already been ground.
This point will be examined in the context of [the statement] "it produces a male."

The phrase "by Tiṣya" means that the *puṃsavana* rite is to be performed under the asterism Tiṣya; this connects with the distant [verb] according to the maxim: "In the absence of a specific context, the primary [action takes its place]. However, regarding the gathering of the *śuṅgā* shoots, there is no fixed rule.
2. Fetching the most excellent sprouts from the fruit of a *nyagrodha* tree;
the principal oblations like those at the *sīmanta* ceremony, as well as the *jaya* and other offerings.

Having fetched a shoot together with its testicles from a branch of the *nyagrodha* tree facing either east or north, one performs the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire as at the *sīmanta* ceremony. (ĀpGs 14.10)

From a *nyagrodha* tree, one should take a shoot (*śuṅgā*)—that is, a terminal sprout—from a branch facing either east or north, along with a "testicle" (*vṛṣaṇa*). It is designated as a "testicle" solely on account of its resemblance [to one]. Having brought that shoot provided with a testicle, one proceeds with the ritual beginning from the kindling of the fire up to the final sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), just as in the *sīmanta* ceremony.
Because of the specific mention of "kindling the fire" and so forth, the feeding of Brahmins and the pronouncement of blessings do not take place prior to that point.
But previously it was stated: "One should feed those who are pure and conversant with the mantras at all rites.

Likewise, that which follows the sprinkling of water and the subsequent instructions does not apply here either, because of the specific instruction given here: "To the west of the fire, facing east... and so forth.
The procedure for that is as follows: on the previous day, the *nāndī-śrāddha* is performed;
on the following day, from the kindling of the fire onwards, there is a single application of the vessels.
The enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) are accompanied by the *śuṅgā* branch alone, and not by the *śamyā* pegs.

At the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, while she maintains physical contact [with him], he performs four verses beginning with "May Dhātṛ grant us wealth," and four verses beginning with "He who [loves] you with a humble heart. He then proceeds with the *jayā* and subsequent rites.
At the end of the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), the ritual action to be described hereafter follows. 12.
It is joined with two fruits that have testicles and the form of testicles;
"śuṅgā" means a terminal sprout.
The rest is clear.

And here, because of the extension [of the rule] from the *sīmanta* rite stating "from the kindling of the fire onwards," the feeding of Brahmins and the pronouncing of blessings are performed once at the beginning of the procedure (*tantra*) and do not recur;
however, they do indeed take place at the conclusion of the rite.
One should feed pure men who are conversant with the mantras at all ritual acts.

This is because of the general statement [in Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.15.11], and also because of the statement: "And in the world, for rites intended for prosperity, there should be sentences beginning with these very ones, such as having [the officiant] recite, 'May it be an auspicious day! Hail! Prosperity! (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 1.13.9).
And regarding the placement of the vessels, items such as the *śuṅga* that are employed for the ritual act are set down only once;
likewise, in this case, it is the enclosing-sticks (*paridhi*) themselves and not the *śamyā* pegs, because the term "clipping and tonsure" (*caulagodāna*) is used here [to exclude the latter].

In the same way, since it is intended to extend the ritual procedure up to the final sprinkling (pariṣecana)—beginning with "the kindling of the fire for the Simantonnayana"—here too, those same eight principal oblations (pradhānahomas) are to be performed. //10//
Now, at the conclusion of the remainder of the Tantra, he states what is to be performed:
Having ground those sprouts with a maiden who has not yet reached puberty, one pours them into the right nostril of a pregnant woman lying on her back.

Having ground [the mixture] with a stone mortar by means of a stone pestle, having sprinkled it, and having caused her to lie on her back facing eastward before the fire, one inserts [the mixture] into the right nostril with the thumb while reciting the Yajus formula following [the pouring].
He causes it to be pounded. (ĀpGṛSū 14.11)
She in whom the menses have appeared is "one who has bathed";
the opposite of that is "one who has not bathed.
A maiden of such a nature is the agent of the grinding.
The prompter is the husband; the son of the grinding-stone is the son of the upper millstone;
even when referring to the purpose of the stone, it is still the "son of the grinding-stone."

There, having crushed a *śuṅgā* shoot and strained it through a cloth, he places another fire to the west; then, having laid her down facing east with her face upward and looking toward the east, he pours that juice into her right nostril with his thumb while facing eastward, using the *yajus* formula: "Thou art the one who brings forth a male. He causes the juice to enter by means of this formula.
He remains facing eastward throughout.
(Covering his own eyes and facing the east. //13//

Since the menses that would necessitate a bath have not yet arisen, she who has not bathed— that maiden, being "unbathed"— should have a stone placed upon the head of a stone-less son (a son born of a woman who has not menstruated), grind it with another stone-less son, and soak the resulting powder in water with a cloth. Then,
[the officiant] should place his wife to the west of the fire, facing east, with her head to the east, lying on her back with her face upward.

Having laid her down, he causes that juice to enter the right nostril by means of his thumb as the instrument, reciting the Yajus mantra: "Thou art the male-impregnator. He thus causes it to reach the embryo;
the meaning is that she should not spit out the juice. //11//
4. Declaration of its fruit:
[The child] gives birth to a male. (ĀpGs 14.12)
Thus, conditioned by this karma, a woman gives birth to a male;
some consider this to be a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda),
because if it were a prescriptive injunction regarding the fruit, it would entail the contingency that the action is not constant due to its connection with desire.
If this were a mere explanatory statement (arthavāda), there would be the undesirable consequence of its repetition in every conception.
Therefore, the phrase "in the first conception" continues to apply;
and for this very reason, its instruction is placed later.
This is clearly stated by the Chandogas: "In the first pregnancy, in the third month, the *puṃsavana* [rite] is performed.
Others consider this to be an injunction regarding the fruit [of the rite].

And in that regard, because of the statement, “He indeed is free from debt who has a son” (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.3.10), the procreation of a son is obligatory; thus, as long as one son has not been produced, it remains incumbent even regarding subsequent pregnancies.
However, once a son exists, [the duty] persists only if there is a desire for further sons; it does not persist if there is a desire for a daughter.
And the mention of "first" does not carry over [from the previous rule], because of the subsequent mention of "pregnancy.
However, the instruction regarding *puṃsavana* is given later so that its performance may take place afterwards, specifically in the fourth month. //14//
The statement that "a woman whose womb has been consecrated by this rite gives birth to a male child" is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), because the *puṃsuvana* rite is obligatory.
Alternatively, it may be a statement of the result (*phala*), since it was taught by the author of the Sūtras; as for example: [text fragment].
"By that, one obtains a thousand wish-fulfilling cows.

Even regarding the fruit [of the sacrifice], because of statements such as "He alone is free from debt who has a son," the procreation of a son is an obligatory duty even if performed only once; therefore, the *puṃsavana* rite, as a subsidiary part of that, must certainly be performed in the first pregnancy.
However, beyond that, it should be performed only in those pregnancies where there is a desire for a son, and not otherwise.
However, for one who has transgressed the injunction and desires, "I shall procreate only females," it does not happen even once.
Others, however, maintain that this statement—"he procreates a male"—is intended to mean that the performance of the rite must be carried out for every single conception. (12)
5. The rite for easy delivery; [it is] an easy delivery. ĀpGs 14.13.
That action by which one gives birth quickly is called the action known as "quick delivery" (kṣiprasuvana). //15//
That by which a pregnant woman gives birth quickly and swiftly, without being afflicted for a long time, is taught as the ritual known as *kṣiprasuvana* (the rite for swift delivery). //13//

Having fetched water downstream with an unbaked earthen bowl, having placed the *tūryantī* plant upon her feet while she is drying her head, and having touched her with the subsequent *yajus*, he should sprinkle her with these waters using the following verses.

[One should offer] with [a ladle] not made of *anāprīta* wood, without touching water, following the flow of the water as it pours out, and not against the current. That plant whose leaves resemble white [objects] and whose flowers resemble yellow, which blooms at midday, and which grows in the forests, is called *tīryantī*.
