And that plant whose leaves resemble bamboo leaves and whose flowers resemble red [objects], which they call *agniśikhā*, [is also used].

As she is about to dry it, she takes those two medicinal plants together with their roots and leaves and places them very closely; "on the head" means on the crown of the head. Others, having ground them, smear [the mixture] over it.

Then, with the following Yajus formula, "I touch you with ten," he touches [the child] with both hands—this being indicated by the word "ten. He should sprinkle him with these very waters brought [to the place], beginning from the face in the natural direction (anuloma).
With the three subsequent Ṛks, "Just as Soma purifies," he should perform the sprinkling for each mantra respectively. //16//

"By one who is unsatisfied" means by one not moistened with water, that is, by one who has not touched water; "by such a vessel" refers to a shallow bowl (*śarāva*). "Downstream" means in accordance with the flow of the current, not against it; having fetched water taken in this manner.
Having placed beneath her feet the medicinal herb called *adhaḥpuṣpī* while she is bearing it,

he should touch with both hands the woman who is withering away due to the pain of childbirth, using the two Yajus formulas beginning with "With these ten fingers I touch you," and then touch her head with the formula beginning with "Upon the head."
With these waters thus fetched, he should sprinkle that [altar] once with the three subsequent verses beginning with "Just as Soma purifies itself";
some, however, do so for each mantra.
"Because its utility is directly perceived.
In that regard, the concluding word of the first verse is "pratitiṣṭhatu," and that of the second is "tā kṛtam."
For the third [rite], [the verse] beginning with "O Sarasvatīs.
Others, however, say: "And [the herb] called śoṣyantī;
having placed that upon her head, he should touch the woman wherever [he chooses]."
That is not so; for the medicinal herb known as *śoṣyantī* is not well-known. Some say there is a medicinal herb named *śoṣyantī* which grows in forests and whose leaves resemble those of the bamboo.
And as for the statement that "the flowers are like red [flames],
and what they call the crest of fire," that is not so; because the relationship between the signified and the signifier is not apprehended through the neuter gender.
As the venerable author of the *Durvārttika* states: "The relationship between the signified and the signifier is not taught by the Teachers;
rather, it is understood through linguistic usage via the principle of *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-unaccountability)."
(Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 1.3.9).
In this case, however, the disagreement arises precisely because there is no common usage;

that [disagreement] is resolved by the fact that in the lexicons composed by those even more authoritative than the author of the Bhāṣya, the word *śoṣyantī* is listed as a synonym for *agniśikhā* (flame of fire).
And it is not seen in that way;
therefore, the previously stated explanation alone is preferable. //14//
Now he states another medicinal rite: 6.
The rite for the purpose of causing the afterbirth to fall.
If the afterbirth does not fall, one should sprinkle it with water prepared in the aforementioned manner, using the two subsequent [mantras]. (ĀpGs 14.15)
The *jarāyu* is the membrane that envelops the fetus; if it does not fall away,
then the following procedure must be performed.
What, then, is this?

It is the procedure prescribed for a swift delivery, beginning with "with an unbaked earthenware bowl" and so forth. With water prepared in this manner, one should sprinkle [the woman] while reciting each of the two subsequent mantras: "O threefold goddess, fall away;
let the speckled Śevala depart."
And these two rites concern one's own wife—whether she is afflicted by consumption or another woman—because effort is required for other rites;
however, others maintain that they apply without distinction. (17)

If, after she has given birth, the placenta—the covering of the fetus—does not come out, then one should sprinkle her with water fetched according to the procedure beginning with "With an unbaked earthenware bowl" (*anāprītena śarāveṇa*), while reciting these two verses: "May the fetus come forth unharmed" (*aitu garbho akṣitaḥ*). Some [teachers] say that this should be done verse by verse.
Likewise, in the previous sprinkling there were three verses with six endings;
here, however, there is one verse, "O god of sesame, O god of grain, be firm," and another Yajus formula, "Let the speckled one go forth. //15//
Thus ends the fourteenth section in the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
Fifteenth Section: 12. The Birth Rite—1.
The consecration by means of the Vātsapra hymn of the newborn boy.
Smelling [the child] on the head, whispering [mantras] into the right ear;

having touched the newborn with the Vātsapra hymn and placed him on his lap with the following Yajus formula, there is the consecration with the subsequent two verses, smelling on the head, and whispering into the right ear. (ĀpGS 15.1)
Because the masculine gender is intended by the word "born" (*jāta*), this sacrament called *jātakarman* pertains only to a male,
not to a female.
Vatsaprī is the name of a seer (*ṛṣi*).

By him [the sacrificer] is seen the *vātsapra* section beginning with "divaspari"; this is the recitation (*anuvāka*). There is touching at each verse (*ṛc*), according to others, at the end of all [verses].
With the following Yajus formula, "In this [I place]," he places [the child] upon his own lap;

for since the word "of the mother" is specified later on, it follows that here he places him on his own lap. Regarding the reading "with the following ones," the three rites beginning with the consecration (abhimantraṇa) are to be performed with the three subsequent Ṛg-verses.
The smearing of the wound with the mantra "From limb to limb" (*aṅgādaṅgāt*);
the smelling of the head with the mantra "May you become a stone" (*aśmā bhava*); and the whispering into the right ear with the mantra "Wisdom for you" (*medhāṃ te*).
The meaning is "recitation" (japa).
However, some, relying on the reading of the two [verses] in the dual number (*uttarābhyām*), maintain that both mantras are to be employed in all three rites.
According to them, by means of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of smelling, the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) and the recitation (*japa*) would apply to the two ears.
And Āśvalāyana says: "Placing [the hand] upon the ears, he mutters the *medhājanana* [verse]: 'May the god Savitṛ bestow wisdom upon you... (Āśva. Śr. 1.13.2). //1//
As soon as he is born— that is, immediately after birth and before the cutting of the umbilical cord— the birth-rite (jātakarman) is prescribed for a male child.
Because of this statement [Manu 2.29], and because this will be clarified further below:
when a son is born, the father [should perform the rite] with the Vātsapra hymn, beginning with "From the sky... (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.2.2).

Having touched [the child] once at the end with this *anuvāka*, and having placed him on his own lap with the *yajus* "In this [I place you]," he should perform the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of the child with the two following verses, "From limb by limb" and "Become a stone," and likewise,
he should smell the child's head with those same two verses.
The meaning is that the recitation (*japa*) of these two verses is to be performed in the right ear;
and by the force of this specific statement, the recitation and the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) override the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of smelling.
The naming [of the rite as "smelling"] occurs, however, due to the commonality of the action of performing a sacramental refinement (*saṃskāra*) upon one who has been born.
And this has been established in the passage: "And this [is done] upon passing a well, a tree stump, or a crossroads" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 5.16).
Some read the text as "with the following [verses]."
Regarding the phrase "nottarābhyām":
by that [phrase], there is the consecration with "from limb after limb";
and there is the smelling with "be a stone."
The recitation is "medhāṃ te devaḥ".
For this very reason, Āśvalāyana states: "Placing [the honey and ghee] near his ears, he mutters the *medhājanana* [verse]: 'medhāṃ te devassavitā'.
As for the consumption of honey and ghee, however, [he uses the verse]: "tvayi medhām".

"Thus, [the ritual is performed] with exactly these three Yajus-mantras"—this is not correct; for if one were to accept a recitation that is not part of the studied text, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga). //1//
2. The Instruction on the Names of the Lunar Mansions:
And he teaches the names of the lunar mansions. (ĀpGs 15.2)

In the formula "I smell this," the word *asau* (this) is replaced by the name of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*). One should specify it in the vocative case, as in: "With the *hiṃkāra*, I smell you, O Aśvayujī, [the lunar mansion] of cattle," and so forth.
Regarding the formation of the forms for those words denoting lunar mansions, there is a verse intended to determine their grammatical derivation:

In *rohiṇī*, *mṛgaśīrṣa*, and *ārdrā*, the vowel at the beginning undergoes *vṛddhi*; in *pūrvaphalgunī* and *uttaraphalgunī*, it is optionally so; and in *aśvinī*, *bharaṇī*, and *śraviṣṭhā*, it is not.
In the remaining [asterisms], there is no *vṛddhi* for the first vowel. For *svāti* and *punarvasu*, the final vowel is short and is desired to be without the visarga (*savisarga*).

The meaning of this is as follows: among Rohiṇī, Revatī, Maghā, Mṛgaśīrṣā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Tisrā—these being indicated by their initial syllables—an augment *vṛddhi* occurs at the beginning; and because of the inclusion of the term "variously" (*bahulam*) in the rule *nakṣatrebhyo bahulam* (Pāṇini 4.3.37), there is no elision (*luk*) of the suffix denoting birth (*jāta*).
And [the names] Rūpa, Rauhiṇa, Raivata, Māgha, Mārgaśīrṣa, Jyaiṣṭha, and Caitra [are formed with the suffix -aṇ].
Furthermore, regarding the rule "je proṣṭhapadānām" (Pāṇini 7.3.18), there is vṛddhi when a *p* follows a *ṣṭh* in the word *proṣṭhapada*. Thus, [the form becomes] *Proṣṭhapada*.
The meaning is that there is vowel strengthening (*vṛddhi*) of the final member of the compound.
As in the previous case, there is no elision (*luk*); thus, *proṣṭhapādaḥ*.
[There is also strengthening] optionally before the words *aśva*, *śravaṇa*, and *aśvayuj*.
The last [nakṣatra] is Apabharaṇī by traditional enumeration.
Regarding these four—Śravaḥ (Śravaṇā), Śraviṣṭhā, Śatabhiṣaj, and Aśvayuj—the suffix *vṛddhi* is optional.
Furthermore, in this context, the optionality of the elision (*luk*) of the suffix applies specifically to Śravaṇā and Apabharaṇī due to the inclusion of the term *bahula*.
In the case of *aśvayuj* and *śatabhiṣaj*, [the form] is derived by the rule *vatsaśālābhijidaśvayukchatabhiṣajo vā* (Pāṇini 4.3.36).
Thus, *apabharaṇaḥ* becomes *āpabharaṇaḥ*.
Śravaṇa is [the month] Śrāvaṇa;
Śatabhiṣaj is [the month] Śātabhiṣaja;
Aśvayuj is [the month] Āśvayuja.

Regarding the remaining [asterisms], there is no *vṛddhi* [substitution] in those other than those already mentioned; for in these cases, the elision (*luk*) occurs by virtue of both the rules *aśraviṣṭhāphalgunyanūrādhāsvātitiṣyapunarvasuhastaviśākhāṣāḍhābahulālluk* (Pāṇini 4.3.34) and *nakṣatrebhyo bahulam* (Pāṇini 4.3.37).
Thus, there is the removal of the feminine suffix, resulting in: Kṛttikaḥ, Tiṣyaḥ, Āśleṣaḥ, Phālgunaḥ, Hastaḥ, Viśākhaḥ, Anūrādhaḥ, Āṣāḍhaḥ, and Śraviṣṭhaḥ.
In the case of *āmvoḥ*, a vowel followed by the letter *k* is the final [element];
that is, in the words *ārdramūla* and others, the final vowel is followed by the word *ka*.
The meaning is that the suffix *vun* is applied according to the rule beginning with *pūrvāhṇāparāhṇārdrahnamūlābhyas tu vun*.
Regarding *ārdraka* and *mūlaka*:

it is desired that the final vowel of *svāpvoḥ*—referring to the constellations Svāti and Punarvasu—is short and without the visarga; thus, the final vowel of *svāpvoḥ*, [meaning] Svāti and Punarvasu, is desired to be short and without the visarga.
By the rule beginning with "śraviṣṭhāphalgunī," there is elision (luk).
Furthermore, the preceding [suffix] retains its visarga because, upon the cessation of the feminine suffix, the elision prescribed by the rule "halṅyābbhyo dīrghāt... does not apply;
however, for the succeeding [suffix], it is like the masculine form because it ends in the vowel u.

Svāti, Punarvasu—thus, for all the names of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), the indication is by means of the nominative case in the *sūktavāka*; however, in the *jātakarman* (birth-rite), it is by means of the vocative case. //2//
That is its secret. ĀpGs 15.3.

The name of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) is secret; the meaning is that it should be spoken in such a way that others do not know it. This is exactly the same in the case of the *sūktavāka* and other such formulas. //3//

Since it is stated that "he indicates the secret name based on the lunar mansion" (*nakṣatranāma*), and since this is formulated as a separate sūtra within what should have been a single sūtra, both that which is based on the lunar mansion and that which was performed on the tenth day must always be indicated as strictly secret during the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), the *sūktavāka*, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*), the formal salutation (*abhivādana*), and so forth. //3//
3. The feeding of honey and ghee for the boy, and the feeding of curd and ghee.
Having mixed honey and ghee together, and having tied a piece of gold with a notch to a blade of *darbha* grass, he takes [the mixture] with the subsequent mantras.

Having fed the boy [the first food] and bathed him with the five subsequent [verses], he should mix curds and ghee; then, having fed the boy the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*) from a bronze vessel with the *vyāhṛtis* followed by the syllable *oṃ* as the fourth, he should mix the remainder with water and pour it out in a cow-pen. (ĀpGs 15.4)
Having mixed these two, honey and clarified butter, in unequal proportions within a bronze vessel, he places therein gold tied with a blade of *darbha* grass using the *niṣṭarkya* knot;
"niṣṭarkya" refers to a specific manner of tying well known in common usage.
Likewise, having taken those two juices with the gold that has been tied [to the boy], he should have the boy consume them with that very [gold].
With the three subsequent mantras beginning with "In thee, wisdom" (*tvayi medhā*), he causes him to consume [the juices] one mantra at a time.
Then, with the five subsequent verses beginning with "For the field-disease" (*kṣetriyai tvā*), he bathes him one mantra at a time.

Then, having mixed curd and ghee in another bell-metal vessel, he feeds him that *pṛṣadājya* from that very bell-metal vessel with each of the *vyāhṛtis* followed by the syllable *oṃ*, beginning with "bhūḥ svāhā" and so forth. Then, having mixed the two remaining portions with water, he should pour them out into the fold of his garment.
The mention of "boy" (kumāra) is intended so that even an incapable boy may perform the eating by means of a ritual expedient.

Therefore, in cases such as "they cause the boys to eat parched grains" (*dhānāḥ kumārān prāśayanti*) and "they cause them to eat the field-producer [grain]" (*kṣaitrapattyaṃ ca prāśayanti*), the eating does not take place for those who are incapable when there is an absence of effort. //4//
He ties it with a knot having a hole, like the tying of the *niṣṭakarya* top-knot, as indicated by the [Vedic] sign "for the impelling of offspring.
He does so with the subsequent mantras, beginning with the verse: "May the god Savitṛ [bestow] wisdom upon you."
With the three *yajus* mantras beginning with "May wisdom [dwell] in you," he performs the consumption;
at the end of the four [substances], having taken them all together once with gold,
there is the consumption of the gold, honey, and clarified butter accompanied by the mantra for him.
This is according to the statement of Manu.
With the five subsequent [mantras], beginning with "For the barren one thee, for Nirṛti thee," and so forth,
the bathing also occurs only once at the end of the five.
*Pṛṣadājya* is curd and clarified butter mixed together. That [mixture] should be fed to him using the very bronze vessel in which it was prepared, and not with the hand.
It should be done with the *vyāhṛtis*, with the syllable *oṃ* as the fourth: "Bhūḥ svāhā! [and so forth].
With these [verses] and others;
here too, at the end, there is a single consumption.
Having mixed the remainder of what was consumed with water, another person should pour it out into a vessel.
Some say that even the mixing of honey and ghee is prescribed for bronze;
[the procedure consists of] two mouthfuls, bathing, and the *prīti* mantra. //4//
4. Giving the right breast:

Having placed [the child] on his mother’s lap with the next [verse], having caused him to take the right breast with the following [verse], having touched the earth with the two subsequent [verses], he places him down while reciting the final Yajus formula. (ĀpGṛS 15.5)
Then, with the verse "O boy, do not [fear]," he places that boy from his mother's lap onto his own lap;
for that long, [the boy] had been on her lap.
Therefore, even the pouring out of the remnants must be caused to be performed by another.

Then, having caused him to take hold of the right breast with the verse "This boy" (RV 10.85.46), he next touches the earth with each of the two subsequent verses, "That which is the heart of the earth" (RV 10.85.47–48).

Then the mother lays that boy down on the ground she has touched, and she touches him as he lies there with the following Yajus formula: "Neither mayest thou be ill, nor mayest thou weep" (ŚGS 2.13.2). //5//
With the verse, "May this [be] for you, O Mother, [this] boy," he places the boy on the lap of his mother;
and because of the mention of the "mother" here, prior to this, [he was placed] on his own lap.
For this very reason, the pouring out of the remnants is performed by another agent.
With the verse, "This boy... (RV 10.183.2), he causes [the child] to take or drink from the right breast.
This rule regarding the mantra and the sequence of breasts applies specifically to the first feeding of the breast, because there is no reason to bypass the first instance.

Consequently, the Jāteṣṭi sacrifice—though prescribed by such texts as, "Upon the birth of a son, one should offer a cake on twelve potsherds to Vaiśvānara; in that there is a cake on eight potsherds, he purifies him with the Gāyatrī through spiritual luster" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.5)—is heard to be connected with the occasion known as the birth of a son; nevertheless, like the Kṣāmavatī offerings and others, it is not to be performed immediately after that occasion.

Why is this so? Because, according to the principle of the *Rātrisatra* sacrifice, it is accepted that birth itself—only when conjoined with the desire for results such as *brahmavarcasa* (Vedic luster) pertaining to the son mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*)—is the cause for eligibility;

furthermore, because the performance of the *Jāteṣṭi* depends on an intense attachment to the result of purity and other qualities pertaining to the living son, if the sacrifice, which requires a long time to complete, were performed and the son subsequently died from natural causes, the child alone would remain as the "residue" (*śeṣin*) and would not survive due to his throat being choked [by the smoke].
Consequently, if this [sacrifice] were dependent on passion (*rāga*), there would be no engagement in it at all.
Therefore, immediately after birth, only the *jātakarman* (birth-rite) should be performed, ending with the naming ceremony (*saṃśāsana*).

However, as for the *iṣṭi* (sacrifice), because it is difficult to avoid violating the natural force of the occasion (*nimitta*) according to the stated reasoning, and because of the favor shown by the general injunction (*codaka*), it should be performed only on an auspicious lunar day (*parvan*) once the period of impurity has passed.
With the two subsequent verses beginning with "The heart of the earth," he touches the ground once;
then, with the Yajus formula, "Wherein the boy lies at ease, neither suffering nor weeping," he touches the spot where the hundred [grains] have been placed. //5//
5. There are five oblations of husks.

Having placed a water-pot at the head [of the child] with the subsequent Yajus formula, he offers mustard seeds mixed with husks three times each with his joined palms using the subsequent formulas, accompanied by the utterance of "svāhā" for each. He then gives the instruction: "Whenever [the child] enters [the fire], let him silently cast [the seeds] into the fire. (ĀpGS 15.6)
Then, to the north near his head, he places a water-pot with the Yajus formula, "The waters sleep" (*āpaḥ supteṣu*).
Thereafter, he offers mustard seeds mixed with husks with his joined palms (*añjali*) using the eight subsequent mantras beginning with "This is Kali" (*ayaṃ kaliḥ*).
And in that rite, there is an offering three times for each *svāhā* utterance.
One should offer once with the mantra and twice silently;
furthermore, the substance must be taken up again and again.
However, some offer three times using only what was taken up once.
And in the two subsequent oblations, they repeat only the utterance of "svāhā";
this oblation is unprecedented because no ritual procedure (*tantra*) has been prescribed,
yet the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*) does take place.
Having offered oblations all around on both sides, he then gives instructions to those who enter the lying-in chamber.
To whom? To those who enter the lying-in chamber.
In that instruction, the particle *eva* has the sense of "thus" (*evam*).
This is what is meant: whenever you enter this maternity chamber, at each such time [you should scatter] mustard seeds and husks.
In this mixed fire, he silently pours [the seeds] in the same manner as when they were sown by me with the joined palms, three times each.
In that context, the word "silently" (tūṣṇīm) is a prohibition of the mantra that would otherwise be obtained by extension (atideśa). They [proceed] according to the formal injunction.
They perform it;
and this fire-oblation (homa) is a consecration for the protection of the boy,
not of the mother.
This is because of the context.
Therefore, although the protection of the mother is also understood from the phrase "for whose [daughter] has been born," nevertheless, the oblation is not for her sake.
Furthermore, in the case of a woman's childbirth or the death of a son within ten days, [the impurity] does not occur. // 6 //

To the north, having placed a full water-pot near the head of the boy with the *yajus* formula, "The waters [are] sleeping" (*āpassupteṣu*), he then brings fire from the house of a *śrotriya* according to the rule beginning with, "Wherever there is fire" (*yatra kvāgnim*, Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.1.23), and having set that down, he offers mustard seeds mixed with husks three times for each of the eight subsequent mantras beginning with, "This is Kali," using his joined palms (*añjali*) with each mantra, twice silently.
The utterance *svāhā* occurs even in silent rites; although it is established that [the offering] is "with each mantra," the phrase "with each *svāhā*" is used because of the additional syllables.
Then he instructs the guardians of the lying-in chamber: "Whenever anyone has entered, you must silently throw [an oblation] into the fire."

And this is the intended meaning of the injunction: immediately upon each re-entry, one should, while remaining silent and restrained in speech, pour mustard seeds mixed with husks into this very fire with both hands (añjali) silently; and by the use of the particle "eva" (only/just), not even a moment's delay should intervene between the entry and the pouring.
The pouring with both hands is to be done of the mustard seeds alone.
Because it is the subject under discussion.
Some [hold] that the particle *eva* has the sense of "thus" (*evam*), and that the word *tūṣṇīm* (silently) is for the purpose of prohibiting the mantras obtained through extension (*atideśa*). //6//
In this manner, [the rule applies] day after day until the ten-day period has passed.
The meaning is that the *homa* and the cremation (*saṃśāna*) must be performed only during the period from the time of identification until ten days have passed,
and they are to be done once, not every day.
Although the cremation follows immediately [after death], this extended application (*atideśa*) does not apply to that specific interval alone.
Because that [sacrifice] has no remnant for the *homa*;
nor [is it applicable] to the *Vātsapra* and others, because the entirety of those is not established in any of the other ritual manuals (*kalpa*). //7//
Just as this silent sowing was prescribed by Āṅgiras, so too must it be performed day after day by the guardians of the confinement room until the tenth day has passed.
The prefix *ā* here denotes a limit;
thus, it refers to that night which has emerged from the ten days and nights, i.e., the night following the completion of the ten days.
The meaning is "until the tenth night. //7//
Having thus explained the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), he states the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) which follows in due order: 13. The Naming Ceremony—6. Its Time.
When the tenth [lunar day] has dawned and she has bathed, the father and mother give a name to the son. (ĀpGs 15.8)
"Rising" (utthāna) means the removal of the signs of childbirth, such as the fire and the water-jars,
and the barbering of the husband;
whatever else women know [to be done], all that takes place on the tenth day for all castes.
By the word "tenth" (daśamī), neither night alone is meant; rather, it refers to the aggregate of day and night, as in the expression, "therefore, of similar nights.
In that context, by virtue of the technical convention (paribhāṣā), the ritual act and the bath must necessarily take place on the very same day, provided it is possible.

Since this is already established by the context itself, the explicit mention of "of the son" (*putrasya*) is intended so that the specific characteristic of the name to be described hereafter applies to him alone.
Consequently, for a girl, there is only this much: "The name of a girl should have an odd number of syllables" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 15.11).
"Not with the noun first and the verb last," and so forth;
as it says, "The father and the mother—may they two give [the gift] first" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.10).
In that regard, the application is: "One should feed those who are pure and conversant with the mantras at all ritual acts" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 2.15.11).

Having fed the Brahmins, the father and mother, having first uttered the name [of the child], should cause the Brahmins to pronounce the words of benediction. This is because it is seen in another ritual manual (*kalpa*) that they should say, "May there be well-being for such-and-such a person.
Some, however, desire the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), saying, "We two shall perform the naming ceremony. //8//
On the tenth night, that is, on the tenth day;
when the woman who has given birth has risen—that is, has emerged from the confinement room—and has bathed:
by saying this, it is stated that she should emerge and bathe on the tenth day.
A father gives a name to his son, that is, he establishes it; he does not, however, create it,
because the relationship between a word and its meaning is eternal.
"And the mother"— the word "and" (iti) has the sense of conjunction; thus, the mother and father together bestow the name.
The meaning of this is also stated in the words of a mantra: "O Jātavedas, that which was my first name, my father and mother gave to me in the beginning" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.5.10). //8//
7. Regarding the number of syllables in a man’s name:

it should consist of two or four syllables; the noun should come first followed by the verb; it should end in a long vowel or a visarga (abhiniṣṭhāna); and it should begin and contain a sonant consonant with a semivowel (antastha) in between. (ĀpGs 15.9)
Now, as for the specific definition of a noun (*nāman*):
whether accompanied by phonemes (*vyañjana*) or devoid of them, a vowel (*svara*) that has syllables (*akṣara*) as its primary substance is a noun.
Wherever that [noun] is the preceding member, it is a "noun-initial" (*nāmapūrva*); [and] a verb (*ākhyāta*) is the cause of action.

That compound whose final member is a past passive participle (kta) following a long vowel is "ending in a long vowel and an abhiniṣṭhāna" (*dīrghābhiniṣṭhānānta*); likewise, that which has a voiced consonant (*ghoṣavat-vyañjana*) as its initial member is "having a voiced consonant at the beginning" (*ghoṣavad-ādi*); that which has a semivowel (*antastha*) in its middle is "having a semivowel within" (*antarantastha*); and among the *varga*s, the third and fourth letters and the letter *i* are the voiced sounds (*ghoṣavantaḥ*).
The semivowels (ya-ra-la-vā) are the internal sounds (*antasthā*). He leads to heaven, thus he is *dyutiḥ*. He rests upon the rays of light (*gāḥ*), thus he is *gośriḥ*.
"Go-prīṇa" means "one who pleases a cow," hence *goptīḥ*; "hiraṇya-dā" means "one who gives gold," hence *hiraṇyadāḥ*;
"bhūri-dā" and "haradatta" are examples of such formations.
Baudhāyana says: "The name should be derived from the lineage of a seer (*ṛṣyaṇūka*) or from the lineage of a deity (*devātāṇūka*), according as the names of their ancestors may be;
'derived from the lineage of a seer' means designated by a seer, such as Vasiṣṭha or Jamadagni."
The *devatāṇūka* refers to those that denote deities, such as "Rudra" or "Viṣṇu. The *pūrvapuruṣas* are the ancestors, beginning with the father. //9//

Now, the definition of the name to be established is stated: it is intended as a compound of either two syllables or four syllables, and not as a conventional term (*rūḍhi*), because of the establishment of its preceding and succeeding parts according to the rule "the noun comes first and the verb follows.
Nor is it a sentence (*vākya*); [for it lacks the necessary expectancy].
This is because it lacks the capacity to denote a substance (*dravya*).

If it is asked: "But why is it that, although there is no difference between a sentence (*vākya*) and a compound (*samāsa*) insofar as both are collections of meaningful elements (*arthavat-samudāya*), only the compound denotes a substance and not the sentence? [The answer is: "A primary derivative (*kṛt*), a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), and a compound (*samāsa*)... (Pāṇini Sūtra 1.2.46).
Thus, because the mention of "compound" (samāsa) serves as a restrictive rule (niyama):
"preceded by a noun" (nāmapūrva); a word ending in a case-suffix (subanta) that denotes a substance (dravya) is a "noun" (nāman); that which has such a [noun] preceding it is "preceded by a noun."
Thus, that name which has a verbal form as its subsequent member is called *ākhyātottara*.
Now, one might object: "Is there not a restriction on compounds by the rule *supsupā* (Pāṇini 2.1.4), such that no compound can occur with a verb ending in *tiṅ*?
True; for this very reason, by the word *ākhyāta* here, what is intended is a base ending in *kvip* which resembles a verb and ends in a *sup* suffix.

And similarity [to a verbal root] exists because of the mere fact of denoting an action, even in the absence of the predominance of action, and because it possesses the designation "verbal root" (dhātu) according to the rule: "A word ending in *kvip* does not lose its status as a verbal root. A name that has a long vowel at the end, a *niṣṭhā* suffix at the end, or both a long vowel and a *niṣṭhā* suffix at the end is described as such.

*Abhiniṣṭhāna* is the designation for the *visarjanīya* according to the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*). A name whose initial phoneme is voiced is called "voiced-initial" (*ghoṣavad-ādi*). Furthermore, the voiced consonants (*ghoṣavat-varṇa*) are well-known from the *Prātiśākhya-sūtras*.
"The sibilants (*ūṣman*), the visarga, and the first and second [classes of consonants] are voiceless (*aghoṣa*), except for the letter *ha*; the remainder of the consonants are voiced (*ghoṣavat*)."

"Containing semivowels within" means that within the middle of which name there are semivowels (antasthā)—namely *ya*, *ra*, *la*, and *va*—it is so described. An example of a two-syllable [name] is *vārdāḥ*:
one who gives (*dadāti*) water (*vāḥ*, i.e., *udaka*) is *vārdāḥ*.
"Gīrdāḥ" means "one who gives speech," and so forth.
Regarding the four-syllable [name], the commentary states "Draviṇodāḥ" and "Varivodāḥ";
both of these are Vedic (chāndasa).
There are also other [gifts], such as the giver of gold, the giver of a young woman, and so forth. //9//
8. "The excellence of a name containing the word *su* [is as follows]:
'Or rather, that in which the prefix *su-* occurs is indeed firmly established,' so says the Brāhmaṇa. (ĀpGS 15.10)
Alternatively, there is this other position: that name in which the prefix *su-* occurs is the defining characteristic of a deity;
nothing else, such as having three syllables and so forth, is [the criterion], for that [three-syllable rule] applies to those [names] established [as deities].
The word *hi* indicates excellence;
it is established with even greater excellence than the former,
by which [it is shown that] even the previous [mantras] consisting of two syllables and so forth are established.

And thus, remaining within that very same definition, Bharadvāja said: "A name consisting of two or four syllables, beginning with a sonant and ending with a semivowel (antastha), and terminating in a long vowel or a visarga (abhiniṣṭhāna)—that indeed is known to be established as the conventional [name]. It is thus firmly established.
The meaning is "that which is constant and indestructible," i.e., that which lasts for a long time.
Examples include *subhadra* (very auspicious) and *sumukha* (having a beautiful face).
Because of the rule concerning prefixes (*upasarga*), forms such as *soma-sut* (Soma-presser) do not become established [as compounds]. //10//
Alternatively, that name in which the prefix *su-* occurs is established as conferring long life and is suitable for rites such as sacrifices;
examples include *sujātaḥ* (well-born) and *sudarśanaḥ* (good-looking), and so forth.
Here, because the term "Brāhmaṇa" is mentioned, the qualification *sv-* is optionally substituted for the qualifications of having two syllables and so on.
The word *hi* is a meaningless particle (*nipāta*), according to the statement: "In the case of *mitākṣara* [compounds], it is meaningless.
The inclusion of the term "prefix" (*upasarga*) is for the purpose of excluding words that resemble prefixes, such as *supasoma* and so forth.

Regarding this, Bodhāyana states other alternatives: "It should be according to the lineage of the sages (*ṛṣyaṇūka*) or the lineage of the deities (*devatāṇūka*), just as the names of their ancestors may be.
Here, *aṇūka* means a designator, because of the context.
The lineage of sages (ṛṣyaṇūka) includes Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, and so forth;
the lineage of deities (devatāṇūka) includes Viṣṇu, Śiva, and so forth;
or the names of one's ancestors, such as father and grandfather, such as Yajñaśarman.
By [the words] "Somaśarman" and so forth. //10//
9. The naming of the girl:
the name of the girl should consist of an odd number of syllables. ĀpGs 15.11.

That number which cannot be measured by its meaning is an "odd" (ayuk) number. Where there are an odd number of syllables, that is called "having an odd number of syllables" (ayujākṣara), such as a single syllable, three syllables, and so forth. This alone is the definition of a maiden's name: *gauḥ*, *vāk*, etc.
O Earth, O Pārvatī! //11//
The name *kumāryā* consists of an odd number of syllables, that is, an unequal number of syllables;
the term *ayujākṣaram* is a Vedic form.
Here, "having an odd number of syllables" is the sole qualifying characteristic.
Because [words] consisting of two syllables and so forth are derived by this [rule], for example:
*śrīḥ*,
*gauḥ*.
Bhāratī, Kamalā, Pativallabhā,
"O lotus-eyed one," and so forth.
Even for a maiden, the rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) and ending with the tonsure (*caula*), which serve to purify the body, must indeed be performed silently.
"However, this entire cycle of rites for women must be performed without mantras."
For the sake of maintaining the body, [one should act] according to the time and in due order.
This is because of the statement of Manu.

Furthermore, in this context, only those ritual acts centered on substances—such as the consumption [of food] and the shaving of hair—which have the nature of being primary actions (*bhāvārtha*), are to be extracted and performed separately, but not the *homās*; for such is the practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).
And because it is seen in the *Smṛtyarthasāra*. //11//
10. Upon returning from a journey, the father should perform the smelling of the son’s head and so forth.
Having returned from a journey, he should consecrate the son with the following two verses, smell his head, and mutter the subsequent mantras into his right ear. (ĀpGs 15.12)
Having returned from a journey, one should perform consecration and smelling [of the child] in sequence with the two following verses:
"From limb to limb" (*aṅgādaṅgāt*) is the consecration;
"May you become a stone" (*aśmā bhava*) is the smelling.
The naming is indicated by the mantra-sign (*mantraliṅga*) "O Yajñaśarman!

and is established by the instruction for another consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) specifically for a girl. The mention of a "son" (*putra*) is intended so that the smelling on the head and the whispering in the right ear—which apply to a son—should not be performed for a girl.
Otherwise, since there would be no contradiction regarding the gender of the mantra, both [rites] would apply to the girl as well.
Since she (the girl) is also the subject under discussion,
the phrase "with the following [mantras] for the maiden" would be a substitute specifically for the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*), and not for the other two rites.
The subsequent mantras, beginning with "Agni is long-lived," which are prescribed as five, he should whisper into the right ear of his son.
The mention of "mantra" is made for the purpose of indicating that the word "five" in the phrase "Agni is long-lived... five" functions as a mantra. //12//

Having returned from a journey, he should perform the consecration (*abhimantraṇa*) of his son with the two verses beginning with "From limb to limb" (*aṅgādaṅgāt*) and "Become a stone" (*aśmā bhava*).
Likewise, he should perform the smelling of the head (*mūrdhnyavaghrāṇa*) with these same two verses.
In place of the word "asau" (so-and-so), he pronounces the name given on the tenth day in the vocative case.
Some say: "The consecration with the mantra 'From limb to limb' and the smelling with the mantra 'Become a stone'—
if that were the case, one should assign them by making such a distinction."
Or he may say "in order.
Then, into the right ear of the son, he should mutter the five mantras beginning with "Agni is long-lived, together with the trees," including their continuations (*sānuṣaṅga*).
And these three [rites] are to be repeated for each son. 12.
11. The same applies to the girl as well. He consecrates the girl with the following Yajus formula: [ĀpGS 15.13]
Having returned from his journey, he addresses the daughter-in-law, the wife, and the offspring with the subsequent Yajus formula, "Thou art born from my entire self.
Although one should have said "daughter" (*duhitṛ*), the use of the word "maiden" (*kumārī*) is intended so that this rite does not apply after she has been given away in marriage.

However, for a son, it applies for as long as he lives; even when a son who had gone abroad returns, the three rites beginning with the addressing [of the wife] take place, because the underlying principle is the same. //13//
The phrase "having returned from a journey" (pravāsādetya) is understood to carry over.
With the subsequent *yajus* mantra, "From every part of myself," he consecrates the maiden, the unmarried girl.
For maidens, this much alone [is required].

But [the rites] arising from smelling [the breath] do not apply, because they are not mentioned [in that context], because the word "of the son" is used there, and because of the contradiction with the masculine gender found in the mantra. //13//
Thus ends the fifteenth section in the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* composed by the venerable Sudarśanārya.
The sixteenth section: 14. The first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana). In this regard, it is the consumption of curd and other such items by the child.

In the sixth month after birth, having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce blessings, one should mix together curds, honey, ghee, and boiled rice, and have the boy eat it with the following mantras. Now follows the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) for the boy;
that should be performed in the sixth month from birth—that is, starting from the second day after the birth itself.
The months are the solar, lunar, and so forth.
Intending to perform that [rite], he feeds an even number of Brahmins and causes them to pronounce blessings: "An auspicious day! Well-being! Prosperity!
On this occasion, there is no *abhyudaya-śrāddha* on the preceding day.
Because of the absence of the sacrifice to the gods;
for where the sacrifice to the gods takes place on the following day, there the offering to the ancestors is performed on the preceding day.
Therefore, it is performed for the ancestors on the preceding day.
Because of the scriptural statement, "He sacrifices to the Uttara-mahar-devas," having caused [the Brahmins] to pronounce benedictions,
one should mix the fourfold substances beginning with curd and have the boy consume them.
With the four subsequent mantras beginning with "Bhūr apāṃ tve" and so forth,
one appends the phrase "tvā oṣadhīnām" to the two middle ones;
the recitation of the word "apām," however, is for the purpose of indicating the fourfold nature of the mantras.
In the phrase "asau," the name is to be taken in the vocative case, as in: "O Yajñaśarman, may there be [prosperity] for you. The consumption [of the food] occurs with each mantra;
others say it occurs at the end of all.

The ritual feeding with solid food (*annaprāśana*) for a girl does not take place on the same day as that for a boy; for the *Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra* states: "The rite for a girl is performed in the same manner" (1.14.7). //1//
"From birth," meaning starting from the time of birth,
"in the sixth month by counting days";
therefore, for one born on the second day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, the month of Mārgaśīrṣa itself is not counted as complete.
Therefore, Bṛhaspati says in the Jyotiṣa: "After fifty days multiplied by three, and after sixty days multiplied by three..."
"...the highest enjoyment is even nearer. The phrase "having fed the Brāhmaṇas" has its meaning already explained.

Immediately after the pronouncement of blessings, one should mix the four items beginning with curd, and with the four subsequent mantras starting with "bhūr apām tvauṣadhīnām," one should have the boy consume [the mixture] only once.
And there is the mention of the name by means of perfect knowledge (*sambuddhyā*).
For the second and third [mantras] as well, the phrase beginning with "O you who are the herbs" (*tvauṣadhīnām*) is to be supplied (*anuṣaṅgaḥ*). //1//
2. In place of curd and other such items, there is the prescription of *taittiriya* meat;
some say it is with *taittiriya* meat. (ĀpGs 16.2)

Some teachers maintain that this first feeding of solid food should be performed with the meat of a partridge (*tittiri*); for them, the meat serves as a condiment for the rice. Others, however, maintain that the meat itself should be consumed while reciting the mantra.
The mention of "flesh" is for the purpose of prohibiting blood and other such substances. //2//
This is for the sake of clarity. //2//
15. Caula—its time: the caulam ceremony takes place in the third year after birth, under the two Punarvasus. (ĀpGs 16.3)

Now, the procedure for the *caula*: that rite in which the hair is first cut is the *caula*, because its purpose (*prayojana*) is the *cūḍā* (topknot). There is no distinction between the letters *ḍa* and *la*. That [is the definition].
Starting from birth, it should be performed again in the third year under the asterism Punarvasu.
Since it is ordained that "one should feed the boy," this *caula* ceremony is for the male alone according to the rule;
for the girl, however, it is merely a repetition.
If it is done in this manner, the masculine gender in the expression "another [fire] facing east" (apareṇāgniṃ prāñcam) becomes appropriate.
The mention of "birth" (janman) is intended so that [the rite] does not occur in the third year from conception, but rather from the time of actual birth. //3//
The birth [rite] is as previously described regarding study.
Consequently, according to the rule "the count of years begins from conception," the year spent in the womb is not counted.
*Caula* is the name of a specific ritual act.
That rite in which the presence of the *cūḍā* (topknot) occurs is the *caula*;
it should be performed under the two *punarvasu* [nakṣatras]—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. //3//
The *nāndī-śrāddha* is like the initiation (*upanayana*);
the feeding of Brahmins is like that of the initiation. (ĀpGs 16.4)
Since there is no distinction regarding the feeding of Brāhmaṇas at the Upanayana, the elision of the initial word (*ādi-pada-lopa*) should be understood here.
Thus, "brāhmaṇabhojanādi" (beginning with the feeding of Brāhmaṇas) is to be understood here as: "having fed the Brāhmaṇas, having caused them to pronounce benedictions, and having fed the boy.
The phrase "with the first [verse] of the Anuvāka," etc., will be extended [by analogy] later on. //4//
And here, the mention of "the feeding of Brāhmaṇas" is intended to indicate the giving of blessings and the feeding of children as well;
or rather, the word "etc. in the phrase "feeding and so forth" should be understood, because of the statement "like the [gift of] a present."
The initiation ceremony (upanayana) itself is the approach (upāyana). //4//
The kindling of the fire and the subsequent rites are performed as at the Sīmantonnayana ceremony. ĀpGs 16.5.
The rites beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the sprinkling of water around it should be performed as in the *sīmantonnayana* ceremony.
On the previous day, the *nāndī-śrāddha* is performed;
the vessels are used only once.

The *śamyā* pegs are used together with the *śalalī* needles and other items; furthermore, in the context of the phrase "while [the teacher] is being touched," it refers to the boy’s act of touching; and there is an extension of the procedure up to the end of the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*).

As for the passage beginning with "The two lute-players should sing," there is no extension of that rule here, because of the injunction "facing eastward behind the fire" which prescribes sitting down again. //5//
The ritual procedure beginning with the kindling of the fire and including the principal oblations, ending with the sprinkling of water (pariṣecana), is performed here as in the Sīmantonnayana rite.
Then, while the boy holds on [to his mother], the principal oblations are offered.
At the time of arranging the vessels, the porcupine quills and other items are placed down only once. //5//
3. The shaving of the boy’s hair and the setting apart of the top-knot (śikhā).
Having shaved the hair, he sets aside the top-knot according to the custom of the ṛṣis. (ĀpGs 16.6)
"Vinayana" means the separation of those [hairs] that are to be sown and those intended for the topknot.

"Silently" is for the purpose of restraining speech, not for the purpose of prohibiting the use of mantras, because there is no prior rule [establishing such a requirement] that would necessitate its prohibition.
According to the number of sages in one's *pravara*, he makes that many tufts of hair: three for one with three sages, and five for one with five sages. //6//
"Prāñcam" means facing eastward. "Vā tūṣṇīm" means remaining silent with speech restrained. "Kesān vinīya" means having arranged the hair in various ways.
The meaning is that those hairs intended for shaving and those intended for the crest should be separated from one another.

He establishes as many tufts [of hair] as there are sages in his pravara; for one who has a single sage in his pravara, there is one tuft; for one who has two sages in his pravara, there are two, and so forth. //6//
According to whatever may be their family custom. ĀpGs 16.7.
Alternatively, in whatever manner the family custom (*kuladharma*) of these [ancestors] belonging to the prince’s lineage proceeds, in that same way he fashions the topknot (*śikhā*).
The use of the plural pronoun "of these" is intended to ensure that the family custom does not belong solely to the agent;
therefore, there is no fixed rule that the father himself must be the performer of this rite.
But elsewhere, when possible, there is a restriction that he alone [the father] shall perform the rites for the boy. //7//
Alternatively, the topknot (śikhā) should be fashioned in such a way that the family custom (kuladharma) of these noble families is maintained;
because of the statement "of these," it follows that the one who performs the tonsure ceremony (caulakartṛ) may be someone other than the father. //7//

The meaning is that everything from "He places [the water] in the cold [water]" and so forth, ending with "or he places it on a clump of darbha grass," should be performed in the same manner as the initiation ceremony (upanayana). //8//

4. Like the initiation ceremony (upanayana), [the rite] begins with the shaving of the hair in all directions and so forth; it is the same as [the initiation] from the pouring together of the waters until the depositing of the hair. ĀpGs 16.8.
This has indeed already been explained in the section on the return ceremony (samāvartana). //8//
Having washed the razor, he sets it down. (ĀpGs 16.9)
The washing of the razor is prescribed; its setting aside follows from the sense of the context. When one sets it aside, then one should wash it. //9//
In this case, washing alone is prescribed; as for the placing [of the vessel], it is obtained by implication. //9//
With the razor used for shaving, one must refrain from performing ritual acts for three nights;
by this, there is a cessation of ritual activity for three days. (ĀpGs 16.10)
For three days and nights, one must not perform the work of a barber with that razor. //10//
With that razor, one should perform the duties of a barber for three days.
He grants a boon. (ĀpGs 16.11)
When this rite is completed, the father of the boy gives a boon to the Brahmin;
it is said that "a cow is indeed the boon. //11//
It is better that the father gives a cow to a Brāhmaṇa seated to his right;
if there is another performer of the *caula* ceremony, then [the gift should be given] to him. //11//
1. The Godāna vow and its timing;
likewise, the Godāna may also be performed under another lunar mansion in the sixteenth year. (ĀpGS 16.12)
Just as the *caula* ceremony is performed, so too should the rite called *godāna* be performed for him;
in that regard, there is an exception to the third year, namely that it may be done in the sixteenth year.
It may also be performed under another lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) on an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*).
The section on Punarvasu is an exception to the rule. //12//
*Godāna* is the name of a ritual act (*karman*),
in which the shaving of the head at two specific regions— the *godāna*s— is an integral part.
Even in that alternative view where there is the shaving of all hair except for the topknot (*śikhā*), [the term applies].
And the tufts [of hair] are according to the ṛṣis;
even there, the shaving of the two *godāna* [tufts] exists as the basis for the application of the name of the rite.
That is the rite called *godāna*.
Thus, just as at the *caula*, the rites beginning with the feeding of Brahmins and ending with the granting of boons (*varadāna*) are to be performed;
that [initiation] may also take place under another lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), such as Rohiṇī and others, and in the sixteenth year. //12//
Regarding this, he states another alternative:
"Or it may be the Agnigodāna. (ĀpGS 16.13)
Where Agni is the deity in the *godāna* ceremony, that is the *agnigodāna*; he whose *godāna* has Agni as its deity is "one for whom Agni is the *godāna*" (*agnigodānaḥ*).
(By the word *agni*, the *godāna* ceremony having that deity is indicated; the analysis of the compound is: "he for whom Agni is the *godāna*").
There is the elision of one of the two words "godāna," as in the compound *uṣṭramukha* ("camel-faced").
Regarding this, Baudhāyana states: "The Godāna ceremony takes place in the sixteenth year."
For that [rite], the performance and the conclusion are silent, like the *caula*.
Alternatively, it may be the *godāna* [rite].
For that, the performance and the conclusion are by means of the opening (*upākaraṇa*) and the completion (*samāpana*) of the section (*kāṇḍa*).
(Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 3.2.52–58).
What is meant by this?

It means that whatever ritual procedure (*kalpa*) applies to the commencement and completion of the sections (*kāṇḍa*) dedicated to Agni, the rules for the tonsure ceremony (*caula*) are to be applied therein.

It occurs in the sixteenth year; the yokes for the sacrificial vessels are not used [at that time], because this [practice] is not taught in this Gṛhya-sūtra. Since the Godāna ceremony is taught [elsewhere], the rule regarding the yoke-pins applies only there.

The procedure for this is as follows: having fed the Brahmins and caused them to pronounce blessings, one has the hair and beard shaved silently; then, having performed the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the final sprinkling (pariṣecana) according to the *Āgnikakāṇḍa* initiation, one performs the worship of the deities according to the *Śukriya* ritual with the formula: "O Agni, Lord of Vows, I shall observe the vow."
Others perform the observance of the vow for one year;
at the conclusion is the dismissal (*visarga*).
In the same way, the modification beginning with "Thus have I practiced" (*evam evācāriṣam*) and so forth is like that of the *Śukriya*, with [the appropriate] deity.
The shaving of the hair and beard;
at the conclusion, the feeding of Brahmins;
in both cases, some perform the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha.
Others say no. // 13 //
"For Agni" refers to the one whose *godāna* [hair-cutting ceremony] has been performed; he is the "Agni-godāna" student (*brahmacārī*).
Because of the masculine gender indication, the analysis of the compound is thus.

In this view, once the *ājyabhāga* offerings have been completed, there is a single principal oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the mantra: "To Agni, the seer of the section (*kāṇḍarṣi*), svāhā!"
Then follows the ritual beginning with *jaya* and ending with the washing of the razor. //13//
Some teachers prescribe the Godāna vow for one year. (ĀpGs 16.14)
Even for one who has performed the *godāna* ceremony, the teachers teach that the observance of the vow (*vrata*) for one year is a necessary supplement to it.
This option applies to the *caula* and *godāna*;

however, in the case of the *agnigodāna*, because of the extension (*atideśa*) of the rules from the *kāṇḍopākaraṇa*, the vow-observance is mandatory. When the vow-observance takes place, then after the granting of the boons (*varadāna*), the worship of the deity at the conclusion is performed as before.
And the visarga is exactly as before. //14//

Even after having studied the Veda, some teachers instruct that the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) known as the *godāna* must necessarily be observed for one year; the meaning is that this is optional. //14//

He states the distinction between both types of *godāna* rites from the *caula*: "In that regard, there is a specific rule concerning the shaving of hair: this much is different—[in the *godāna*,] he has all the hair shaved off. (ĀpGS 16.15)
In this *caula-godāna* ceremony, however, there is this much difference from the *caula*:
here one has all the hair shaved, including the topknot (*śikhā*); but in the *caula*, one leaves the topknot according to the number of one's ancestors (*ṛṣi*).
Others explain that the inclusion of the word "all" (*sarva*) is for the purpose of including the beard and so forth;
for them, the word "hair" (*keśa*) is intended as an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Thus says Āśvalāyana: "He issues the command regarding the hair of the head, the beard, the body hair, and the nails, [to be trimmed] while standing in water."
(Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.18.6) //15//
The difference is only this much:
that even with a crest-lock intended for the purpose of concealment, one causes all the hair to be shaved.
Therefore, because there is no act of training (*vinayana*) here, there is an exclusion of the *śalalya* and other such items.
And here, because of the mention of the causative form *vāpayata* ("he causes to shave"), the teacher alone is the performer of the *godāna* rite;
the gift to the bridegroom (*varadāna*) is also for the teacher alone.
Likewise, there is the shaving of the topknot (*śikhā*) as well, based on this very statement: "The difference is only this much: he has all the hair shaved," which is like the *satra* sacrifice.
Others say: "This [head] is indeed empty and uncovered when it is shaven; the lock [of hair], however, is its covering.

But because of the scriptural statement regarding sacrificial sessions (satras)—"In sacrificial sessions, there is the shaving of the lock" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.10.8–9)—and because this prohibits the shaving of the lock elsewhere than in sacrificial sessions, here too there is certainly no shaving of the lock. //15//
"The touching of water," so say the Chandogas. (ĀpGs 16.16)
Regarding this Godāna vow, the Chandogas instruct that one should perform the ritual touching of water (ablution) every day;
some, however, say it should be performed at the three sessions of the day.
Thus ends the sixteenth section in the Anākula commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra composed by Śrī Haradatta.
The Chandogas teach that, within the context of the annual *godāna* vow, there should be a daily ritual bathing in water; the meaning is that this is an alternative option. //16//
Thus ends the sixteenth section in the Gṛhyatātparyadarśana composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
The sixth chapter is completed.
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Seventeenth Section: 16. Construction of the House—1. Therein, the digging out and the carrying away [of earth] are performed with a spade.
Having leveled a site for the village that slopes toward the south-west, he sweeps it toward that same direction with a broom made of *palāśa* or *śamī* wood while reciting the subsequent [verse].
The purificatory rites for the body of a person about to be initiated into sacrifices have been explained.
And these, in the absence of the statement "having departed from the house of a settled householder," must be performed in the very house;
that is, in a house constructed according to the prescribed rules.
Through entry according to the prescribed rule, there is the attainment of desired results such as longevity, wealth from sacrifice, and so forth.

Therefore, the procedure for the construction and entry of a house, which follows the sequence of the transmission of the mantras, is now explained: (Paṭala 6, Khaṇḍa 17–1) Now begins the procedure for the consecration of the house.
And the honor of the householder is neither obligatory like all the sacrifices and so forth, nor is it occasional like rites for miracles or expiations;
what then? It is optional (kāmya).
Therefore, there is no fault in non-performance;
however, regarding performance, there is a rule concerning the northern solstice and so forth.
In that regard, the site where a house is intended to be built is the "space for the house," and it should slope toward the south and west.
The ground is sloping toward the intermediate direction between south and west;
the meaning is that a dwelling should be constructed in such a location. One digs that site for the house, excavating it with a spade until the loose soil is brought forth.

Having gathered up those particles of dust with a shovel made of *pālāśa* wood or with a wooden scraper, he sweeps them toward that same direction with the following verse, "Whatever of the earth is cruel" (*yad bhūmeḥ krūram*). He sweeps them from a higher place down to a lower one.
It is called a *udūha* because by means of it [the dust] is swept away (*udūhyate*). //1//

That portion of ground intended for the purpose of a house, which slopes toward the south and west— that is, it is low in the south-western direction— one should raise it up by means of a spade or similar tool, having excavated the soil;
[one should do this] with a broom made of *pālāśa* or *śamī* wood—
an "udūha" being so called because by it the soil particles (*pāṃsu*) are swept away (*udūhyante*), that is, moved to another place.

The meaning is "one who speaks like an owl"; by means of this [phrase], he pushes up this very corner of the direction with the following verse, "That which is cruel of the earth," and so forth. //1//
In this manner, three times. (ĀpGs 17.2)
Having thus raised it up three times, he fans it upward. //2//
The connection is "he draws up.
Here, there is a repetition of the mantra for both the second and third drawings as well,
because of the statement "in this manner."
Otherwise, he would have simply said, "He stirs it upwards three times with the following [verse]," and would not have composed another sūtra stating, "In this manner, three times. //2//
2. The digging of the post-holes and the planting of the posts:

Having touched the prepared [site] with the next [verse], having caused the post-holes to be dug while moving clockwise, and having thrown the earth inside [the holes], he sets up the southern door-post with the two next [verses]. ĀpGS 17.3.
Having thus removed that portion of earth, they prepare it so that it becomes level on all sides.
Then, he touches that prepared ground with the subsequent verse, "The Earth is pleasant," while reciting this [Ṛgveda 1.22.15].
Thereafter, he digs the holes for the pillars in a clockwise direction; the absence of the letter *n* [in the word *sthūṇāgartān*] is due to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
The meaning is: starting from the outside and ending in the middle, in such a manner.

In that context, regarding the central pillars intended for supporting the beams, because the qualifiers "clockwise" (*pradakṣiṇam*) and "inwardly" (*abhyantaram*) are impossible [there], it applies only to the peripheral [pillars].

There, in a house with an eastern door, having caused the holes for the pillar of the southern door to be dug clockwise up to the hole for the pillar of the northern door, then as many intermediate pillars as there are—of those...
Starting from the south, the arrangement ends toward the north.

In the same way, even in a house with a different orientation of its door, one should ensure the circumambulation is clockwise (pradakṣiṇa) and that the interior space is properly formed as far as possible.

Having had the pits dug in this manner and having removed the earth from them by throwing it out, he then places the southern door-post into its pit using the two verses beginning with "ihaiva tiṣṭha" (Stand right here). //3//

Having prepared the site by leveling it with a shovel so that it slopes toward the northeast, and having touched it with the verse "O Earth, be pleasant for us," he should have the laborers dig pits for the pillars— pits intended for the division of the pillars— clockwise, beginning from the inside and not from the outside.
Having thrown out the earth, he should, while stepping out toward the south, recite the two verses beginning with "Stay right here."
They do not enter;
he fixes [the post] into the pit of the door-pillar.
Here, the prescription for the clockwise direction and for being on the inner side applies only to the pillars of the *paḍayantī* verses.
But not during the intermediate [periods]. //3//
In the same way for the other [wife]. (ĀpGS 17.4)

The meaning is that with these same two verses he fixes the other two door-posts, the northern and the southern. Regarding the statement "the southern one [is fixed] first," it should be understood as referring to the left and right [posts] for one who is exiting, not for one who is entering. 4.
In the same manner, he fixes the other doorpost on the left side with these two [formulas]: "Stay right here! //4//
Having placed the other [posts] around it exactly as they were dug, he consecrates the bamboo pole being set up with the *utteraṇa* formula.
The two door-posts are set in their respective holes with the recitation of mantras;
for the others, however, they are set in their respective holes silently, in the same order as the pits were dug.
When all the middle posts have been thus set, the workmen place the beam upon them.
He consecrates the beam being placed by them with the subsequent Yajus formula, "By Truth,
the pillar," and by the mention of the "beam" (vaṃśa), the spinal column is understood,
because it is the primary one.
This is clearly evident in the Bhāradvājaka [Kalpa]: "With the verse 'Upon the pillar by Truth,' he places [the beam] upon the backbone.
In that mantra, the word *sthūṇau* is a Vedic [form] involving a change of gender;
and the dual number is to be understood as occurring according to the requirements of the context. //5//

Having silently set down the other pillars in the order in which they were dug, he consecrates the bamboo beam—when it is being placed evenly upon the pillars—with the following Yajus formula: "By Truth, ascend the pillar. //5//
The response should be measured and superior, according to the specific characteristics of the person addressed.
Then, he consecrates that house, which has been measured out and prepared, with the six subsequent mantras beginning with "Brahma ca te kṣatram.
What does he do? He consecrates it—this is the meaning.

"According to the characteristic mark" (yathāliṅgam) means that he faces each specific part of the house and consecrates it with whichever mantra contains the characteristic mark corresponding to that particular part.
Even when the front pillar has been fixed, the consecration is performed with reference to only two [pillars],
because the word for "house" (*agāra*) is used in the dual number.
Thus, in every case, the central king-pillar within the house is the *stūpa*.

Regarding the spine: here some teachers desire the ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) in the four mantras for the pillar-sockets (*sthūṇāliṅga*), such as "May the pillar protect [the left]," and "May sacrifice and sacrificial fees protect the right pillar.
Others [apply it] even to the word "those" (*te*), as in "May sacrifice and those sacrificial fees [protect the right pillar]."
We say "no," because the mantras are expectant;
for it is impossible to connect the plural-ended words *dakṣiṇā*, *iṣaḥ*, and *ūrjaḥ* with the singular-ended word *abhirakṣatu*.

Furthermore, there is no injunction for modification (*ūha*), nor is there an absence of recitation as in the case of the *Abhyātāna* formulas; and finally, there is no repetition at the end of all the *anupaṅgas* (supplementary insertions) as is observed in other instances.

As for the "expectancy" (sākāṅkṣatva) that was mentioned, even that is not a cause for ellipsis (anuṣaṅga), because expectancy is satisfied by mere proximity alone. Alternatively, in the case of "May Dharma protect you" (*dharmas te sthūṇārāja*) and "May Śrī [protect] you" (*śrīs te*), there is no requirement for the word "abhirakṣatu" (may he/she protect),
since both [words, *dharmaḥ* and *śrīḥ*,] end in the nominative case.
Thus, words such as "dakṣiṇā" (the sacrificial fee) and so forth should be understood as being in the nominative case.
Therefore, there is no expectancy [for another word].
Furthermore, because of proximity, the pillar is understood [as the object of the action]. //6//

He consecrates the constructed house with the five mantras beginning with "sammitaṃ nirmitam agāram uttarā brahma ca te kṣatraṃ ca," facing the respective directions as determined by the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the mantras; among these,
he faces the center with the fifth mantra, because it is not connected to any specific direction.
Some [construct it] with six [verses].
In that context, "Dharma is your central pillar" refers to the middle pillar, and "Glory is your stūpa" refers to the backbone.
Here, although the components of the house are praised as pillars by means of mantras;
Nevertheless, by these [verses], the house itself is praised as if it were a pillar,
just as one who possesses feet is saluted when his feet are saluted.

On this point, some consider that in the three mantras beginning with the second, the phrase "May the pillar protect [us]" (*sthūṇe abhirakṣatu*) and so forth is an *anūṅga* (supplementary addition) for the sake of completing the sentence.
Others say that this [supply] applies even to the word "aśabda" (non-verbal),
as well as to "abhirakṣatu" (may he protect) in such passages as "adharmaḥ te" (unrighteousness to you).
Still others, however, maintain that here there is no supply of anything whatsoever anywhere.
Because there would be a structural inconsistency in what is being connected, and because it is not recited even at the end;
rather, the completion of the sentence is established through the connection of the word-meanings present in the mind by virtue of their being the subject under discussion.

Just as, for instance, because the mantra "iṣe tvā" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.1.1) is connected with the act of cutting present in the mind, the sentence is completed by the word "chinadmi" ("I cut"). //6//
Now he describes the ritual for entering the house—17.
The Ritual for Entering the House:
1. The installation of the fire in the northeast direction of the house.

Having kindled a sacrificial fuel-stick made of *pālāśa* or *śamī* wood with the following [verse], he takes up the fire with the next [verse] and, having led it into the house with the following *yajus*, he establishes the fire in the north-eastern part of the house with the next [verse]. Now follows the rule for entering:
this same rule applies to the entry even into a house that has been measured out differently.
Some say it depends on the summer solstice and so forth;
others say no.
"He enters the house containing seed" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 2.10.2).
Thus says Āśvalāyana.
The mention of "seed" (bīja) is an elliptical designation for all household implements.
Intending to enter there, he kindles a fuel-stick made of Palāśa wood or of Samī wood in the fire.
And here, the fuel is determined by its purpose rather than having a fixed measure.
Having ignited it, one should lift up that fire-vessel with the subsequent verse consisting of five quarters beginning with "uddhriyamāṇa.
If the entry occurs during the day, the mantra containing the characteristic mark of night should be employed without dispute.
Likewise, at night, the *aharliṅga* [mantra] should be employed without dispute,
because there is no separate application [of it].
However, those who require the northern solstice (*udagayana*) do not desire its use at night.
The meaning is that the removal (*viniyoga*) of evil committed during the day and during the night is brought about.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction, as in the passage: "Whatever evil we have done at night, O Waters... (*yad āpo naktaṃ duritaṃ carāma*).
Having lifted that fire, he causes it to enter the house with the northern Yajus formula, "O Indra, your houses are wealthy and protective," by means of this [verse].
Having caused it to enter, he establishes that fire in the north-eastern part of the house with the following Ṛc, "The immortal oblation. In this context, the word "of the house" need not be stated.
And [the word] "fire" [is mentioned].
Why? Because both [are heard] in this very sentence.
If that is so, then this word *agāra* (house) is not intended as a qualification of the location.
What then? It is for the purpose of qualifying the fire; [the text] says, "he establishes the fire of the house.
But what is the fire of the house?
It is the cooking fire.
Therefore, some maintain that the taking out of this fire does not proceed from the *aupāsana* fire, but rather from the common (*laukika*) fire;
others, however, hold that because of its connection with the *homa*, this fire is indeed the *aupāsana* fire itself.
In that case, the two words "of their house" (agārasya) and "fire" (agni) would be redundant;
furthermore, oblations are observed even in the context of cooking during the Vaiśvadeva rite.
Therefore, this [text] refers specifically to the cooking fire.

Even though this is so, nevertheless, the consecration of the site (*deśasaṃskāra*) certainly takes place because of its connection with the *homa*. At that very time, the installation of the *aupāsana* fire and the fires used for sacrificial sessions (*vaihārika*) occurs in their respective places;
and at that same time, the entry of the wife and others [into the house] takes place. //7//
He kindles a sacrificial fuel (idhma) made of *śamī* wood in the *aupāsana* fire.
Regarding the word "fuel" (*idhma*), as in the expression "he places large fuel-sticks upon the fires," the specific number and other such details are not intended to be restrictive.
[He does so] with the following verse: "Being lifted up... (*uddhriyamāṇaḥ*).
Thereupon, he takes up that fire.
In this context, two verses in the *triṣṭubh* meter, consisting of four feet each, are traditionally handed down with five feet including their appendages (*anuṣaṅga*).
Of these two, only one is intended for the purpose of taking up [the fire].
The other [clause], however, is for the purpose of providing an option,
because of its application through the singular number in the word "uttarayā" (with the subsequent one). And this option is intended to be fixed, like the case of the *agnihotra*.
If the entry occurs during the day, it should be with the night-sign;
if at night, it should be with the day-sign.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that entry at night is well-established by the practice of the learned (śiṣṭas).

With the Yajus formula, "To the north are the houses of Indra," he brings the excavated fire into the fire-hall; immediately thereafter, in the northeastern part of the hall which has been consecrated according to rule, he establishes that fire with the verse, "The immortal oblation" (RV 10.87.19).
Likewise, at this very time, having brought the Śrauta fires according to rule into the hall, he establishes them in the fire-hall according to the prescribed ritual.

Some [teachers] maintain that because these two phrases— "having taken up the fire here" and "having brought it into the house"— are repeated even though they were already established in the original context, they must have a purposeful meaning; thus, by connecting them as "the fire of the house," they hold that everything from the kindling to the final installation pertains only to the ordinary fire used for cooking,
and not to the *aupāsana* (domestic sacrificial) fire.
For them, when entering the marriage rite (*vivāhāṅga*) according to this *Tulyasūtra*, the kindling of the fire and so forth should be performed using the cooking fire itself.
If it is argued that the *Tulyasūtra* does not apply there because the word "house" (*agāra*) denotes a place for sleeping, whereas the word "home" (*gṛha*) does not—[we reply: no;
for there is no dispute regarding the two words "home" (*gṛha*) and "house" (*agāra*) having the same meaning.

And here, because the word *gṛha* in the mantra "The houses of Indra are rich in wealth" denotes a dwelling, on the contrary, it is stated in the Dharmaśāstra: "In the middle of the house, with the tenth and eleventh [verses], ending toward the east;
in the north-eastern part of the house, with the four following [verses]."
Furthermore, because the rule *śayyādeśe kāmaliṅgena* (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.3.22,
23; 2.4.1) specifies that the place for sleeping is distinct from the house,
the apparent tautology may also be resolved by considering it to serve a clear purpose.
Furthermore, although there is a grammatical connection between "house" (agāra) and "fire" (agni)— such that *agārāgni* means *śālāgni*—
since ritualists employ these terms as synonymous for the *gṛhyāgni* and *aupāsana-agni*, it is the *aupāsana* fire alone that should be established,
not the cooking fire (*pacanāgni*). //7//
To the south of the fire, one prepares the site for the water-vessel;
therefore, the site for the water-vessel is to the south. (ĀpGs 17.8)
Once the fire has been thus established, the site for the water-vessel (udadhāna) should be prepared to the south.
That in which water is placed is called the *udadhāna*, also known as the *maṇika*.
Therefore, the site for the water-vessel—the *maṇika*—is to the south of the established fire. //8//
There, at that place, he establishes the water-vessel.

Having spread darbha grass with its tips pointing in various directions upon it, and having poured rice and barley grains over them with the following verse, he places the water-vessel there. (ĀpGs 17.9)

In that place, having spread out Darbha grass with its tips pointing in all directions and facing every quarter, he pours rice and barley grains mixed together upon those Darbha blades while reciting the following verse, "O Lord of Food...
Then, in that same place, he establishes a water-vessel, setting it down so that it remains steady and does not move. //9//

Having spread out darbha grass with tips pointing in various directions at that place where the water-jar is to be set, he scatters rice and barley mixed together upon those darbha blades while reciting the verse "O Lord of Food, of food" (RV 1.187.1), and then establishes the water-jar upon them.
The filling of the water-vessel with water;
to the north of that, he brings four water-jars while reciting the subsequent Yajus formula. (ĀpGS 17.10)
With the subsequent Yajus mantra, "ariṣṭā asmākam" (May we be unharmed),
there is a repetition of the mantra for each jar.
In that regard, one may either bring [the water] separately with four jars, or else fill it again using a single jar.
As in the case of the statement: "One should pour out the three ladles. //10//
To the north of that water-vessel, he brings four water-pots with the *yajus* formula, "May we be unharmed on this side. The mantra is repeated for each pot,
because the action to be manifested differs according to the difference in the substances.
Furthermore, where there is a rule for repetition regarding an action such as the consumption of the madhuparka offering, the mantra is to be recited only once for that very same action. //10//
