5. There is a consecration for its breaking. He consecrates that which has been broken with the following verse. (ĀpGS 17.11)
Now, if that water-vessel breaks, he consecrates it with the subsequent verse, "The earth, the earth...
This same procedure applies at another time if it cracks, even when it is situated inside another water-vessel. 11.

If the water-jar should break, then he consecrates it with the subsequent verse, "The earth has gone to the earth," and this, by virtue of the context, is indeed an integral part of the ritual action. //11//

6. The principal oblations: Having performed the subsequent oblations after the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the *ājyabhāga* portions, he proceeds with the *jaya* and following offerings. (ĀpGs 17.12)
There are four additional principal oblations: “O Lord of the Dwelling, acknowledge us;
O Lord of the Dwelling, with your auspicious [favor]; O Lord of the Dwelling, be our protector.”
"O Vāstoṣpati, the dispeller of disease..."—
in this case, the extension of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is established by the very mention of the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings,
just as in the rule: "as at the *Pārvaṇa*, ending with the *ājyabhāgas*."
What is the purpose of the statement regarding the kindling of the fire and so forth?

It is for the sake of restricting the fire; that is, so that the kindling may apply only to that very fire which has been established in the house for the purpose of cooking, and not otherwise. Otherwise, the oblation would have to be performed in the *aupāsana* fire alone for the sake of all *pākayajña* sacrifices.

The mention of "victory" (*jaya*) and so forth is for the purpose of prohibiting the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering). But what is the basis for the application of the *sthālīpāka*? It is because it is observed in other [texts].
But how is it that the *sthālīpāka* is prohibited by the mention of the *jaya* offerings and so forth?

It is said: first, the prohibition of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is understood; having offered the subsequent oblations, one proceeds with the *jaya* offerings and so forth—thus the prohibition of the *sviṣṭakṛt* is indeed understood. Having offered the subsequent oblations, one proceeds with the *jaya* offerings and so forth.
"One does not perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
And that [offering] occurs in the case of *sthālīpāka* oblations;
therefore, by means of this prohibition of the *sviṣṭakṛt*, it results in a prohibition of the *sthālīpāka* itself. //12//

There are four subsequent oblations, which are the principal oblations; these consist of two beginning with "O Lord of the Dwelling, acknowledge us" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.4.10) and two beginning with "O Lord of the Dwelling, our furtherer.
Because clarified butter is the sacrificial offering, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) is prescribed.

The statement "ending with the *ājyabhāga* offerings" is for the purpose of establishing the sequence, indicating that the principal oblations (*pradhānahoma*) occur immediately after the *ājyabhāga* offerings and not for any other purpose. Since the performance of the ritual framework (*tantra*) is already established by the phrase "ending with the *ājyabhāga*," the further statement "beginning with the kindling of the fire for Agni" is intended to show, according to his own view, that only the cooking-fire (*pacanāgni*) established here is the one used for the oblation.
That is incorrect,

because all Smārta oblations are prescribed to be performed in the *aupāsana* fire without distinction, according to the rule: "The householder should perform the Smārta rites daily in the marriage fire."

Because this Sūtra has another meaning according to the manner stated above, and because the practice of performing the Vāstu-homa exists only in the *aupāsana* fire for both our own followers and those of other Gṛhya traditions. //12//

7. The sprinkling around for the house. Having performed the rites ending with the sprinkling around, he should sprinkle water three times clockwise around the interior of the house or the dwelling with a water-pot while reciting the following *yajus* formula. He should then feed the Brahmins with cakes, barley meal, and boiled rice.
The statement that the rite ends with the sprinkling around is intended to ensure immediate sequence [with the subsequent feeding].
Having completed the remainder of the *tantra*, one should perform only the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) of the house; nothing else, such as the *vaiśvadeva* offering and so forth, is required.
This is done with the subsequent *yajus*: "The inauspicious is auspicious" (*aśivaṃ śivam*).

Since the act would already be accomplished by the mere mention of "with the water-pitcher in hand," the explicit statement "to the right" (pradakṣiṇam) indicates that this single sprinkling must be performed three times clockwise; furthermore, it must be done continuously and without interruption using the very same water-pitcher taken up once.
By the mention of "encircling with a girdle," it is established that there are three sprinklings;
the statement "between" is intended so that the sprinkling may not take place outside the house,
but rather strictly within.
The house is the dwelling,
and the residence is the place for reclining;
one should feed an even number of Brahmins with cakes and other such foods.
The word "iti" has the sense of conjunction. //13//
Thus ends the seventeenth section in the Anākula commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra composed by Hārīta.

Having sprinkled water three times clockwise around the house or the dwelling from the inside— not from the outside— using a water-pot filled once with the Yajus formula "The auspicious [makes] the inauspicious auspicious" (Śivaṃ śivam), ending with the ritual sprinkling, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas with cakes and other foods.
The word "iti" has the sense of inclusion (samuccaya).
However, the consumption of roasted barley flour (saktu) must take place only before the meal, not during it, as this is not established by worldly custom.
As it is said: "One should feed those who are pure and learned in the mantras at all ritual acts" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.15.11).
Thus, the reiteration of the prepared food is for the purpose of enjoining qualities such as cakes and the like. //13//
Thus ends the seventeenth section in the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
The eighteenth section: 1. The ritual for averting [the affliction] of a boy seized by a *bālagraha*.

When a boy has been seized by the dog-demon (*śvagraha*), one who is devoted to austerity should cover him with a net, ring a bell or a small gong, and lead him into the assembly hall through a door other than the main entrance. Having cleared a space for gambling in the middle of the hall, sprinkled it with water, and scattered dice upon it, he should lay the boy down face upward on the dice and sprinkle him with his joined palms using curds mixed with salt, reciting the following [mantras], in the morning, at midday, and in the evening. (ĀpGS 18.1)
There are many child-seizing spirits (*bālagraha*) associated with days, months, years, and so forth.
Among them, he by whom a child is seized and acts like a dog is the Dog-seizing spirit (*śvagraha*). By that [spirit], the boy is seized.
Some say that because of the masculine gender used in the reference, it does not apply to a maiden;
some say the performer endowed with austerity is the father;
others say it refers to whoever [performs the rite].

*Austerity* (*tapas*) refers to celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth; the meaning is that he performed as much austerity as he considered sufficient for success. *Jālam* means a net for catching fish; having covered [the vessel] with it, [he placed] the well-known *kaṃsa* [vessel].

A *kiṅkiṇī* is a particular kind of bell. Causing one of those two to ring—that is, making it produce sound—by means of another person, while he himself takes the prince and causes him to descend to level ground; the meaning is that he does so by opening a path by pushing aside the roof-panels at a place other than the door.

What is that place? It is the assembly hall (*sabhā*). In its center is the gambling area (*adhidevana*), the spot where gamblers play; having raised up that ground and sprinkled it with water, he casts the dice (*akṣān*) there. The dice are the *śārāḥ*.
Others say they are *vibhītaka* fruits;
having spread them out wide, he lays him down on his back and makes him lie there.

Then, one should sprinkle [the ground] with curd mixed with salt using both hands, reciting the subsequent mantras beginning with "kūrkuraḥ sukūrkuraḥ" and ending with "śvānam icchvādan pūruṣaṃ chaṃt.
There is a sprinkling for each mantra.
Among these, the first three are verses (ṛc).
Then two Yajus formulas: "That is truth" and "Having stretched out his arms"; then five Ṛcs beginning with "Bearing a golden disk"; then one Yajus: "The dog."

Thus, these are the eleven mantras. As long as the ritual action is not completed, one should cause either of the two small bells (*saṃsakiṅkiṇī*) to ring. In this manner, this ritual—from the covering with the net up to the sprinkling—should be performed at the three junctions of the day. //1//
That by which a youth is seized, who then barks like a dog or behaves like a dog, is the "dog-seizure" (śvagraha).
One seized by that is "seized by the dog-seizure" (śvagrahagṛhīta).
Bitten by a *piśāca* or a dog;
one endowed with austerity (*tapas*), meaning one engaged in fasting and so forth until the mind is satisfied; the performer of rites for the ancestors and others;
and a net, which is the means for catching fish.

Having struck the bronze gong (*kaṃsa*) and the small bell (*kiṅkiṇī*), and having caused the iron bell (*lohaghaṇṭā*) to ring out by means of an intermediary person, he should clear away the elephants, walls, and other obstacles, thereby making a path.
The gambling ground (*adhidevana*) is where gamblers play.
The *akṣas* are the fruits of the *vibhītaka* tree;
some call them *śāras*.
[One should offer them] with the ten subsequent mantras beginning with "kūrkuraḥ sukūrkuraḥ," which belong to the Yajurveda.
Alternatively, there are eleven [verses].

In that case, the division is as follows: first, three ṛcas; then, the two verses beginning with "tatsatyaṃ yattvendraḥ" and ending with "vigṛhya bāhū," which are treated as a Yajus; then, the five verses beginning with "bibhranniṣkam";
and finally, the eleventh, "śvānam," which is indeed a Yajus alone. This is the division.

And the sprinkling (avokṣaṇa) for all the mantras should be performed only once at the end; some, however, say it should be done with each mantra because it provides a visible benefit. Thus, this entire procedure, beginning with the covering with the net and ending with the sprinkling, is to be performed during the three specific auspicious days (puṇyāha), such as the morning and so forth.
And the sprinkling [of water] up to the final sprinkling is the act of refreshing. //1//
It becomes a remedy. ĀpGs 18.2.
*Agada* means "free from disease";
the meaning is that its purpose is the cessation of disease. What is established by this?
If the prince were to become free from disease through medicine alone, then this [ritual] should not be performed;

otherwise, it would be understood that for the father, in the event of such a disease of the prince, this rite of the soothsayer must necessarily be performed, just like the *gṛhadāheṣṭi* (the sacrifice for a house on fire) and other such rites.
For those who speak thus, there is a fault: even when the disease is pacified by other means—such as another woman seized by consumption—the rite must still be performed.
It may be so. Therefore, this is considered the purpose:
when this rite has been performed in these three sessions, the boy becomes free from disease;
if he does not become so, it must be performed again, joined with austerity. //2//

And here, in the phrase "one who has a conch-like [protuberance]," there is a statement of the result; this is to demonstrate that the instruction for ritual action (karma-upadeśa) is intended for one who desires [a result]—whether that desire is understood from the Vedic text itself or through the sense—and that, by implication, it extends until the accomplishment of the result is realized.
Therefore, [the text says] "one seized by consumption" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 9.10).
In such cases, even in the absence of an explicit statement regarding the fruit, the instruction extends until the desired result is achieved.
Some [commentators] say: "When this rite is performed at the three junctions of the day in this manner, one becomes free from disease."
If it does not occur, then this ritual action must be performed again until the medicine becomes effective.
This is not so, because there is no word indicating that one's own preferred practice [is required]. //2//

Having consecrated the boy Śaṅkhin with the two [verses] beginning with "uttarābhyām" while engaged in austerity, he should pour water from the northern water-pot over his head in the morning, at midday, and in the evening, using the following [verse]. (ĀpGs 18.3)
There is a seizing spirit named Śaṅkha that causes terror among children;
one who is seized by it cries out like a conch shell.

When a child has been seized by that [spirit], one should consecrate him with these two verses, "These two are the counter-foes" (*ete te pratidvaṣī*), and then pour water from a water-pot over his head.
One should consecrate [the disciple] with the following verse, "The seer Bodha, the awakener...
and so forth; in this manner, this ritual of addressing and so on is to be performed at the three times of day. //3//
Śaṅkha is also a Graha; he by whom it is held is "Śaṅkhin," because it sounds like a conch when held.

With the two following [verses], "These two are seen as a pair," and with the next, "The seer Bodha and Prabodha," he should pour water from the head downwards—that is, he should sprinkle him on the head—with a water-pot at the three junctions of the day (trisandhya). //3//
He becomes free from disease. (ĀpGs 18.4)
Its purpose is as stated previously. //4//
The meaning has already been stated. //4//
Now he describes the time at which and the procedure by which the snake-offering (sarpabali) is commenced: 18. Snake-offering—At its commencement, there is a cooked oblation (sthālīpāka).
On the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, at sunset, a sthālīpāka offering is performed.

Now, the ritual known as the *sarpabali* (serpent offering), which is to be performed annually, is taught. Its commencement takes place on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, and its conclusion on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa.
At its beginning, on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa after the sun has set, there is the preparation of a *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice oblation).
Even when there is no conjunction with a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa is called "Śrāvaṇī" by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

Regarding this, two verses state: "Whichever new moon (*darśa*) occurs while the sun is situated in Aries and the other [signs], those twelve months ending with it are traditionally known as Caitra and the rest."
Among those [lunar days], whichever is the full moon is traditionally designated as Caitrī and so forth;
the determination is based on the occasional conjunction with a lunar mansion.
Thus [it is said].
There, having offered the evening oblation, one undertakes the *sthālīpāka* rite; it is stated that other [rites] follow the *pārvaṇa* model, and specifically the *paurṇamāsa* on the full moon day.
Having set aside rice or barley intended for the full moon of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one performs the ritual up to the point of the final sprinkling over the established offering.
Having performed the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire, he should place the vessels in pairs facing downwards, together with *kiṃśuka* flowers and fuel-sticks made of *āragvadha*. //5//

The full moon day conjoined with the asterism Śravaṇa is called Śrāvaṇī; however, even when not so conjoined, it is intended here [to be used] for the regular offering to the serpents (sarpabali), because of its constant occurrence.
The meaning is the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa; it does not refer to the Śravaṇa lunar mansion of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
because "of Śrāvaṇa" serves as a qualifier for the full moon day.
And because of the statement, "On the full moon day" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 2.20),
[this refers] to the lunar months beginning with Caitra.
There are two verses for the purpose of determining the full moon days of Caitra and the others:
"Whichever new moon occurs while the sun is situated in Aries and the subsequent signs, those twelve lunar months ending with that [new moon] are traditionally known as Caitra and the rest."
Among those, whichever is the full moon day is considered to be Caitrī and so forth;
the determination is that this is based on its occasional conjunction with a lunar mansion (nakṣatra).
Thus,
on that full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa,
when the sun has set.

At the conclusion of the evening *homa*, in accordance with the injunction "the wife threshes [the grain]" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 7.2), the *sthālīpāka* must be prepared after the *pratiṣṭhitābhighāraṇa* (the sprinkling of clarified butter over the established oblation). //5//

2. Therein, the *kiṃśuka* oblation: after the *ājyabhāga* offerings as at the *pārvaṇa*, having offered from the *sthālīpāka*, he offers *kiṃśuka* flowers with his joined palms (*añjali*), one by one with each of the subsequent mantras. (ĀpGs 18.6)
It is said, "Everything is like the Pārvaṇa": one offers from the sthālīpāka alone according to the Pārvaṇa rite, but not with *kiṃśuka* flowers.
Therefore, the rule for taking portions (*avadāna*) does not apply to them.
And there is no taking of a portion for the Sviṣṭakṛt from them.
The fuel-sticks made of *kiṃśuka* wood have already been explained.
The mention of the conclusion at the Ājyabhāga offerings is for the purpose of establishing the general ritual procedure (*tantra*).
The oblation from the *sthālīpāka* is performed with the formula, "To Śrāvaṇī Paurṇamāsī, svāhā!
followed by the three subsequent mantras beginning with, "The mosquito has been eaten."
*Kiṃśuka*s are *palāśa* flowers;
others say they are the flowers of the thorny *palāśa* trees.
It is said that "with each mantra" (pratimantram) is intended so that there may be a multiplicity of *kiṃśuka* flowers for each mantra;
otherwise, it would follow that there is an offering (*homa*) of each individual *kiṃśuka*, just as is the case with fuel-sticks (*samidh*). //6//

Then, as in the *pārvaṇa* rite, from the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings— that is, up to the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*)— because the "mouth of the fire" is prescribed for all ritual procedures involving vegetable oblations that follow a common framework (*tantra*).

Having taken portions from the *sthālīpāka* according to rule and offered them with the formula, "To the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, svāhā!", he offers *kiṃśuka* flowers of the *palāśa* tree with each of the three subsequent mantras beginning with, "The mosquito has been eaten."
One offers flowers;
some say these are the flowers of a thorny plant resembling the palāśa.
And these [limbs] are to be collected only during the spring season.
In this context, the ritual treatment of the ointment (añjali) includes the rules for portions such as the under-layer (upastaraṇa) and so forth;
furthermore, even from the remnants of the *kiṃśuka* flowers, one should take the portion for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
Even with the hollowed palms or with a ladle, the application of ointment and collyrium certainly takes place;
for it has been stated that the practice of dharma proceeds according to what is primary. However, another person may perform what is prohibited.
Some maintain that añjali-homas possess exactly those ritual properties that have been stated, just like lāja-homas. //6//
3. The oblation with fuel-sticks of *āragvadha*: with the following three verses, one offers fuel-sticks made of *āragvadha* wood. (ĀpGS 18.7)
The *āragvadha* is the *rājavṛkṣa*,
which has golden-colored flowers and fruits the size of a cubit (*aratni*).
[One should worship it] with the three subsequent *ṛc*s beginning with "O Indra, slay the biting serpent" (*indra iti jahi dandaśūkam*).
He places the fuel-sticks or offers oblations;
in every case, the mantras end with the utterance "svāhā. //7//

Then, with the next three verses beginning with "O Indra, slay the biting one" (RV 10.87.1–3), he offers fuel-sticks made of *āragvadha*— that is, fuel-sticks which are modifications of the *āragvadha* tree— verse by verse. What [is the purpose]?
The connection is with the word "he offers" (*juhoti*).
Therefore, in this case, the renunciation (*tyāga*) must indeed be performed by means of the deities indicated by the wording of the mantras for the fuel-sticks (*samidh*). //7//
There are four oblations of clarified butter;
the subsequent [oblations] are also of clarified butter. (ĀpGs 18.8)
He offers four subsequent oblations of clarified butter with the verse, "That is the truth which [is yours] on the new moon day," and three with the formula, "Homage be to the serpents. //8//
The four following [verses] are: one beginning with "That is the truth which you [spoke] at the Abhīvarta," and three beginning with "Homage be to the serpents. //8//
He undertakes the Jaya and other [oblations]. (ĀpGS 18.9)

Having thus offered these eleven principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) and having offered the *sauviṣṭakṛta* oblation from the very *sthālīpāka*, one then proceeds with the *jaya* and subsequent rites. This statement is intended to make known the primacy of the oblations beginning with the *kiṃśuka*; otherwise, since it is prescribed that "on the full moon day, after sunset, [one offers] the *sthālīpāka*" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.10.2), and because the name of its deity is given as "Paurṇamāsī" on the full moon day and because that rite consists of only two offerings, the primacy of the *kiṃśuka* oblations would not be established.
It would not be understood [as such].

Consequently, having performed everything up to the secondary oblations (upahoma) as in the case of the *pārṇa* sacrifice, it would follow that the offering of *kiṃśuka* and other materials occurs thereafter. //9//

And this statement is for the purpose of attaining victory and other such results, as well as for the purpose of establishing the primary status of the eleven offerings consisting of the *sthālīpāka*, *kiṃśuka* wood, and oblations of clarified butter.
It has already been stated that the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering follows immediately after the *jaya* and other rites. // 9 //
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the northeast direction of the house and having scattered barley meal (saktu) there,

and having performed the rites up to the sprinkling of water (pariṣecana), he— remaining silent and taking the necessary materials— goes out toward the east or north, prepares a sacrificial mound there,
draws three lines toward the east and three toward the north, pours water over them, and [proceeds] with the following [verse].
He pours out parched grain flour.

The statement ending with the sprinkling (pariṣecana) is for the purpose of indicating immediate sequence. What is established by the fact that the exit (upaniṣkramaṇa) occurs immediately after the sprinkling? By this, the displacement (utkarṣa) of such rules as "one should feed a Brāhmaṇa with ghee" is established.

Restraining his speech and making no sound, he prepares the materials: parched grains (*dhānā*), fried grain (*lāja*), unguents (*añjana*), *sthagara*, *uśīra*, and a vessel of water. The ground that has been smeared is the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).
Because of the word "having prepared" (*kalpayitvā*), the preparation must be done by himself; one does not accept what has been prepared by others.
From the word "therein" (tatra), it follows that the abode of Bala is situated in the middle of the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
And there is this verse:
"One should first draw lines toward the east, arranged toward the north, beginning from the south."
Then, one should draw lines facing north, beginning from the west and ending at the east.
Others, however, desire that the laying out begin from the south of the eastern lines (*prācī*).
(The eastern lines run eastward, and likewise the northern lines run northward, because the sequence is intended to be significant.
First the eastern lines, and then the northern ones.
Furthermore, this action called "drawing the lines" has been described as "beginning in the east and ending likewise.
In this case, since beginning in the east is impossible, the lines begin in the north and end in the east.
By this, the drawing of the lines for "wherever the fire may be" is explained.
Having thus drawn the lines, he pours water near them; he offers water to all the divine beings, just as in the offering of rice balls (piṇḍa) to the ancestors.
Then, over those lines, he scatters groats with his hand or with a ladle, using the next verse, "Homage be to the serpents who are on the earth," as seen in the Āśvalāyana [Gṛhyasūtra].
The use of the plural "in them" (tāsu) is for the purpose that Bali may pervade all those lines. //10//
Then, having completed the remainder of the ritual manual,
and having taken up the sacrificial materials such as parched grain flour which are to be employed in the subsequent [rite],
he should go out toward the eastern or northern direction while maintaining silence.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) as a seat, he draws three lines on that seat starting from the south and directed eastward,
and three lines starting from the west and directed northward; having sprinkled water over them, he pours parched grain (saktu) into those six lines in the order they were drawn,
with the verse beginning with "Homage be to the serpents who are terrestrial" and ending with "I shall offer the oblation."
The mantra is recited only once,
and there is no utterance of "svāhā," because it is not an act of offering.
And because it has been stated that even the *namaskāra* offering is characterized by being "proffered" (*pradīna*).
Some [teachers] say: "He pours out [the grain] in such a way that the oblation may reach all the lines simultaneously. (10)
6. Therein is the pouring out of the unbroken grains and so forth:
silently [are offered] the *sampuṣka* grains, parched grains (*dhānā*), fried grains (*lāja*), collyrium, ointment, *sthagara*, and *uśīra*. (ĀpGS 18.11)
He pours these six substances into them: *saṃpuṣka* (flowers), unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), whole grains (*akhaṇḍita-taṇḍula*), *sthagara*, and *uśīra*—these being fragrant materials.

The word "and" (*iti*) has the sense of conjunction; thus, since it might follow that the pouring should be done everywhere with the aforementioned mantra alone, the phrase "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*) serves as a prohibition of the mantra. //11//
"Sampuṣkāḥ" means "well-nourished," specifically referring to fried grains (*dhānā*) made from unbroken rice grains;
"sthagara" refers to a fragrant substance found in the marketplace.
The others are well known.
The word "iti" (thus) has the sense of inclusion.
These six substances he pours silently upon the lines themselves. //11//
After the other *upasthāna* rites, having returned home and sprinkled that [water] there, he then feeds the Brahmins.

Having performed the *upasthāna* with the subsequent [verses] and having sprinkled water, he returns silently without looking back. With the two verses beginning "O white-footed one" (*apaśveta pada*), he sprinkles three times clockwise around the inside of the house or the dwelling with a water-pot;
then he should feed the Brahmins. (ĀpGS 18.12)
In this very manner, having offered this oblation with seven substances,
he then worships that deity of the oblation with the eighteen subsequent mantras beginning with “*Takṣaka veśāleya*.”
The phrase "to them this great offering of food" (*tebhya imaṃ balimahārṣam*) is a modification of the final quarter of the preceding [verse] itself, not a separate mantra;
as he will state later: "the modification of the *bali* mantra.
Having thus performed the worship, he sprinkles water around, pouring it out on all sides.
Because Bali has been offered as the subject under discussion,

he then returns without looking back— that is, not looking behind him— silently and with speech restrained. Having returned, he sprinkles water from a water-pot to the north of the house or the dwelling with these two verses beginning with "O white one, do not step with your foot," and he should feed the Brahmins to the extent of a yoke's length with the remains of the *sthālīpāka* and other offerings.
Thus ends the eighteenth section in the Anākula commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra composed by Śrī Haradatta. //17//
Then, with the eighteen subsequent mantras beginning with "O Takṣaka, son of Veśālī," he worships the deity of the offering (balidevatā) as indicated by the words of the mantras themselves.

And in that context, in the four successive sections beginning with "Ojasvinī by name you are," there is an ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*) from the ten words [of the first section] onwards for the passage beginning with "the protector and the overlord."

Likewise, in the case of the five [verses] beginning with "You are called weapons" (*hetayo nāma stha*), after the eleventh [verse], there is the name [section] beginning with "Homage to you, whose name is Wind" (*vātanāmaṃ tebhyo vo namaḥ*).

As for the phrase "To them I have offered this oblation" (*tebhya imaṃ balimahrṣam*) occurring in the middle, it is a name intended for the purpose of discarding the latter part of the very preceding verse which was for the purpose of offering the oblation (*baliharaṇa*).
For he will state there: "The modification of the *bali* mantra is 'I have taken' (*ahārṣam*)" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 19.4).

Then, having sprinkled water around the offered *bali*, without looking back, silently and with speech restrained, he returns home and performs the rites beginning with the verses "O white one, with thy foot" (*apa śveta padā*) according to the Sūtra.
In that context, the mention of feeding the Brāhmaṇas is for the purpose of establishing the proper sequence.
The pronouncement of blessings is performed by those who have eaten, just as it is in the Upanayana ceremony. //12//
Thus ends the eighteenth section in the Gṛhyatātparyadarśana composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
Nineteenth Section: 8. The Feeding of Parched Grains Remaining from the Bali Offering to the Boys.
They cause the boys to eat the parched grains. (ĀpGs 19.1)

They feed the *dhānā* grains remaining from the *bali* offering to the boys who are capable of eating; the girls also partake of the food, as indicated by the use of the elliptical compound (*ekaśeṣa*). (1)

Until the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, the offering of the bali-oblation is performed every day. Likewise, from this point forward until the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should offer that same bali-oblation consisting of whatever food is available or of barley meal (saktu). ĀpGs 19.2.
They feed the boys with the remnants of the offering of parched grains. Who [are they]? The remnants, by implication. //1//
10. The procedure for the *sthālīpāka* on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa. On the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, after sunset, the *sthālīpāka* is performed. (ĀpGs 19.3)

That which begins with "the offering of the bali, having taken the materials while restraining speech" and ends with "without looking back, silently" (ĀpGṛ 18.10–12)— after this rite, until the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, every four months, one should perform daily the offering of whatever specific food is available, or of groats (*saktu*). Whatever food is prepared in the house for the purpose of eating, that is what should be eaten [in the offering].
The scattering around the house and so forth, however, is a remainder (śeṣa) of the *sthālīpāka* alone, not of the *bali*.
Therefore, this is prescribed here [as part of that].
Although items such as collyrium are for the purpose of adornment and are not edible, nevertheless, "in those [vessels] he pours out groats with the following [verse]."

"Silently, the *saṃpuṣka* parched grains," and so forth; since the sensation [of hunger] is equal for all, and there is an equal mention of them in the mantra, "I shall offer this *bali* to them," therefore all seven are indeed *balidravya* (substances for the *bali* offering).
For all of these, this substitution applies only to the first three;
however, it does not apply to water, because of the difference in the injunction.
"Having brought [the water] near and having sprinkled [it]"—
the word "thus" (evam) is for the purpose of prescribing the time;
just as here, the offering of the bali-oblation is performed after sunset.
"In this same manner, it should be performed even after [the sun] has set," so he thought. However, this was for the purpose of establishing the ritual law;
this offering is indeed of such a nature.
Nor is the establishment of both [rites] achieved by either one alone.
For if the word *eva* were intended for the sake of both, then the *pārvaṇa* would apply at night.
How so? Because the *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Agni arises at night, and the rule "from this point onward" establishes the *pārvaṇa*.

Likewise, if this word were to have both meanings, then [the rule] "this should be done for those who attend after a full year" would imply that the honoring (*apaciti*) occurs at night; for the honoring arises at night during the *samāvartana* ceremony. Therefore, if it has both meanings, both must be stated.
Thus, first of all, there is the offering of the *bali* once at night.

Another says: "The offering of the *bali* is at both times. How so? Because of the statement, "of whatever is fit for eating"; since it is stated "of whatever is fit for eating," the meaning of that is: whenever any food is prepared for the purpose of eating, the [offering] must be performed for each of those at that time.
And there is eating at two times,
because of the statement "eating at [these] two times.
Therefore, just as the Vaiśvadeva— which has arisen when there is an offering of food and oblations for the householder— is performed at two times, so too is this [rite].
And this is clear from the Āśvalāyana [Gṛhyasūtra]: “One should offer the bali with the mantra ‘svāhā to the Sarpadevajanas’ every evening and morning until the *pratyavarohaṇa*” (Āśva. 2.1.14).
In this view, the word *evam* is for the sake of what follows;
the statement “from this point forward” is intended so that no option regarding the substance might be understood in relation to this first offering of the bali.
"Until the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa" is an instruction regarding the time for concluding the offering of oblations (*baliharaṇa*).
If this is so, there is no need for this [statement], since it has already been said:
"He releases it at this point" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 19.5).
He will state [the purpose];
we shall explain its purpose in that very place.
"From this point forward" means after the rite performed on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa.
"Until the Mārgaśīrṣī" means until the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, that is, until the *utsarjana* (the concluding rite).
This refers to the aforementioned offering (*bali*) associated with the barley meal (*saktu*).

Thus, having taken the ritual materials, with speech restrained, facing either the east or the north— and so forth, ending with "returning silently without looking back" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 18.10–12)—
one should offer the *bali* every day at evening according to this procedure.
The word "or" (*vā*) connects with the distant term "that which belongs to the food" (*yadaśanīyasya*).
Because the phrase "of what is to be eaten" (yadaśanīyasya) serves to exclude parched grains (*dhānā*) and other such items;
furthermore, the sprinkling around the house and so forth is a remnant of the *sthālīpāka* sacrifice alone and not of the *baliharaṇa*,
since they occupy different locations.
Some [hold] that there is an offering of oblations at both times, because of the statement "of that which is to be eaten," and because eating—
at both times— is prescribed for food, just as in the case of the Vaiśvadeva, by the rule: "Eating at two times" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.1.20).

Furthermore, according to the statement of Āśvalāyana, "One should offer the bali-oblation every morning and evening until the pratyavarohaṇa," the word *evam* (thus) in the subsequent sūtra serves as the meaning of that [preceding] word *etam* (this), because the word *etam* alone brings about the application of all required dharmas.
Because there is a contradiction in all the words uttered together producing a single unified meaning, [the rule is:
"On the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, after sunset, the *sthālīpāka* [is performed]. //3//

This is explained by the phrase "on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa. The word "thus" (evam) also carries over here; that is, just as this rite is performed on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, so too is it performed on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa.

Therefore, the entire ritual procedure (kalpa) beginning with "as in the Pārvaṇa rite, up to the end of the Ājyabhāga offerings" and ending with "they cause the boys to eat the parched grains" is to be applied here.
The only difference is that the oblation of the *sthālīpāka* is performed with the mantra: "To the Full Moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, svāhā!
The term "on the full moon" is stated again, even though it was already mentioned in the context of "on the full moon of Śrāvaṇa," for the purpose of providing specific instruction.
The mention of the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) does not carry over into this section;
therefore, in the preceding sūtra, "of Mārgaśīrṣa" is not taken as the terminus for the ritual action.
That which was enjoined there by that [preceding] sūtra is not the time [enjoined] by this sūtra.
Therefore, on the day of the full moon in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, there occurs the offering of the bali-oblation of whatever is to be eaten;
however, if [the suffix] denotes time, it would not apply, provided that the vowel *ā* signifies a limit (*maryādā*).
But if it signifies pervasion (*abhividhi*), [it applies].
Even when [the sun] has set, that which is to be eaten belongs to him alone;
and it is accepted that at the time of the *sthālīpāka* rite after sunset, there is an offering of food (*baliharaṇa*) with seven substances, as well as that which is to be eaten during the day.
Therefore, the instruction regarding the previous rite should apply accordingly.
The qualification "on the full moon day" (paurṇamāsyām) is provided so that there may be no designation of [any] time [at random].

And thus, what was stated—that the offering of the bali is performed at both times by means of the word "food" (aśanīya)—remains established. It is said "when the sun has set" (astamite) so that it might not occur during the day.
It has been stated that the word "evam" (thus) possesses no power with respect to either the attainment of the dharma or the prescription of time. //3//
Because there is a requirement for this, the word "evam" (in the same manner) is carried over [from the previous rule].
Just as the *sthālīpāka* was performed on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, so too must it be performed on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa after sunset.

The meaning is that the entire ritual procedure, beginning with "the wife threshes [the grain]" and ending with the consumption of the parched grains (*dhānā-prāśana*), is to be executed. However, regarding the *sthālīpāka* oblation, the specific modification is: "To the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa, svāhā! //3//
"I have taken [it]"—this is the modification of the *bali* mantra. (ĀpGs 19.4)
The modification (*sannāma*) consists of changing "I shall carry" (*hariṣyāmi*) to "I have carried" (*ahārṣam*).

Although this modification is already recited within that very mantra, nevertheless, in the absence of this specific statement, there would be no separate application of the fourth quarter of the *baliharaṇa* mantra; therefore, since it consists of four quarters, the rule for the modification is now commenced.

This [verse] consists of three feet; this supreme third foot is recited here because it is the time for its specific application (*viniyoga*), and not previously. Furthermore, this entire rite, ending with the consumption of the *dhānās*, is designated by the term *sthālīpāka*; this is what is being demonstrated. The purpose [of mentioning this now] is for the subsequent sūtra concerning the offering of the *bali*. //4//
This has already been explained. //4//
11. The offering of the snake-oblation (*sarpabali*).
One offers this here. (ĀpGs 19.5)
In this rite known as Mārgaśīrṣa, one offers this bali-oblation.

By the word "thus" (evam), the entire procedure prescribed for the Śrāvaṇī is extended [to this rite]; consequently, the offering of the bali is obtained as a subsidiary part of this sthālīpāka as well.
In that case, the term "in the Śrāvaṇī" would be understood as the temporal limit.

Therefore, the rule "I have taken [the portion]" applies specifically to the remainder of Mārgaśīrṣa; this is for the purpose of prohibiting [the taking] of the remainder of Balih. As for the phrase "until the full moon of Mārgaśīrṣa," however, it is for the purpose of prescribing the *asāna* (placing) of the *balih* from the remainder of Śrāvaṇa. //5//
When this dismissal has been performed here,
he offers this oblation (*bali*) being made for the day;
yet this is not a final dismissal.
Because, by virtue of its permanence, the snake-sacrifice must be performed every year. //5//
For one who has not maintained the sacred fires, there is the Āgrayaṇa offering.
The root *i* here has the sense of "eating. That in which the first (*agra*) moving (*ayana*) occurs is the *āgrayaṇa*.
Although *agrāyaṇa* would be the expected form, the lengthening of the vowel is a Vedic anomaly (*chāndasa*).

That ritual act will now be described. In this context, the mention of one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) is for the purpose of prohibiting its combination with the *āgrayaṇa* rite performed according to the Śrauta tradition by one who has maintained the fires (*āhitāgni*) and possesses the *aupāsana* fire. Consequently, a combination [of both rites] occurs during the *pārvaṇa* and other such ceremonies.
In that case, if the Smārta rite is performed, there is spiritual merit (*abhyudaya*).
There is no transgression in its non-performance.
By the name "Āgrayaṇa," the ritual details of the Śrauta Āgrayaṇa are obtained through the rule:
"One who has established the sacred fires (āhitāgni) shall not eat of the new grain until he has performed the Āgrayaṇa."
(Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 6.29.2) One should sacrifice with *śyāmāka* millet in the rainy season,
with rice in the autumn,
and with barley in the spring.
And as in the case of "with seasonal bamboo and barley. //6//
The word "it is taught" (*upadiśyate*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

Here, the mention of one who has not established the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*) is for the purpose of showing that even for an *āhitāgni* who has performed the fire-establishment with remnants, this Smārta Āgrayaṇa is not to be combined with the Śrauta [rite].
However, in the case of the *aupāsana* oblation and so forth, there is indeed a combination with the *agnihotra* oblation and so forth.
The Piṇḍapitṛyajña and the monthly Śrāddha are to be performed in combination by both those who have maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni) and those who have not;
for there is the statement: "This very [rite], as thus prescribed, is [performed] by one who has not maintained the fires on the Āvasathya fire" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 6.28).
Having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors at the waning of the moon, a Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires should perform the Piṇḍānvāhāryaka Śrāddha every month.
And because of the statement of Manu:

"Thus [one should perform the rites] for one who has established the sacred fires" (MaSmṛ 3.122), even for one who is dependent on others, the monthly *śrāddha* must indeed be performed, excluding the *homa*.

However, according to the view of Upadhyāya, for one who has established the fires with remnants (*saśeṣādhānin*) and for one who maintains the *āhitāgni*, there is a cessation of the *pārvaṇa* rites and the *aupāsana-homa*.
Because one's purpose is fulfilled by the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and the Agnihotra,
and because there is a contradiction due to the identity of time;
"Āgrayaṇa" is thus the name of a ritual act.

By which ritual action one first causes the nine substances to reach the gods; or rather, by performing that very action, the *āgrayaṇa*—the first journey—becomes the attainment of the consumption of new grain. //6//
19. The Āgrayaṇa Sthālīpāka:
First, the performance of the Āgrayaṇa rite with cooked grains of new rice and so forth;
thereafter, the procedure for digging up a lump of cooked rice at the household stūpa.

Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* of new grain and offered oblations to the deities of the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice, with *Sviṣṭakṛt* as the fourth, he should fill his mouth with rice grains, swallow them, sip water for purification, form a ball of the cooked rice, and deposit it upon the roof-peak of the house with the following Yajus formula. (ĀpGS 19.7)

Having cooked fresh rice or barley on the *aupāsana* fire, having poured clarified butter over it once it is established, having kindled the fire, strewn grass around it, and silently sprinkled water all around, he cleanses the ladle (*durvī*) and offers four oblations from the *sthālīpāka*,
taking portions for each, to the deities of the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice with Sviṣṭakṛt as the fourth: "To Indra and Agni, svāhā!"
Or [he offers] to Agni and Indra;
then to all the gods,
then to Heaven and Earth.
"To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt"—
the sprinkling around is as before;
this much alone is the ritual action, and nothing else.
Because there was no other means of sustenance,
some performed all the tasks;
then, he filled his mouth with rice grains.
In this context, the word "taṇḍula" (rice) refers to the grains of boiled rice (*pulāka*),
as in the expression "the rice-grains on the stirring-spoon.
Therefore, the filling is done by taking portions from the remainder of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
Others desire only pure rice grains;
having ground them and eaten them, and having sipped water (ācamya), he then carefully prepares a lump of cooked rice.

Having prepared it so that it does not crumble while being pierced into the stūpa, he should pierce it into the house-stūpa from above with the following Yajus mantra: "Thou art the Supreme Lord (Aparameṣṭhin). With this, he should pierce it upwards.
Just as it falls upon a stūpa—
the stūpa being the backbone— "viddhet" is a corrupt reading for "viddhyet."

Or it is according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*). Since the result is already established by the very mention of the *āgrayaṇa* offering, the specific statement "of new grains" is intended so that for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), there may be only a *sthālīpāka* (pot-cooking) of new grains; thus, other rituals seen in the Śrauta texts shall not apply here.
The mention of the *sviṣṭakṛt* as the fourth [offering] is for the purpose of excluding Soma;
by this, the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice of *śyāmāka*, *veṇuka*, and *veṇuyava* grains takes place even for one who has not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*). //7//

Having prepared the *sthālīpāka* (cooked rice offering) from fresh grains of either *vrīhi* rice or barley according to the injunctions such as "the wife threshes [the grain]," and having performed the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire up to the end of the *agnimukha*, he offers oblations to the principal deities of the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice as prescribed in the *Śrauta* ritual—those for whom Sviṣṭakṛt is the fourth.
Among these, he first offers, saying: "Svāhā to Indra and Agni," or "Svāhā to Agni and Indra."

Then [he offers] with "Svāhā to the Viśve Devas," then with "Svāhā to Heaven and Earth," and then with "Svāhā to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt"; and in all cases, according to the specific rule for the portioning of the sacrificial material.
Now follows the conclusion of the remainder of the Tantra, beginning with "Then, of the two ointments" (*atha lepayoḥ*).
An objection is raised: In the Vedic [text], it says, "He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni of old rice-grains," so Agni is the first deity.
How then, in this case, can there be the first oblation to Indra-Agni or to Agni-Indra?
True; however, Agni Āṅgirasa is merely a subordinate deity (āṅgadevatā) there, not the principal deity (pradhānadevatā);
and by the phrase "to the deities of the Āgrayaṇa," there is an understanding of only the principal deities.

Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, fire (*agni*) is not the primary element, because in the passage "The *āgrayaṇa* belongs to Indra and Agni for the sake of the offering," only Indra, Agni, and others are taught; and since the *aindrāgna* [offering] is the principal primary, the rule of the *tantra* (shared ritual procedure) is justified by the fact that it is the *tantra* of the new moon sacrifice (*amāvāsyā*).
Regarding the statement, "There are two [verses] for the *daśahavis* and two for the *sviṣṭakṛt*," this is because there is an absence of the *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses dedicated to Agni.

Furthermore, the rule here that "the *sviṣṭakṛt* follows the fourth" is intended to prevent the optional commonality of ritual procedure (*samānatantratā*) between the *vrīhi-āgrayaṇa* and the *śyāmāka-āgrayaṇa*, as occurs in the Śrauta rites.
Consequently, for those who have not maintained the sacred fires (*anāhitāgni*), the ritual procedures must indeed be distinct (*nānātantra*).
During the rainy season on the full-moon day, the *Āgrayaṇa* sacrifice of *śyāmāka* grain must be performed;
for even though the substance, deity, and time are not explicitly mentioned, they are understood from the very name "Āgrayaṇa," and there is no contradiction in accepting these required elements.
By this same principle, the *Āgrayaṇa* of rice (*vrīhi*) is performed in the autumn.
And in the spring, [the offering] is on the very *parvan* day of barley.

Some maintain that, because of the mention of the *Sviṣṭakṛt* as the fourth [offering], there is no *Āgrayaṇa* at all for one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) regarding *śyāmāka* and other grains or bamboo-barley.
That is not so; for if one were to admit the eating of new *śyāmāka* and other grains by one who has not performed the *Āgrayaṇa*, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
And because the meaning of the statement regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* being the fourth has already been explained.
Then, when the remainder of the ritual manual has been completed, he fills the mouth— that is, the opening— with rice grains;
and these rice grains are uncooked,
as this is well known.
Others say they are boiled (*śṛta*), because of the scriptural observation: "The grains which [remain] in the stirring-spoon.
According to the view that they are boiled, one takes from the remnants of the oblation—which require disposal—and fills the mouth.
Then, having swallowed the rice grains, he sips water; "sips" means he drinks it once.
And this injunction for sipping water is an auxiliary part of the ritual action, because of the context.

Even the sipping of water for purification (ācamana), though its purpose is already established, must indeed be performed as prescribed by other scriptures, being endowed with numerous ritual details such as "sitting down, one should sip water three times" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.16.2).
Then, he forms a rice-ball (piṇḍa) from the remainder of the oblation of cooked rice; he makes it very firm so that, while being rolled out, it does not break apart.
Then, with the Yajus formula "Thou art the Supreme Lord" (*aparameṣṭhy asi*), he should throw that lump upwards;
he should cast it so that it falls upon the backbone of the stupa of the house.
The elision of the letter *y* is a Vedic (archaic) usage. //7//
20. The descent for the winter season—the descent for the winter season. (ĀpGs 19.8)
Having descended, they lie down upon a new grass mat.
Having descended with the subsequent Yajus formula, they lie down on their right sides using the following [formulas]. (ĀpGS 19.9)
The rite called *hemantapratyavarohaṇa* (the descent from the bed in winter) is an obligatory duty to be performed every year;
it is now taught: when winter has arrived, having left the couch, one sleeps on a bed of *palāśa* leaves.
The term *hemantapratyavarohaṇa* refers to the descent from the couch (*khaṭvā*) in relation to the winter season (*hemanta*).
After that, it should be performed with the Yajus formula: "May winter descend upon us.
What, then, is its time?
It is when the night has dawned and winter begins while autumn departs.
That night is the time for this [rite].
Another says: "The *pratyavarohaṇa* takes place on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, after sunset and after the *sthālīpāka*, because it is well-known for all [rites].
Others maintain that the phrase "on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa" is to be supplied here as well.

Having descended there, they lie down with their right sides underneath— meaning they sleep on their right sides— upon a bed prepared with nine fresh Palāśa leaves, using the five subsequent mantras beginning with "pratikṣatra.
This includes the householder, his dependents such as sons and others, and the unmarried daughters.
This is a restrictive injunction (niyamavidhi) concerning sleeping: that which is sleeping at night for the purpose of dreaming must be performed on this very night alone.
The *pratyavarohaṇa* rite should also be mentioned at that same time. //8//
The remainder of the sentence is that the ritual performed in the winter season after having performed [the other rites] is taught as the rite named *hemantapratyavarohaṇa*.

From this very etymological name, and from the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "The winter has descended upon us," it is inferred as the injunction that this rite is to be performed in the first night of the winter season; some, however, hold that it should be performed on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, after sunset (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 19.3).
Because of this continued application, the following must be performed therein. //8//

With the subsequent Yajus mantra, "May winter not descend upon us," the householder and his wife and others, having ascended the new layer of straw (navasvastara), descend from the straw-mat during the winter; that is to say, they form the intention: "Having left the straw bed for as long as the winter lasts, let us sleep only upon the new layer of straw."
Furthermore, it is not the case that they first ascend the *khaṣṭvā* for an unseen purpose and then descend onto the *svastara* with a mantra;
rather, immediately thereafter, with the first five subsequent mantras beginning with "pratikṣatre," [they descend] upon the *navasvastara*—
a bed prepared with nine *palāśa* leaves— lying on their right sides.
Placing their right sides downward and with their heads turned toward the east, they lie down. //9//
Furthermore, by means of two further sūtras, he specifies the very manner of lying down—the method of lying down:
"The father lies on the right side, the mother on the left; in this same way for the remaining [sons], each elder brother lies immediately next to the one before him. (ĀpGS 19.10)
Among those lying down, he who is the father lies on the right side and she who is the mother lies on the left;

their status as right and left is relative to one another. Regarding this, Āśvalāyana says: "Together with his wife, [the husband] should lie with his head toward the east and facing the north" (Āśvalāyanagṛhyasūtra 2.3.6).
And [it is said]: "Those who know the mantras should mutter the mantras" (Aśvagṛhya 2.3.9). //9//
Of the remaining ministers, whichever son or daughter is the eldest sits to the right of the father; the next in order sits to the left of the mother.
The third sits to the right of the first, the fourth to the left of the second, and so on.
They maintain that the one who cannot be led [the youngest] sits only to the left of the mother, according to seniority.
All those who know the mantras, facing eastward with their faces turned toward the north, should mutter the mantras;
the mention of "immediately" is for the purpose of indicating immediate succession. //10//
"Father to the south, mother to the north"—thus, the status of south and north is relative to one another.

Among the remaining [relatives], such as sons and so forth, whichever is the eldest—whether son or daughter—is to the south and immediately adjacent; whichever is younger is to the north and immediately adjacent.

Because of the extension [of the rule] by the word "thus" (evam), this is what is meant: he who is the eldest of all is the immediate successor of his mother; he who is the second eldest is the immediate successor of the eldest of all, and so forth.
Some say that the eldest son is on the father's right side, the next eldest on the mother's left, and so forth. //10//
Having risen, there is the touching of the earth; having sat down, they touch the earth with the two subsequent [verses]. ĀpGs 19.11.

Having thus lain down and slept for a short while, he should rise from his bed with the verb *jahati* preceded by *sam* (*saṃjihāna*). It is seen [in scripture]: "While lying down he is Kali; but as he rises, he is Dvāpara" (Aitareya Brāhmaṇa Pañcikā 7).
Having risen and sipped water, they touch the earth with the two subsequent verses, namely "O Earth, be pleasant" (*syonā pṛthivi*) and "O Baḍittha," both of which concern the pleasant earth.
And in this case, there is recitation only for those who are fit for the utterance of mantras, but not even for those who are without mantras. //11//
In this manner, the laying down [of the child] and so forth is performed three times. (ĀpGs 19.12)
The meaning is that the lying down, the recitation, and the touching should be performed three times with the accompaniment of mantras;
however, the descent [from the couch] is done only once.

"When the sun has risen, having muttered the hymns to the Sun and the auspicious prayers (*svastyayana*), having prepared food, having fed the Brahmins, and having caused them to pronounce auspicious blessings" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 4.6.18).
And on this point, Tāṇḍya says: //12//
In this manner, these acts beginning with the settling [of the fire] must be performed three times accompanied by the respective mantras.

Furthermore, since there is a rule regarding auspicious days (*puṇyāha*) stating that "rites should be performed during the northern course of the sun, during the bright fortnight, and on auspicious days" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 1.2), how is this to be understood?
Is it taught that this should be performed at night because it is contrary to that?
It is said: here, lying down is not being enjoined, such that this would have to take place during the day on an auspicious day.
What then? It is precisely with reference to that lying down at night which is prompted by natural desire (*rāga*) that the mantras and restrictive rules (*niyama*) are enjoined;
just as the acts of spreading the under-layer (*upastaraṇa*), the *prāṇāgnihotra*, and so forth, are enjoined with reference to eating which is prompted by natural desire.
Or, for example: "The husband and wife should eat before the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) is brought, [thinking] 'the plants are full of sap'" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 4.2.3), and so on.
Therefore, it is logical that this rite should take place at night;

furthermore, there is the feeding of Brahmins at the conclusion, according to the injunction: "In all rites, one should feed those who are pure and accompanied by the sacred mantras" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.15.11). //12//

Now, the eternal *pākayajña* named Īśānabali, which follows the sequence of the traditional recitation of mantras, is being explained. Its time is established by the general rules as being during the northern solstice (*udagayana*) and so forth; for here, unlike the *sarpabali*, no specific time is prescribed. Consequently, this rite is not to be repeated every year.
This is because of the maxim that "when it has been performed once, the purpose of the scripture has been fulfilled.
Some maintain that, according to another scripture, there is an option between repeating the rite every year and performing it only once;
likewise, from yet another scripture, it should be understood that the performance is for the sake of pacifying cattle or for the sake of desiring sons and so forth.
21. The Īśāna-bali: 1. Cooking the *sthālīpāka* (offering of cooked rice) and, having gone outside the village, preparing the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*).

Having cooked a *sthālīpāka* offering for Īśāna and one for Kṣetrapati, he goes out toward the east or the north, prepares a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), and performs the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire. (ĀpGs 19.13)

Now, the domestic sacrifice (pākayajña) called Īśānabali will be described; it is commonly known as the Śūlagava. In that rite, the immolation of a cow is enjoined in other scriptures, but for us, it is merely a cooked rice-offering (sthālīpāka), because of the restrictive rule that this much constitutes the place for the immolation of the cow.

And this consecration of the person is obligatory; it is neither optional nor occasional, because neither optionality nor occasionality is mentioned in the scripture. Furthermore, it is to be performed once, as there is no connection with a specific time.
For repetition occurs in connection with time,
due to the repeated association with that time.
But what is its time?

"Either in autumn or in spring," according to another scriptural authority; "it should be performed under the constellation Ārdrā," and for us, there is the restriction of the northern solstice and so forth.
In that regard, when the eighth lunar day of the bright fortnight in the month of Phālguna coincides with the Ārdrā nakṣatra, that is his primary time [for the sacrifice].
Intending to sacrifice at that time, he cooks a *sthālīpāka* in the domestic fire (*aupāsana*) for the god Īśāna, having dedicated one portion to him.
And another [offering] to Kṣetrapati.

Together with them, having gone out from the village toward the eastern or northern direction to where he intends to sacrifice, he should prepare there a single sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) sufficient for a place of sacrifice (*devayajana*) and two temples for the gods; then, having scraped out the fire-pit (*agnyāyatana*) in the eastern half of that mound, [he should place] the fire.
Having established [the fires], one proceeds with the ritual procedure beginning with the kindling;
there are pairs of vessels and enclosing-sticks. //13//

Since the meaning of the verbal root *īś* is "to rule" (*aiśvarye*), he whose sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is unsurpassed is *Īśāna*; the meaning is that he is Maheśvara, who is to be worshipped through the meditation on the *Praṇava* and other means.

For that *Īśāna*, having cooked a *sthālīpāka* (pot-offering) in the domestic fire according to the *Pārvaṇa* rite—sufficient for the oblations (*homa*) and so forth—he performs the ritual up to the point of the established sprinkling of clarified butter (*pratiṣṭhitābhighāraṇa*).
Some, having prepared three portions of the offering and brought fire to them, establish it outside and perform the pouring of clarified butter over the three;
by that method, he cooks the *sthālīpāka* for Kṣetrapati on the common fire (*laukikāgni*),
because it is not to be offered into the sacred fire.

Then, having taken the necessary materials according to the requirements, having gone out from the village toward the east or the north, and having prepared a leveled sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) and so forth away from the fire-shed (*agnikuṭī*) and other such places, he should establish the fire upon that ground according to the rule: "Wherever there is fire" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.1.23).

One undertakes the ritual procedure beginning with the kindling of the fire; and it has already been stated that the performance of the ritual procedure is for the sake of establishing the proper sequence. //13//
2. Construction of two huts behind the fire:
having constructed two huts to the west of the fire. (ĀpGS 19.14)
Then, to the west of the fire, he constructs two huts for the god and the goddess;
they may have doors facing west or doors facing east, with the northern hut being to the south and the southern hut to the north, so that the sequence ends toward the north.
Having fashioned images of both the god and the goddess. //14//
Thus ends the nineteenth section in the Anākula, a commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
When the conclusion of the fire-rite has been performed, one should construct two huts to the west of the fire, with doors facing east and arranged from north to south. //14//
Thus ends the nineteenth section in the Gṛhyatātparyadarśana composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
The twentieth section:
Invoking Īśāna in the southern hut.
With the following [verse], he invokes Īśāna in the southern [hut]. (ĀpGs 20.1)
Having fashioned an image of Jayanta in the very sky in the middle, he invokes Īśāna in the south with the subsequent Ṛc, namely "ā tvā vahanti.

Since the procedures beginning with the kindling of the fire have already been stated, and since the principal oblations are yet to be described, only the construction of the hut takes place at the conclusion of the two portions of clarified butter (ājyabhāga). //1//
Then, with the following verse, "May they bring you hither," he invokes Īśāna at the southern corner;
he should meditate, thinking, "May you come here in embodied form. //1//
To the north of the goddess and in the middle for Jayanta; with worldly speech, [he should place] Mīḍhuṣī to the north. ĀpGs 20.2.
In the middle, [he places] Jayanta.
With ordinary speech, he invokes the goddess Mīḍhuṣī in the north;
in the center, he invokes Jayanta with ordinary speech: "Come, O Jayanta!"
Or one may say, "I invoke Jayanta.
Jayanta is Skanda.
If the word "laukikī" (worldly) were not stated, the invocation would result in being performed with the preceding mantra. //2//
Likewise, in the northern wall, with worldly speech, he invokes Mīḍhuṣī, the wife of Īśāna, saying, "Come, O Bountiful One," and likewise Indra, whose function is victory. //2//

In the space between the two huts, he invokes Jayanta, the son of Indra, or Skanda, with the mantra "Come, Jayanta. Although not explicitly stated in this sūtra, it is appropriate that one provides seats for those who have been invoked. //3//
5. The offering of water for the feet and other honors to those who have been invited,
the principal oblations, and the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.

Having offered water as it was brought, having prepared three portions of cooked rice, having brought fire forward, and having caused [the sacrificer] to touch the northernmost portion, he should offer oblations from each of the portions of cooked rice with the subsequent [verses] according to their respective order; then, having taken portions from all [portions], he should offer the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation to Agni with the subsequent *yajus*.
(With the specific mantra, at the specific locations, and in the specific sequence by which the invocation was enjoined, he offers the *arghya* waters for those respective deities.
These are prepared in separate vessels because they constitute *arghya*, and are joined with flowers and unbroken rice (*akṣata*). [He says: "O Īśāna, this is your *arghya*."
"Victory! Here is the *arghya* for you.

Then, having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, incense, and lamps, he takes portions from the *sthālīpāka* and prepares three portions of cooked rice in three vessels: for the Goddess, for Skanda, and for the God—for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*) and for the offering (*upahāra*).
He leaves a large quantity of cooked rice in the pot for the purpose of feeding the Brahmins.

Then, having brought those portions of rice near the fire, he places them upon the sacrificial grass (barhis) to the west of the fire—at the southern, northern, and middle points. Upon their being thus established, the sprinkling of clarified butter (abhighāraṇa) takes place.
Then, with the three subsequent mantras, he causes [the bride] to touch the three portions of cooked rice as they were brought;
he effects the relationship between master and servant with the subsequent mantras beginning with "Let the Bountiful One touch me."
He touches [the portions] according to their respective deities, as in the case of the portion for Agni with the formula, "This is for Agni.
Having thus caused [them] to be touched, he then offers the seventeen principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) with the subsequent mantras, each to its own rice dish.
The meaning is that he offers from whichever rice dish there is a connection with whichever deity, as indicated by the act of touching.
There, from the *odana* of Deva, [he offers] with the eight [verses] beginning with "To Bhava, to Deva... and so forth;
from the *odana* of Mīḍhuṣī, with the eight [verses] beginning with "To the wife of the god Bhava, svāhā";
and from the *odana* of Jayanta, with [the verse] "To Jayanta, svāhā."
Having thus offered the principal oblations, he then takes portions from all [the offerings] and sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the subsequent Yajus formula, "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, well-offered.
It is said that one should take portions from all [the offerings] so that there may not be a separate Sviṣṭakṛt offering for each individual portion of rice.
Although this [rite of] worship and so forth is mentioned immediately after the Sviṣṭakṛt, [it is to be performed here].
Nevertheless, because the word "upa" (after/along) is heard in the injunction "he offers the Jaya and other oblations," the Jaya and subsequent offerings take place after the principal oblations;
and the worship (upasthāna) and so forth occur at the end of the sprinkling (pariṣecana). //3//
Now,

just as they were married and invited here, in that same order he offers the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the other items individually with their respective names followed by "namaḥ," giving them with great devotion.
Since the mention of "water" is intended as an illustration, the instruction is that he offers everything up to the lamp.

Then, having taken three portions of cooked rice from the *sthālīpāka* for Īśāna, he prepares them in three vessels: one for Īśāna, the *īḍhuṣī*, and the *jayanta*s for the purpose of the oblation and the food offering (*bali*);
and in the pot itself, he leaves a large quantity of rice for the purpose of feeding the Brahmins.
Then, having brought those portions of rice near the fire, he places them to the west of the fire.
Then, with the three subsequent mantras beginning with "Let the Bountiful One touch [me]," he causes [the sacrificer] to touch [the waters] respectively, according to the respective deities.
And the purpose of this rule for touching is to convey the connection of the two latter *odana* offerings— which have been divested of the deity Iṣāna— with other deities named Mīḍhuṣī and Jayantī,
just as in the case of the *Iṣṭi* for prosperity (*abhyudayeṣṭi*) and similar rites.

In the first [offering], however, because the word *mīḍhvān* denotes Īśāna, one establishes the connection with Īśāna. Then, with the seventeen subsequent mantras beginning with "To the god Bhava," he offers the principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*) from each respective portion of cooked rice— taking portions according to the specific characteristics (*liṅga*) of whichever deity each rice belongs to— in accordance with the rules for the *parvan* offerings.
In that context, the phrase "for the sake of existence" (*bhavāya*) refers to the cooked rice of Īśāna by means of eight [verses];

and this is appropriate because words such as *bhava* and *śarva* denote Īśāna. However, the phrase "of the god Bhava" (*bhavasya devasya*) refers to the offering of Mīḍhvāṃs by means of eight [verses].
"Jayantāya" means for Jayanta, [the portion] from his own [rice].

Then, having taken portions from all three types of rice according to the rule for the *avaddāna* (cutting-off) of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, and having combined them, he offers to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt with the subsequent *yajus*: "To Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, well-offered, offered.
With this, he sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.

Therefore, the statement "cutting from all sides" is intended to dispel the doubt that, as in the case of the *āgrayaṇa* sacrifice or the monthly *śrāddha*, one should perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering after cutting only once.
6. He gives leaves with boiled rice to the deities.

Having approached them from the north with the following *yajus*, he gives two leaves with boiled rice for each deity using the subsequent formulas, ten to the divine armies (*devasenās*) and ten to those that follow them. (ĀpGs 20.5)
And there is the worship of Mahādeva with the subsequent Yajus mantra, "May there be well-being for us from Pūrṇamukha";
"Pūrṇamukha" is also a designation for him alone.
With full oblations, his mouth full,

he worships with the subsequent mantras beginning with "O householder, touch [the water]," and so forth; with these eighteen [mantras], he gives the rice-filled leaves to the deities known from the mantras.
In that rite, he gives two leaves with each mantra for the first seven [mantras].
With the eighth mantra, saying "to the ten divine armies," he indicates the deities understood from the mantras.
Therein, "Gṛhapati" is considered a designation for Mahādeva, as he protects the houses (*gṛhān pāti*).
And there is another mantra: "Obeisance to Rudra, the Lord of the Dwelling.
Therefore, with this [mantra], two leaves are offered to the deity from that very same cooked rice.
The goddess Gṛhapī—
Therefore, with this mantra, one should give [the offering] from that very cooked rice to the Goddess.
Ghoṣiṇī and the others are all the hosts who are the attendants of the God.
From them as well, near the temple of the gods, there were two leaves from which his boiled rice was prepared;
[these were offered] to the hosts of deities and spirits.
From those too, it was like [the offering] to the hosts of serpents.

From the ten *uttarābhyaḥ*—the higher deities understood from the subsequent mantra beginning with "those which have been declared"—ten portions are taken from the very same mantra, from the rice of the god himself. //4//
With the subsequent Yajus mantra, "May there be well-being for us, O full-mouthed one," he circumambulates Agni and Īśāna.
And this [mantra] is used according to its recited text immediately after the Sviṣṭakṛt offering.

Then follows the completion of the remainder of the ritual procedure (tantra), beginning with the words "of the two smears" and so forth; for the author of the Bhāṣya states: "Having performed [the rites] up to the final sprinkling (pariṣecana), the offering of the leaf (parṇadāna) is made."

Some say that the conclusion of the remaining portion of the ritual consists of the attendant services (*upasthāna*) and so forth. Then, having prescribed in general that one gives sacrificial leaves from the respective portions of cooked rice with the seven [verses] beginning with "O Householder, touch [them]" (*gṛhapo 'paspṛśa*), he specifies: "two leaves with each mantra."
Now, with the words "ten," and so forth, he sets aside the statement "two by two.
The *devasenās* are the armies of the god Īśāna;
having taken ten leaves from the very same cooked rice of the god, he gives them in the southern hut.
Likewise, there are ten leaves for the northern divine armies (*devasenā*).
In the subsequent mantra, "those that are named and those that are unnamed," these northern divine armies are characterized by two qualities. //5//
As before, [the rites are performed] with the subsequent [mantras].
As before, with the four subsequent mantras beginning with "dvārāpo 'spṛśe," two parched grains (parma) each should be offered; the meaning is that this is done one by one, two at a time.
In this context, Dvārāpa is the male deity and the door-guardian (dvārapāla), while Dvārāpī is the female deity and the door-guardianess (dvārapālā).
The attendants of the Goddess were also wanderers;
Niṣiṅgin was the name of Jayanta.
To them, he gave gifts of cooked rice there and there, each according to his own [rank]. //5//

Just as previously, with the mantras beginning with "Touch the door-posts" (*dvārau prokṣasva*), he gave two leaves each from his own portions of boiled rice between the southern and northern walls while reciting the respective mantras, so too should he give them now with the four subsequent mantras beginning with "Touch the door-posts" (*dvārā prokṣasva*).
Now, the ritual procedure: when the sprinkling around [the fire] has been completed, one says "O householder, touch water! toward the south; "O housewife, touch water! toward the north;
and "O you who possess voices! in the middle.
And then, "the panting ones" [are assigned] to the south;
"the searching ones" to the north.
In the middle [of the leaf], [he places] the verse beginning with "prapuṇvantaḥ"; then, on the southern [leaf], the verse beginning with "samaśnantaḥ".
There are two leaves for each of these sections.
Then, on the southern [branch] itself, there are ten leaves with the words "The divine armies" (*devasenāḥ*).
Likewise, there are ten leaves with the words "Those which are proclaimed" (*yā ākhyātāḥ*).
Then, on that very same [branch], once again, there are two leaves with the words "Touch the door-posts" (*dvārāpopaspṛśa*).
"‘Through the gate’—two in the north; ‘The followers’—two in the middle;
‘O you with the quiver’—two in the south.
Although some of these mantras here have unexpressed gender markers or plural gender markers, [they are to be applied accordingly].
Nevertheless, the deities are indeed Jayanta and Īśāna;
and the authority for this is the observation of the indicative marks (*liṅga*) in the mantras: "gṛhapati," "dvārāpati," and "niṣaṅgin."

Regarding the phrase "ten [times] more than the ten divine armies (*daśadevasenā*)," according to the statement of the author of the Sūtra, the "divine armies" (*devasenā*) are indeed deities who are the armies of the god Īśāna. Furthermore, even the worship of those such as sons and servants who have become objects of one's sense of possession is simply the worship of the ancestors and the master.
Because when there is worship of the son and others, the mental perception arises that "I myself have been worshipped" by the father and others;
for this very reason, the *Jāteṣṭi* sacrifice possesses a combined entitlement (*saṃvalitādhikāra*).
Therefore, in this case, the giving of rice from the deity [Dhātṛ] to the Devasenās is not contradictory.
