Some [hold] that the deities are indeed those indicated by the words of the mantras; therefore, [the offering is made] to the deity Vāstoṣpati, because of the Śruti text: "Rudra, indeed, is Vāstoṣpati" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.4.10).
"Gṛhapī" is for the Goddess;
"Ghoṣiṇaḥ," however, with five [verses], is for the attendants of the God who move with the *sarṣaga* [birds],
because it is explicit in the Āśvalāyana [Śrautasūtra].
Then, with the two [verses] beginning with "devasenāḥ," [one offers] to the divine armies;
with "dvārāpā" to the door-keeper of the deity;
and with "dvārapī" to the female door-keeper of the deity.
The term "anvāsārin" (follower) refers to the attendants of that very goddess;
the term "niṣaṅgin" (quiver-bearer) refers to Jayanta, because he too, having been invoked, must be provided with an offering. //6//
7. Hanging [the food] on the tip of a tree:
Having formed a ball of boiled rice and placed it in a leaf-cup, he hangs it on a tree with the subsequent Yajus formula. (ĀpGS 20.7)

Then, having formed a ball from that very same boiled rice with both hands, making it firm, and having placed it in a hollow made of sewn leaves, he suspends it on a carrying-net by means of the northern *yajus* formula: "Homage to the quiver-bearer, to the one possessing the arrow-case," and thus attaches it to a tree.

Then, taking portions from the three remaining offerings— the *homa*, the *bali*, and the *odana*— he rolls them into a ball (*piṇḍa*) and makes it very firm, because the remainder requires a proper disposal. Some say [the ball is made] from the *jayanta-odana*.

Then, having placed that rice-ball in a leaf-cup, he hangs it upon some tree by means of a sling, using only this much of the mantra as it occurs in the liturgical collection: "Homage to the one who carries a quiver, to the one who possesses a bow-case. //7//
8. Here follows the recitation of the Rudra hymns.
Here one should recite the Rudras. (ĀpGs 20.8)
At this time, one should mutter the eleven sections beginning with "Obeisance to your wrath, O Rudra" (*namaste rudra manyave*).
The meaning is that one should worship the deity with these very [sections].
In that regard, among the verses of the final section, after the tenth verse, the supplement is: "Of them, [the distance] of a thousand yojanas... (*teṣāṃ sahasrayojanam*).

Finally, there are three mantras: "Salutation to the Rudras who are on earth, whose arrows are food"; "Salutation to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space, whose arrows are wind"; and "Salutation to the Rudras who are in heaven, whose arrows are rain"—this [formula] is to be supplied everywhere. // 7 //
"At this time";
others, however, say "here, near the tree. [He recites] "O Rudra, homage to your wrath" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5.1).

One should recite these eleven sections (*anuvākas*) with the fourfold intonation (*cātussvaryeṇa*). Among them, in the final section beginning with "In this great [world]" (*asmin mahati*), there is an addition (*anuṣaṅga*) starting from "Of those [who are] at a distance of a thousand leagues" (*teṣāṃ sahasrayojane*, Taittirīya Saṃhitā 8.5.11).

Likewise, [the additions are]: "Homage to the Rudras who are on earth, whose arrows are food; homage to the Rudras who are in the intermediate space... (*namo rudrebhyo ye pṛthivyāṃ yeṣāmannamiṣavastebhyaḥ | namo rudrebhyo ye antarikṣe...*)

"To those Rudras whose arrows are the wind, to them [be] homage; to those whose arrows are the rain—to them [be] homage. The phrase "ten to the east, ten to the south," and so forth, is to be supplied as an *anuṣaṅga* (continuation).
Or rather, [the formula applies] to the first and the last [groups]. 8. ĀpGS 20.9.
Alternatively, the worship should be performed with only the first and the last sections. //8//
Alternatively, one should mutter only the first and last anuvākas of the Rudras. //9//
Now, he states what is to be done at the very time of the principal oblations:
9. The placement of the cows around the fire. He places the cows around this fire so that the smoke may reach them. (ĀpGS 20.10)
While this Agni is being offered into, he should place his own cows around him so that the smoke may reach them;
the meaning is that they should be nearby, downwind.
And at the time of the principal offering, it is said "this very [Agni] while being offered"—that is, for the sake of that very purpose. //9//
He places his own cows around this Agni afflicted by the oblation— that is, in the vicinity of the sacrificial fire— downwind,
so that the smoke of the oblation may reach them.
Some say that this [statement] serves as an indicator (jñāpaka) for the view that even this ritual action is for the sake of pacifying the cow. //10//
10. The sprinkling of the cows: he sprinkles them with perfumes using a handful of *darbha* grass, beginning with the bull, [saying] "O Agni... (ĀpGS 20.11).

One sprinkles it with fragrant substances such as sandalwood and the like using a handful of *darbha* grass, not with the hand. "A handful of *grumuṣṭi*"—the elision of the vowel *u* is a Vedic (*chāndasa*) usage; the meaning is "with a handful of *darbha* grass having its tips intact."
In that regard, the statement concerning the time for the *homa* refers to the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) at that same time. //10//
One sprinkles that very bull, the male, first. Even if it does not stand at the beginning, nevertheless, because it is a subordinate part (*aṅga*), its sprinkling takes place first;
the time for that purpose is indeed at the outset. 11.
"With perfumes" means with those consisting of sandalwood and so forth.
"A handful of *darbha* grass" (*darbhagrumuṣṭi*) refers to a large handful (*guru-muṣṭi*) of *darbha* grass;
the elision of the vowel *u* is a Vedic archaism.
"Sannakha" means one with a firm fist;
with that [fist], he sprinkles.
In this regard, there is a distinction: [he sprinkles] the bull.
Or he sprinkles water first upon the bull;
by the use of the word "only" (*eva*), it is indicated that while that [bull] is being sprinkled, no other cow is sprinkled.
Then he sends out the cows to graze. //11//
11. On the path of cattle, there is the sacrifice to the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati). On the path of cattle, he sacrifices to the Lord of the Field even without fire. (ĀpGS 20.12)
Now follows the procedure for the *sthālīpāka* dedicated to Kṣetrapati: the word *anagnau* (not in the fire) uses the Vedic short vowel *u*. It is performed on the ground itself, not in the fire;
since the sacrifice is prescribed to be performed on the path while the cows are departing, this is a prohibition against using the fire when it would otherwise be required. //12//
Then, as the cattle set out, at every step along the way—
using the short vowel [for "mārge"] according to Vedic usage—
he sacrifices to the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati) upon the bare ground, not on the fire. 12.
The invocation of that Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati) should be performed like that of Īśāna;
the meaning is that it should be done with this verse, "ā tvā vahantu.
Furthermore, the word "Śarva" should also be understood as a synonym for him. //13//
The invocation is like that for Īśāna. ĀpGs 20.13.
The invocation of the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati) is like that of Īśāna;
the meaning is that it is performed with the verse beginning, "May they bring thee hither" (ā tvā vahantu). //13//
12. To him, the gift of leaves is given;
he places the name [of the child] upon four or seven leaves. (ĀpGs 20.14)

Having invoked [the deity] and offered the *arghya*, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, and having placed the *sthālīpāka* (cooked sacrificial rice) and poured clarified butter over it, he places four or seven leaves near the deity.
Addressing them by name and designating the destination, he offers a ball of rice from the *sthālīpāka* upon those leaves.

Since there is a rule that the mantras for offering the leaves in previous instances must end with the word *svāhā*, here too the leaf-offering is made with the mantra: "To the Lord of the Field, *svāhā*!"
This indeed is his sacrifice. //14//

Having placed four or seven lumps of earth on the ground, he takes cooked rice from the *sthālīpāka* offering dedicated to the Lord of the Field (*kṣetrapati*), pronounces the name [of the recipient] in the dative case, and offers it with the formula, "To the Lord of the Field, thee!
This is because of the traditional rule (smṛti) that the root *dhā* (in *ḍudhāñ*) signifies "placing" and "nourishing."
Some offer [the oblation] with the formula, "To the Lord of the Field, svāhā! because the utterance of *svāhā* was observed in the preceding bali-mantras.
However, in this case, cooked rice mixed with meat should not be offered.
Because of the use of the locative case in the word "parṇeṣu" (on the leaves). //14//
13. The procedure for the quick rite:
one should sacrifice quickly; the deity is Pāka. (ĀpGS 20.15)
The ripening is like that of a child; this deity is likewise prone to moving away. Therefore, the meaning is that one should sacrifice quickly. //15//
And this sacrifice consisting of the offering of cooked rice (odana) should be performed immediately after the invocation, having first offered water alone;
however, the offering of perfumes and other items occurs only after the sacrifice,
because the deity is "the small one" (alpa) regarding the cooked food.
The following is what is meant: because the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati) is characterized by impermanence, an offering (bali) must be given to him immediately.
Some say that "pāka" means a child—one whose nature is to move like a child—and likewise, even here, an offering is to be made after giving perfumes and other such items. //15//
14. His worship: he worships him with the two following [verses]. ĀpGs 20.16.
With the two following verses, "We [choose] the Lord of the Field," [he should offer]. //16//
He worships with two verses beginning with "By the Lord of the Field, we... (RV 4.57.1–2). //16//
By the passage beginning with "having formed a ball of rice," the disposal of the remnants of the oblation and the *bali* offering has been stated.
Now, he describes the disposal of the remnant of the *sthālīpāka* for Īśāna:
15. From the remnant of the *sthālīpāka*, the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas [takes place].
One should feed the Brāhmaṇas with the cooked rice from the sacrificial pot.

Since this is already established by the extension (atideśa) from the Pārvaṇa rite through the phrase "with that [oblation] mixed with ghee," the statement is intended for the purpose of prescribing plurality. //17//
And this restatement of the ordinary understanding is intended either to enjoin a plurality of Brahmins or to exclude the presence of clarified butter. //17//
He states the ritual disposal for the Kṣaitrapatya offering:
16. "The consumption of the Kṣaitrapatya caru together with one's kinsmen; those who are uterine siblings consume the Kṣaitrapatya. (ĀpGS 20.18)
"Sons and brothers" refers to those who share the same navel and the same womb;

although this is already established by the term "sanābhayaḥ" (those sharing the same navel), the explicit statement is made for the purpose of including other relatives such as daughters' sons and so forth in the act of acceptance. //18//
Those who share the same navel and the same funeral oblation (sapinda) are kinsmen. //18//
It should be according to what constitutes their family custom. ĀpGs 20.19.

Regarding those born into the family of the sacrificer, the consumption [of the remains] should be according to the family custom; that is, if it is for the sons alone, then the consumption is in that manner;
or if it is for all those born into their own respective families.
Likewise, the consumption [of the remainder];
and likewise, the consumption by the sister's son and others as well. //19//
Thus ends the twentieth section and the seventh chapter in the *Gṛhyavṛtti* composed by Haradattamiśra, known as the *Anākulā*.
If, for these performers, the consumption [of the offering] by one who is not a sapinda-kinsman is also a family custom, then it may be so. //19//
In the seventh chapter as well, the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* was thus composed by the venerable Sudarśanārya in accordance with the Bhāṣya. //1//
Whatever has been left unsaid or poorly expressed here, whether caused by negligence or other factors, should be forgiven by the wise, as this work follows the path of the Vedas. //3//
Thus ends the twentieth section in the Gṛhyatātparyadarśana composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
The seventh chapter is completed.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
The Twenty-first Section.

Furthermore, another *pākayajña* is taught—a rite for the ancestors known as the *māsi-śrāddha*, which is offered to three persons and serves as the archetype for the *aṣṭakā* and other such rites—[Section 22:
The Chapter on the Māsi-Śrāddha].
The time for the monthly *śrāddha* is as follows:
the times for the monthly *śrāddha* during the fortnight of the waning moon are according to the traditional instructions. (ĀpGs 21.1)

The ancestral rite called *māsiśrāddha* is to be performed month after month. Regarding that, the specific times within the dark fortnight (*aparapakṣa*) are established in the *Sāmayācārika* section, such as “if it is performed on the first day” (*Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra* 2.16.8), and so forth, as well as “the afternoon of the dark fortnight is superior” (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra* 2.16.4).
And all those [details] regarding conduct (*nīti*) should be understood month by month exactly as they were taught in the instruction;

even though those specific details are established from that very statement, this statement is made for the purpose of indicating that the procedural rules (*prayoga-vidhāna*) for that ritual action will be set forth hereafter. Otherwise, one might wonder in which ritual action such rules as "those who are pure and possess the mantras" are prescribed.
If that is so, then let this very [statement] serve as the basis for the eligibility (*adhikāra*) for the monthly *śrāddha*.

Therefore, its purpose is this: so that, regardless of the measurement of the month, the festival times (*parvakāla*) may occur according to the instruction by virtue of the latter fortnight (*aparapakṣa*).

Consequently, for one who has not performed the *śrāddha* on the fifteenth day of the former fortnight, the performance takes place on all lunar days (*tithi*), starting from the first, in the latter fortnight, for one who desires those respective results. //1//

Regarding the *māsi-śrāddha*, which is to be performed with faith month after month during the latter fortnight— the dark fortnight— it satisfies the ancestors when performed on any day of the latter fortnight, according to the instruction: "On all days of the latter fortnight, one gratifies the ancestors."

The times [for rites] are determined in accordance with the instructions established in the Dharmaśāstras, such as: "A distinction in the fruit results from the performer's restriction regarding time" (Āpastamba Dharmasūtra 2.16.7).
"In the dark fortnight, the times are according to the instruction."
The purpose of this repetition has been stated in the passage, "Rites for the ancestors are performed in the dark fortnight" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 1.7).
Some maintain that there is no fixed rule requiring that the subsequent performance must take place on the very same lunar day as the initial commencement.

Kunti, even when the month is full, [the rite] occurs specifically during the dark fortnight; according to the instruction, the performance is both obligatory and optional even on other lunar days. //1//

2. Brahmins who are worthy of being fed—those who are pure, learned in the mantras, and not related by birth, lineage, or mantra—he should feed them in uneven numbers, at least three, without regard for material gain. (ĀpGs 21.2)

Regarding the phrase "pure, clean, possessing mantras, and perfected in sacred learning": although this is already established by the rule, "In all rites, one should feed those who are pure, clean, and possess mantras" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.15.11), the repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
"Brāhmaṇas related by birth" refers to fathers-in-law, maternal uncles, and others.
Those connected by lineage are those of the same *gotra*; those connected by mantra are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the preceptors (*ācārya*), and the resident pupils (*antevāsin*).
He will state later that this applies "except when others have lost their qualities.
The term "an odd number" is for the purpose of prohibiting an even number.
The phrase "at least three" is intended to exclude the case of only one [offering];
for Āśvalāyana says: "But by no means [should there be] only one for all."
The meaning is that in the case of an *āmaśrāddha* performed at the beginning [of a lineage], or during a famine, one should feed even a single person from the family.
Although the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) is seen to be made for women as well, nevertheless, the feeding of Brāhmaṇas on their behalf does not take place here,
because the performance of the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the touching of the offerings (*abhimarśana*) are not observed in this context.
And because of the contradiction regarding the statement of "pairs," the feeding of Brahmins is therefore for the three ancestors— the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather alone;
three or five [Brahmins] for each one.

Because it is seen in other Kalpas and in the Dharmaśāstras that the feeding of Brāhmaṇas for the Viśvedevas is done in pairs: "The same applies to the maternal grandfathers; there is either a separate rite or a common one (tantra) for the Vaiśvadeva" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.228), so says Yājñavalkya.

The meaning of the sentence is that one should feed Brahmins endowed with qualities such as purity, being "without regard for worldly motives" (anarthāvekṣaḥ), which means having no expectation of visible purposes such as a reciprocal favor.
The meaning of the term *padārtha* here is those who are pure, being purified in speech, mind, and body.

Nor should it be argued that the statement in the Dharmaśāstra, "One should not feed those who are impure, even if they know the mantras, at any ritual act" (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.15.11), renders the repetition of the requirement for purity here superfluous, since that rule is stated as a general principle applicable to all matters.

Since one should feed even those with little learning provided they are pure, it is better to omit the ritual performance in their absence than to feed the impure; thus [the text speaks] out of respect for purity.

Regarding the phrase "those unrelated by birth, lineage, or mantra" (*ayonigotramantrāsambandhān*), according to the grammatical principle that "a term heard after a *dvandva* compound is connected with each member individually," this means they are unrelated by birth (*yoni*),
unrelated by lineage (*gotra*), and [unrelated] as those who sacrifice for one another or teach one another (*yājyayājakādhyetradhyāpayitṛ*).

As for the statement in the *Dharmaśāstra*, "those related to non-mantric students" (*āpastamba-dharmasūtra* 2.17.4), which speaks of relationships with students (*antevāsī*) apart from relationships with mantras, that is intended to prohibit the relationship with mantras characterized by being students of or listeners to the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*).
Now, one might object: is it not already established that among the *Sāmayācārika* [rites], Brahmins possess mantras, or rather, lack connection to the mantras of their *yoni* and *gotra*?
Why, then, is this stated again here?

It is said: in the case of the monthly *śrāddha* performed regularly, one should feed those possessing the qualities mentioned in the *Gṛhya-sūtras*, but it is not necessary that they be knowers of Brahman (*brahmavit*), students (*antevāsī*), or relatives; this is for that purpose.
"Odd" means an uneven number.
"Tryavarāḥ" means those for whom three is the minimum number;
this refers to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather.
Consequently, one should invite three or five of each of these three—such as the father and so forth—but not seven or more.
One should feed two Brahmins at a rite for the gods and three at a rite for the ancestors, or one for each of the two;
even if one is very wealthy, one should not be overly attached to a large number of guests.
This is because of the statement of Manu: "Thus says Manu" (Ma.smṛ.

3.135). Now, one might object: in this statement of Manu, having said "three for the rites for the ancestors," it was further stated that "one should not be overly attached to elaboration"; so why then was "or even five" mentioned?
It is said: because of the author of the Sūtra’s statement, "an odd number, at least three.
If that is so, then [the rule] "one for each, or both together" is contradictory.
No; for that is a secondary alternative (anukalpa).
In this regard, although the offering of the rice-ball (piṇḍa) is seen as being performed separately for the mother and others,
nevertheless, there is no separate feeding of Brahmins for them, because no such separateness is observed in the cases of the gold-giving (hema) and the touching (abhimarśana).
Because, when counting the number of fathers, mothers, Brahmins, and [other] groups, there is a contradiction with the requirement of being an even number, and because such a practice is absent;
furthermore—

On the Aṣṭakā days, on occasions of prosperity, at Gayā, and on the anniversary of her death, one should perform the Śrāddha for the mother separately; on other occasions, it should be performed together with the husband.
From this statement of Manu, it is clearly understood that there is no separate performance [of the rites] for the monthly *śrāddha* and so forth, other than for the *aṣṭaka* and similar occasions.

Furthermore, although not mentioned here by either the author of the Sūtra or the commentator, the feeding of an even number of Brahmins for the sake of the Viśvedevas must be performed, because it has been stated by both Manu and Yājñavalkya: "Two for the gods.
Likewise: "Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, and various kinds of Bhūtas..."
They suddenly plunder the faithful offering when it is unprotected;
therefore, the Viśvedevas were ordained by the Self-Existent One for its protection.
This is because of such statements as those of Jhāgaleya,
and because of the uncontradicted practice of the learned (*śiṣṭācāra*).
However, when only a single Brāhmaṇa is available, [the following applies].
In that case, one should feed him for the sake of the father and others alone,
because they are the primary [recipients].
But as for the Vaiśvadeva, which is a subsidiary part— if one feeds only one person at the Śrāddha, how then can there be a portion for the gods (daiva) therein?
Having taken up food from the vessel, [he should offer] of everything that has been prepared.
Having prepared it in a temple of the deities, one should offer a śrāddha there;
one should either cast that food into the fire or give it to a celibate student (brahmacārin).
Thus is the performance according to the rule stated by Vasiṣṭha. Now, one might object:
"In this same manner, the Vaiśvadeva rite for the maternal grandfathers is either performed as a separate ritual or as part of the main procedure."
Likewise—

the wise person should perform the śrāddha for the maternal grandfather in this same manner; according to the rule, it should be done with the omission of the mantra, while the remainder is performed without mantras.
In the same manner,

one who is endowed with devotion should perform the rite for the maternal grandfathers separately, either accompanied by the Vaiśvadeva offering or as a single integrated ritual (tantra) including the Vaiśvadeva.

Thus, because the injunctions are seen in the *Yājñavalkya-smṛti*, the *Viṣṇu-smṛti*, and the *Viṣṇu-purāṇa*, it is understood that the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* (ancestral rite for the maternal grandfather) is indeed obligatory (*nitya*).
Why, then, do the author of the Sūtras and the commentator not mention it?

It is said in reply: even there, in other Smṛtis, it is not intended as a rule that every living twice-born man must necessarily perform the *mātāmaha-śrāddha* in the same manner as the rites for the paternal ancestors (*pitrya*). Once [the paternal rites] have been performed...

If it is argued that [the injunction] is a rule (*vidhi*) because prosperity (*abhyudaya*) results from its performance and no transgression (*pratyavāya*) occurs from its non-performance, then for whom must it be performed as a mandatory duty? If this is asked:

If a son— whether born of a woman who was made a *putrikā* (an appointed daughter) or wed by an *āsura* or other such form of marriage— performs the *sāpiṇḍya* with his maternal grandfather along with his mother, for him the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather is absolutely mandatory; and if he fails to perform it, there is sin.

However, in the case of the monthly *śrāddha* (māsi-śrāddha), since there is no separate *śrāddha* for the mother, it is logical that she partakes in a portion of the *śrāddha* for the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*).
Alternatively, this *śrāddha* is obligatory for that daughter’s son who removes all the suffering of his childless maternal grandfather.
As Laugākṣi said:
"A son of a daughter who inherits wealth must always perform the Śrāddha for his maternal grandfathers according to the rules and in accordance with the prescribed ritual."
Thus it is said.
Bārci also stated this very same point:
"In that case where the maternal grandfather is without a son..."
By such passages as, "The son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra) shall take the entire estate; in that case,
there is a rule for him to offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍa)," the procedure for the Śrāddha for the maternal grandfather (mātāmaha) is to be understood from other Smṛtis and through logical reasoning.

Therefore, since there is no restrictive rule stating that for every daughter’s son (dhauhitra) the rite must necessarily be performed exactly as for a son (pitryavat), neither the author of the Sūtra nor the author of the Bhāṣya states so. // 2 //
3. There are three oblations of food.
He offers the food with the following verses. (ĀpGs 21.3)
With the seven verses beginning with "yan me mātā" (RV 10.85.46–52), which contain feminine gender references, he offers a portion of the food.
The meaning is that he takes [the portion] from the food prepared for the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas and offers it.
In this regard, in place of the word "amuṣmai," the name of the father is to be mentioned at the beginning of the first two verses.
"To the two middle [pindas] belongs the grandfather;
to the last two, the great-grandfather.
'If one should have two fathers, he should designate both on each individual pinda'" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 1.27).
By this principle, the two fathers are indicated by the dual form "amuṣmā amuṣmā";
at the end, there is the utterance of *svāhā*.
Some perform the modification (ūha), saying "the two parents should choose," or they perform a variation of the Ṛgveda verse;
by this, the grandfather and great-grandfather are explained [by analogy].

Likewise, regarding the mantra "svāhā pitre," some perform modification (ūha), while others do not, on the grounds that here the fatherhood is intended to be expressed, whereas the singular number is not intended to be expressed. Some [hold this view].

They also perform the *ūhana* (adaptation) and the *homa* for the maternal grandfathers: "Whatever [fault] is mine from my maternal grandmother, whatever [fault] is mine from my mother’s paternal grandmother, whatever [fault] is mine from my mother’s great-grandmother..."
"May my maternal grandfather accept that for me," and so forth. //3//
Here, by the word "food" (anna), food intended for the feeding of Brahmins is meant; and by the genitive case, the relationship between the source and that which is derived from it is expressed.

Therefore, the meaning is this: having drawn out together into a single vessel from all the various kinds of sacrificial oblations—such as boiled rice, cakes, and so forth—which are intended for the feeding of Brahmins, for the purpose of the oblation (homa).

Therefore, having cut portions according to the ritual rule for the *pārvaṇa* sacrifice, he offers the principal oblations with each verse of the seven [mantras] beginning with "yan me mātā," one by one.
It is not a single oblation accompanied by many mantras; for it is said: "Or rather, this is the reverse" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 21.5).
This is because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of plurality.
This indicative mark will become clear in the commentary on the sūtra "etad vai" [Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 1.24.3].
Here, in place of the word "Agni" in the first and second mantras, one should utter the name of the father in the dative case, such as "Viṣṇuśarmaṇe."
In this manner, for the third and fourth [ancestors], it is the grandfather; for the fifth and sixth, it is the great-grandfather.
However, because the word "you" (*tvad*) is absent in the seventh [generation], there is no mention of the name.
And in this case, there is no modification (*anūha*) even for one who has two fathers (*dvipitṛka*), and so forth.
Furthermore, because of the prohibition against omitting a *ṛc* in the rule, "Therefore, one should not omit a verse" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra*),
the singular number in the phrase "May the father choose [the portion]" (*pitā vṛṅktām*) and so forth refers to the general category of the father and others.

For this very reason, in the archetype (prakṛti) of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, even for one who has multiple wives, the directive (sampraiṣa) "Having girded the wife" (patnīṃ saṃnahya) is given using the singular number alone.
This is taught as an instance of modification (ūha),
because in the archetype itself— the Dvādaśāha sacrifice— a modification is observed in the statement "Today [is] the Soma-pressing," according to Ālekhana.

This same principle applies to [mantras] such as "eṣa te tata madhumān... and so forth. However, one whose father is living takes the names of three ancestors, beginning with his own father; whereas, if this person whose father has died were to have his grandfather still living, [he would take the names of those three].
He should utter the names of his father, as well as those of his grandfather and great-grandfather.

Thus, even though there is a difference in the objects of address in the mantras, only the words *pitṛ*, *pitāmaha*, and *prapitāmaha* are employed. However, according to the view that allows for modification (*ūha*), [the names should be substituted].
The application [of the formula] is preceded by the specification of each respective counter-correlative, such as "May the father’s father partake" or "May the father’s grandfather partake.

Nor should it be suspected that one whose father is living has no monthly *śrāddha*, for [it is said]: "But while the father is still living, one should offer [the oblation] only to those who precede him."
It should be given in the first three [houses], provided that the triad [of planets] is alive.
This is because of such a collection of statements [beginning with] *Manusmṛti* 3.220.
But even so, for one whose father and others have died out of the natural order, this would not be possible at all; for it is said:
"Sapiṇḍana should never be performed for those who have died out of the natural order."

[Objection: "This is not so; because of the prohibition of *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* for those who have died out of the natural order (*vyutkrama*), the sons and others of such persons lack the entitlement to perform a *śrāddha* where the ancestors for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed are the recipients. [Reply: It is not thus. For it is said: "But he whose father has passed away while his grandfather still lives, should pronounce the name of his father and then mention the great-grandfather."
"Or the grandfather may eat that śrāddha," so Manu has declared.
Since the performance of the Śrāddha rite is prescribed even for one whose father and others have died out of the natural order by the words of Manu (M.Smṛ.

3.221, 222), it follows that the prohibition "and because of the reverse order" is merely optional; from this certainty, it is understood that the entitlement [to perform the rite] is also merely optional. //3//
4. There are oblations of clarified butter; the subsequent [verses] are for the offerings of clarified butter. (ĀpGS 21.4)

He offers six oblations of clarified butter with the mantras beginning with "Svāhā to the Pitṛs. In that context, because the word "svāhā" occurs at the beginning of the mantra "Svāhā to the Pitṛs," there is no "svāhā" at the end.

On this point, they say: in the monthly *śrāddha*, the feeding of the Brahmins is the primary rite (*pradhānakarma*), while the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*) and the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) are its subsidiaries (*aṅga*). Therefore, the performance of the *śrāddha* for one whose father is living does not take place; as it is said: "If the father is living, he shall not give [the offerings]."
Because of the prohibition;

this [injunction], "one should desist after having performed the *āhoma*," is also not a primary injunction (*vidhi*), because the *homa* is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the meal, whereas in the *Piṇḍapitṛyajña*, the *homa* is the principal act (*pradhāna*).
Others, however, say that the son should give to the very same persons to whom the father would have given.

Another says: "There are three principal elements in the *śrāddha*—the offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), the feeding, and the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*). Therefore, this rule—"having performed [the rites] up to the *homa*, one should desist"—is the scope for this as well; thus, having performed the food-*homa*.
Immediately thereafter, he offers six oblations of clarified butter with the northern [mantras], beginning with "Svāhā to the Father. //4//
Or rather, it may be the opposite of this. (ĀpGS 21.5)
The meaning is that there are seven preceding oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*) and six subsequent oblations of food (*anna*).
As for the mantras, they are exactly as recited in the traditional texts.
The ritual procedure (*prayoga*) is as follows: on the previous day, after the evening meal, one makes the announcement: "Tomorrow, the *śrāddha* will take place."
From that point on, the practice of the vow applies to all.

We, however, maintain that there is no eating on the evening of the preceding day, based on the indicative mark (liṅga): "If one were to fast without having eaten [the previous meal], it would belong to the ancestors and the gods."
Then, on the following day at dawn, the second announcement is made: "It shall be performed today.
Then, in the afternoon, having bathed and purified themselves with clay and water, he invites them.

First, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), for the Viśvedevas, he should offer an invitation to two or four even-numbered [guests] at the monthly Śrāddha, saying: "An invitation is to be made for the Viśvedevas.
The response is: "Om, so be it. Then, according to their seats, he should lead them to their places, saying: "May you be seated, sir."
"May I obtain [it]" is the response.
For the gods, the Brahmins face eastward upon Darbha grass whose roots are directed eastward;
for the ancestors, they face northward upon grass that is doubled over and bent, with the tips pointing southward; for the youth, it is for the father.
The *vṛddhas* for the grandfather;
the *vṛddhatamas* for the great-grandfather;
three or three each for each one.
In a pure place sloping toward the south, one should construct a Śrāddha hall enclosed on all sides with its door facing north. In the north-eastern part of that hall is the *aupāsana* fire.
To the south of that fire is a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) for the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍas*).
To the south of that, those intended for the ancestors sit facing north, and behind them, those intended for the gods sit facing east.

On that very sacrificial ground, as space permits, he places water for the *arghya* offering for the ancestors in three vessels containing sesame seeds, ending toward the south; for the gods, he places it in one vessel containing barley.
Having scattered flowers over them and set them down upon *darbha* grass, he covers them with *darbha* blades and [places them] in the hands of the Brahmins who have taken their seats.
Taking water from each respective water-vessel into another vessel, [he says]: "O Viśvedevas, this is your *arghya*;
O Father, this is your *arghya*; O Grandfather, this is your *arghya*."
The great-grandfather says, "This is for you, O Arghya," and thus he offers the arghya waters, or silently;
before and after [the offering], he gives pure water. Then, having honored the twice-born with perfumes and other items, as well as with garments.
He addresses [the Brahmins] with the words, "Let it be taken up, and let it be offered in the fire.
The response is, "Let it be taken up at will; let it be offered in the fire at will.

Then, having taken a portion from the food prepared for the Brahmins, having placed it to the west of the fire upon the sacrificial grass, and having sprinkled clarified butter over it, he performs the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, and then offers thirteen principal oblations (*pradhānāhuti*).

Alternatively, there is a different classification: the seven preceding oblations of clarified butter beginning with "What my mother [did]" (yan me mātā), and the six subsequent oblations of food beginning with "Svāhā to the father" (svāhā pitre). //5//
5. Touching the food: one should touch everything with the subsequent [mantras]. (ĀpGs 21.6)
Having thus offered the principal oblations and having offered the *sauviṣṭakṛt* (oblation to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt), he proceeds with the *jaya* and subsequent rites.
When the principal rite along with its ancillaries is performed, the sacred thread is worn over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvīta*) in all cases;
others say that the heirs do not [participate].

Having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling (pariṣecana) and released the *praṇītā* water, he should then place all the food intended for the offering together with the remnants of the oblation (*huta-śeṣa*) upon it. Having set that aside, he should touch it with the three verses beginning with "This [is] for you, O father, full of sweetness" (*eṣa te tata madhumān*).
Here too, there is an adaptation (*ūha*): "This [is] for you, O maternal grandfather, full of sweetness," and so forth.
among them //
Then, one should touch all the food—both that fit for the Brahmins' meal and that which is not—with these three subsequent mantras beginning with "This, O father, is honeyed.
If it is impossible to touch everything in a single effort, there is a repetition of the mantras;
for the subordinate elements (śeṣas) are dependent upon the principal element (śeṣin). //6//
Or, having prepared [the portions], he should offer them one for each person.
Alternatively, one should touch the various kinds of cooked rice prepared in the food vessels for each individual separately, according to their respective gender.
In that regard, as many persons as are fed for the sake of the ancestors, the first mantra is repeated for that many; the same applies to the two subsequent ones.
Then, [one touches] the remnants of the food placed in the vessels. (7)

Alternatively, one should touch with each respective mantra, according to its indicative mark (*liṅga*), the food items that have been prepared and placed in the eating vessels for the Brahmins representing the ancestors and others.
Here too, if there is a plurality of Brahmins for each ancestor and so forth, and simultaneous touching is impossible, there must be a repetition of the respective mantras. //7//
6. The touching of food by those who are about to eat: having caused them to touch it with the subsequent Yajus formula, [one should proceed]. (ĀpGs 21.8)
Having caused the Brahmins to touch [the vessel] with the subsequent Yajus formula, "The earth is thy vessel," he should feed them; this is the remainder [of the sense].

And although in that context the plural number is seen in the words "I thee for the Brahmins" and "Mayest thou not fail for them," nevertheless, there is a repetition of the mantra for each individual person, as in the case of the mantra for the *uparava* holes.
And like the mantra for driving away the calves, there first follows the sipping of water by the gods with this verse: "O All-Gods... (viśve devāsa).
Because it is seen in another Smṛti;
others say [it is] "belonging to Viṣṇu," with the words "O Viṣṇu, protect the oblation" at the end of the verse "idaṃ viṣṇuḥ."
Likewise, at the end of the rites for the ancestors (pitrya), he says, "O Viṣṇu, protect the kavya! While they are eating, he turns his face away;

he causes them to hear mantras that destroy demons, those pertaining to the ancestors, those pertaining to Viṣṇu, and other purifying, righteous mantras, as well as the Dharmaśāstras, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas.
Then, knowing them to be satisfied, he should cause [the recitation of] the *Madhumatī* verses and the verse beginning with "akṣann amīmadanta.

Then he scatters food upon the ground, saying: "Those who were cremated by fire, those who were not cremated by fire, and those born in my family—may they reach the supreme goal, satisfied by this ball of food given upon the earth."

Then, after they have sipped water, he gives water again and causes those representing the ancestors to say, "It is well-tasted" (*svaditam*), and those representing the gods to say, "It is pleasing" (*rocate*).

Then, having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his faith, he sets aside from all the remaining food portions for the sake of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) and for eating; he then presents the remainder, asking, "What shall be done with the remains of the food?
The reply is, "Let it be enjoyed together with those you wish."
"May our donors increase, may our Vedas and our progeny flourish;
may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give."
Thus he makes his request.
The response is made with the modification: "May you, the givers, increase.
Having circumambulated those who have finished eating, keeping them to the right, [he performs the remaining rites].
Homage!
"Oṃ svadhā" for the ancestors;
"May the Viśvedevas be pleased" for the Viśvedevas.
In that regard, among all ritual acts, the precedence belongs to the Vaiśvadeva offerings and the succession to the Pitrya offerings;
however, there is a reversal at the time of dismissal.

From the pouring of the oblation until before the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas), one should wear the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), according to the observation of other ritual manuals.
With the subsequent Yajus mantra, "The earth is your vessel," having taken hold of the hands of the Brāhmaṇas who have been provided with specific kinds of food, he causes them to sip water.
"He should feed him"— this is the ellipsis.

And although the plural number "of the Brāhmaṇas" (*brāhmaṇānām*) occurs in this mantra, nevertheless, because it is impossible to touch [them all] simultaneously, there must be a repetition of the mantra for each individual person,
just as in the case of the mantra "You are the winds" (*vāyavas stha*).
Thus the mantra is [recited] for each year.

In such cases, the use of the plural number is for the sake of the grammatical correctness of the performance, or it refers to the multiple individual instances that are to be employed within a single performance statement. //8//
7. Following those who have finished eating,
the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍas),
and the consumption of the remnants.

Having followed [the guests] after they have eaten and circumambulated them from left to right, he spreads darbha grass with the tips pointing south in two rows; having poured water over them with the following [mantras], he offers the rice-balls (piṇḍas) ending toward the south with the following [mantras]; having again poured water as before with the following [mantras], having worshipped with the following [mantras], and having sprinkled water three times counter-clockwise around [the balls] with a water-pot using the following [mantra], he turns the vessels upside down and recites the subsequent Yajus formula three times without pausing.

Having sprinkled the vessels and brought them forward two by two, having taken portions from all of them, he should consume the remainder—the best morsel—as an offering, with the *uttara-yajus* formula. (ĀpGS 21.9)

Then, having followed after them once they have finished eating, and having performed the ritual circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇīkṛtya*), he returns; wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), he spreads *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south at the place where the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) are to be offered.
"In two places" means he spreads them in two distinct locations so that they do not overlap.
Therein, he first spreads [the grass] for the ancestors (*pitṛ*).
Afterwards, for the mothers;
and likewise Āśvalāyana says: "Some [place] them in two or six furrows;
one should offer to the paternal ancestors in the eastern ones."
Regarding the phrase "from other women" (*aparāsu strībhyaḥ*) [Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.56,

7.8], since the rule "with the tips pointing south in rites for the ancestors" (*dakṣiṇāgraiḥ pitryeṣu*, Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 14) pertains specifically to the act of strewing grass (*paristaraṇa*), the term "pointing southward" (*dakṣiṇāgrīni*) is used here.
Having spread [the grass] upon them with the subsequent mantras beginning with "May they purify my ancestors," he offers water.
The phrase "as before" implies that the mantras to be mentioned later are also drawn back [to this point].
He offers the rice-ball (piṇḍa) as before; the meaning is that it is the same as the offering of the rice-ball performed in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
Therefore, specific details such as "three handfuls of water" and so forth apply here as well;

therein, [the offerings] are made for the fathers with mantras containing paternal characteristics when strewn upon the mats, and for the mothers with mantras containing maternal characteristics when strewn upon the mats.

Having thus given water, he then offers rice-balls (*piṇḍas*) upon those *darbha* grasses—arranged with their ends pointing southward—for both [the paternal and maternal ancestors], using the subsequent mantras beginning with "This for you, O Father, Sāva," according to the respective gender-markers (*liṅga*), [addressing] the fathers and the mothers.
In every instance where "Sāva" occurs, the name is to be inserted according to the respective gender.
Here too, because of the connection with the phrase "as before," the rule regarding bending the left knee and placing the hand downward, and so forth, applies here as well.
Regarding one who has multiple fathers, the Paiṅgi-sūtra states:
"O Yajñaśarman and Viṣṇuśarman, this is for you two, your fathers, and those who follow you; this is for you two, your grandfathers," and so forth.

Regarding the statement, "O Mothers, this [is for you] both, and those who follow you," and so forth, it is said that they end toward the south so that both sets of rice balls (piṇḍas) may individually terminate toward the south.
Therefore, the mother's rice balls do not lie to the south of the father's rice balls;
rather, they are behind them.

Having thus given the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*), he gives water with the subsequent [mantras] as before, for the fathers and the mothers. Since these mantras beginning with "May my fathers wipe themselves" are prescribed again in the collection of mantras (*mantrasamāmnāya*), the phrase "as before" is an extended application (*atideśa*) intended to refer back to the Piṇḍapitṛyajña; [the procedure applies] both to the rice-balls and to the handfuls of water.
Then he worships them with the subsequent mantras according to their respective characteristics: "And those who of you... for the fathers; "And those women of you... for the mothers;
and "May they bear [the offerings]... for the fathers.
And he says, "May they carry [the offerings]," for the mothers; "May you be satisfied," for the fathers;
"May you be satisfied," for the mothers.

Saying "Be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied," he sprinkles water over both [sets of ancestors] with the following verse, "May sons and grandsons... three times, moving from right to left (prasavya) with a vessel of water. Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the phrase "may they be satisfied together," the sprinkling of the *piṇḍas* is performed simultaneously. The mention of a "vessel of water" is so that it should not be done with the hand.

The statement regarding "counter-clockwise" (prasavya) is an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*). It means that the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) should be performed as a single continuous act three times over, rather than there being three separate sprinklings as in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.
Having sprinkled in this manner, one then [places] the vessels which are relevant here: the three *arghya* vessels, the vessel for sprinkling, and the water-pitcher.

Having turned down—that is, having turned face downwards—the vessel from which the food for the rice-ball was taken, he then recites the subsequent Yajus formula, "Be satiated, be satiated, be satiated. He repeats this at least three times without pausing and without taking a breath; that repetition of which three times is the minimum measure is called *tryavarārdhya*.
The mention of the *yajus* is for the purpose of indicating that the formula "tṛpyate," which has been recited three times, constitutes a single *yajus*.
When that is repeated three times, there is a ninefold repetition.
Having thus repeated it, he sprinkles the vessels that have been tilted downward and draws them up—that is, he lifts them out.
The meaning of the word "abhī" (towards) is that he offers the subsequent rite [to them].
Therefore, some say that those same vessels are to be used even for the subsequent śrāddha rite;
others say no.

Having spoken thus, he should eat from the remainder of the food that which is "having a morsel as its lowest portion" (*grāsavarārdhya*)—meaning that whose smallest measure is a single morsel; the short vowel here is a Vedic anomaly.
He should eat this with the following *yajus*: "Seated in the breath, I offer the nectar. This means [he eats] from all [the remnants], that is, from all the remnants of the *śrāddha* food.
This eating is an integral part (*aṅga*) of the *śrāddha*.
There is no restrictive rule for eating that which is constant;

therefore, even in that case, the sacred thread must be worn over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta). However, in the case of sipping water (ācamana), the sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta) is not required, as it is not an integral part of that act.
Then follows the performance of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*).
When the Brahmins have eaten and are departing, he follows them as far as the boundary of his house and circumambulates them.
During these two [acts], the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) is worn over the left shoulder.

How so? First, regarding circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa), it is because of the association [with the rule]: "One should circumambulate from left to right while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder" (yajñopavītinā pradakṣiṇam).
Regarding following after (anuvrajana) as well, it is because of the association with circumambulation in the phrase: "having followed after and having circumambulated from left to right."
And these two [methods] are by way of a tantra because it is possible;
however, if due to some cause there is an absence of a tantra, then they are separate and distinct.

Then, having returned and wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he spreads darbha grass with its points directed southward at the place where the rice-balls (piṇḍas) are to be offered, arranging it in two double layers;
there, first, for the sake of the ancestors and so forth.
Afterwards, for the sake of the mother and the others,

water should be poured from right to left (dakṣiṇāpavarga) upon those Darbha grasses with the subsequent mantras beginning with "May my mothers purify themselves" (*mārjayantāṃ mama mātaraḥ*), according to the rule and custom seen in the *Āśvalāyana* [Gṛhyasūtra].

Immediately after giving [the water], he offers three balls of rice (piṇḍas) each, ending toward the south, according to their respective gender, with the subsequent mantras beginning with "This for you, O father, [Name]" and "This for you, O mother, [Name].
These balls of rice should be prepared by taking portions from both the remnants of the oblation and the remnants of the meal.

In this context, in the first three mantras, he takes the names of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather in the vocative case in their respective order, substituting them for the word *asāvi*. In the subsequent three, however, he does so for the mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother.
According to the rule "the completion is from the south" (Āpastamba Gṛhyasūtra 1.20).
The repetition here of what is already established by the general rule is for the purpose of making it known that,

regarding the offering of the *piṇḍas* alone, the conclusion is toward the south (*dakṣiṇāpavarga*), whereas in the case of the spreading of the *darbha* grass, the conclusion is toward the west (*paścimāpavarga*); likewise, it is also for the sake of establishing that each of the *piṇḍas* for both groups concludes toward the south.

Then, as before, he offers water with the mantras beginning with "mārjayantām. Some explain that by drawing back the word "as before" (pūrvavat) from both of these [sūtras]— namely, "having offered water over them with the subsequent [mantras]" and "having offered the balls ending toward the south with the subsequent [mantras]"— it is enjoined that in all three sūtras it should be performed "as before," that is, like the Piṇḍapitṛyajña.

The purpose, however, is that the injunctions such as "he pours out three handfuls of water" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 1.8.10) and "having bent the left knee, with hands turned downwards" (Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra 1.9.1) apply here as well.
That is not so; for a reduction [of the ritual] is itself improper, and because the notion that "as before" means "like the Piṇḍapitṛyajña" does not arise.
However, if it is argued that by the force of established custom (ācāra), the rule "having bent the left knee" and so forth must indeed be performed here as well, [we reply:]...
In that case, there is no fault.

Then, with the six subsequent mantras beginning with "And those who are here among you," he worships the ancestors three times each, according to the sequence and according to their respective characteristics.
He does so by repeating the mantra "Be satisfied" (*tṛpyata*) three times, applying it to both [groups] by means of the common ritual procedure (*tantra*).
Some [teachers] hold that there are four mantras, not six;

among them, the first mantra, beginning with "And those who here" (*ye ca vo 'tra*) and ending with "may they carry [the offerings]" (*tāśca vahantām*), is for the purpose of worshiping both [classes of ancestors].
[The second is] "May you be satisfied" (*tṛpyantu bhavantaḥ*).
Thus for the ancestors;
"May you be satisfied," for the mothers;
"Be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied," for both.

Then, with the verse beginning "O sons and grandsons" (*tata uttarayā 'putrān pautrān*), he simultaneously sprinkles water from the water-vessel three times around the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) of both groups in a counter-clockwise direction (*prasavya*) without interruption.

The repetition here of the counter-clockwise direction—which is already established by the general rule—is for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that the clockwise direction (*prādakṣiṇya*) might apply here as well, due to the statement "having circumambulated clockwise" (*pradakṣiṇīkṛtya*) in the preceding section.
Immediately thereafter, [he sets aside] the vessels used for the oblations and those used for the offering of the funeral cakes.
Some say they are for the purpose of eating or for the purpose of giving water, but not for the purpose of the *homa* sacrifice;
having turned them face down, that is, making their openings downward.

Following that, the Yajus mantra "Be satisfied, be satisfied, be satisfied," as it is handed down in the tradition, is recited thus three times. Without pausing and without inhaling, he repeats it three times; "tryavarārdhya" means that repetition which has three as its minimum measure, and he repeats it in such a manner.
Then, one should practice this nine times, saying "be satisfied even with a small measure.
Having thus repeated it without pausing as far as possible according to one's capacity, one should then sprinkle water upon the vessels placed face down.
He cites a pair [of examples].
Here, he provides a counter-example following the prefix *abhi*.

The sense is that there is no fault of "having been used up" (*niriṣṭika*) regarding those vessels. Now, "grāsāvarārdhya" means having the size of a mouthful as the minimum portion of the remaining food.
The vowel is short due to Vedic usage;
he should consume [the food] with the subsequent Yajus mantra: "He is established in the breath."

And this should be done by collecting portions from all the remaining food from every [dish]. Furthermore, this consumption must necessarily be performed even if there is no desire to eat, taking at least one mouthful as the minimum;
for it is an integral part of the ritual action (*karmāṅga*).
Having thus consumed it,
one should then sip water for the sake of purification while wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder.

Now, since the rules here are incomplete, having supplemented them with matters established from other sources, the ritual application is set forth according to its manifestation: Having performed the *aupāsana* oblation on the evening of the previous day, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), and having performed breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*): "Tomorrow I shall perform the monthly *śrāddha*. Then, one should inform the Brahmins—who are endowed with qualities such as purity, who are free from defects such as leprosy, and who have completed their evening daily rites—of this intent. Therein, first becoming invested with the sacred thread (*yajñopavītī*), [one says]: "Tomorrow there will be a monthly *śrāddha*."

In that regard, one should announce to the Brahmins invited for the Viśvedevas: "A seat (kṣaṇa) should be prepared by you for the sake of the Viśvedevas. Then, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), [one should announce] to those invited for the sake of the ancestors: "A seat should be prepared for the sake of the fathers," and "A seat should be prepared for the sake of the grandfathers" to those invited for the sake of the grandfathers.

One should offer the invitation (*kṣaṇa*) for the sake of the great-grandfather (*prapitāmaha*), as in: "The invitation is to be made for the sake of the great-grandfather. However, according to the view that there is only one Brahmin, one should say: "The invitation is to be made for the sake of the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather. If the performer is also offering a Śrāddha for the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaha*), he should announce it with the appropriate modification (*ūha*), beginning with: "The invitation is for the sake of the maternal grandfather," and so forth.

In that regard, one should wear the *yajñopavīta* during the two oblations for the bases (*ādhāra*), the two fuel-sticks for those [bases] (*tadartha-samit*), the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, the oblation to Agni as the mouth (*agnimukha-huti*), the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, and the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta-huti*);
likewise, the *yajñopavīta* alone is used for all matters pertaining to the Viśvedevas, as well as for circumambulation and following behind [the fire] from left to right (*pradakṣiṇa*).
Other than these, until the completion [of the rite], the *prācīnāvīta* alone is used everywhere.
And this has already been established previously.
Furthermore, for the performer here, there is the practice of vows such as celibacy and fasting, beginning from the initial resolve until its completion;
and for the partakers as well, there is the state of being free from anger and so forth, as stated by Manu.
Then, on the following day at dawn, having invited those Brahmins to his house and seated them on their seats after they have sipped water (ācamana), the second invitation is performed as before;
however, the distinction here is that one says, "Today the Śrāddha will take place.
This is because of the scriptural injunction: "The notification is on the previous day, and the second and third invitations are on the following day."

Then, having washed their feet in vessels containing water, *kūrca* grass, and sesame seeds, and having given them water for sipping (*ācamana*), as well as *kṛsara* rice, betel leaves, and other offerings, he should anoint them and send them forth for the purpose of bathing; and they should bathe.
Then, having bathed himself, he should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite and the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña) using food other than that intended for feeding the Brāhmaṇas;
some say this is done when the Śrāddha is completed.

Then, in the afternoon, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he seats the Brāhmaṇas—who have washed their hands and feet and sipped water for purification—upon their seats.

There, one should place those intended for the Viśvedevas facing east upon Darbha grass whose tips point east; and those intended for the ancestors (pitṛs) and others facing north upon Darbha grass that is doubled over, bent, and whose tips point south.

Furthermore, the Śrāddha hall should be located in a clean place, sloping toward the south, enclosed on all sides, and having its door facing north. In the northeast corner of that hall is the domestic fire (aupāsana).
To the south of the fire, one should prepare a mound for the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas);
to the south of that, the seats for the sons and other descendants;
and behind those, the seats for the Viśvedevas.

On sacrificial mounds (*sthaṇḍila*) as space permits, water is taken for the purpose of the *arghya* offering according to the procedure taught in other scriptures, using three vessels for the ancestors (*pitṛs*) and so forth, or a single vessel;
and [water] is likewise taken in another vessel for the *Viśvedevas* according to the rule.
Having honored those [vessels] with perfumes (*gandha*) and other offerings, [one proceeds].

Having placed [the vessels] upon *darbha* grass and covered them with *darbha*, he takes water from each of his own water-pots into another vessel and pours it into the hands of the seated Brahmins, saying, "O Viśvedevas, this is your *arghya*; O Father, Grandfather, and Great-grandfather, this is your *arghya*.
This very act of offering the *arghya* is called the "pouring of the *svadhā*" and the "bringing of the water-pot" in the *śrāddha* rite.
Before and after the offering of the *arghya*, pure water is poured into their hands.
Then, the Brahmins are honored according to one’s means with perfumes and other offerings, garments, rings, and so forth.
Thereafter, they should reply to them, "Let it be taken up, and let it be offered into the fire."
The practice of the Northern region (Udīcya-vṛtti), however, is as follows: while seated, he brings water-pots to their hands;
he addresses them, saying, "Let it be taken up" and "Let it be offered in the fire.
When they have given permission, saying, "Let it be taken up at will" and "Let it be offered in the fire at will," he may take it up and offer it in the fire. (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 2.17.17, 18, 19)

This is because of the statement in the Dharmaśāstra. Furthermore, this bringing of the water-vessel and the invitation with the words "let it be drawn out" are optional, as they were not mentioned by the author of the Bhāṣya.

Furthermore, because the compound *udīcyavṛttiḥ* admits both analyses—namely, "the conduct of the northerners" (*udīcyānāṃ vṛttiḥ*) and "conduct toward the northerners" (*udīcyeṣu vṛttiḥ*)—[it is appropriate].

Then, having set aside from the food intended for the Brāhmaṇas' meal the sacrificial oblation (*haviṣya*), such as boiled rice and cakes, into one vessel, and having set aside the non-sacrificial food mixed with pungent substances (*kṣāra*) and so forth into another vessel, he then consecrates the established sacrificial oblation with clarified butter; [then follows] the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire and ending with the "mouth of the fire" (*agnimukha*).

Having performed the thirteen principal oblations with the mantras beginning with "This for my mother," and having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, he then removes the hot ashes toward the north, offers non-sacrificial food with the utterance of *svāhā*, and completes the remainder of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) beginning with "The two smearings. Then, having touched all the food with the mantras beginning with "This for you, father," he performs the third invitation separately for each, just as before.
Having performed the three invitations, the Brahmins give the response "Oṃ, so be it.
Then follows the request of the performer.
Then follows the acceptance by the diners with the words "May I obtain [it]."

Others state another sequence: after the Vaiśvadeva and the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña), in the afternoon, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī), he performs the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire.
In that procedure, according to the view that includes the pouring of the *svadhā* libation, at the time of arranging the vessels, the *svadhā* vessels are also set down.
Having brought forward the *praṇītā* waters, he takes up the *svadhā* offerings according to the prescribed rule.
Then, having seated a non-Brahmin to the south,
and having performed the rites beginning with the washing of the feet up until the conclusion of the *agnimukha*,
he addresses [the officiant] with the words, "Let it be lifted."

"Having taken up the food, [one performs] the principal oblations and so forth. Even in this view, the pouring of the *svadhā* is merely optional. Others, however, maintain that in the monthly *śrāddha*, in accordance with other scriptures, there is the consecration of the place of eating along with mantras and fixed rules, as well as the invocation (*āvāhana*) of the Viśvedevas.
Having fed [the guests], they desire the ritual dismissal (udvāsana).

Regarding these items and their sequence, the determination is made solely from the practice of the learned (śiṣṭācāra), as it has not been stated by either the author of the Sūtras or the commentator.

Now the subject at hand is stated: he causes the specific foods arranged in the eating vessels to be touched by the Brahmins individually with these two verses, "The earth is your vessel" and "Viṣṇu strode across this," and at the end of that [first verse],
[he says] "O Viṣṇu, protect the sacrificial food" for the Viśvedevas.
"O Viṣṇu, protect the *kavya*," [he says] for the ancestors and others.
Having thus caused them to touch [the food], he should then feed them.
When there is the means, he should offer special items such as clarified butter (*sarpis*) and meat (*māṃsa*).
In the absence [of other offerings],
one should regard the oil and the vegetables as the *āhavanīya* fire while the Brahmins are eating,
and one should regard the ancestors and others as deities.
He regards the food as nectar and himself as Brahman;
and while they are eating, he turns away and [recites] the Rākṣoghna, Pitrya, Vaiṣṇava, and other purificatory (pavitra) mantras.
He causes them to hear the Pāvamāna mantras, the Dharmaśāstras, the Itihāsas, and the Purāṇas.
Knowing that they are satiated, he causes them to hear the Madhumatī verses and the verse beginning with "akṣannamīmadanta."
Then, he scatters food upon the ground:
"Those who were cremated by fire, those not cremated by fire, and those who were born in my family..."
May those who are satisfied by the rice-ball (piṇḍa) offered upon the ground attain the supreme goal.
Thus it is said.
Then, after they have sipped water (ācamana), he again gives them water and causes those for the ancestors and others to say "It is well-tasted" (*svaditam*),
and those for the Viśvedevas to say "It is pleasing" (*rocayate*).

Then, having given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability, and having set aside portions from all the remaining food for the sake of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*) and for consumption,
one should offer the remainder by asking, "What shall be done with the remains of the food? (*annaśeṣaiḥ kiṃ kriyatām?*).
And they should reply, "May you eat together with those you desire. Then the performer says:
"May our givers increase; may the Vedas and our progeny flourish."
May our faith not depart, and may we have much to give.
Thus he prays:
"May your donors increase, may your Vedas and your progeny flourish."
May your faith not depart from you, and may there be much for you to give.
Such was their reply.
Then [they said]: "May we have abundant food; may we receive guests;
may there be those who ask of us, and may we not have to ask anything of anyone."
And thus he prays:
"May you be free from those who do not offer a way across; may there be supplicants for you, and may you not have to supplicate others."
(Thus, more: To the [query], "May there be much food for you," the reply is given with the very few words, "Oṃ svādhā. Immediately thereafter, he says, "Oṃ svādhā."
"Let it be, svadhā," is the response.
Then, the dismissal of the Brahmins representing the ancestors and others occurs first;
the dismissal of the Viśvedevas follows afterwards.
In all the aforementioned items, such as the offerings and so forth, the priority belongs to the gods alone. Then,

wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder (yajñopavītī), having followed those who have eaten and circumambulated them, he should wear the thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvītī) and [arrange the grass] in two parts with the tips pointing south, and so on.
He performs everything up to the point ending with "he should eat the remainder, [taking] at least one mouthful," according to the sūtra.
And here this must be stated: the feeding of Brahmins, the fire-oblation (*homa*), and the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*)—these three are the primary elements in the monthly *śrāddha*.
This is because it was stated by Dhūryasvāmin [in the context of] the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*). (The reading "by Bhāṣyakera" is an addition found in manuscripts ṅa and ja.)
Regarding the phrase "the Viśvedevas in the Vaiśvadeva," this is because it has been stated by Kapardisvāmin.
Some maintain that here the feeding of the Brāhmaṇas alone is the primary act,
while the offering of gold and the giving of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) are its subordinate members.
Having established that "one should feed [the Brahmins] without regard for wealth," because those two [rules] are prescribed therein;

now, in the event that the primary ritual procedure (*mukhyakalpa*) is impossible, the rule for the *āmaśrāddha* (the śrāddha with uncooked food) is stated as a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*): "In times of distress, when one lacks a sacred fire, at a holy ford (*tīrtha*), and likewise during an eclipse of the moon or sun..."
The twice-born should perform the *āmaśrāddha*, while a Śūdra should indeed always perform it.
Thus, [it is established] by the statement of Bṛhaspati and the statement of Bṛhatpracetā (alternatively: by the statements of Bṛhaspati and Pracetas). By the statement of Bṛhatpracetā.
On this point Vyāsa says:
"The invocation must be performed, and likewise the offering of the *arghya*;
this very same procedure applies wherever [the term] *anna* (or *āma*) occurs."
Wherein the ancestral rite (śrāddha) is performed.
Whatever one gives to the Brahmins, whether it be cooked or uncooked,
with that one should perform the fire-oblation (agnaukaraṇa) and with that very same substance one should offer the funeral cakes (piṇḍas).
Thus it is said:
"In this regard, when one performs the *āmāśrāddha* according to the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*, how should the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) be done?
Having brought cooked food from the house, one should offer the rice-balls together with sesame seeds."
Thus.
As for the summary of the ritual procedure: having invited the Brahmins on the previous day or the following day, and having bathed in the forenoon, one should summon the Brahmins.
Having performed the rites from the washing of the feet up to the offering of the *arghya*,
and having honored [the deity] appropriately according to one's means with perfumes, garments, and so forth, one should announce,
"I shall perform the oblation in the fire," and then, at the conclusion of the *agnimukha* rite, perform the homa with materials such as rice and other non-sacrificial substances.
Then, having completed the remainder of the ritual manual,
he offers unhusked rice and other materials for the sake of the śrāddha;
since there is no boiled rice (caru), there is an absence of its specific ritual requirements.
And due to the absence of food, there is likewise an absence of those things related to it;
therefore, the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is made with either raw grain or with cooked food brought from the house.
But in the case of extreme distress, "even with gold there is merely the act of giving," and even with gold—(as in the variants kha, ga, ṅa:
"merely the principal")—there is merely the act of giving; or even with roots and fruits, there is merely the act of giving.
Based on such statements by Bodhāyana and others, one should perform at least the mere offering of gold and other items, even if devoid of all other ritual details.
Thus, in every respect, the Śrāddha must necessarily be performed;
there is no omission under any circumstances whatsoever.

And in this matter concerning the śrāddha, although there is the eternal Vedic revelation: "The Vasus are to be known as the fathers, the Rudras as the grandfathers, and the Ādityas as the great-grandfathers."
There is much more that could be said regarding what is established in other such scriptures; nevertheless, we shall desist here for fear of prolixity. //9//

Having thus explained the monthly *śrāddha*, which constitutes the archetype (*prakṛti*), he now intends to explain another *pākayajña* called the *aṣṭakā*, which is its modification (*vikṛti*) and is to be performed annually;
he states the rule for its timing: 23. The *aṣṭakā-śrāddha*.
Its time is as follows: the eighth day after the full moon of Māgha, which coincides with the asterism Jyeṣṭhā—that they call Ekāṣṭakā. (ĀpGS 21.10)
The rule regarding faith has been explained.

Now, the *pākayajña* known as the *aṣṭakā*, which is dedicated to the ancestors (*pitrya*) and must be performed year after year, is being taught. This is its rule for the time: following the month of Māgha, in the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) that follows it, on the eighth day—that is the *ekāṣṭakā*.
Thus they say: "If that [eighth day] coincides with or is joined by the month of Jyeṣṭha, they call that too 'Ekāṣṭakā'. These are two applications [of the term].
Otherwise, it is established by the mere statement: "The eighth day following the full moon of Jyeṣṭha, when it coincides with [the constellation] Jyeṣṭhā, they call that 'Ekāṣṭakā'.
What, then, is the significance of the term *aṣṭakatva*?
The purpose of including the term "two sets of eight" (dvyaṣṭaka) must be investigated. Why is it said, "it is joined with Jyeṣṭhā"?
It is so that when the eighth [tithi] falls on two days, the ritual may be performed when it is conjoined with the constellation Jyeṣṭhā. //10//
The meaning is: following the night of the full moon belonging to the month of Māgha, that which occurs in the dark fortnight is the *vyaṣṭakā*.

On that *vyaṣṭakā*, the eighth lunar day (*tithi*) which coincides with or is joined by the constellation Jyeṣṭhā—that eighth day the exponents of the Veda (*brahmavādinaḥ*) call the "Single *Aṣṭakā*.
The ellipsis to be supplied is: "On that [day], the *Aṣṭakā* is to be performed."
The meaning is that on the Ekāṣṭakā day, the primary rites beginning with the offering of the omentum (vapāhoma) must be performed.

The statement "they call that [day] Ekāṣṭakā" indicates that whatever other rites are prescribed for the Ekāṣṭakā— such as the initiation (dīkṣā) for the Gavāmayana sacrifice, or, for instance, the fasting of the underwood with cakes during long sacrificial sessions (dīrghasatra) for the sake of spiritual knowledge— all are intended here.
And for the purpose of gathering the necessary materials as required, and so that all of these may be performed on the eighth day possessing the characteristics already described;
herein is the intention: although not every eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha coincides with the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra.
Nevertheless, the Ekāṣṭakā must indeed be performed therein;
for it is obligatory as a *pākayajña*, and because of the specific mention [in the scripture] that "the Aṣṭakā is on that [Ekāṣṭakā]."
The statement "it is accomplished with the Jyeṣṭhā [nakṣatra]" refers to the general rule;
therefore, even when [the moon] is not in conjunction with Jyeṣṭhā, the initiations (*dīkṣā*) for the Gavāmayana sacrifice and other rites are still obtained.

Some hold the view that the intention is as follows: when the eighth day falls on two consecutive days, or in a year in which there are two Māgha months, one should perform the rite on that eighth day which coincides with the Jyeṣṭhā nakṣatra, and not on one that does not so coincide. //10//
Its evening [rite] is performed in the *aupakārya* hall.
That which is performed in proximity (*upa*) is called an *upakāra* (benefit). That which exists therein is *aupakārya*. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is "the *aupakārya* belonging to that."
The rite which is performed near that Ekāṣṭakā on the preceding day, the seventh [lunar day], there he cooks a cake (*apūpa*) in four *śarāva* measures.
The meaning is that on the evening of the seventh, after the sun has set, the ritual involving the cake as the oblation must be performed.
Thus, the word *aupakārya* is intended to prescribe the time;
when it is construed with "in the evening" (*sāyam*), one obtains the cake on the eighth day after sunset,
and the animal on the ninth day.
"The Anvaṣṭakā [is performed] on the tenth day"—this is not well-known in those scriptures;
furthermore, the word *aupakārya* is meaningless. //11//

This sūtra consists of three words. Regarding the term *aupakāryam*, it means "that which assists" (*upakārakam*) that group of eight; the suffix *-ya* is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*), according to Vedic usage (*chāndasa*).
