The meaning is that it is a ritual action that constitutes a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the Aṣṭakā. On the evening of the seventh day [of the dark fortnight] preceding [the eighth], a ritual action that is a subsidiary part of that Aṣṭakā must be performed, just as the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice is a subsidiary part of the Soma sacrifice; thus, it is to be performed on the evening of the seventh day preceding [the eighth].
This is the meaning of the Sūtra:
however, the connection here is not "of that Aṣṭakā," because the primary ritual acts, such as the offering of the omentum (*vapā*), occur on the ninth day;
and this [interpretation] is not tenable.

The phrase "yā mādhyā" [is not a time-injunction] because it is logically possible for it to serve as a subordinate element (upakāryārtha) of the injunction; furthermore, this would contradict the maxim "from the context, [the reference is] to the principal," and because such an interpretation is unestablished in other scriptural traditions. //11//
Now he states the procedure for this rite:

having silently measured out four *sarāva* measures of rice, she cooks the cake (*apūpa*) according to the procedure beginning with "the wife threshes [the grain] as in the *Pārvaṇa* [rite]," and so forth.
A *apūpa* is well known as a cake whose constituent parts are spread out.
And he performs [the rites] ending with the sprinkling of clarified butter upon the established [fire]. (ĀpGs 21.12)
2. [The section] on the cake-offering: he cooks a cake prepared from four measures of parched grain. //12//
Some say it should be on eight potsherds. (ĀpGS 21.13)
Some maintain that the evening oblation consists of a cake (*apūpa*) prepared on eight potsherds (*aṣṭākapāla*).
That which is prepared on eight potsherds is called *aṣṭākapāla*.
According to this view, the baking is performed according to the procedure for a sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
However, for the former [rite], the procedure follows that of the worldly *apūpa* offering;
in both cases, the cooking is performed on the *aupāsana* fire.
And although this is an ancillary rite belonging to the ancestral (*pitrya*) ceremony, it does not itself become a rite dedicated to the ancestors.
Therefore, the wearing of the sacred thread over the left shoulder (prācīnāvīta) and so forth does not take place. //12//
Thus ends the twenty-first section in the Anākula commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra composed by the venerable Hara-datta Miśra.
The sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) prepared on eight potsherds is called "aṣṭakapāla. According to some, it should be cooked [on the fire].
Furthermore, since "puroḍāśa" refers to a well-known specific form, its cooking should be performed in the manner of common practice, specifically on the *aupāsana* fire. 13.
Thus ends the twenty-first section in the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
Chapter Twenty-Two: Section Three.
The Oblation of Cake with the Joined Palms.
At the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, as in the *Pārvaṇa* rite, he offers portions of cake with his joined palms while reciting the following verse. (ĀpGs 22.1)

When the *pratiṣṭhitābhidhāraṇa* (the pouring of clarified butter over the oblation) has been performed and the fire has been replenished with fuel, having completed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he offers from the cake (*apūpa*) with his joined palms (*añjali*) using the subsequent Ṛc, according to the procedure for portions (*avadāna-kalpa*) as in the *Pārvaṇa* sacrifice, with the verse: "The one whom people welcome...
By implication, there is another person to perform the under-pouring (*upastaraṇa*), the over-pouring (*abhighāraṇa*), and the taking of the portion (*avadāna*).
The mention of "up to the *ājyabhāga*" is for the purpose of establishing the ritual framework (*tantra*).
This very point serves as the indicator that this rite is not for the ancestors (*pitrya*).
Otherwise, just as the *tantra* (the common framework) proceeds even in the absence of a specific effort in the monthly *śrāddha* and the *aṣṭakā*,
it has been stated that the *tantra* would likewise proceed in the rites for the ancestors even in the absence of a specific effort.
In the same way, it would be established here as well.

The statement "like the Pārvaṇa" is for the purpose of obtaining the ritual procedure for the portions (avadāna-kalpa), because the *añjali*-offerings do not adopt the properties [of the standard offerings]. Thus, even when offering with the joined palms (*añjali*), one offers according to the Pārvaṇa procedure by means of the portion-division rite.
However, the acts of placing [the portions], sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), and wiping (*saṃmārjana*) do not apply to the *añjali*. //1//

Then, having performed the rites from the kindling of the fire according to the *pārvaṇa* procedure up to the end of the *agnimukha*, he takes a portion from the cake or the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) according to his own rule for taking portions, and offers it with his joined palms while reciting the following verse: "Her whom people welcome... and so forth.

Regarding the *añjali* (the hollowed palms), one other person should perform the smearing with the residue of the consecration (*saṃskāralepa*), the anointing (*añjana*), the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*), the over-pouring (*abhigāraṇa*), and the portions of the oblation (*haviravadāna*), because these are prohibited [for the primary agent].

However, one offers the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation with the ladle (*darvī*) and not with the *añjali*; for according to the logical principle that "a ritual duty (*dharma*) enjoined in a modification (*vikṛti*) serves the purpose of the primary rite."
Nor should it be said that because the *aupakārya* [rite] is a subordinate member (*aṅga*), it lacks primacy (*prādhānya*) altogether;
for even this [rite] possesses primacy in relation to its own subordinate members.
For this very reason, it is stated: "One should recite softly during the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering]" (Āpastamba Śrautasūtra).

(ĀpŚS 10.4.11) Thus, the restriction on speech is for the sake of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice—which is a primary constituent of the Soma sacrifice—alone, and not for its subsidiaries such as the *prayāja*s.
Similarly, (ĀpŚS 5.17.6) "Then he offers the *agnihotra* silently":

the quality of silence is a property of the primary *agnihotra* itself, which is a modification (*vikṛti*) of the obligatory (*naiyamika*) *agnihotra* that is a subsidiary of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*), and not a property of its own subsidiaries.

It has already been stated that the repetition of the established ritual procedure for the guest-house (*aupakārya*)—which is itself proven by the fact that it is a medicinal herb and a *havuṣka* offering—is for the purpose of extending its application to this bath-offering of curd (*snāpannadadhihoma*). ĀpGS 22.2:
"The distribution of the remainder divided into eight parts to the Brahmins:
the remainder is prepared; having divided it into eight parts, he distributes it to the Brahmins."
The remainder of the tantra becomes established as unmodified; this is the meaning.
"He offers with joined palms"—the meaning is that both [of these] are excluded from the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
Therefore, having offered the *sviṣṭakṛt* with a ladle according to the rule for portions, and having placed twenty-one fuel-sticks, he proceeds with the *jaya* and subsequent rites. //2//

Regarding the statement, "O Brāhmaṇas, [eat] that which is mixed with clarified butter," when the eating by a single person would otherwise result, the withholding from eight [Brāhmaṇas] is prescribed.
In that case, having announced [the matter] to those Brāhmaṇas who are to eat on the following day, he observes the fast. // 3 //

The statement, "He brings the remainder of the cake, mixed with curds, for the purpose of tasting," is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to enjoin that one should divide that remainder, along with clarified butter, into eight portions and give them to eight Brahmins. Consequently, in this case, there is a sublation of the singularity of the Brahmin.
Some maintain that the sutra should be divided as "siddhaḥ śeṣaḥ" (the remainder is established).
This means the remainder of the ritual procedure is established in its unmodified form;
by this, the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation is performed with the wooden ladle (*darvī*).

And since it is established that one should begin with the Jaya and other [mantras], in the phrase "that [offering] eightfold," there would be a reference to the *apūpa* (cake) which is separated [from it].

Thus, having performed the *aupakārya* rite, he should inform the Brāhmaṇas who are to be the recipients—just as in the case of the monthly *śrāddha*—"Tomorrow there will be the Aṣṭakā-śrāddha"; this is the distinction. //2//
5. The dedication of the cow.
On the following day, he dedicates the cow with darbha grass, saying: "I dedicate you, acceptable to the ancestors. (ĀpGs 22.3)
In the phrase "with darbha grass," the singular number is not intended to be significant; [the word] "cow" refers to a female,
as indicated by the gender of the term *juṣṭām*.
Standing to the east facing west,
as is seen in the Śrauta ritual; and also the rite for the ancestors (paitrya).

Because of the observation of the formula "ṭakākarma, pitṛbhyas tvā juṣṭām," it was stated previously that in rites for the ancestors (pitrya), the ritual procedure (tantra) proceeds even without a formal effort [to initiate it]. Therefore, once the *ājyabhāga* offerings have been performed at the conclusion of the *tantra*, the commencement of the *upākaraṇa* and subsequent rites takes place.
We shall state the authoritative evidence for this:
"The afternoon of the dark fortnight is preferable"—this is the time;
and in all cases, the sacred thread is worn over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīta). //4//
Then, on the following day, the eighth lunar day,

having invited the Brahmins to his house and performed everything up to the *agnimukha* rite as in the monthly *śrāddha*, he then, with a single blade of *darbha* grass, dedicates the cow to the females, saying: "I dedicate you, who are pleasing to the ancestors (*pitṛs*), to the ancestors."
With this mantra, he performs the introductory rite (upākaraṇa). //3//

6. The offering of the omentum (vapā-homa). Having silently offered five oblations of clarified butter and having cooked its omentum, he offers it—after spreading a base of ghee and pouring ghee over it—with either a middle or a terminal leaf of the Palāśa tree, reciting the subsequent [verse]. (ĀpGs 22.4)

If "silently" (*tūṣṇīm*) were not stated, then in the absence of a recipient (*sampradāna*), the oblation (*homa*) would not take place; consequently, since the necessity of postulating a deity (*devatā*) would arise, one might understand [the oblations] to be those five animal-offerings prescribed by the rule, "Having brought [the animal] forward, he offers five," which belong to the animal sacrifice (*pāśubandhika*).
Therefore, even though the mantras would have been applicable [by default], the word "silently" is stated.
By stating this, he shows that the ritual processing (*saṃskāra*) of the animal prescribed by the Śruti applies even to the animal [offered] on the *āvṛt* day.
Therefore, specific details such as "standing facing west in front" and so forth also apply here.
The mention of "of that" (*tasyāḥ*) is intended so that the specific details enjoined here—such as the cooking (*śrapaṇa*) and so on—should pertain specifically to its omentum (*vapā*).

It is not for the purpose of [defining] an *avadāna*; therefore, the preparation of meat, rice, and so forth should take place in another fire, as in the case of the monthly *śrāddha*. Consequently, the mention of clarified butter (*ājya*) is redundant.
This is already established by the rule "one offers with the following verse," yet it is stated here for the sake of providing an explanatory indication (*jñāpaka*);

it indicates that once the *tantra* (the common ritual framework) has been completed up to the end of the *ājyabhāga* offerings, the *upākaraṇa* and subsequent rites for the animal sacrifice are to be performed.
How does this serve as an indicator?

In all primary offerings where there is a plurality of tantric oblations possessing the same characteristics, a qualification is observed— such as "an offering of clarified butter from the cooked rice"—
and that same [qualification] is seen here as well.
This indicates that only the Tantrika priest performs the two oblations with clarified butter (*ājya*).

Furthermore, the immediate succession between the *upākaraṇa* rite and these [oblations] is observed in the text: "Having performed the *upākaraṇa*, he offers five oblations" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.1.5).
Therefore, it is established that the dedication (*upākaraṇa*) of the animal takes place at the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings.
Having thus offered the five *ājya* oblations, having quieted the animal silently, having extracted the omentum (*vapā*) silently with the two omentum-spits (*vapāśrapaṇī*),

having cooked it on the *aupāsana* fire, having sprinkled it with clarified butter, having placed it upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and having sprinkled it again, one then [takes] that omentum which has been spread under and sprinkled over with butter.
He offers with either the middle or the last leaf of a Palāśa tree, using the following verse, "Bring the omentum" (avaha vapām).
The placing and other rites for the spit of the supreme [victim] take place together with the vessels of the two omentum-roasting spits.
He offers five oblations of clarified butter silently, even without the utterance of *svāhā*, because there is an absence of any [prescribed] mantra;
and their deity is Prajāpati alone.
The passage beginning with "tasyai vapām" has been explained;
[it is performed] with the verse "uttarayāvaha vapām. //4//
7. Offerings of meat-rice:
one offers meat-rice with the following [verses]. (ĀpGs 22.5)

When the omentum has been offered, having had the animal slaughtered for the sake of the Anvaṣṭakā rite, one should cook it along with other sacrificial foods such as boiled rice in the house; then, having sprinkled them with clarified butter, placed them upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), and sprinkled them again, one offers them with the *darvī* spoon according to the procedure for taking portions (*avadāna-kalpa*).
In this case, the procedure of offering a single oblation (*sakṛdupaghāta-kalpa*) does not apply.
Because of the contradiction regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering;
because [the offering] is absent in the case of clarified butter (*ājya*), while it is present in the case of meat, flour, and cooked rice.
There, one offers *māṃsaudana* (meat-rice) with these seven [verses] beginning with "yāṃ janāḥ pratinandanti.
*Māṃsaudana* is rice mixed with meat;
and the mixing takes place at the time of the oblation (*homa*).
Not at the time of boiling,
because of the unevenness of the cooking;
in this ritual, eighteen offering-mantras are recited.
There are ten *ṛc*s and eight *yajus* formulas.
Among them, the first *ṛc* is for the sake of the *apūpa*,
and the subsequent one is for the sake of the *vapā*.

The feminine designation "with the *uttarā*s, etc. is used because he will later state, "with the *uttarā* [verses], [he offers] flour-food. Therefore, the oblation of the rice cooked with meat is performed with seven verses.
"Meat-mixed rice" is *māṃsaudana*; he offers that with the seven [verses] beginning with "That which people welcome" (*yāṃ janāḥ pratinandanti*).
And this must be stated here:

at the end of the offering of the omentum (*vapā*), having caused the cow to be slaughtered, one should set aside some meat for the purpose of serving as a condiment for the Brāhmaṇas who are to be fed at the subsequent *Aṣṭakā* rite.
Having cooked the rest of the entire [offering] in the manner prescribed for worldly rites,
one mixes a portion of it with the rice set aside for the purpose of the oblation— just as in the *māsi-śrāddha*— from the food intended for feeding the Brahmins;
then, one offers the oblation with that very same rice mixed with meat.
Nor should it be suspected that the meat and the rice were cooked together,
because the food intended for the oblation was set aside even before the cow was slaughtered, and because there is a difference in the cooking times of the meat and the rice. //5//
8. Oblations of ground-grain food:
one offers the ground-grain food with the following [verse]. (ĀpGs 22.6)
He offers into the milk food prepared from flour, using the subsequent verse, "And the Ukthya," for its cooking.
*Piṣṭānna* is well-known as food made from flour cooked in milk.
One offers that with the next verse, "And the Ukthya" (*ukthyaś ca*).
In this rite, *piṣṭānna* must necessarily be prepared for the purpose of feeding the Brāhmaṇas and other such needs.
The extraction of the boiled portion for the sake of the *homa* must be performed separately beforehand;
as for the meat-rice and the flour-rice, their own rules regarding the cutting of portions (*avadāna*) apply just as in the *pārvaṇa* sacrifice.
In this rite, however, the *palāśa* leaf is used solely for the offering of the omentum (*vapā*).
The other [oblation] is offered with the *darvī* ladle alone. //6//
There are nine oblations of clarified butter;
the subsequent [oblations] are also of clarified butter. (ĀpGs 22.7)
The meaning is that he offers eight oblations of clarified butter with the subsequent mantras beginning with "bhūḥ pṛthivyagninarcā" (Bhūḥ! Earth, Fire, and the Ṛgveda). //8//

The meaning is that one offers eight oblations of clarified butter (ājyāhuti) performed with the subsequent mantras; and these, beginning with "bhūḥ pṛthivyagninā," are in the form of Yajus formulas. //7//
10. The *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and so forth.
From the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering onwards, the procedure is the same up to the placing of the rice balls (*piṇḍa*). (ĀpGS 22.8)

The meaning is that the entire ritual procedure, beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and ending with the placement of the *piṇḍas*, should be performed here just as it is in the monthly *śrāddha*.
In this case, the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is made from the meat-rice and the flour;
after that, the *jaya* and subsequent rites follow.
Then follows the seating of the Brahmins, the bringing of water-vessels into their hands, and their adornment.
Thereafter, he should touch everything with the subsequent [mantras], beginning with "adityai rāsnāsī" and ending with "he should consume [the food] up to the best morsel.
On this day, this alone constitutes the meal; there is no other.
And once begun, there shall be no eating until its completion;
furthermore, the five sacrifices are thereby omitted. //9//

The remainder of the ritual procedure (tantra-śeṣa), beginning with the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and including the touching of all [the offerings] and ending with the circumambulation; the feeding of the Brahmins;
the placing of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-nidhāna*);
and the eating of the first portion of the morsels (*grāsa-varārdhya*)—all this is to be performed.
The meaning is that the entire collection of ritual items must be prepared here as well, just as in the monthly *śrāddha*.
In this regard, however, there is a distinction: from both the meat-rice and the flour-rice, a portion is to be cut off together for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering. //8//
Some teachers prescribe the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa-nidhāna) specifically on the Anvaṣṭakā day.
If it were said that "the placing of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) does not take place," then the placing of the rice-balls would also not occur at the Anvaṣṭakā;
however, the Aṣṭakā is the subject under discussion. Therefore, what possibility is there that it would not occur at the Anvaṣṭakā?
If that is so, then this makes it known: here, this is an option (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, it becomes the object of the entire ritual action, namely "together with the cake" (*sāpūpa*) and "together with the Anvaṣṭaka rite" (*sānvaṣṭaka*).
Consequently, some hold that the handful of curd (*dadhyañjali*) is optional because it is performed as part of the entire Aṣṭakā rite, being [alternatively] "with the cake" or "with the Anvaṣṭaka."

We, however, say: the statement that "there is no eating for him if the Aṣṭakā has not been performed" is precisely for this purpose—that the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) which occurs at the Anvaṣṭakā need not be performed separately in this ritual. //10//

Regarding that which will be prescribed as "the Anvaṣṭakā on the following day," some teachers teach that the depositing of the *piṇḍas*—that is, the offering of the *piṇḍas*—should take place specifically at that Anvaṣṭakā and not at the Aṣṭakā itself.

Some [commentators] say: since it should have been stated simply as "some [do not perform] the depositing of the *piṇḍas*," this specific phrasing—"only at the Anvaṣṭakā, according to some"—indicates that the option being prescribed applies to the entire ritual procedure, including both the *Sāpūpahoma* and the *Anvaṣṭakā*.
Therefore, the curd-offering (*dadhi-homa*) is an alternative to the entire *Aṣṭakā* rite ending with the *Anvaṣṭakā*.
However, some maintain that the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa-nidhāna*) which occurs on the *Anvaṣṭakā* day is itself [the substitute] for this [curd-offering].
Furthermore, by the phrasing "it should not be performed separately in this place," there is an indication that this ritual action is incomplete.
Consequently, if the Anvaṣṭakā has not been performed, the performer must neither eat nor perform the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña).
In reality, however— since no specific meaning has been stated here by the author of the Bhāṣya,
since it will be stated later that "the Anvaṣṭakā [rite] belongs to both fortnights," and because the completion of the intermediate performance is clearly evident—

Regarding the statement, "Only on the Anvaṣṭakā," it should be understood that this designation is intended to convey the result: namely, that the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍa) takes place specifically on the Anvaṣṭakā and not on the Aṣṭakā itself.

Now, the distinction between the *yajñopavīta* (sacrificial thread over the left shoulder) and the *prācīnāvīta* (thread over the right shoulder): [the latter is used] at the *aupakārya* rite, during the offerings of meat and rice in the first four [oblations],
during the offering of flour-food in the sixth, and during the offering of clarified butter in the first six.
In the *dadhi-homa* and in the *āghāra* offerings and so forth, the *yajñopavīta* is likewise prohibited (the phrase "prior to those" is added).
Because mantras have the characteristic of being divine;
elsewhere, as in the original state, the sacred thread is worn over the left shoulder (prācīnāvīta).
But is it not the case that in this Kali age, the slaughter of cows is forbidden according to the consensus of those who know the Dharma?

Therefore, although in the case of the injunction "one should offer meat-rice with the [next] verses," the performance of the *aṣṭakā* rite is established by means of oblations consisting solely of cooked rice (*odana*)—accompanied by other principal rites—even in the absence of meat which is subordinate to the sacrificial offering (*havis*), such an interpretation is nonetheless untenable regarding the offering of the omentum (*vapā*), because its very essential form (*svarūpa*) would be absent.

This is not so; for even when a certain principal rite is prohibited on the strength of authoritative evidence, the fulfillment of the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is still possible through other principal rites, since the recognition of the subject matter (*viṣaya-pratyabhijñāna*) remains intact.

For this very reason, although the *sānnāyya* and the *āgnīṣomīya* are prohibited for those who have not performed the *soma* sacrifice— by the injunctions "One who has not sacrificed with *soma* shall not offer the *sānnāyya*" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.5.5) and "The *āgnīṣomīya* cake does not exist for a Brāhmaṇa who has not sacrificed with *soma*" (*Āpastamba Śrauta Sūtra*)— the entitlement to perform the primary rites of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* is nonetheless established through those principal offerings other than these two.
However, this is the distinction: in some cases it is the Vedic revelation that is prohibitive, while in others it is the convention of those who know the Dharma.
The convention of those who know the Dharma is also an authoritative means of knowledge, just like the Veda.

Alternatively, clarified butter (*ājya*) alone should be employed in place of the omentum and the flesh; for this is seen in the case of the *pātnīvata* offering in the injunction, "One should conclude the remainder with clarified butter," and also in the injunction, "One should cut off [the portions] from clarified butter. (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 3.1.3).

As for the attainment [of the result], it follows from the very fact that the entire set of eight [offerings] is permanent. Alternatively, a goat alone is to be sacrificed in place of the cow; this is because it shares the same status as the subject at hand, as in the passage: "One should sacrifice a bull let loose again to Indra and Agni" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.1.5).

In this regard, because the *Bharadvāja-sūtra* is observed to state, "In place of the cow that has been released again, there is a goat not to be released again," one should understand that even the alternative of offering curd—a rite which is extremely light—is established for the Kali Yuga. As for the authority [for this], it is the learned elders (*vṛddha*) among the *traividya*, who are themselves the cultured (*śiṣṭa*). //9//
11. The Oblation with a Handful of Curd.
Now, this is another [rite]: he offers curd itself with his joined palms, in the same manner as the cake. (ĀpGS 22.10)

Thus, the primary ritual procedure (*mukhya-kalpa*) for the Aṣṭakā has been shown. Now follows the secondary procedure (*anukalpa*): with the verse "yāṃ janāḥ" (RV 10.57.3), one offers an oblation from a full handful (*añjali*) of curd.
Because of the injunction regarding the *tantra* (the ritual framework) and because it is an offering made with a handful, this handful of curd constitutes a unique rite (*apūrva*).
By the statement "with joined palms" (*añjalinā*), the ladle (*darvī*) is excluded.
(2 ka, kha: Neither the preliminary ritual (*purastāttantra*) nor the concluding ritual (*upariṣṭāttantra*) is performed in its entirety;
furthermore, the two-fold ritual framework (*tantradvaya*) does not exist.)
What, then, is its time? It is on the eighth day. And the performance takes place in the forenoon because it pertains to the deities.

After the morning *homa*, having kindled the *aupāsana* fire, strewn it around, and silently sprinkled water all over it, he fills his joined palms with curds and offers the oblation with the verse, "yāṃ janāḥ."
There is no *sviṣṭakṛt* offering;
however, the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*) is performed again silently.
Others, however, desire the *purastāt-tantra* ritual sequence including the *sviṣṭakṛt*, but not the *jaya* offerings and so forth.
The source for this must be sought;
this is the proper time because it is the practice of the Teacher.
For this indeed is the Teacher’s practice regarding the secondary options (*anukalpa*).
For example: "At the return ceremony (samāvartana), one should simply bathe at a sacred ford (tīrtha) in silence.
Furthermore, this offering of a handful of curd (*dadhyañjali*) supersedes those oblations (*homa*) performed on the eighth day (*aṣṭakā*), because it is mentioned immediately following them.
There is no *apūpa-homa* (offering of cakes),
nor is there an *anvaṣṭakā*;
however, the feeding of Brahmins and the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa-nirvāpaṇa*) do take place.
"This handful of curd is the displacer of the oblation alone.
If that is the case, then the meaning of the statement here is revealed as: 'That which one offers, that is [to be done] with curd, and specifically with a handful.
Another says: 'It is the displacer of both the cake and the eightfold offering.'"
[This applies] not to the Anvaṣṭakā;
for if there were a substitute even for that, then after mentioning it, this secondary rule (anukalpa) would have to be stated.
Others, however, hold that the handful of curd is a substitute for the entire Aṣṭakā rite, including both the offering with cakes and the Anvaṣṭakā. 10.
With the verse "yayā yāṃ janāḥ," he offers a cake;
with that same verse, having cut off portions of the curd according to the rule for the Svāvadāna, he offers it with his joined palms.
And like the Pārvaṇa rite, the offering of curd takes place at the end of the Agnimukha.
The portioning of the offering is like that of the cake-oblation (*apūpa-homa*).
The rule beginning with "that by which one offers, having heated it over the fire," and so forth, as well as the smearing and anointing, should be performed by another person.
And this curd-oblation (*dadhi-homa*) takes place on the eighth day in the forenoon.

Some [teachers] maintain that all *añjali-homas* (handful-oblations) are *apūrva* (unprecedented rites), and that in their case there is no ritual framework (*tantra*) either before or after; furthermore,

this alternative procedure (*anukalpa*) should be understood as applying specifically in place of the cake-oblations (*apūpa-homa*) and those ending with the subsequent clarified-butter oblations (*ājyāhuti*).
Nor does it apply to the Anvaṣṭakā [rite] itself,
because after prescribing the ritual up to the oblation of clarified butter (ājyāhuti), an alternative procedure is prescribed even before the Anvaṣṭakā; therefore,
in both fortnights, the Anvaṣṭakā on the ninth day is indeed obligatory.
Therefore, the claim that there is no *anvaṣṭakā* rite in the case of the curd-oblation (*dadhihoma*) is baseless.
Furthermore, this injunction for the curd-oblation applies specifically to the place of the [regular] oblations;
this is because of the natural sense of the word *juhoti* in the statement, "He offers with a handful of curd alone."
Therefore, even in this view, there is a repetition of both the feeding of the Brahmins and the offering of the rice-balls (piṇḍas).
Consequently, on the seventh night, having invited the Brahmins, the curd-oblation (dadhi-homa) is performed at the place of the fire-sacrifice (homa) on the eighth;
thereafter, in the afternoon, everything beginning with the meal remains unchanged.
It is thus established that the Anvaṣṭakā rite also takes place on the ninth day.
12. The Anvaṣṭakā [rite]: For this very reason, having set aside meat according to the requirements, on the following day one performs the Anvaṣṭakā.

Therefore, when this very cow has been sacrificed on the Ekāṣṭakā day, having set aside as much meat as is required for each person according to their need, the rite named Anvaṣṭakā must be performed on the following day, the ninth tithi. The word "eva" (only/very) is used precisely to exclude [the practice] of using more meat, such as that of a buffalo, and so forth. //11//
On the following day, the rite known as the Anvaṣṭakā is to be performed on the ninth lunar day (navamī).

For this very reason, the statement "having set aside the meat of the cow sacrificed at the Aṣṭakā according to its purpose and according to the requirement" refers specifically to the first alternative view.
The ritual procedure for that [offering] has been explained by the rules for the monthly śrāddha.
The meaning is that the Anvaṣṭakā rite is to be performed like the Māsi-śrāddha.
Because of the extension of the ritual procedure (kalpātideśa), everything—including the materials and the deities—is obtained here.
Regarding the statement, "There, one offers oblations of food with the subsequent verses," they maintain that the offering consists of food mixed with meat.
Because it is seen in the *Aṣṭakā* [rites],
and because of the statement here that "meat is according to the purpose" (*yathārtha māṃsam*),
others maintain that there should be no offering of food from the monthly *śrāddha* by extension.
"In whatever ritual occasion meat is prescribed for the monthly *śrāddha*, it is also [prescribed] here in that same context.
On this point, some maintain that even in the case of the "handful of curd" (*dadhy-añjali*) rite, one should perform the *anvaṣṭakā* offerings,
because they are enjoined in the middle of that sequence.
For if this were indeed a substitute for the *anvaṣṭakā* as well, then after mentioning that too, it would have had to be stated;

therefore, the connection with what precedes is: "Having set aside meat according to the purpose, on the following day the *anvaṣṭakā* [is performed]; its ritual procedure is explained by the *māsi-śrāddha*. Thus it is linked to the previous section.
Now, the procedure for the *ekoddiṣṭa* [śrāddha] according to another treatise:
that śrāddha which is performed with reference to a single deceased person (*preta*) is the *ekoddiṣṭa*. An odd number of Brahmins are invited—namely, one, three, or five.
Through increase, there is a greater abundance of fruit;
in that case, there is no offering into the fire,
nor is there the formal announcement.
There is no prior invitation, no offering to the gods, and no incense.
Neither a lamp, nor the svadhā offering, nor prostration.
The Brāhmaṇas face north.

Having taken a single portion from all the food, they should draw out embers mixed with ash toward the south and offer the oblation upon those very embers, saying: "Svāhā to the deceased, to such-and-such a person, and to Yama.
The mention of "to the deceased" (pretāya) is for the purpose of specifying the name of the deceased; they desire the practical application to be: "Svāhā to Yajñaśarman and to Yama."
Others [say it is] "for the deceased Yajñaśarman" and "for Yama.
The receiving and dismissal of the water is performed with the formula, "May there be satisfaction for such-and-such," and the response is, "There is satisfaction.
The dedication is performed with the formula, "May it attend upon such-and-such."
And "offering a ball of food" (piṇḍadāna) refers to the place of eating;
"be satisfied" refers to the rinsing of the mouth.
This ekoddiṣṭa rite is well-known for all castes to be performed at the end of their own period of impurity.

Now, there are other [śrāddhas], namely the *navaśrāddha*, the monthly (*māsika*), the tri-monthly (*traipakṣika*), the six-monthly (*ṣāṇmāsika*), and the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*). That which is performed first is the *navaśrāddha*;
it is so called because it is both new (*nava*) and a śrāddha.
According to the sequence of castes, the [proper] time is on the fourth and fifth days, as well as on the ninth and eleventh;
whatever is given here for the sake of a living being is called the *navaśrāddha*.
Thus [it is said].
Others maintain that for all castes (*varṇa*), there are four types of *navaśrāddha* (new funeral rites).
In these, the term "new" (*nava*) applies to the second and subsequent [offerings].
There are twelve monthly rites (*māsika*) which must be performed on the anniversary of death every month.
The first [of these offerings] they perform while still in their own state of impurity;

the last is performed on the anniversary of death itself along with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*. The third-month, sixth-month, and annual offerings are performed on the anniversary of death itself during the second and subsequent years—this being the annual (*sāṃvatsarika*) rite.
These sixteen are *ekoddiṣṭa* rites, and regarding the annual rite, there is an option between the *ekoddiṣṭa* procedure and that for the *kṣetraja* and *jāraja* sons.
For others, there is only the *ekoddiṣṭa*.
For those who maintain that there is a combination of the nine *śrāddhas*, even their well-known position that "there are sixteen *ekoddiṣṭas*" would be difficult to justify.
On this point, they recite:
The perpetual *śrāddha* should be performed every month; if that is not possible, it should be done every season, or every twelve days, or all twelve at once on a single day.

Now, the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* [rite] takes place after one year, or in the eleventh, fourth, third, or third-fortnightly month, or in the half-month, or on the twelfth day, or upon the attainment of the initiation (*upanayana*) or an auspicious occasion (*abhyudaya*).
In that case, there is a combination of the *ekoddiṣṭa* and the monthly *śrāddha*.
The *ekoddiṣṭa* is for the deceased (*preta*), while the monthly *śrāddha* is for his father and the others; and there is no modification whatsoever in the mantras.

In the verses beginning with "O my mother," just as they were previously employed by the deceased father, so too must they be employed by the son. Furthermore, no one other than the son has the authority to perform the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite, because there is no monthly *śrāddha* for anyone else.
And because the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* is a modification of the procedure for the monthly *śrāddha*,
therefore, for a deceased person who has no son, the wife offers the monthly *śrāddha* to her husband according to the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite alone for as long as she lives;
and a son who has not yet been married does exactly the same.
When one begins the monthly *śrāddha* after marriage, one begins it together with the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the father;
however, the performance of this may also occur in other ways.

In that case, for the deceased father, there is an oblation into the ashes as before, while for the others, it is performed from food and clarified butter according to the rules of the monthly *śrāddha*.

Regarding the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍadāna*): having offered the rice-balls as in the monthly *śrāddha*, one should offer a rice-ball for the deceased (*preta*) on separate *darbha* grass spread near them.

Having offered water as before, one should pour half of the *arghya* water from that vessel into the vessels of the ancestors with the verse "Ye samānā" (RV X.14.3–4). One should then merge the rice-ball into the other rice-balls.
This is the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa*.
When this has been performed, the deceased attains the status of an ancestor (pitṛ).
And the fourth [ancestor], having been requested for permission, becomes one whose portion is relinquished.
Regarding this, there is a disagreement: some mix the vessel and the rice-ball (piṇḍa) of the great-grandfather (prapitāmaha) with those of the others.
By the word *preta*, that very person is meant, as one who has "gone away" (*pra-ita*) in an eminent sense;
for he is permitted [to depart] here. However, the established custom is that he for whom the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite has been performed is a *preta*.
Furthermore, there is a commingling of his very vessel and alms-food with those of the others;
even so, the permission belongs specifically to the great-grandfather.
This is the case in the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* of the mother, provided she was an appointed daughter (*putrikā*).
Alternatively, for a woman married through an Āsura or other such form of marriage, there is a connection with the *piṇḍas* of her maternal grandfather and others;
some establish that her *piṇḍa* is joined with those of the father-in-law and so forth, while for one who has ascended the same funeral pyre, it is joined with the *piṇḍa* of the husband.
However, the actual practice should be performed in accordance with the established customs of the ancestors.
On this point, some read as follows: "A brother, or a brother's son, a sapinda, or even a disciple—
having performed the sapinda-rites, he should then perform the auspicious rite."
Thus.
Likewise:
"But when a woman dies without a son, her husband shall perform the sapindikarana."

Now, regarding the *nāndīśrāddha*: on this point, Bodhāyana states—“Now, in the case of auspicious rites (*abhyudayika*), the procedure is clockwise; the sacred thread is worn over the left shoulder (*yajñopavīta*); the *darbha* grass blades have their tips pointing eastward;
an even number of Brahmins are invited; and barley is used in place of sesame seeds.”
The oblation consists of speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*).
With the vessel accompanied by the *upayāma* formula, there is the receiving of water with the words, "May the *nāndīmukha* ancestors be pleased," as well as the mixing [of the water].
The offering into the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*) and the assignment of portions is performed with the formula: "Svāhā to the Nāndīmukha ancestors.

When the vessels have been swept clean, the offering is made upon the *darbha* grass with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), using the formula: "Svadhā and obeisance to the Nāndīmukha ancestors," twice for each [ancestor] (Baudhāyana Gṛhyasūtra 3.12.2–5).

In that very same section, at another point: "When they have eaten their fill, having murmured the Yajus-mantra, 'I shall meditate on honey, I shall produce honey,' in the place of the *svadhā*, he pours water [with the words], 'May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased.'"
He leads [the offerings]; thus it is said that this is indeed the *svadhā*.

They do not perform the rites for the gods and the ancestors on the same day; for him who performs the ancestral rite and the divine rite on the same day, his offspring will be subject to premature death.
Therefore, the rite is performed for the ancestors on the preceding day.
"On the following day, [the offering] belongs to the gods" (Baudhāyana Gṛhyapariśiṣṭa 1.3.10–11).
Likewise, having smeared [the ground] with barley mixed with flowers, fruits, and unbroken grains, and having scattered curd-rice for the sake of the sesame seeds;
therein, the monthly *śrāddha* is the archetype for all ancestral rites.
Our specific details, however, are to be learned from other treatises.
Therefore, everything beginning with "the announcement on the previous day" also applies here.
There should be an even number of Brahmins—either eight or sixteen.
If there are eight [cakes], two are for the gods and two each for the ancestors;
if there are sixteen, four are for the gods and twelve for the ancestors, and so forth.

Barley is to be used in place of sesame: whatever function of sesame is performed in the monthly *śrāddha*, such as the offering of water (*arghya*) and other rites, that should be done here with barley.
And there is a mixing with flowers and other substances, because of a statement in another section;
the sacrificial oblation (havis) is speckled butter (pṛṣadājya).
Some say that the *pṛṣadājya* (spotted butter) should be mixed with rice boiled in milk (*rmāsaudana*), while others say it should be used alone.
"With an *upayāma*" means that the vessel by which the *arghya* is offered is covered with another vessel.

"May the Nāndīmukhas be pleased," [one says] for the gods; "May the Viśvedevas be pleased," [one says] for the gods. In that rite, there is a single vessel for the ancestors, not three; for there is no instruction regarding the distinction between the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather.
Since there is an instruction that for all mantras [the offering is made] to "the ancestors with joyful faces" (nāndīmukhāḥ pitaraḥ),
therefore there is only one vessel for the ancestors and one for the gods.
There, having seated the Brahmins, the installation of the fire and of the two *arghya* vessels takes place;
and the fire is specifically the *aupāsana* fire,
because it is not possible [to obtain] one for marriages.

Having offered the *arghya* water and adorned [the ancestors] with perfumes and other offerings, and being granted permission, he takes up the sacrificial food (*havis*), mixes it with speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*), and pours clarified butter over it. At the conclusion of the *ājyabhāga* offerings,
he offers one principal oblation (*pradhānāhuti*) with the mantra, "Svāhā to the Nāndīmukha ancestors," and he should offer a second oblation for the *Sviṣṭakṛt* with pure speckled butter alone.

Having completed the remainder of the *tantra* according to the principle "or [one may offer] for each person separately," he assigns [the oblation] to the ancestors with the mantra "To the Nāndīmukha ancestors, Svāhā! and to the gods with "To the Viśvedevas, to the gods, Svāhā!
These are the mantras for the fire-oblation in the monthly *śrāddha*.
And there is the cessation of those mantras used for the assignment [of portions].
However, the ritual rinsing (*upasparśana*) certainly takes place, because there is no substitute rite (*pratyāmnāya*) for it.

Regarding the phrase "when the vessels have been swept together in the receptacles" (*pṛthivī te pātram ity āśayeṣu ca parisamūḍheṣu*), "receptacles" (*āśaya*) refers to the places where the food is set out.

When the [seats] have been purified by sweeping, the offering of the rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) is performed with the *pṛṣadājya* mixed with curdled milk (*bavīṣā*), using that very *pṛṣadājya* while reciting "Svadhā namaḥ to the Nāndīmukhas. In this manner, everything is done twice each.
The meaning is that a double effort must be made in each instance, such as the offering of seats and so forth.
Having smeared [the ground] and scattered curd-rice, this occurs in place of the verse "In this fire, those not consumed by fire" (*tate 'gnau ye 'gnidagdhāḥ*).
Then, having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the dismissal is performed with the words: "May the Nāndīmukha ancestors be pleased."

Then, having murmured the *yajus* formula, "I shall produce honey from this water-vessel," and having poured [the remainder] into the vessel upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) with the two *visarjana* mantras, he turns it face down.
In this manner, the *nāndīśrāddha* should be performed there where the performance of the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajyā*) takes place on the following day.
However, some read it otherwise:
The Śrāddha for the mother should come first, followed immediately by that for the paternal ancestors;
thereafter, for the maternal grandfathers—thus they know there to be a triad of Śrāddhas on the occasion of a Vṛddhi ceremony.
Thus [it is said].
In this view, there are two each for the mother and the others;
likewise for the father and the others,
and likewise for the maternal grandfather and the others.
"Twenty twice-born men for the sake of the gods"—
thus it is shown by Manu in another statement:
"The neighbor and the next-door neighbor [should be invited] among twenty twice-born men on an auspicious occasion."
The *yātrābhyudaya-śrāddha* (auspicious śrāddha for a journey) takes place; that is auspicious when performed for twenty twice-born men.
Furthermore, they recite:
"At the birth of a son, at the first feeding, the tonsure, the ceremonial bath, and the taking of the hand in marriage..."
Likewise, in the establishment of the sacred fires and in the Soma sacrifice, ten types of prosperity are traditionally recorded.
Thus it is said.

And the procedure for the offering is exactly like that of the pārvaṇa śrāddha; the difference here is this much: an even number of Brāhmaṇas, the movement is clockwise, the sacred thread is worn over the left shoulder (yajñopavīta), and barley is used instead of sesame seeds. //12//
The meaning is that the ritual procedure for this Anvaṣṭakā is to be performed like the monthly śrāddha (māsi-śrāddha).
Because of this extension of the ritual procedure (kalpātideśa), everything here—including the materials, deities, and so forth—is obtained.
Therefore, everything from the invitation (nimantraṇa) up to the consumption of morsels (grāsa-prāśana) should be performed without modification, just as in the monthly śrāddha. //12//
Now he explains the rites for which the remaining mantras are to be employed:
1. One who goes for the purpose of begging should perform a recitation (*japa*). Having recited the subsequent [mantras] with a specific motive, he should state his request. (ĀpGS 22.13)
Having approached a donor for the sake of alms,
the wealth obtained through begging is called *sanis*.
Having performed the *sanimantra*, one should mutter seven times the subsequent mantras beginning with "May I be like food for you to behold."
One should state the purpose for which he has come;
in the seventh mantra, at the word "asau" (so-and-so), the name of the giver should be uttered with the intention [of addressing him]. //13//
*Saniryātṇā* means begging.
Some say it refers to wealth obtained through begging.

Regarding *sanir*, Āpastamba Dharmasūtra (2.10.1, 2) states: "The occasions for begging are: [the need for] a teacher, marriage, a sacrifice, the desire to support one's parents, and the breaking of a religious vow; having considered the merits in these cases, one should give according to one's ability."
Thus it is understood in the Dharmaśāstra; having approached her with that in mind— that is, having gone to her—
and having recited the seven subsequent mantras beginning with "May I be like food for you to behold," he should state that purpose or objective.
Whatever he should beg for, he informs that person, saying, "I beg from you for the sake of my teacher.
In the same way, there is a distinction regarding the subsequent purposes for begging, such as "for the sake of marriage" and so forth.
And in the seventh mantra, at the point where it says "asau," the name of the giver is to be uttered with an even mind.
Now, if chariots and other such items have been obtained through begging,
by what procedure should they be accepted? To answer this, the following rules are commenced:
2. Regarding the acquisition of a chariot:
having obtained a chariot, having yoked it, and having stationed it facing eastward, he touches the two wheels of the chariot—or the two side-pieces—with the following [verse]. (ĀpGS 22.14)

If a chariot is obtained, then having obtained it, he has it yoked by laborers and prepares the yoke-pole. Having stationed it facing the east, he touches both wheels of the chariot together with the verse "The two hooks, the two descending ones, on both sides," which is the next ṛc.
The word "of the chariot" is to be supplied as the object; others say it refers to the two side-panels (phalaka), while others say it refers to the two rims (nemi).
The mantra is recited only once.
The touching with both hands is likewise prescribed;
thus Āśvalāyana says: "One about to mount the chariot should touch the two wheels separately with both hands" (Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra 2.6.1).

If a chariot has been obtained, he should have it yoked by workmen with two draft animals; then, having stationed it facing east with its front toward the east, he simultaneously touches both wheels of the chariot with his hands while reciting the verse, "The two hooks,
the two downward-hooks," or else he touches the two side-pieces.
They state that the meaning of a word can be understood in other ways as well. //14//
3. The mantra for mounting the chariot:
Having mounted it with the subsequent *yajus*, and having set out toward the east or the north with the following [mantra], he should proceed as required. (ĀpGS 22.15)
Then he mounts his own chariot with the Yajus formula for crossing, "Of paths,
the path-leader," and then with the following Ṛc verse, "This chariot of yours, O Aśvins."
Having set out toward either the eastern or the northern direction, he should proceed as required; he should go wherever there is a purpose.
The long reading *adhīruhya* is Vedic (*chāndasa*).
This rule applies even to a chariot obtained through purchase or other means when it is being mounted for the first time.
However, it does not occur in the second [moment] and those following, because of the statement "having obtained. //15//
Having himself mounted the chariot by means of that northern path with the *yajus* formula, "O Lord of the Path,"—
the lengthening of the vowel being Vedic— he [proceeds] with the following verse, "This [chariot], O Aśvins..."
Having set out toward either the eastern or the northern direction for a purpose not visible [to the senses], he should then proceed according to his actual requirements. //15//

Some maintain that because of the word "having obtained" (*labdhvā*), this injunction applies even to chariots and the like obtained through purchase and other means at the time of first mounting them.

This is not so; for the meaningfulness of this statement is established precisely by its referring to chariots and such items obtained through the specific acts of begging and so forth under discussion, and because it contradicts the Bhāṣya, which states: "having obtained chariots and the like by means of begging. (15)
4. The mantra for mounting a horse:
One should mount the horse with the following verses. (ĀpGs 22.16)

The word "having obtained" (labdhvā) carries over [from the previous section]. By means of the eleven subsequent mantras beginning with "Thou art a horse, thou art a steed" (*aśvo 'si hayo 'si*), the obtaining of the horse is explained in the same manner as the obtaining of the chariot. // 16 //
If the horse has been obtained through a request, he should mount it with the subsequent mantras beginning with "Thou art a horse. (16)
5. The mantra for mounting the elephant:
[he should mount] the elephant with the following verse. (ĀpGs 22.17)
Having obtained [the name], the word "agoha" follows. With the subsequent verse, "thou art Hastiyaśas," there occurs the mention of the name of that elephant by saying "asau" (this one).
"I press down, O Queen of Naga-kings!"—
having ascended [the throne], one should silently utter the name "Goad" (*aṅkuśa*);
and in the mantra, it should be understood that the word "I press down" (*abhinidadhāmi*) is to be applied.
Therefore, there is no contradiction with the indicative mark in the mantra. //17//

The explanation is as before. With the following verse, "He who possesses the glory of an elephant," the name of the elephant, Airāvata, is mentioned by means of the vocative case in the word "asau" (O such-and-such).

In this case, although the mantra's purpose appears to be the naming of the goad based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) in the phrase "I strike him down with the thunderbolt," nevertheless, because the application (*viniyoga*) prescribed by direct statement (*vacana*)—"one should mount the elephant with the following [verse]"—is more powerful, the mantra must be explained in accordance with that. //17//
If they cause a wound, he should touch the earth as before.
When injury to the body occurs due to those two, the horse and the elephant, he should touch the earth as before— just as at the descent for the winter season—
with the two verses, "O Earth, be pleasant" (*syonā pṛthivi*) and "O Baḍittha.
By the phrase "as before," the birth-rite (*jātakarma*) is not included.
Because of the intervention. //18//
When there is injury or death to those two, the horse and the elephant,
as before— just as at the winter solstice descent— he should touch the earth with these two verses, "Gentle is the earth... and so forth.
Some say it was due to those two, the horse and the elephant;
that when he fell to the ground through negligence, scratching occurred and injury to the body ensued. //18//
1. Taking up the umbrella and the staff:
when about to enter into conversation, he takes hold of the umbrella and the staff with his left hand. (ĀpGs 22.19)
Where there is a place characterized by objects and other such causes, and where one is in agreement with the opponents, that is "agreement" (saṃvāda).
Desiring to go there for the sake of non-defeat, he takes up the umbrella and the staff with his left hand. The mention of "hand" is for the sake of what follows.
In this case, however, it is established precisely because of the emphasis on taking up [the material].

Therefore, the *khalīkaraṇa* oblation must be performed with the hand alone, not with a vessel; otherwise, since the word "handful" (*muṣṭi*) is also seen to denote a specific measure, this [rule] would not apply. //19//
Thus ends the twenty-second section in the Anākula commentary on the Gṛhya-sūtra composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
"Samvāda" refers to legal proceedings such as the recovery of debts and so forth.
Some explain it as "the place where litigants debate.
The meaning is that one who intends to engage in a legal proceeding—such as the recovery of debts and so forth—and desires victory in that lawsuit; the rest is clear. //19//
Thus ends the twenty-second section in the Gṛhyatātparyadarśana composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
Now begins the twenty-third section.
2. The mantra for the oblation of a handful of husks:
Having offered a handful of husks with the southern [hand] using the subsequent [mantra], and having gone [to the north], he should mutter the following [mantra]. (ĀpGs 23.1)
[In the opinion of Haradatta, these first three sūtras are counted as a single sūtra; this is noted in the Kha and Ḍa manuscripts.

Holding the umbrella and the staff with his left hand, he offers a handful of *phalīkaraṇa* husks with his right hand, while reciting the following verse (as indicated by the presence of the word *avajihvaka* in verse 1–ga.gha).
[One should perform the rite] with this [verse], "O little tongue.
In that context, the word "this one" (asau) is the mention of the name of the adversary in the nominative case;
and this oblation is an unprecedented (apūrva) one.
The placing [of the fire], the strewing [of grass], and the sprinkling of water on both sides—this much is done silently.
Then, having entered into a discussion and having seen the opponent, he should mutter the subsequent verse:
"I have brought thy speech into my mouth."
Here too, "asau" (this one) is the designation of the opponent's name in the vocative case;
the oblation is offered with the fist turned downward, as indicated by the characteristic mark [of the mantra]:
"avayaja."

The mention of "with the right hand" is for the purpose of holding the umbrella and the staff with the left hand at the time of the fire-oblation (homa); since the left hand is occupied, the oblation is performed with the right hand alone. //1//
Holding the handle of the umbrella with his left hand, he offers a handful of *phalīkaraṇa* husks into his own fire with his right hand, using the verse "ava jihvaka" as the subsequent [mantra].
In the phrase "asāv," he utters the name of the opponent in the nominative case, such as "Somaśarman.
This rite possesses the properties previously described.
And it has already been stated previously that this [rite] is a *homa* sacrifice.

Some [teachers] maintain that the strewing of grass (*paristaraṇa*) should be performed silently on both sides, as should the sprinkling of water (*paryukṣaṇa*), and that the offering should be made with a downward-turned fist.
Then, having gone to the place of the legal assembly and seeing the defendant, he should mutter this verse, "ā te vācam," while addressing the defendant by name in the vocative case.
3. The consecration of one who is angry:
One should consecrate an angry person with the two following [mantras]; he becomes free from anger. (ĀpGs 23.2)
[The rite is performed] with the two subsequent [verses], namely "yā ta eṣā rarāṭyā" and so forth.

Since there is no distinction in the indicative power (*liṅga*) of those two mantras, the specific gender [indicated by the word] *kuddham* is not intended to be significant (*avivakṣita*). Therefore, it applies to a female as well.
[The objection is: "Does this [rite] also apply to Śūdras and others?
[The reply is: "No," say others.
Since it might be argued that this occasional rite must necessarily be performed upon seeing someone who is angry, he says: "He becomes free from anger."
The meaning is that one should perform [the practice] toward that person whose anger one wishes to remove.
And this anger may have oneself as its object or another person as its object. //2//
If the adversary or the judge of the legal proceeding is angry,
yet he desires the pacification of that anger,
then one should address the angry person— or the other— with the two subsequent verses beginning with "yā ta eṣā."
By this consecration, one who is angry becomes free from anger;
and this is the ritual procedure for the fruit [of the practice],
not merely a figurative statement.
Because it has been composed by the author of the Sūtras. //2//
4. The rite for obstructing another man’s connection with one’s own wife:
Desiring to prevent [the union], one should have coarse *sthūlāḍhārikā* life-powders prepared and, while she is asleep, sprinkle them into her private parts with the following verse. (ĀpGS 23.3)
"One who desires non-origination, that is, one who desires non-sexual union. "Origination" means sexual union.
And it is heard in scripture: "Let us come into being from the source of desire" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.5).
The absence of that is impossibility.
A particular kind of *āḍhārikā* or serpent, desiring the impossibility of other persons,
[is called] "the hundred-footed" (*śatacaraṇā*).
And that [destruction] is of two kinds: gross and subtle.
It is gross in the forests and subtle elsewhere.
Regarding that, while the gross one is still active, it causes [the seeds] to be reduced to powder.
The performer himself, having caused those [seeds] to be sown, when his wife sleeps, should then sow them in her *sambādhā*, that is, in her lap (*upastha*), with the following verse:
"As one unstrings the bow... and so forth.
When this has been done, the private parts are no longer fit for enjoyment; this [rule] applies when there is suspicion of infidelity, or it concerns prostitutes. // 3 //

He who, about to depart on a journey, or while remaining at home, desires to protect the continuity of his progeny by ensuring that no semen from another man enters his wife—such a person is one who desires the non-occurrence of others.
For him, the instruction regarding the means is as follows:
he has the powder of a living *sthūlāḍhārikā* prepared by someone else.
The *āḍhārikā* is a type of centipede (*gaulikā*), which is a specific kind of reptile; it is also known as the *śatacaraṇā*.
And that [reptile] is of two kinds.
It is both village-born and forest-born;
of these two, the forest-born is thick, while the village-born is thin.
When she is being struck with a heavy blow from a stone or similar object, the vital powders (*jīvacūrṇāni*) are released.

Then, while she is asleep, one should scatter those powders into her vaginal canal (*sambādha*) with the following verse: "As one unstrings the bowstring... (*ava jyāmiva dhanvana*). When this is done, the vaginal canal is no longer fit for sexual enjoyment. //3//
Furthermore, it should be performed again in the shade;
for the sake of success, one should wash it with the urine of a brown cow. (ĀpGs 23.4)
(From this point onward, according to the opinion of Haradatta, five sūtras are counted as two sūtras; this is noted in manuscripts *ka* and *kha*.
The method of division is as follows: *sidhyarthe babhru... palāyeran*.)
In that [vessel], they wash the grains.
Thus.

The meaning is: for the sake of success—that is, when there is a prayer for the accomplishment of a task and one desires to make [the organ] fit for enjoyment—at that time, the washing of the vulva with the urine of a brown cow (*ābhrū*) must be performed;
this is the medicine in this case.
A tawny cow is one that has a reddish-brown color. //4//

Now, when the suspicion of another man has departed, then for the sake of accomplishing the production of one's own semen, the following medicinal procedure is prescribed: one should wash the private parts with the urine of a tawny cow. //4//
6. An oblation for the success of merchandise:
for the sake of success, he should offer with the following verse whatever merchandise he may have in his house. (ĀpGS 23.5)

For the sake of the success of whatever wealth, merchandise, or goods for purchase may be in this householder’s home— so that success may be achieved through the reduction of half [the price] and so forth—
one should take a portion from that wealth and offer it with the following verse, "Whatever I [have gained] by means of wealth," and thus success is attained.
In this context, there is also an oblation of alkaline substances, salt, and so forth.
The optional rites have been described according to the instruction;
among those, for liquid substances, a ladle is used.
In other cases, the hand is used;
and like the oblation of husks (*phalīkaraṇa-homa*), this is for the sake of an unprecedented (*apūrva*) result.
The statement "of this" (*asya*) is intended so that the oblation may be performed even by another person desiring his welfare with whatever merchandise is in his house.
Nor is there any contradiction with the mantra "I am [the deity]," for it is said that "having become that very [deity], he performs [the rite].
Because of the statement "merchandise in the house," this does not apply to matters such as fields and the like.
Furthermore, the statement regarding the accomplishment [of the goal] is for the purpose of making known that this is a distinct ritual action;
otherwise, it might be suspected to be merely an optional alternative (vikalpa) to the preceding one. //5//

Having performed the rites up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, or up to the *agnimukha*, according to the nature of the commodity for sale, one should take a portion from that merchandise and offer it with the following verse, "Whatever wealth I [have gained] by means of wealth.
Because of the word "from that" (*tataḥ*) used here, the oblation is not to be made from a living being as the substance.
Consequently, because it would result in a deficiency of parts in the *avadāna* (cutting-off),
some maintain that, based on the statement "of this," the oblation must be offered by another person desiring the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) [suffix].
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the word "I" (*aham*) in the mantra.
"Having become that very thing, he offers the oblation. //5//
7. An act that produces affection among servants:

If one should desire of someone, "May this person not be separated from me," he should pour his own urine into a living horn, and while the person is asleep, he should sprinkle him three times counter-clockwise with the two following verses. (ĀpGs 23.6)

Thinking, "May this servant not be separated from me; may he not depart; may he remain entirely under my control for as long as he lives," one should take a horn that has fallen off a living cow of one's own, bring one's own urine, and while the servant is asleep, sprinkle it three times counter-clockwise around him with the two verses beginning with *pari tvā girer*.
The mention of "living" is for the purpose of excluding [the offering] when [the animal] is dead.
The instruction is "a cow.
Because of the word "having brought," one should first urinate in another vessel, perform purification, and then bring forward the horn.
Based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "Thou art completely cooled," this [rite] does not apply to women.

However, if a woman should desire a husband who—due to weakness of his senses—is attached to a co-wife or another woman, thinking, "May this husband not be separated from me; may he have uninterrupted affection for me," she [should perform it] with the horn of a living cow.

While the cow is still alive, one should forcibly cause its urine to be poured into its own horn. Then, with the two verses beginning with "pari tvā gireramiham" (RV 10.172.1–2), he should sprinkle it three times from right to left over his sleeping husband.
Regarding this, because of the expression "having caused [it] to flow," one should first urinate into another vessel, perform purification, and then pour it into the horn.
Some say this refers to the master’s duty regarding his servants.
Now, he states the duty for those such as servants who have fled and desire to return:
8. The rite for the return of those who have fled, such as slaves and others.
On the path by which the slaves and laborers might flee, he should kindle fires and offer the subsequent oblations. (ĀpGs 23.7)
Now, those who perform work for the sake of bringing back servants who have fled—whether they be slaves or others—are called *dāsakarmakāras*.

By whatever means they might flee on that path, [the practitioner], having prepared and ignited iron or wooden shackles (*nigalas*) in a fire, should offer four subsequent oblations (*āhutis*) into that fire with these [verses]: "O Returner, cause them to return," and so forth.
Regarding that, some maintain that for four *iṇvān* [offerings], there is a gradual, distinct settling on the path and the recitation of mantras in sequence;
others hold that for many *iṇvān* [offerings], there is a simultaneous settling and the *homa* offering occurs right there at once.
This *homa* occurs even when one or two [slaves] flee; it does not apply only to many.
This is because of the singular designation used for slaves and laborers: "a slave and a laborer," "two slaves and two laborers," or "slaves and laborers.
Furthermore, the plural number is employed when the matter is uncertain.
For example: "How many sons do you have?
In this case, the plural number is employed even when the matter is not yet determined.
For example, [in the question] "How many sons do you have?",
and in mantras such as "parikrośo vaḥ," the plural number is not intended to be significant,
because the purpose is to establish the deity.
This too is an unprecedented oblation;
in all these cases, as far as possible, the fire is the *aupāsana* fire alone. //7//
And the slaves, laborers for hire, and servant-laborers—

on whatever path they might flee, on that very path, having piled up pieces of wood well-known as "the earth" (bhūmi) and "the wind" (anila)— that is, wooden pieces— in the absence of fire, he should offer the four subsequent oblations of clarified butter with the mantras beginning with "āvartana vartaya," just as in the case of the injunction, "he offers on the footprints [without fire]."
This is an unprecedented legal matter;
for although the term "servants and laborers" is used here in the plural, this penalty applies even if only one or two have fled.
Some, having kindled fires on the paths, perform the oblation (homa) in those very fires. // 7 //
9. There are nine incidental [impurities]:

if fruit should fall upon him from a tree, or a bird should drop something upon him, or a drop of water should fall when there is no expectation of rain, he should wash those [parts] with the subsequent [mantras] according to their respective characteristics. (ĀpGs 23.8)

If a fruit fallen from a tree should fall upon this Snātaka, whether on his head or another part of his body; or if a bird, such as a crow or the like, should alight upon him, whether on his head or another part of his body;

or if, at a time or in a place where rain is not expected, a drop of water should fall upon his limb—then [he should touch it] with the subsequent mantras beginning with "yadi vṛkṣāt," according to the respective characteristics of each.
One should wash them with water:
[using] "If the trees... for fruit; [using] "Those who are birds... for birds.
“*Divo nu mā bṛhata* [RV 10.121.1]” is for the *bindu*.
The mantras in all three cases follow their respective gender and number so that they do not apply to a single instance.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of them applying even when crossing a ford (*tīrtha*) and the like.
Because the injunction is more powerful. //8//
If a fruit should suddenly fall from a tree down upon this twice-born man;
or if a bird should strike him with its wings, shaking him with the wind of its wings;
or if a drop of water—a small particle of moisture—should fall upon him from a sky that is cloudless and where rain is not expected.
This has been explained.
If a limb of the body is struck by the falling of fruit or similar causes, one should wash it with the subsequent mantras according to their respective indicative marks (*liṅga*).
In that regard, the mantra "yadi vṛkṣāt" is for the falling of fruit.
The phrase "ye pakṣiṇaḥ" [is used] when birds scatter [dirt], and "divo nu mā bṛhataḥ" when drops fall upon him.
However, the statement "according to the respective signs" is intended so that there should not be a washing with three verses for each individual cause. //9//
Now, the expiation for portents (adbhutaprāyaścitta): [This is] the expiation for portents.
[It is performed] when a pillar in the house sprouts, when bees settle [there], when pigeon tracks are seen on a thatched roof, or when the bodies of ministers are infested with worms.

And during other extraordinary portents, on the night of the new moon, in a place where one cannot hear the sound of water, having performed the rites from the kindling of the fire up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings, he offers the subsequent oblations and proceeds with the *jaya* and following rites. (ĀpGs 23.9)

Now follows the expiation for extraordinary portents (*adbhutotpāta*). An "extraordinary" event (*adbhuta*) is one that is unprecedented and has never been seen before. Of such an [extraordinary and unseen] event—
An *utpāta* (portent) is a sudden occurrence; or rather, extraordinary phenomena arising from above—whether celestial or atmospheric—are specifically called *utpātas*.
Examples include a rainbow at night, a red sky, or the appearance of a pillar-like object in the sun.
In that view, the word *adbhuta* (marvel) refers to terrestrial phenomena according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull" (*govālīvardanyāya*).
The compound is a *dvandva*.
Therein, he shows some marvels by way of illustration, beginning with "the pillar of the house" (*agārasthūṇā*).
The term *virehaṇa* refers to the production of sprouts.

Because of the mention of "in a house" (*agāre*), this does not apply even to one's own houses belonging to Śūdras and others. In the case of honey, however, it applies specifically when it is placed in a house.
*Kuptuḥ* and *cullī-bhrāṣṭram* are synonymous.
The meaning is that upon seeing the footprints of the wild bird, the pigeon, he entered that cooking-shed;
"ministers" refers to his sons and others.
When many of these are simultaneously subjected to bodily injury, death,
or other such conditions as those occurring in anthills and the like, or in rainbows and the like.
From the statement "in others," it is understood that even the harming of ministers' bodies is considered a wonder;
it does not occur when there is harm to only one or two, nor when there is a difference in time.
Regarding the expiation for this: on the night of the new moon, the night is divided into four parts, and the third part is the night [for the rite].

In a place where one does not hear the sound of water-jars being brought to the reservoirs, in that place one should perform the rites beginning with the kindling of the fire, followed by the eleven subsequent oblations: "This [is my] Varuṇa," "O Prajāpati," and "O Prajāpati, none other than you... This last verse is taken because it is well-known [from the Gṛhyasūtras].
The verse "O Prajāpati, you are the guardian of the treasure" is not [the concluding formula].
Having offered with "O Prajāpati, not thee," one should offer the principal oblations; thus one proceeds to the remainder of the ritual procedure (*tantra*).

Since the completion of the *tantra* is established by the rule "ending with the butter-portions" (*ājyabhāga*), the mention of "kindling the fire" (*upasamādhāna*) and so forth is for the purpose of kindling the fire itself alone.
Therefore, in the absence of the *aupāsana* fire, [the rite] may take place even in the common (*laukika*) fire.

This effort at the very end to prescribe the fire is intended to demonstrate that these various occasional rites (*naimittika*), as well as those with visible results such as the *paṇyahoma* and others, proceed even in another fire.
The mention of "compassion" and so forth is for the purpose of indicating immediate succession (*ānantarya*).

It is understood that immediately after the principal oblation (*pradhānāhuti*), only the *jaya* and subsequent offerings are to be performed; it does not mean that the oblations seen in other sūtras are to be offered in this tantra.
What, then, are these [mantras]?
If a dove should strike or alight upon the house, one should offer oblations or recite verse by verse the mantra beginning with "devāḥ kapotaḥ.
Thus says Āśvalāyana.
By the very statement "it is victorious," there is a prohibition against the *Tantrasamuccaya*.
That expiation (*prāyaścitta*) also occurs optionally as a separate ritual procedure (*pṛthaktantra*).
In that case as well, the *śamyā* serves the purpose of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).
Because this expiation is also taught in this very scripture. //9//

In this context, "marvels" (*adbhutāḥ*) are those things which, being non-existent previously, come into existence by way of their own nature. "Portents" (*utpātāḥ*), however, are those which arise upwardly or reach a state of manifestation. The term "marvels and portents" (*adbhutāś cotpātāś ca*) is a *dvandva* compound.
The distinction in terminology, however, is intended to differentiate between terrestrial and celestial [omens].

Among these, the celestial portents are earthquakes, rainbows at night, "suns" (halos), and so forth; whereas the terrestrial ones, such as the miraculous appearance of pillars in a house and the like, he himself illustrates with the phrase "the pillars of a house" (*agārasthūṇā*).
[The compound *agārasthūṇāḥ* means] the pillars (*sthūṇāḥ*) of a house (*agārasya*).

Regarding their "growing," which means the production of sprouts: the mention of the "post" is intended to indicate any other bamboo pole belonging to the house that has been driven into the ground, since it serves as a qualifying attribute of the occasion (*nimitta*). As for the "sitting down of the honey," this occurs specifically within the house itself.
Even though the word *agāra* (house) is a subordinate member [of the compound], it is connected by means of mental analysis (*buddhi*) according to its fitness [with each member],
because it is not uncommon [to find houses] in gardens and other such places.
*Kuptuḥ*, *cullī*, *bhrāṣṭra*, and *ambarīṣa* are synonymous.
"In that" means in the kitchen;
"even upon seeing the footprints of a pigeon"— that is, a specific kind of wild bird—
"in that" is used for the purpose of illustration.
Even within the house, because of its wondrous nature:

"amātyas" are those who dwell together (*amā vasanti*), such as sons, brothers, and others who eat from a single vessel; for these many, there is the constant seeking of the body's end, which means the destruction of the body, i.e., death.
Some say that even when there is a simultaneous outbreak of disease among ministers,

or when other extraordinary portents (*adbhutotpāta*)— other than those already mentioned— such as the appearance of anthills within houses and so forth, are observed, one who desires the pacification of the misfortune indicated by them should perform [the rite] on the night of the new moon (*amāvāsyā*),
two *muhūrtas* after midnight.
Some say [it should be done] during the second watch;

some say when one no longer hears the sound of flowing waters; some say when water is being brought in jars to the water-reservoirs. In such a place, one proceeds with the ritual procedure beginning with the kindling of the fire.

And its ritual procedure (*tantravidhāna*) consists of clarified butter as the oblation (*ājyahaviṣṭva*), because of the rule "at the end of the portions of clarified butter" (*ājyabhāgānte*), which serves to prohibit other ritual duties.
