Having offered the eleven subsequent oblations beginning with "imaṃ me varuṇa" and "tat tvā yāmi," one proceeds to the *jaya* and other offerings by the force of the scriptural injunction.

Here, by the introductory phrase "Prajāpati," this very [verse], "O Prajāpati, these worlds are not yours alone," is understood, just as in the case of the statement, "The Vyāhṛtis belong to Prajāpati. //9//
Having performed the rites up to the final sprinkling, he places a stone as a boundary-marker to the south for those who have died, using the next [verse]. He places it. (ĀpGS 23.10)

Therefore, regarding this wonder called the "search for the bodies of the ministers," there is a specific distinction: those whose ancestors and descendants die in succession are called *abhimṛta*; for them, and for the sake of pacifying their death, one performs this subsequent rite of oblation (*homa*).
At the conclusion of the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), one establishes a stone as a boundary (*paridhi*) and as a screen (*antardhāna*) for the purpose of warding off death, using the subsequent verse.
[One should recite] with this [verse], "imaṃ jīvebhyaḥ.
The repetition indicates the completion of the exhalation.
Because of the mention of the "enclosing-stone" (paridhi), one must not move that stone from its place.
He becomes firmly established right there. //10//
Thus ends the twenty-third section in the *Anākula*, a commentary on the *Gṛhya-sūtra* composed by the venerable Haradatta Miśra.
And thus the eighth and final chapter is completed. The commentary on the Ānākula [Tantra] is finished.
Then he performs the remainder of the ritual procedure (*tantra*) up to the final sprinkling (*pariṣecana*).
It has already been stated previously that "the *śamyā* sticks serve the purpose of the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*).

Some maintain that since the application of the *tantra* is already established by the rule "up to the *ājyabhāga* offerings," the explicit mention of "laying the fire" (*upasamādhāna*) and so forth is for the purpose of laying down the fire alone.
Therefore, for one who lacks the *aupāsana* fire, this rite may be performed even in a worldly fire (*laukika*).
Likewise, other rites of this kind—occasional (*naimittika*) rites with visible results, such as the *paṇyahoma* and others—are also permitted;
for it is understood that this entire section on the prescription of fires serves all purposes at the conclusion of [the discussion].
By the words beginning with "abhimṛtebhyaḥ," a certain specific detail is stated regarding this wonder, namely, "in the search for the bodies of the ministers.

"Abhimṛtāḥ" means those who have died facing [the enemy]; by implication, they were as good as dead while still living, being themselves afraid of death due to the constant sight of the deaths of their ministers.
For them—that is, for the sake of removing their constant fear of death—the subsequent verse [is recited]: "imaṃ jīvebhyaḥ."
Thus, with this [verse], he places the stone— which serves as a screen against death— on the south side;
and this occurs at the conclusion of the ritual procedure (tantra), by virtue of the force of the suffix -ktvā in the word "having done" (kṛtvā).

Some [teachers] say that "he places" means he establishes it; and because of the word *paridhi*, one must not cause that stone to be moved from its place. The analysis of the root as "he places" (*dadhāti*) meaning "he gives" (*dadāti*) is for the purpose of indicating the conclusion of the inquiry. //10//
Thus, by the noble Sudarśana, this *Tātparyadarśana* has been composed in accordance with the Bhāṣya, according to his own understanding and as he had heard it.
Whatever has been left unsaid or poorly expressed here, whether due to the dullness of my intellect or my lack of learning,
the wise should forgive us, for we are intent upon the path of the righteous.
Thus ends the twenty-third section and the eighth chapter in the *Gṛhyatātparyadarśana* composed by the venerable Sudarśanācārya.
This commentary on the Gṛhyasūtra is completed.
